title: Canadian tariffs to further raise prices, a top concern for voters
text: WASHINGTON — A developing trade war with Canada could bite Republicans ahead of the upcoming midterm elections as voters worry about rising prices and industries in states with competitive races could suffer.Maine’s lobster industry dodged what officials had warned could be economic havoc Thursday morning when Canada reversed its decision to tax lobster imports at 25%. But states including Ohio, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Michigan and Wisconsin could see effects if Canada follows through on retaliatory tariffs on alcohol, automobiles, dairy, home appliances, steel and other goods.Those products are among the 629 categories Canada’s Department of Finance announced Tuesday in response to President Donald Trump’s most recent tariffs on Canadian goods that went into effect over the weekend.“On one hand you have the issue of the U.S. import tariffs, which voters are associating with affordability, but then on the other hand you have the retaliatory Canadian tariffs, which are going to impact businesses in those states,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst with the libertarian think tank Cato Institute. “So you could have a sort of double whammy where there's pressure on behalf of voters for the president to recede this policy,” he said.Trade talks have completely stalled between the U.S. and Canada, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Canadian Broadcasting Corporation News on Wednesday evening, a day after Canada announced retaliatory taxes to start Sept. 8 on $27.6 billion worth of American goods. The duties on U.S. imports will match Trump’s new 50% tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products “dollar-for-dollar,” according to Canada’s Department of Finance.Individual businesses and importers, rather than governments, pay the tariffs on goods. Economists warn increased costs on either side of tariffs can affect investment decisions and increase consumer prices.States Newsroom documented accounts from numerous small business owners affected by Trump’s tariff policies during his second term.Small portion of trade volumeThe Yale Budget Lab estimates that under the Trump administration’s current tariff schedule, including its latest tariffs on Canadian goods, Americans will spend an additional $1,100 annually on household costs.The increase in annual household costs pre- and post-Trump’s newest duties on Canadian goods, which took effect Aug. 22, ranges roughly between $27 and $33, according to the Yale Budget Lab’s comparison.Of the massive and intertwined trade relationship between the U.S. and Canada, the new tariffs account for a small fraction of all goods traded. Canada is the U.S.’s second-largest trading partner, and the two countries exchanged $879.9 billion in goods in 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.Major areas of trade between the two countries that are subjected to tariffs include automobiles, industrial supplies, steel, iron and aluminum.“It's not a huge magnitude. Both the Canadian and the American tariffs cover only about 5% of what each country exports to each other. We're not talking about all of a sudden everything we get from Canada is going to get tariffs. It's only a share of that. But this is the initial salvo,” Obregon said.“If you are a company that relies on imports from Canada, and you're sort of doing production on both sides of the border in that sense, then you are worried about where this could lead in the future,” he added.Outsized politicsWhile tariffs are small in proportion to Canada and the U.S.’s entire trade portfolio, the politics are outsized.Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who faces a tough race to keep her seat, told local reporters Wednesday she spoke with the Trump administration about protecting her state’s major lobster and seafood industry, which was spared Thursday.Collins’ opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, attacked the incumbent on social media Wednesday, blaming her for having “completely failed” to stop Trump’s tariffs.The Republican candidate for Michigan’s open Senate seat, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, has not commented on the new tariffs, but Democrats in Michigan are seizing the issue.Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel told the Michigan Advance the tariffs will “throw Michigan’s economy into chaos.”Rogers’ opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, on Tuesday responded to Trump’s threat on Truth Social to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.“Whatever you call it, you just made all the goods we buy that come across our border more expensive,” El-Sayed wrote on X. “Michigan, he’s asking us to pay for his vanity trade war with our money.”Trump signed an executive order Thursday renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America.During comments to reporters, Trump said Canada “has been ripping us off a long time on trade, very sadly, even the military. You know, we defend Canada for nothing.”He added: “They don't pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they're not a state.”Imran Bayoumi, an expert on U.S.-Canada relations with the Atlantic Council, said Canadians are “angry, hurt and upset” about Trump’s rhetoric toward their country’s sovereignty. The country, which has long received scrutiny over its defense spending, has increased the allocation in recent years, said Bayoumi, a Canadian-American.“There's a recognition that you can't change your geography, and so the two are going to need to find a way to work together … on shared defense challenges, economic priorities, the Arctic, the defense of North America,” Bayoumi said. “The challenge now is to either find a narrow way off this path that both sides are on, which seems to be spiraling downwards, or ensure the deterioration of relations in the economic and trade sector doesn't spill into other areas.”Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney enjoys approval from 76% of Canadians for his decision over the weekend to walk away from trade talks with the U.S., according to the Canadian Angus Reid Institute. But the poll found two in five Canadians also fear for their job security.Carney has already pledged a $7.5 billion package for businesses and workers who might be affected by the tariffs.Trump administration officials remain dug in on the tariffs and denied any major effects of the Canadian retaliatory tariffs.“The concept that this could have any kind of meaningful effect on the United States is quite limited,” Greer told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham Wednesday. “And guess what? If there's something in there that has some negative effect that is brought to the attention of President Trump, he can do what he needs to do,” he added. “I mean, this is just not going to lead to any economic Armageddon.” Jennifer Shutt contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Are the kids all right? Mental health issues drop — but disparities remain
description:
The latest data from a statewide youth survey shows signs of progress, but that’s partly because our comparison is from a “horrible” pandemic peak, experts say.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Are the kids all right? Mental health issues drop — but disparities remain.
text:
The Middlebury Union High School marching band prepares to march in the Memorial Day parade in Vergennes in May 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
After years of nationwide concerns about teen mental health, the latest data from Vermont’s largest survey of its kind suggests that the situation for the state’s youth might finally be improving. 
The Vermont Department of Health released a report on Aug. 18 showing that fewer teens say they feel depressed or anxious, and a smaller percentage of  teens are vaping, drinking or using cannabis. Experts said that may be partly the result of a slow recovery from the mental health struggles of the Covid-19 pandemic.  
“I do think some of this is, ‘Hey, our country went through this horrible event of a pandemic,’ and it affected all of us, including our youth and teens,” said Vermont Department of Health Commissioner Dr. Rick Hildebrant. “We’re seeing a bit of a return to less of that poor mental health that we were seeing around the country and around the world.”
The data comes from the 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, sent to high school and middle school students around the state every two years since 1995. More than 15,000 students completed surveys last year.
Despite progress, Hildebrant noted that mental health issues in teens were still “way too high.” One in four high school students reported poor mental health, down from one in three in 2023.  
“I think it’s the collective desire of every parent to have children who are able to live their best life,” Hildebrant said. “And when you are struggling from depression and mental health disorders? That’s a concern, and to have the number be as high as it is, (is) alarming and concerning to me.”
Also concerning are the disparities reported for girls, LGBTQ+ teens, and high school students with educational disabilities. Female high school students were more than twice as likely as male students to report poor mental health. LGBTQ+ students were far more likely than their peers to feel sad or anxious, to self-harm or make a suicide plan. 
Hildebrant said those groups were also less likely to say that they feel like they mattered in their community, and more likely to drop out of activities due to poor mental health. 
“This feeling of connectedness —  there’s more and more research showing how important that is to your self-esteem and to your mental health,” he said. 
Dana Kaplan is the executive director of Outright Vermont, an organization that supports LGBTQ+ youth. He said it was important to highlight that queer teens’ poor mental health “is not based on anything being wrong with a young person’s identity,” but says more about “the level of bullying, harassment, rejection (and) isolation” they’re navigating. 

Several hundred queer and transgender kids and their supporters gather at the Statehouse in Montpelier to celebrate International Transgender Day of Visibility in March 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Vermont has great policies to protect LGBTQ+ people, “but there is a real gap between the actual lived experience of young folks and what those policies say on the books,” he said. 
“There’s things that happen on a daily basis, of being misgendered, or not being referred to by your right name,” Kaplan said. “(We get) phone calls from young folks saying, ‘Am I allowed to go to school and be who I am?’”
“Whack-a-mole”
Another highlight from the survey is that e-cigarette use among Vermont’s teenagers has dropped precipitously from pre-pandemic levels. About 14% of high school students reported using a vape or electronic cigarette in the past 30 days, down from 26% in 2019. 
In total, 18% of students said they’ve used any form of tobacco, including vapes, cigarettes, cigars and smokeless tobacco pouches, according to the survey. 
Elias Klemperer, a researcher at the University of Vermont who studies tobacco use, said the drop among Vermont’s teens was a “very good sign” that parallels a national fall in e-cigarette use. “Anytime we can keep kids from using nicotine products, that is a good thing,” he said. 
Hildebrant praised youth-led anti-tobacco initiatives like Unhyped for spreading awareness of the harms of vaping. “It’s peer pressure in the positive direction,” he said. 
But it’s not entirely clear whether the drop signifies a shift away from tobacco products entirely, or just a shift to other tobacco products. Cigarette use remained low — just 6% of high school students — but early reports have shown a rise in smokeless tobacco pouches from brands like Zyns.
Jill Sudhoff-Guerin, a lobbyist and spokesperson for the Coalition for a Tobacco Free Vermont, said it can feel like a “game of whack-a-mole” trying to keep up with new products. Along with pouches, she noted that e-cigarettes are coming on the market that look like toys or phones. 
“This industry is highly, highly skilled at communications, highly skilled at marketing,” she said. “And kids know when things are made for them.” 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Are the kids all right? Mental health issues drop — but disparities remain.

name: Michigan Advance
title: New House committee to examine signature verification sampling process for ballot initiatives
description: A new select committee in the Michigan House was established on Wednesday to examine the rules and procedures of the Board of State Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections — specifically the sampling process used to verify signatures for ballot initiatives.  Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) introduced a resolution to establish the commit[...]
text:
All four members of the Board of State Canvassers gather with Bureau of Elections staff to review signatures on the citizens-only ballot petition on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)A new select committee in the Michigan House was established on Wednesday to examine the rules and procedures of the Board of State Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections — specifically the sampling process used to verify signatures for ballot initiatives. 
Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) introduced a resolution to establish the committee, which passed along party lines. The vote came two days after the Board of State Canvassers deadlocked on a vote on whether to approve a ballot petition to establish strict voter ID laws in the state — meaning the measure will likely not be on the November ballot. 
The decision was made on the margin of just a handful of votes. Based on the more than 709,000 signatures submitted, compared with the required 446,198, at least 629 signatures in the 1,000-signature sample needed to be valid. 
After reviewing information provided by lawyers both in favor and opposed to the proposal, and voting on a number of individual signatures, the four-member Board of State Canvassers had identified 626 valid signatures — just three signatures below the needed threshold. A number of those decisions were contentious, many ending in a 2-2 vote — meaning that those signatures did not count towards the needed 629.
That decision is likely to hold for the November ballot, unless an appeal filed Thursday with the Michigan Supreme Court were to prevail. The appeal was made by Americans for Citizens Voting, which backed the measure. Because the Bureau of Elections also does not have the power to overturn the decision of the Board of State Canvassers, only a court order could put the initiative on the ballot.
However, with absentee ballots for the general election becoming available starting Sept. 24 and Michigan law requiring that the ballot must be finalized by Sept. 4, the committee — which is “expected to begin its work in the coming weeks,” according to press releases from various Republican members — will likely not have time to change the outcome for this proposal on the 2026 ballot.
“We can’t let this stand. What Jocelyn Benson has done here to disenfranchise the voice of hundreds of thousands of people who signed this petition for very political reasons. It’s just a disgrace what’s happened, and I hope you get to the bottom of it,” Hall said in a press conference on Wednesday evening, referencing state Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township), who will chair the committee. 
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) and state Rep. Mike Harris (Waterford Township) speak to reporters on Aug. 26, 2026 about a new legislative committee created to examine the petition signature verification process. (Screenshot)
Harris said the goal of the committee will be ensuring that the rules of signature verification were followed and appropriate, and that people’s voices are heard.
“I think we owe it to the people of Michigan to accomplish that,” Harris said. “We have almost 700,000 people that I feel have been disenfranchised by this decision to deny this ballot initiative, and I think it’s important we get them answers on what that process actually is and what it looks like.”
Michigan has used a form of a sampling process for signature verification since 1980, though that process has changed over time. It was reviewed in 1990 and again in 2022, after which it was updated. 
“The Bureau of Elections fulfills its nonpartisan administrative and advisory role to the Board of State Canvassers in accordance with Michigan law,” Angela Benander, a spokesperson for the Michigan Department of State, said in a statement. “Legislators who are unsatisfied with the current longstanding process have the power to propose bills to change the law.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The sampling process allows the Bureau of Elections and Board of State Canvassers to determine whether enough signatures are valid without examining every signature individually, since petitions generally contain hundreds of thousands of signatures.
“Practically speaking, the board’s view for decades is that it’s not really practical to review, in this case, over 700,000 signatures individually,” Jonathan Brater, director of the Bureau of Elections, explained about the sampling process during Monday’s meeting of the Board of State Canvassers.
In 2024, a package of bills introduced by Democrats passed both chambers of the Legislature but were vetoed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, which would have amended Michigan’s election law to allow the Board of State Canvassers to use a statistical random sampling methodology when reviewing petition signatures for authenticity, among other changes to the petition filing and review process. 
Those bills stemmed from a lack of statutory guidance for the Board of State Canvassers when reviewing petitions from five gubernatorial candidates, who were disqualified over signature fraud, and sought to codify the recommendations from a working group on the process. 
However, Whitmer said in her veto letter that the bills’ effort to utilize statistical sampling “move Michigan in the wrong direction” as opposed to “requiring exhaustive review of signatures to ensure no fraud exists.”
Currently, according to Michigan Department of State guidance, “the selection of random signatures is completed utilizing a custom-designed computer program.” After that selection takes place, “sampled sheets are face reviewed for validity, then signatures on valid sheets are compared to the Qualified Voter File.”
Sean Dutton, a lawyer supporting the citizens-only voting ballot petition, provides information to Jonathan Brater, the director of the Bureau of Elections, at a Board of State Canvassers meeting on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Along with Harris, four other Republicans will be members of the committee — Majority Floor Leader Bryan Posthumus (R-Rockford) will serve as the majority vice chair of the committee, alongside Reps. Ann Bollin (R-Brighton), Rachelle Smit (R-Martin) and Jason Woolford (R-Howell). 
In a press release about his placement on the committee, Posthumus emphasized that members of the Board of State Canvassers or Bureau of Elections “don’t have to like the proposal to agree that 709,841 signatures deserve a serious look.”
“This is a lot bigger than a spreadsheet or a sample of signatures. More than 700,000 Michiganders signed their names, and they deserve a straight answer about what happened,” he said. “Maybe everything was done exactly right. I want to see the process, see the numbers, and let the facts speak for themselves.”
Two Democrats will also be on the committee: Rep. Denise Mentzer (D-Mount Clemens) was named minority vice chair, and Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) will also serve as a member. 
“My goal is for this committee to provide the public with a clear and accurate understanding of the signature verification process. The discussion is not simply about the total number of signatures submitted, but also about their validity. What I question is why they’re only raising these concerns now,” Mentzer said in a statement to the Michigan Advance. “I have a long track record of working across the aisle, and I intend to approach this committee in the same spirit. Michiganders deserve a transparent, consistent, and fair process.”
Hall also indicated his belief that partisan bias played a role in the board’s decision not to put the petition on the ballot. 
“They’re rejecting other proposals over the years, and they seem to be only one-sided,” he said. “Whenever a Republican-affiliated group submits something on the ballot, it takes months and months and months to review it, and then they always figure out a way to disqualify it. If it’s a Democrat group, they review it much quicker, and they always find a way to approve it, even if it’s suspect.”
Some of that sentiment came out of the approval for the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics proposal, which did pass through the signature verification process in July. 
Benander rejected this idea, and emphasized that the Bureau of Elections is nonpartisan and follows the same process for every petition. 
“The final determination is made by the Board of State Canvassers which is comprised of two Republicans and two Democrats,” she wrote. “The ACV petition got the exact same treatment as MMOP. While the outcome was different the signature sampling and verification rules were the same. The Board of State Canvassers uses the same standards to verify the validity of signatures as clerks do when they verify signatures on ballots.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: At least some new NC voting rules may be delayed until after the midterms
description: A state commission that okays administrative rules unanimously approved changes for elections and voting on Thursday, though at least some of those rules may not be ready in time for the midterm elections. The Rules Review Commission is usually a final stop for administrative rules changes before they’re activated. That’s unless at least 10 people […]
text:
Robert Rodriguez of Democracy Out Loud objects to proposed voting rules at the NC Rules Review Commission on Aug. 27, 2026 (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)A state commission that okays administrative rules unanimously approved changes for elections and voting on Thursday, though at least some of those rules may not be ready in time for the midterm elections.
The Rules Review Commission is usually a final stop for administrative rules changes before they’re activated. That’s unless at least 10 people object to a rule. When 10 or more people write acceptable letters of objection, rules effective dates are delayed for legislative review in the General Assembly’s next regular session. The legislature is on a break but is still in session. The next regular session won’t start until next year.
As of Wednesday, the proposed rules for photo ID and for voting site conduct received more than 10 objection letters, as did one section of a proposed rule on recounts. The deadline for objection letters is 5 p.m. on Friday, so it’s possible more rules will be delayed. 
Brian LiVecchi, state Board of Elections chief of staff, said the board would consider issuing the rules as “numbered memos,” instructions to county elections boards that are less formal than rules.
“We probably will discuss that if anything is deemed critical,” he said. 
Members of Democracy Out Loud – a group that says it wants a “fair and inclusive democracy” – spoke against the rules Thursday, saying they were not clear or that the board went beyond its legal authority to make the changes. Jim Womack, president of the conservative North Carolina Election Integrity Team, objected to a rule on buffers around voting sites. 
Gov. Josh Stein sent the commission a letter Wednesday asking it to delay one of the rules for absentee ballots and the rules for throwing out ballots when members of local boards believe that voters are lying about why they don’t have photo ID. 
As it stands now, a county board of elections must vote unanimously to discard the ballots of people who members think lied about the reasons they didn’t present an ID. The proposed rule would allow a simple majority to make that decision, meaning Republican majorities on boards could vote to toss ballots.
NC elections board moves to make it easier to toss voters’ ballots

The rule on absentee ballots makes it hard to vote by mail, Stein wrote, and “increases the likelihood that more voters casting absentee ballots will see their votes thrown out. Many North Carolinians, including people who are elderly, disabled, or ill, choose to vote absentee by mail, and there is no evidence that the additional proposed requirements for these votes to be counted are necessary.”
The News & Observer first reported on Stein’s letter. 
Stein also objected to the rule making it easier for local boards to toss ballots if members decide a voter lied about photo ID. 
“Making the rejection of voters’ ballots a partisan decision will undermine voters’ trust that their ballots will be counted,” Stein wrote. 
The photo ID rule drew vigorous public objection when it went before the Board of Elections earlier this year. The board received 161 pages of emailed comments about the rule, and 1,506 comments through an online portal. Most were opposed to dropping the need for unanimous votes to toss ballots.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas awards nearly $150 million in rural health program funding
description: Arkansas awarded $149.3 million in federal funding to 50 projects to support rural healthcare efforts statewide, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced Thursday.  Created last year through a federal tax and spending law called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Rural Health Transformation Program will provide $50 billion to states over five years. Arkansas i[...]
text:
A man who currently doesn't have dental insurance has his blood pressure checked at a mobile dental and medical clinic in August in Terre Haute, Ind. States have submitted grant applications to the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, showing a variety of priorities from rural workforce development to technological advancements. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)Arkansas awarded $149.3 million in federal funding to 50 projects to support rural healthcare efforts statewide, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced Thursday. 
Created last year through a federal tax and spending law called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Rural Health Transformation Program will provide $50 billion to states over five years. Arkansas is expected to receive more than $1 billion, including $209 million for this year. 
Critics of the program have said it lacks transparency, which could make it difficult to protect against fraud, according to KFF, a nonprofit health policy and research group.
Applications open for Arkansas rural telehealth projects to receive federal funding

The initial funding announced Thursday included $55.7 million through the state’s Telehealth, Health-Monitoring and Responsive Innovation for Vital Expansion initiative and $93.6 million through the Promoting Access Coordination and Transportation priority, according to a press release. 
Funding for the remaining two initiatives in Arkansas’ program will be announced soon, Sanders said during a press conference at the state Capitol. The initial round of funding will support projects that reach all 75 of the state’s counties and “help every single Arkansan lead a better, healthier life,” she said. 
“Thanks to the grants we’re announcing today, we’re giving a lifeline to providers, who are in turn giving a lifeline to small communities in Arkansas,” Sanders said.  
The funding will support a variety of projects, including helping Arkansas Children’s provide remote monitoring and virtual care coordination for rural children with chronic diseases, and Conway Regional Health System’s deployment of a maternal mobile health unit.  
The funding comes as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act could reduce federal Medicaid funding in rural areas by $137 billion over 10 years, according to KFF estimates. Rural providers see larger proportions of patients insured through Medicaid.  
The federal law is expected to reduce federal spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion during the next decade to help pay for tax cuts that disproportionately benefit the wealthy. 
The funding also comes as providers warn that the state’s healthcare system could be further strained by the end of Arkansas’ hybrid Medicaid expansion that covers more than 200,000 people. 
The Trump administration has said it won’t renew the program, and the state has asked for a two-year temporary extension to come up with a replacement.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Albuquerque homeowner says Republican candidate doesn’t live at contested address
description: Republican candidate for New Mexico House of Representatives District 27 Jahnelle Garcia has repeatedly listed her address as a home on Walnut Creek Road, but she hasn't lived there for more than a year, the current homeowner told Source NM.
text:
Republican New Mexico House of Representatives candidate Jahnelle Garcia has repeatedly listed the home in Albuquerque pictured above as her residence as she runs to represent House District 27, but the owner told Source NM on Aug. 25, 2026, that he has lived there for more than a year. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Republican candidate for New Mexico House of Representatives District 27 Jahnelle Garcia has repeatedly listed her address as a home on Walnut Creek Road, which sits in the middle of the district in Albuquerque’s Northeast Heights. She’s listed that address in at least four campaign finance filings this year, most recently in early July.
But Daniel Olufemi, an education professor at New Mexico Highlands University’s Rio Rancho campus, told Source NM in an interview outside the home this week that he’s lived there for more than a year, which county property records confirm. He said he recently recognized Garcia’s name from campaign advertisements as the person whose mail he still receives, he said. 
“The letters come in here, and I pick them up, and I just put them back in the mailbox,” Olufemi said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Abby Foster, a lawyer and the Democrat running against Garcia, sued Garcia, who owns several healthcare-related businesses, in the Second Judicial District Court on Monday. The lawsuit argues that Garcia violated state law that requires candidates to live in the district they hope to serve if elected. 
The lawsuit alleges, citing property records, that Garcia actually lives about 30 miles away in Los Lunas, along with her husband.
Garcia did not respond to multiple requests for comment this week from Source NM, including phone calls and text messages, and she has not yet responded to the lawsuit in court. Her campaign treasurer also did not respond to a phone call seeking comment.
The lawsuit urges a judge to remove Garcia from the ballot in one of the most competitive state House races in the Nov. 3 general election cycle. Of the roughly 23,000 registered voters who live within the 6.5-square-mile district, 40% are Democrats, 34% are Republicans and 27% are “other,” according to New Mexico Secretary of State data.
Democratic Party of Bernalillo County Chair Jacob Trujillo told Source NM that he ranks House District 27 as one of the top three races this year in Bernalillo County that Republicans hope to flip. Even if Garcia were to win, however, Democrats would maintain a sizable majority in a chamber where Democrats currently outnumber Republicans 46-26.
Foster and Garcia both won primary elections this June in the only state House race that featured primaries in both Democratic and Republican races. Foster narrowly bested Rep. Marian Matthews (D-Albuquerque) in the only primary legislative race in which an incumbent lost. 
Garcia also narrowly defeated her challenger, Robert “Bob” Godshall, by fewer than 100 votes in a race where 2,251 were cast. 
Godshall told Source NM on Thursday morning that he was unaware of any discrepancies in his former opponent Garcia’s address when the pair faced off in the months-long primary, though he said he will keep tabs on the lawsuit as it proceeds. 
Officials from the Republican Party of Bernalillo County, as well as the state House Republican caucus, did not respond to Source NM’s requests for comment this week.
Incumbents mostly win in contested New Mexico legislative races

New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office Deputy Secretary Sharon Pino told Source NM in an email that her office first learned of the lawsuit Wednesday and “is in the process of reviewing it” with the office that processed Garcia’s campaign filings, which is the Bernalillo County Clerk’s Office. The clerk’s office did not respond to Source NM’s inquiries about whether Garcia’s initial campaign filings raised suspicion. 
Foster told Source NM earlier this week that she hopes Second Judicial District Judge Joshua Andrew Allison rules quickly on removing Garcia from the ballot, given that the Nov. 2 general election is only a few months away. 
“It goes to our values as New Mexicans,” she said. “We take pride in our well-run elections, and by running in a district that she doesn’t live in, she’s making a mockery of the system.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Backers to pull Colorado road funding ballot measure after deal with state lawmakers
description: Backers of a ballot initiative that would funnel more money into Colorado road maintenance and repair announced that they will withdraw the measure after negotiating a funding strategy with state lawmakers. The measure, known as Initiative 175, would have created a constitutional amendment to direct taxes and fees related to transportation, such as the 22-ce[...]
text:
Southbound traffic on Interstate 25 in Denver on July 29, 2021. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Backers of a ballot initiative that would funnel more money into Colorado road maintenance and repair announced that they will withdraw the measure after negotiating a funding strategy with state lawmakers.
The measure, known as Initiative 175, would have created a constitutional amendment to direct taxes and fees related to transportation, such as the 22-cent state gas tax, to physical road construction and maintenance. Democratic lawmakers warned that it would create a massive hole in the state budget by requiring around $540 million per year in transportation spending, jeopardizing funding for services like public education and healthcare.
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser in a statement highlighted the potential for a compromise transportation ballot measure in a future election, but participants in the negotiations did not detail the provisions of such a measure or the new funding strategy. Restore Our Roads co-chair Jeff Keller said the funding strategy “goes beyond what the ballot measure contemplated” for revenue. Restore Our Roads was the committee that backed the ballot measure and was funded by construction groups.
“It will also prioritize long-needed maintenance and repair to ensure the safety of our roads for all Coloradans,” Keller said in a statement. “Our goal has always been to give Colorado taxpayers a voice in how the taxes and fees they pay for transportation are used. And now they finally will.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Democrats passed a bill this year to effectively neutralize the measure’s potential impact by lowering the gas tax. Withdrawal of the initiative means the bill will not go into effect. Sponsors of the bill, including Rep. Andy Boesenecker of Fort Collins and Sen. Judy Amabile of Boulder, worked with Weiser, a Democrat who is running for governor, and Restore Our Roads on a transportation funding framework.
“Maintaining Colorado’s roads and bridges is not only right for safety but also prevents Coloradans from spending more time in traffic and more money on car repairs,” Weiser said in a statement. “I’m grateful that the Initiative 175 proponents were willing to collaborate and find a path forward — one that will produce a ballot measure that we can all get behind.”
Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, in a Thursday statement thanked those involved with the compromise and highlighted increased transportation funding during his two terms.
“I am glad to see that through collaboration, state leaders and Restore our Roads were able to come to an agreement that removes Initiative 175 from the ballot and builds on our administration’s historic investments in our roads, highways, bridges, and tunnels,” Polis said. “Legislation written in collaboration with hundreds of stakeholders that I signed is investing more than $600 million in our roads in (fiscal year 2027) alone, and this agreement builds on that good work.”
Colorado voters will likely decide on over 10 ballot questions this November.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Pennsylvania measles deaths prompt concerns for NJ health leaders
description: New Jersey health officials are urging people to stay up to date on immunizations following two measles-related deaths involving unvaccinated people in Pennsylvania, the first in the nation this year.
text:
New Jersey Health Commissioner Dr. Raynard Washington is urging people to stay up to date on immunizations in the wake of two measles-related deaths of unvaccinated individuals in Pennsylvania, the nation's first such fatalities this year. (Photo by Illustration Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)New Jersey’s health commissioner is urging residents to ensure they are immunized against measles after Pennsylvania announced earlier this week that two unvaccinated people there had died from the highly contagious and preventable disease. 
Pennsylvania has not reported a measles-related fatality in at least 35 years, state officials there said, and the deaths are the first nationwide that have been tied to measles in 2026. Both were residents of Lancaster County, some 50 miles west of Philadelphia.
New Jersey is not experiencing a measles outbreak, but people “must remain vigilant” because of how contagious it is, New Jersey Health Commissioner Dr. Raynard Washington said in a statement.
Dr. Denise Rodgers, a family medicine expert and public health leader in Newark, said parents should understand the need to get their kids vaccinated, adding that there is “significant and incontrovertible evidence” that the measles vaccine is safe.
“No childhood vaccines have been found to cause autism and yet misinformation is causing thousands of children to be at risk because they are unvaccinated,” Rodgers told the New Jersey Monitor.
People who are unvaccinated are more likely to spread the disease to others, even if they don’t show symptoms themselves, experts note. Rodgers, previously a leader at Rutgers University’s biomedical programs, said this can be particularly dangerous for children and adults who have underlying immune issues.
“For example, children with asthma who get measles are more likely to have an asthma attack that could lead them to be hospitalized. I would hope that we take public health precautions that not only protect those that we love, but also protect our friends and neighbors,” Rodgers said.
Washington said the measles virus, which is spread when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes, can hang in the air for up to two hours, making it easy to transmit to others. If one person has measles, 9 out of 10 people who are in close contact with them will also become infected if they are unvaccinated, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.  
“So my ask is simple: Please, check your immunization record and your children’s, especially if you are planning to travel internationally or to areas in the United States currently experiencing an outbreak,” Washington said.  
New Jerseyans can ask their doctor if they are up to date. If you have signed up for myHealthNJ.com, a free software tool available under a partnership the state launched last year with the tech firm Docket, you can review your immunization record there.
Nationwide, nearly 2,800 measles cases have been reported from dozens of states in 2026, according to the CDC, which confirmed just under 2,300 cases last year. Active outbreaks continue in multiple states, including Pennsylvania, which has identified 424 cases in 2026, including more than 30 over the past week. New York has reported 29 cases this year, while New Jersey logged just one so far, in April, after confirming a dozen cases in 2025.
The recommendation from Washington, a public health specialist, comes a week after he urged parents to ignore President Trump’s executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccines, a shift Washington said would increase infectious disease and death nationwide. Trump and U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr have taken multiple steps to reduce the use of vaccines, despite extensive research proving they are safe and effective.  
Washington encouraged families to continue to follow state guidance, which is based on recommendations from professional organizations and public health collaboratives. The state backs the combined MMR vaccine — which guards against measles, mumps, and rubella — something Trump said should be split into three separate shots and given one at a time. MMR is considered 97% effective after the two-dose course. 
Measles first shows up as a high fever, cough, and runny nose, followed in three to five days by a rash that spreads downward from the head. The virus can be spread even before symptoms appear. While some people recover, others experience pneumonia, brain swelling, deafness, or even death. 
“When more than 95% of a community is protected, the virus runs out of people to infect, and an outbreak cannot take hold,” Washington said.
Federal data shows just 92% of kids in New Jersey had at least one MMR shot by age 2. In all, New Jersey requires eight different vaccines for kids to attend school. 
Immunizations are generally covered by insurance and are also available at low or no cost from local health departments. The state also maintains a list of community health events that includes back-to-school vaccine clinics. Shots are also available from most doctors’ offices and many drug stores.

text:
A woman uses the TikTok app. (Photo by Thicha Satapitanon/Getty Images)The State Board of Higher Education on Thursday voted to repeal a ban on TikTok for devices owned by North Dakota public colleges and universities.
The move follows Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s action that rescinded a 2022 executive order banning TikTok from devices owned by state agencies. 
The restrictions were prompted by national security concerns related to the app’s ownership by China-based company ByteDance. TikTok’s U.S. operations are now led by a U.S.-based joint venture.
State Board of Higher Education Chair Kevin Black said the decision seeks to balance security with access to communication and educational tools.
“The Board reviewed the latest information regarding TikTok’s ownership structure and cybersecurity risk profile,” Black said in a statement. “Based on those developments and the state’s updated assessment, the Board determined that a systemwide ban is no longer necessary.”
North Dakota University System campuses can request access to TikTok on university-owned devices.

title: Postal Service pushes ahead on Trump order limiting vote-by-mail
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Postal Service took another step Thursday in implementing a Trump administration policy to restrict mail-in voting, even as a high-stakes legal battle plays out and midterm elections approach.The agency published an FAQ about its new rule that compels states to send their voter rolls to the federal government and only deliver mail ballots to voters who match federal citizenship data. The rule also updates standards for mail ballots that states have said would be difficult to implement before the Nov. 3 elections that will determine the balance of Congress.The controversial rule, which two dozen Democratic states and voting rights groups are challenging in federal court, increases the federal government's role in elections and voting. The states have argued the rule violates the U.S. Constitution, which grants them the power of administering elections.In a Thursday brief defending the rule, the U.S. Justice Department said it only contained “modest improvements and modernizations of the Postal Service’s infrastructure” and would have minimal effect on states’ election administration.“The Rule does not displace a single State election law,” the brief said. “And it need not and should not prevent a single voter from voting by mail.”Democrat-led states and voting rights groups re-filed lawsuits Wednesday to block the Trump administration from executing the rule after a Supreme Court ruling Monday that temporarily greenlit the policy on procedural grounds.USPS acknowledged pending litigation in the FAQ, and noted it would make any changes spurred by the suits. Republicans, including Trump, have long made the accusation that noncitizens vote in federal elections, which multiple studies have shown occurs rarely.   On Thursday, Trump said he believed states could implement the new rule, even in North Carolina where ballots are set to be mailed next week.  “North Carolina is great,” Trump said. “And they do some mail-in ballots. But basically they ruled on the legitimacy and the way we want to make them legitimate. And it was a great ruling for the Republicans.”Those states suing to block the rule are California, Massachusetts, Nevada, Washington, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, as well as the District of Columbia.Jennifer Shutt contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Mary Henry left a NH school district amid a $5 million deficit. Woodstock says she’s exactly who they need.
description:
The superintendent of Mountain Views Supervisory District said the hiring committee reviewed 17 applicants and chose Henry for her experience in public school finance.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Mary Henry left a NH school district amid a $5 million deficit. Woodstock says she’s exactly who they need..
text:
Woodstock Union High School in August 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Molly Hughes was first published in the Valley News on Aug. 24, 2026.
Nine months after leaving a New Hampshire school district in the middle of a $5 million budget crisis, Mary Henry has a new job, a new state and a new administration standing firmly behind her.
Henry says she inherited the Claremont financial crisis, not caused it — and that she became the scapegoat for a problem she was brought in to fix.
Board members learned in August 2025 that Claremont’s SAU #6 was facing a multimillion-dollar deficit. Weeks later, the district placed Henry on unpaid suspension over what the interim superintendent at the time described only as “additional concerns” about her performance. Henry left in November after she and the district negotiated a separation agreement rather than go through a termination hearing.
In July, Henry started as director of finance and operations for the Mountain Views Supervisory District, which serves Woodstock and several surrounding Vermont communities.
Henry remains “one of the finest professionals that the Mountain Views Supervisory District has ever had the pleasure to hire,” said Keri Bristow, who chairs the Mountain Views school board.
However, the Claremont portion of her resume still follows her.
“I really don’t think the hiring district did their due diligence in hiring her,” Candace Crawford, a member of the Claremont school board, said by phone Monday.  
Current Claremont Superintendent Timothy Broadrick declined to weigh in on her specific performance, as he started his position after she left. But he was direct about who is responsible for the district’s finances.
“The business administrator and I are always responsible. Period,” Broadrick told the Valley News. “It’s any business administrator’s job and responsibility to know that the books are right, or if they’re not, to be the one who raises the alarms.”
The superintendent of Mountain Views, Sherry Sousa, said the hiring committee reviewed 17 applicants and chose Henry for her experience in public school finance.
“If there have been problems about Mary executing her position, the (Claremont) board would have had cause for termination,” Sousa said. “If the licensing board in New Hampshire believed that Mary had done something incorrectly or in violation of a license, it would have been rescinded. … That did not happen, and that gave us cause to pursue her as a candidate.”
“We know we have the best candidate for the position,” Sousa added.
What happened in Claremont
Claremont’s fiscal crisis didn’t start with Henry, and it didn’t end when she left. Broadrick said the district’s books had been in disarray for roughly seven years and that Claremont hadn’t completed an annual audit since around 2020 or 2021 — spanning two or three business administrators before Henry.
“It wasn’t that some new problem emerged — it’s that they ran out of cash,” he said, and compared it to checking a bank balance without accounting for checks already written.
Henry said she was told when she was hired in July 2023 that Claremont was five years behind on audits and already in a fiscal emergency. She traces the deficit to two sources: money returned to taxpayers after a prior tax rate was miscalculated, and unbudgeted special-education placement costs. The bulk of it, she said, ties to 2020 and 2021 audits she said she flagged to the district’s auditor in May 2025.
One of her first moves in Claremont, she said, was digitizing a paper-only system, which added to the district’s confusion: “Everything was to be scanned into the system and was paid. (But) nothing was, and everything was by paper and by hand, and you were constantly trying to find things.”
Henry wasn’t the only administrator to leave Claremont. Superintendent Christopher Pratt resigned in September 2025, and several others left around the same time.
“I can’t answer for other people and why they left,” Henry said. “I don’t think there is one administrator left from when I was there.”
The leaked letter
An internal SAU #6 “findings of fact” letter dated October 2025, a month before she left the district, outlined a dozen allegations against Henry, ranging from improper insurance paperwork to unreconciled bank statements.
Due to the separation agreement between Henry and the district, the document was never approved for public release, but it was leaked anyway — months later, Henry said, when a Claremont resident posted it to Facebook in January.
“I don’t know how they got their hands on it,” she said. Neither Henry nor Mountain Views officials could say who leaked it, though both believe it was released to damage her reputation.
Since none of the findings were adjudicated and SAU #6 had not made the letter public or confirmed its contents, Sousa declined to address the substance of the letter. Analyzing the findings “line by line,” she said, was “a rabbit hole that can be contested and has been contested, and it’s not proven for cause of termination, nor has it impacted her license.”
Henry said she was never formally notified of a license investigation. “In the state of New Hampshire, they have to tell me they’re investigating me and put me on notice,” she said.
“I was never put on notice that there was an investigation.”
Her New Hampshire license expired at the end of June 2026, and she is working toward Vermont certification, which requires a year in her current role before she can apply.
A district that’s all-in
Mountain Views officials describe a hands-on onboarding and finance plan: weekly check-ins between Henry and Sousa; continued contact with her mentor and predecessor, Jim Fenn; and a six-month evaluation planned for December or January.
Bristow, the board chair, told the Valley News that the board had held off on a statement while coverage played out, but was unambiguous.
“Why did Claremont try to destroy the person who was trying to fix the problem?” she said, adding that it’s “very infuriating to me that we have to put out fires like this when what we’re really trying to do here is build a new high school, middle school (and) keep moving forward with our successes in literacy and mathematics.”
The board didn’t wait long. On Aug. 20, Bristow sent a message to district families that said there was a “poisonous attempt” by “a relatively small group of individuals” to ruin Henry’s career. It closed with an endorsement from Fenn: “They’ve hired one of the most accomplished and talented Directors of Finance and Operations to support our District’s schools that you’ll find anywhere — in New England or beyond.”
Henry said the scrutiny weighs less on her than on the people around her. “The worst part of all of this isn’t about how much this has come back on me,” she said. “It’s about how much it’s coming back on others — this district, my family.”
Asked why she’s staying in public education rather than returning to the private sector, Henry didn’t hesitate: “I contemplated it. I looked into it. I want to be here, and I’m not going to let someone take away what I work so hard for, and what I want to do with my life.”
Before Claremont, Henry was a business administrator at the Fall Mountain Regional (2022-23), Hillsboro-Deering (2020-22) and Winchester (2018-20) school districts in New Hampshire. She holds a master’s degree from Plymouth State University, a bachelor’s in accounting and finance from Granite State College, and a certificate in education finance from Georgetown University. She also served for roughly a decade on the Fall Mountain Regional School Board.
“I was not terminated from Claremont. We negotiated out of my contract,” Henry told the Valley News.
Claremont, meanwhile, still hasn’t replaced her. The district’s business administrator job has been open since Henry left.
“The job has been posted since January. We are actively looking for a business administrator,” Claremont board member Crawford told the Valley News. “Things are much better than they were a year ago. Things have stabilized, and I encourage people to apply.”
Crawford said the vacancy isn’t unusual. “If you look around the state, we are not unique,” she said. “There are many schools with vacant business admin positions.”
The New Hampshire School Administrators Association currently lists at least nine open financial positions at schools across the state.

title: State approves funding to kickstart 122nd Fighter Wing modernization
description: The State Budget Committee on Thursday approved $1 million to help the Indiana Air National Guard’s 122nd Fighter Wing in Fort Wayne land a future F35-A base. Indiana Brigadier Gen. Matt Brown told the panel of lawmakers the 122nd is “locked in a fierce multi-state competition to secure the next-generation F-35 fighter jet, a designation […]
text:
An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 122nd Fighter Wing takes off at the 122nd Fighter Wing, Fort Wayne, Indiana, July 30, 2026. Training sorties were an essential part of the wing’s readiness to respond to a critical aerospace defense tasking. (Photo by U.S. Air National Guard Tech. Sgt. David Sherman)The State Budget Committee on Thursday approved $1 million to help the Indiana Air National Guard’s 122nd Fighter Wing in Fort Wayne land a future F35-A base.
Indiana Brigadier Gen. Matt Brown told the panel of lawmakers the 122nd is “locked in a fierce multi-state competition to secure the next-generation F-35 fighter jet, a designation that would solidify Fort Wayne’s fighter role in defense economic impact for decades.”
In June, Indiana’s entire congressional delegation sent a letter to the U.S. Air Force urging it to consider the Fort Wayne base for two new F-35A units. The letter highlighted the adaptability of the 122nd Wing and guaranteed the same seamless transition to F-35’s as its recent conversion from using the A-10 to F-16 in the last year.
But Brown said other states are investing heavily to improve their chances. For instance, the Michigan Legislature recently approved $152 million to upgrade the Selfridge Air National Guard Base.
“While Fort Wayne is one of nine F-16 wings competing and will score exceptionally high in performance and readiness, our outdated infrastructure will hold us back in the final scoring,” Brown said. 
He described two projects Thursday that will jumpstart base modernization.
The first costs $517,000 and covers the final design work on a revamped squadron operations building. It will include a mission planning cell, a secure vault area and maximizing the weapon system’s full capability. Federal funds covered the initial 35% concept phase, but the money is needed to position the base to secure an $8.8 million dollar federal construction investment.
The second project costs $500,000 for a comprehensive area development plan to map out future F-35 infrastructure requirements. One part of the roadmap will include mitigating a high-risk security and logistics challenge caused by a bisecting Norfolk Southern railroad.
“Established in 1947, the Fort Wayne base must look beyond its current F-16 operations and plan now for the next generation of aircraft,” Brown said. “Because he National Guard Bureau doesn’t provide federal planning funds until after the final basing decisions are made, Indiana must invest now to remain competitive for the headquarters U.S. Air Force basing decision, which is occurring in the next 18 months.”
The investments, he said, will help position the 122nd to secure an F-35 aircraft delivery by 2034, ensuring the long-term credibility of the Indiana Air National Guard.

title: US Education Secretary McMahon visits rural North Dakota school
description: The top U.S. education official on Thursday visited a small rural school in the rolling hills west of Mandan, part of her national education tour. Education Secretary Linda McMahon visited the Sweet Briar School, joined by U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, R-N.D., and Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler, who was North Dakota’s[...]
text:
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon sits with kindergarteners, first and second graders at the Sweet Briar School near Mandan, North Dakota, on Aug. 27, 2026. 
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)The top U.S. education official on Thursday visited a small rural school in the rolling hills west of Mandan, part of her national education tour.
Education Secretary Linda McMahon visited the Sweet Briar School, joined by U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, R-N.D., and Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler, who was North Dakota’s K-12 superintendent from 2013-2025.
School board members, state lawmakers, State Superintendent Levi Bachmeier and others watched as McMahon, Fedorchak and Baesler moved between grades and chatted with the approximately 25 students in kindergarten through eighth grade.
Trump, McMahon promote school voucher program as students return to class

One girl showed McMahon her classroom’s hydroponic garden on the wall. Older students told the secretary about their sports. McMahon sat among kindergarteners, first and second graders, and posed for photos with the students and teachers by the playground. 
The students are split between a 1936 stucco schoolhouse and a newer building. The school community is small enough that a few students are siblings or cousins. At least two teachers count their own children among their pupils.
McMahon’s visit is part of her 50-state “Returning Education to the States Tour. Education is “not one size fits all,” she told reporters, flanked by Fedorchak, Baesler and Bachmeier near the playground.
“Look at the school where we’re standing here today,” she said. “This is an obvious example of an innovation that is education for the students in the place where they live, and the president certainly believes the best education is that that’s closest to the child, and I think we can see evidence of that clearly here today.” 
North Dakota is McMahon’s 41st state since she took office, she said.
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon visits the Sweet Briar School near Mandan, North Dakota, on Aug. 27, 2026. At right is Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler, who was North Dakota’s K-12 superintendent from 2013-2025.(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
“My goal is to see what is taught, how it’s taught, what are the reactions of the students, where are we making the greatest progress, etc., because states are the innovators,” McMahon told reporters.
Baesler and Fedorchak touted the Education Freedom Tax Credit, which rolls out in January and North Dakota will participate in. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill last year created the tax credit, which provides up to $1,700 per taxpayer for cash contributions made to nonprofits known as scholarship-granting organizations that give the funds to families for education expenses, including private K-12 school tuition.
“The key piece here is that that scholarship-granting organization is going to be granting those scholarships to parents to use that money and those dollars how they choose – it’s a choice – to help benefit the education,” Fedorchak told reporters. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Burlington artist, dug Nap, struck and killed e-bike rider in crosswalk, new court filing alleges.
description:
Fatal crash brings outpouring of grief for 16-year-old who died as filing in case states that an “attentive driver” should have seen the crosswalk flashing lights and stopped “before crashing into” her.   
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington artist, dug Nap, struck and killed e-bike rider in crosswalk, new court filing alleges..
text:
Doug Knapp appears in Chittenden County Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Knapp is charged with negligent operation of a motor vehicle with death resulting in the death of cyclist Shiloh Skalka. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON – A Burlington folk artist pleaded not guilty Thursday to a charge alleging he struck and killed a 16-year-old cyclist in a crosswalk with warning lights flashing.
Douglas Knapp, 79, faces a misdemeanor offense of negligent operation of a motor vehicle resulting in the death of 16-year-old Shiloh Skalka, a high school student from Burlington, on July 16, who had been riding her e-bike,
Knapp, through his public defender Austin Howard, pleaded not guilty to the offense during an arraignment in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington. If convicted of the charge, Knapp faces up to two years in jail. 
Judge Robert Katims released Knapp on conditions requested by the prosecution, including that he not drive a motor vehicle. Knapp’s next court hearing is set for Oct 27
Skalka’s death has led to tributes in her honor and calls for enhanced bike safety protections. A ride in Skalka’s honor and vigil earlier this month drew hundreds of people, Seven Days reported.
Several of Skalka’s family members, friends and other community members filled several rows of seats in the courtroom Thursday, and declined to comment following the hearing.
Knapp, a well-known Burlington folk artist using the name dug Nap, did not speak during the hearing or after it. 
Instead, Howard, his attorney, made a brief statement on his client’s behalf to reporters outside the courtroom. 
“First, and most importantly, he wants to extend his sincere condolences to the Skalka family,” Howard said of Knapp, who was seated on a bench next to Howard in a courthouse hallway. 
Howard also said that the defense had only recently received the state’s charging documents, 
“Our investigation is just beginning,” the defense attorney said, adding, “Mr. Knapp looks forward to engaging in the process and letting that process play out.“
Chittenden County Deputy State’s Attorney Kelton Olney referred questions from reporters regarding the investigation to the charging documents. 
“Obviously,” Olney added, “it’s very early in the prosecution but the state is pleased that the court imposed the conditions that the state requested, which in this case include a prohibition on driving a motor vehicle on a public highway.”
Knapp was issued a citation by Burlington Police to appear in court on the misdemeanor charge late last month. However, few details were made available at that time regarding what took place leading up to the fatal crash.
A 14-page charging affidavit made public following Knapp’s arraignment Thursday outlines the police investigation leading to the charge that included taking statements from witnesses and analyzing video footage captured from cameras near the scene. 
Burlington Detective Cpl. Padric Hartnett wrote in the filing that the crash took place on the afternoon of July 16 at the intersection of Pine and Locust streets. 
Hartnett added that the investigation showed Skalka was traveling east to west on her e-bike on Locust Street and stopped at the pedestrian crosswalk. Skalka then activated the crossing signal and waited about 3 seconds before entering the roadway, Hartnett wrote.  
While crossing the intersection, Hartnett wrote, Skalka, who was wearing a helmet, was struck seconds later by a Dodge Grand Caravan, driven by Knapp, and traveling south on Pine Street. 
“It is reasonable to believe an attentive driver would have noticed the amber LED lights engaged and upon observing the cyclist in the crosswalk, come to a stop prior to crashing into them,” Hartnett wrote. “Knapp was also traveling at a constant speed just prior to crashing into (Skalka), which further indicates his inattention to the roadway and failure to yield.”  

Doug Knapp appears in Chittenden County Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Knapp is charged with negligent operation of a motor vehicle with death resulting in the death of cyclist Shiloh Skalka. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Skalka was taken to the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington where she later died from her injuries. 
Knapp told an officer at the scene that he was pretty shook, adding that all of a sudden Skalka was in front of him and “I’m hitting her,” the affidavit stated. Knapp also said he had no memory of seeing the crosswalk warning lights or if he hit the brakes of his vehicle, according to the affidavit.
Knapp said he hadn’t consumed any alcohol, and noted that he was on prescribed medication, though the officer did not ask him what that medication was, Hartnett wrote. 
Police later tried to interview Knapp about two weeks after the crash, the affidavit stated, but he told the investigator that based on an attorney’s advice he would not provide a further statement. 
“Knapp was asked if he was on phone during the time of the crash to which he stated he did not have his phone, it was at his studio and not in the vehicle at the time of the crash,” Hartnett wrote.
Hartnett added that it appeared from video footage that Knapp’s vehicle was moving at a consistent speed, estimated at 28 mph in the 25-mph zone leading up to the crash.

title: IRS delays filing, paying of taxes for residents in 22 Nebraska counties after wildfires and storms
description: LINCOLN — The U.S. Internal Revenue Service is postponing the filing and paying of 2026 taxes for affected Nebraskans and businesses in 22 counties due to wildfires and storms this year. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announced the delay Thursday as a result of five separate state disaster declarations. Affected taxpayers now have until Feb. 1, […]
text:
Gov. Jim Pillen surveys burned land in Nebraska on Saturday, March 14, 2026. One person died as four major fires continued to burn in western and central Nebraska. (Photo courtesy of the Governor's Office)LINCOLN — The U.S. Internal Revenue Service is postponing the filing and paying of 2026 taxes for affected Nebraskans and businesses in 22 counties due to wildfires and storms this year.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announced the delay Thursday as a result of five separate state disaster declarations. Affected taxpayers now have until Feb. 1, 2027, to file their tax returns and pay any taxes originally due during the disaster periods. Four of the five disasters are due to wildfires between March and June. The fifth is due to severe storms in May.
“When a disaster strikes, surviving the immediate aftermath takes priority,” Pillen said in a statement.
The counties with the approved delay: Arthur, Buffalo, Custer, Dawes, Dawson, Fillmore, Frontier, Gage, Garden, Grant, Howard, Jefferson, Keith, Lincoln, Morrill, Nemaha, Red Willow, Richardson, Saunders, Sioux, Thayer and Thurston.


Federal legislation now allows the IRS to grant a governor’s request for delay based on a governor-declared disaster or emergency. Before, a federal declaration, which can take longer, was needed. 
This is the first time Nebraska has requested the relief under the new law.
Pillen said this year has “undoubtedly” weighed heavily on those who experienced losses and/or damage from the fires and storms just months ago.
Said the governor: “This determination from the IRS will hopefully provide a little respite to Nebraskans in those counties who were affected by allowing them the time to meet their tax obligations without incurring additional penalties.”
Additional counties could be added to the previously declared disaster areas. Residents and businesses in those counties would also be eligible for postponement. Individuals who receive late filing or payment notices during the postponement can call the IRS to have the agency abate the penalty.
More information on each disaster is available from the IRS at https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/around-the-nation-nebraska.
