name: VTDigger
title: Burlington’s public safety problems require more than new gun laws
description:
Another gun ordinance won't fix a city that lacks secure juvenile detention, psychiatric beds and enough police to patrol its streets.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington’s public safety problems require more than new gun laws.
text:
This commentary is by Matt Swenson, the founder of Omnidex Solutions, an independent research and strategic analysis company. He lives in Vermont.
Burlington’s latest outbreak of violence should prompt a broader discussion about the city’s public safety system, not simply another debate over gun laws.
Over a single weekend, Burlington police investigated a fatal stabbing, a second stabbing, gunfire following an argument and the alleged accidental discharge of a firearm downtown. In a separate daytime incident, three juveniles allegedly attacked a man with a knife near the bike path. These events involved different weapons and circumstances, but together they suggest weaknesses in Burlington’s ability to deter dangerous behavior and intervene effectively when it occurs.
Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak responded by renewing calls for stronger gun laws, including prohibiting firearms in establishments serving alcohol. These proposals may be well-intentioned, but they address only one part of a larger problem.
Reckless endangerment, assault and unlawful discharge of a firearm are already crimes in Vermont, as is carrying a weapon with intent to injure. People carrying weapons while committing other crimes are unlikely to be deterred by another ordinance. Additional restrictions will be followed primarily by people who already obey the law, while having less effect on those creating the danger.
The fact that several recent attacks involved knives illustrates the limitations of concentrating mainly on firearms. Burlington appears to be facing broader problems involving enforcement, detention, treatment and institutional capacity.
The alleged juvenile attack is particularly concerning. Having worked with juvenile offenders involved in nearly every level of felony conduct, I have seen the difference between a young person who can be redirected and one who presents an immediate danger to others. Treatment and rehabilitation should remain central goals, but they may not always be a viable substitute for secure custody when public safety is at risk.
Vermont closed the Woodside Juvenile Rehabilitation Center in 2020 and has never established an adequate replacement. The state is now proposing a locked 14-bed Green Mountain Youth Center in South Burlington. Fourteen beds may not be sufficient if Vermont intends to stop placing juveniles accused of serious or repeated violence in caregiver-style facilities that were not designed or staffed to contain them securely.
Vermont should explore establishing a larger secure juvenile corrections facility supported by personnel specifically trained as juvenile corrections officers. It should be capable of providing secure detention while also offering clinical care, education and meaningful rehabilitation. Treatment and security need not be competing objectives.
The Burlington Police Department is unlikely to restore its former staffing strength quickly. The city could temporarily supplement police coverage with qualified armed security officers on selected streets and in parks and commercial areas. This could provide a visible public safety presence while the department rebuilds.
The city should also consistently enforce conduct-based public space rules addressing threats, obstruction, open drug use and aggressive harassment. Residents should be able to use public parks without navigating discarded needles, drug activity or threatening behavior. Enforcement should focus on conduct rather than poverty or housing status, while recognizing that public spaces must remain accessible to the entire community.
Burlington’s approach to harm reduction also deserves careful evaluation. Howard Center previously distributed syringes and smoking pipes intended for crack cocaine or methamphetamine use before discontinuing the practice. Supporters argue that these programs reduce infections and help maintain contact with people who might eventually seek treatment. Those goals should be considered alongside the effects on surrounding neighborhoods.
Publicly funded nonprofits should report measurable outcomes, including how much material is recovered, how many people enter and remain in treatment, and whether surrounding areas become safer. Harm reduction should be one component of a larger strategy, not a substitute for treatment, public order or accountability.
Enforcement alone will not repair Burlington. Vermont also lacks sufficient inpatient psychiatric and substance-use treatment capacity. Chittenden County should examine building a second, smaller hospital in Williston or Colchester, including a full-service emergency department and approximately 100 psychiatric and substance-use treatment beds.
This would give residents an alternative to the congestion, limited parking and public disorder encountered when seeking emergency care at the University of Vermont Medical Center. The facility could provide routine emergency medicine, acute psychiatric care, substance-use stabilization and longer-term behavioral health treatment.
Vermont should solicit proposals from experienced nonprofit hospital systems capable of recruiting clinicians and developing modern treatment infrastructure. A second emergency department would also reduce pressure on UVM Medical Center rather than routing nearly every serious medical or psychiatric emergency in the county through one congested location.

READ MORE

Such a facility would require substantial investment, but Vermont is already paying for its lack of capacity through overcrowded emergency departments, repeated police calls, correctional placements, homelessness and victimization.
The state’s economic stagnation and difficulty modernizing essential systems cannot be separated from these issues. A state that struggles to build housing, recruit doctors, retain police officers and develop effective institutions will eventually see its social systems deteriorate.
Burlington needs a balanced response: secure juvenile detention, trained juvenile corrections officers, greater medical and psychiatric capacity, measurable standards for publicly funded programs, temporary security support where police coverage is inadequate and stronger coordination from state government.
New gun laws may be part of the political discussion, but they will not correct the broader institutional limitations contributing to Burlington’s public safety problems.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Here’s what the Meta settlement means for Montana
description: Montana’s portion of the landmark $17.1 billion settlement from Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, could vary depending on several final settlement factors. It is guaranteed to get at least $89 million and could get as much as $127 million, according to Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen, whose office was part of the […]
text:
In this photo illustration, social media apps are displayed on an iPad on Feb. 26, 2024, in Miami, Florida. (Photo illustration by Joe Raedle | Getty Images)Montana’s portion of the landmark $17.1 billion settlement from Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, could vary depending on several final settlement factors. It is guaranteed to get at least $89 million and could get as much as $127 million, according to Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen, whose office was part of the 47-state coalition which had brought the lawsuit.
“This settlement agreement is the culmination of years of hard work to hold Meta accountable for their dangerous and deceptive practices that put the health and well-being of Montana kids at risk,” Knudsen said in a press release. “I’m glad Meta has taken responsibility and I hope other social media companies will follow suit. This settlement money will be put to good use to improve safety and mental health resources for kids and teens in the state.”
Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen testifies before the U.S. House in an impeachment hearing for Homeland Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas on Jan. 10, 2024 (Committee webcast).
At least half of the money must go to remediate harms caused by social media such as:

Crisis intervention services, specifically the expansion and operation of the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and text-based youth crisis lines.
After school or summer programs, such as sports, literacy, dance, and other activities.
Public health advertising credits.
A digital wellness public education fund.
Funding outdoor activities.
Youth mental health programming.
Support the hiring of digital literacy counselors or implement phone-free school zones.
Training for medical providers on interactive media use and body dysmorphia.
Grants to school districts or other local government entities to accomplish any remedial purpose encompassed here.
Any similar remedial or restitutive purposes as those described above; and
Investigation, litigation, and related efforts to improve teen safety on social media.

Montana also resolved its claims against Meta for Meta’s sharing of nonpublic information about Facebook users with third parties, like Cambridge Analytica, leading up to the 2016 election. Montana will receive an additional $4.3 million under that settlement agreement.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Amidst politicos and athletes, Crafts and Central Bank again buy country ham for $10 million
description: LOUISVILLE — In what’s become a tradition for them, Republican megadonors Joe and Kelly Craft joined Central Bank in buying a country ham for $10 million.  At the end of the Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast on Thursday, attendees have a chance to bid on the Kentucky State Fair Grand Champion Country Ham, though the […]
text:
UK basketball player Malachi Moreno holds the $10 million country ham above the winning bidders, Kelly and Joe Craft at the Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast on Aug. 27, 2026. UK basketball coach Mark Pope is next to Moreno. Central Bank CEO Luther Deaton is seated next to Miss Kentucky. (Photo by Chris Hughes for Kentucky Lantern)LOUISVILLE — In what’s become a tradition for them, Republican megadonors Joe and Kelly Craft joined Central Bank in buying a country ham for $10 million. 
At the end of the Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast on Thursday, attendees have a chance to bid on the Kentucky State Fair Grand Champion Country Ham, though the Crafts and Central Bank have outbid everyone else for a few years. The breakfast typically brings together Kentucky politicians with farmers from across the state. 
Malachi Moreno, a center for the University of Kentucky men’s basketball team, made bids for the Crafts, who are long-time sports boosters for both UK basketball and football. UK basketball coach Mark Pope also sat at their table.
The money from the auction will go to organizations  around Kentucky, including the Boys & Girls Club of Glasgow-Barren County, the FFA chapters in Barren and Glasgow counties, University of Kentucky Athletics, Keeneland, St. Elizabeth Healthcare, The Hope Center and more. 
Kelly Craft, a former U.S. ambassador, said her family plans to get the ham sliced thin and serve it with biscuits to share with others. This year’s winning ham was produced by Tim Berry of Clifty Farm Country Meats in Scottsville and weighs 16.7 pounds. 
The winning $10 million ham was produced by Tim Berry of Clifty Farm Country Meats in Scottsville and weighs 16.7 pounds. The Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast took place on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Chris Hughes for Kentucky Lantern.)
Craft, who previously ran for governor in 2023, said she is planning to work to elect more Republicans next year when asked if she is considering another foray into politics. 
“As you’ve heard today, our legislators have made the state a huge success in our farming and  our agri industry. So that is what Mr. Craft and I — that’s what our goal is,” she said. 
Asked about candidates she might support, Craft said she was looking forward to “working really, really hard to elect Jamie Comer governor.” 
Comer, Kentucky’s 1st District congressman, was at the breakfast, as well as Democratic candidates for governor — Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear. Even though Louisville isn’t in the 6th Congressional District, both the Republican nominee, Ralph Alvarado, and Democratic nominee, Zach Dembo, attended as well.
While Comer is currently seeking reelection for his U.S. House seat, he has been a speculated candidate for governor, and received numerous public endorsements from Republicans already. During his remarks at the breakfast, Republican Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell referred to Comer as “Governor Comer” before correcting himself when listing guests he brought. 
Comer told reporters he was honored to have the support so far, noting that “the entire slate of constitutional officers, except for lieutenant governor, have all expressed their support for me.”
“We’re going to make a decision very soon. There’ll be an announcement probably a week after the November election,” Comer said. “But I will tell you this: everything looks good. I think the people of Kentucky are ready to go in a different direction, and I look forward to traveling the state.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: McConnell misses annual Kentucky ham breakfast despite frequent attendance in years past
description: LOUISVILLE — Kentucky Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell continues to be absent from public life after he was hospitalized in June.  McConnell did not attend the Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast at the state fair Thursday morning, an event he usually attends, and often uses to discuss the congressional farm bill.  Kentucky’s two senators and […]
text:
Kentucky Farm Bureau President Eddie Melton speaks during the KFB Country Ham Breakfast on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026 at the Kentucky State Fair in Louisville. (Photo by Chris Hughes for Kentucky Lantern)LOUISVILLE — Kentucky Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell continues to be absent from public life after he was hospitalized in June. 
McConnell did not attend the Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast at the state fair Thursday morning, an event he usually attends, and often uses to discuss the congressional farm bill. 
Kentucky’s two senators and the governor are typically invited to address the breakfast, which gathers a crowd of hundreds, including politicians and farmers from across the state. Republican U.S. Sen. Rand Paul and Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear also did not attend this year, but KFB President Eddie Melton said staff for both senators were present. 
“He’s been here as long as I can remember coming to this Country Ham Breakfast. He’s been here every year,” Melton said of McConnell, adding that he wishes McConnell “can improve and get back and run this thing through the tape at the end of the year.”
McConnell, 84, was hospitalized in June and said on July 12 he would enter a rehabilitation center. Since he has been absent in the U.S. Senate, speculation about his vitality has run rampant online. His office has shared photos of him with his wife, former Secretary of Labor and Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao. He has not made any video appearances.
Asked on Wednesday about if McConnell was planning to go to the ham breakfast and for updates on his health, a spokesperson for the senator referred to an Aug. 6 statement where McConnell had said he will “an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period” and continue to work with staff and colleagues. 
U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, the Republican candidate running for McConnell’s seat this year, told reporters he last spoke to McConnell three weeks ago and “he was in good spirits and recovering.” Barr added that Republican Senate Leader John Thune had said McConnell is expected back in the Senate when it returns on Sept. 14 to make critical votes throughout the rest of the year. 
U.S. Rep. James Comer, another Republican, said he spoke to McConnell’s staff Thursday morning and they “hope he’s on the Senate floor very soon.” 
“That farm bill — something he’s always been involved in. He’s won a lot of awards from Farm Bureau over the years, so he wants to certainly cast a vote for the farm bill,” Comer said. 
Earlier this month, McConnell was not present at an Agriculture Committee committee to advance this year’s farm bill to the floor. He had attempted to cast a vote by proxy but Senate rules prevented it.
Comer said he will be on the conference committee for the bill after it makes its way through the House and Senate. The legislation is a “little bit of a safety net” for American farmers, he added. 
“We’re going to do everything we can because the tariffs have not been good for agriculture in America, especially Kentucky, and with the rising cost of gasoline, it’s really affected the input costs,” Comer said. “Fertilizer costs are directly related to fuel costs. So, the farmers are under a lot of challenges.”
President Donald Trump, who has made tariffs a cornerstone of his foreign policy in his second term, signed a proclamation on Wednesday to boost lean beef imports from other countries to lower prices for consumers. American farmers have been critical of the policy. Earlier this week, Melton released a statement saying the president’s plan to move to “greater reliance on foreign beef could hurt American farmers and create long-term consequences for consumers.” 
U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, who is running for Sen. McConnell’s Senate seat, spoke to reporters at the Kentucky Farm Bureau Country Ham Breakfast on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Chris Hughes for Kentucky Lantern)
Comer said farmers “are overwhelmingly opposed to this decision,” though he understands Trump’s goal of lowering grocery prices. The best solution is to “increase the cattle inventory,” Comer said before adding that it does take longer to raise cattle compared to other farm animals, such as chickens. 
“I’ve expressed my displeasure with the president and the secretary of agriculture, explained why we don’t buy beef from Argentina,” Comer said. “And when you talk about America First, if we’re going to have tariffs — we should stick with it one way or the other.”
Barr has set up a Friday meeting between U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnik and Kentucky cattle farmers. Barr also said “the long-term solution to this is to build up our herd.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: NABJ honors Mississippi Today for prison homicides project
description: The year-long project, involving Mississippi Today, The Marshall Project - Jackson and the Clarion Ledger, found that over a decade at least 42 people were killed in the state’s prisons with just six people convicted in those deaths.
text:
The National Association of Black Journalists has honored Mississippi Today, The Marshall Project and the Clarion Ledger with an NABJ Salute to Excellence Award for coverage of deaths inside Mississippi prisons.
The year-long project, which involved Mississippi Today’s senior investigative reporter Jerry Mitchell and criminal justice reporter Mina Corpuz and Justice Editor Debbie Skipper, also included the contributions of the Hattiesburg American and Mississippi Link. It chronicled dozens of killings that went unpunished. 
Over a decade, at least 42 people were killed in the state’s prisons with just six people convicted in those deaths. Often families contacted by the reporters didn’t know their loved ones’ deaths were ruled a homicide. In one case, a prosecutor forgot to serve an indictment until a reporter on the team called about the homicide. 
New evidence Mitchell uncovered offered hope to the mother of a son killed in the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman five years ago that she would finally have some answers about what happened.
Faced with these facts, Mississippi Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain told Mississippi Today that he would reopen investigations of the homicide cases as well as deaths ruled undetermined.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Flock backlash growing in some Western NC communities
description: Law enforcement agencies across North Carolina have been using automatic license plate reader, or ALPR, technology quietly for the past several years to little knowledge of residents. But this technology has become controversial nationwide and synonymous with Flock cameras, which take images of license plates at a singular point in time and enter them into a[...]
text:
Flock Safety license plate readers are typically mounted on tall poles, with a camera and solar panel on top. The company says its technology is used in more than 6,000 communities across 49 states in partnership with thousands of law enforcement agencies nationwide. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)Law enforcement agencies across North Carolina have been using automatic license plate reader, or ALPR, technology quietly for the past several years to little knowledge of residents. But this technology has become controversial nationwide and synonymous with Flock cameras, which take images of license plates at a singular point in time and enter them into a database where artificial intelligence catalogs vehicle characteristics, like a vehicle’s make, model and color.
Communities in rural parts of Western North Carolina, who are used to the kind of privacy that comes with winding mountain roads, have been surprised to find that their local governments may have a contract with Flock and several of Flock’s cameras installed on roadways. Some say the technology is a violation of the Fourth Amendment.
In Madison County, about 50 community members came to speak about their sheriff’s office’s contract with Flock during the public comment period of a Board of Commissioners meeting in June. Madison is a mountainous county that touches the Tennessee border. It is home to the towns of Marshall, Mars Hill and Hot Springs.
[Subscribe for FREE to Carolina Public Press’ Daily, Weekend and Election 2026 newsletters.]
Privacy advocates were met with Council Chairman Michael Garrison telling the dozens of county residents who wanted to speak on Flock that only one of them could talk about the issue. Though it was disappointing for those who wanted to speak, allowing one person to speak for a large group during a public comment period for the purpose of time is acceptable under the North Carolina Open Meetings Law.
Members of Madison for Privacy, a local advocacy group, told Carolina Public Press that they are also having a difficult time receiving records requests from the sheriff’s office about contracts with certain surveillance technologies. Members of the group, Joe Stanis and Sean Phillips, said the group isn’t inherently political — they are just wary of outside surveillance in their community.
“Most Republicans, at least in Madison County, have libertarian values and don’t want to be surveilled,” Stanis said.
Local governments like Madison County are actively debating the use of the technology and some disgruntled citizens have even taken to removing Flock technology from their local street corners. Earlier this month, someone removed a camera in Asheville’s Carrier Park, prompting the city police to reinstate it. Flock cameras are having a national reckoning right now — and Western North Carolina is no stranger to it.
What is Flock?
Atlanta-based tech company Flock Safety is by no means the only company that provides this kind of technology — other ALPRs across the country come from vendors such as Axon and Motorola — but Flock is unique. The company has a network of data on every car it has detected, allowing law enforcement agencies across the country to search for a specific vehicle’s location history across thousands of camera feeds.
Because of this, Flock and ALPRs have only become more synonymous as the cameras have become a point of contention across the country.
Agencies can access and search data from others across the more than 120,000 Flock cameras in the country. Madison County, for example, has access to a network of more than 1,500 law enforcement agencies and shares its data with 725 of them, according to records obtained by CPP.
Though Flock denies a direct partnership, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Center for Border Patrol sometimes receive data from local law enforcement agencies through indirect sharing.
Flock was founded in 2017 and originally served HOAs and neighborhoods that wanted to prevent petty crimes like break-ins, but quickly contracted with law enforcement agencies. The company also makes audio detection technology called Flock Raven that can sense gunshots and loud noises.
Cameras store information in audit logs, which track who in an agency searched for a license plate and the reason for the search. Different types of audit logs include those of an agency’s own Flock cameras and network audits, which show searches conducted by other agencies through network sharing agreements. Some agencies have transparency portals where they release redacted audit logs to the public.
On Aug. 13, Flock announced that its cameras will now only store information for seven days, unless the data is related to a criminal investigation. Previously, the number was 30 days.
Flock in NC
Some communities in North Carolina are actively debating ending their contracts with the tech company because of public concerns. Some already have. But, a number of sheriffs are reluctant to give up the technology. Many say Flock is a necessary evil for catching criminals, especially in rural areas with smaller numbers of law enforcement personnel.
A number of cases have also involved law enforcement misuse of the cameras. An officer in Mooresville, in Iredell County, searched for her boyfriend’s ex-wife over 30 times in the Flock database, according to reporting from The Charlotte Observer. The officer was arrested and charged with misuse of the technology “for purposes other than official law enforcement duties.”
Macon County, which is in the southwest corner of the state, let its Flock contract expire without renewal in a unanimous vote by county commissioners on July 14. Six cameras installed in public schools across the county will remain, but all others will be removed this month.
In the Piedmont, Chatham County and the town of Hillsborough also canceled their contracts with the tech company earlier this year. Davidson County is also set to vote on its Flock contract this week.
“I feel the Flock cameras are a necessary evil, but due to paranoia and uncertainties about people’s motives, we group to protect ourselves via our US Constitution,” Macon County Commissioner Gary Shields said in an email statement to Carolina Public Press.
Some 85% of the 2,819 ALPRs in North Carolina are operated by Flock, according to DeFlock, an advocacy group that has created a crowdsourced database of surveillance technology nationwide. Wake County has the most cameras.
Asheville Mayor Esther Manheimer called on the City Council to end the area’s contract with Flock in a video statement posted on social media last week. The council voted to cancel the contract during its meeting Tuesday. Right now, the city of Asheville operates 11 Flock cameras, but more cameras are operated by other entities, like the public school system, inside the city limits.
“We need to do this to make sure that this technology is not moving faster than we are,” she said in the video. “We need to protect our citizens and our civil liberties.”
But Manheimer, along with every City Council member except for Kim Roney, voted to approve a 24-hour Real-Time Intelligence Center for the Asheville Police Department worth $1.4 million earlier this year. The center would synchronize license plate readers, public and private surveillance cameras in the city and police dash cameras. The City Council also approved a new contract with Axon in May, so just voting out the Flock contract wouldn’t be likely to rid the city fully of ALPRs.
Asheville Police Department Lieutenant Josh Meindel said private entities like homeowners’ associations can also purchase Flock cameras that local law enforcement agencies wouldn’t have access to.
“There are a lot of people on social media who have misinformation about Flock and this technology,” he said. “Other states have different rules and different laws.”
Sheriff’s offices double down
Many counties and municipalities have adopted contracts with Flock, or other ALPR companies, without the approval of local governments.
“The sheriff asked for the funding, and the county manager signed the contract with Flock,” Mark Spencer Williams, an attorney who founded the Wilmington-area DeFlock ILM, said. “It’s just hard to believe that you could put a mass government surveillance system in place, monitoring a quarter of a million people based on a signature.”
Williams has sent demand letters for stonewalled records requests about Flock in other North Carolina counties. DeFlock ILM is an independent group, though it mirrors the national DeFlock organization, which has built an open-source database of ALPR technology across the country.
There are currently 12 Flock cameras in Madison County, according to records obtained by Carolina Public Press. There were initially 17 cameras, but in June, the sheriff’s office amended its contract with Flock to remove five of them, according to the amendment, which was also obtained by records requests. Flock costs Madison County $30,000, according to an April information release from the sheriff’s office.
The Madison County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to interview requests for Carolina Public Press.
The sheriff’s office only adopted Flock cameras this year, but has had a contract with the tech company Rekor Systems, which also supplies ALPRs, since 2021. Rekor does not provide physical cameras, but tracks vehicles by way of software that can be integrated with existing third-party cameras. Stanis said Madison for Privacy was already wary of Rekor cameras, but Flock poses a different challenge because of its network.
Stanis said Madison for Privacy requested records from the sheriff’s office, which were only partially fulfilled. When the group requested the county’s Flock contract, they only received the signature page. In response to a records request filed by Carolina Public Press, the sheriff’s office said Flock was the holder of some of the requested records, not the sheriff’s office.
Similarly, some Henderson County residents are aggravated by the use of Flock. But like in Madison, the sheriff’s office is standing firm, saying technology is crucial in solving crimes. After a popular petition circulated in Henderson County, the sheriff’s office doubled down on its support of the technology.
In a press release, Henderson County Sheriff Lowell Griffin referenced crimes in the county that were solved with the help of ALPRs. He also emphasized that Flock deletes data after 30 days unless it is involved in a criminal case.
“Our agency has maintained an ALPR policy for years, and the use of Flock is specifically addressed within that policy,” the statement read. “We are committed to ensuring technology is used responsibly, lawfully, and in a manner that protects both public safety and individual privacy.”
‘The range is stark’ 
While there does not look to be an end in sight to the use of surveillance technology and artificial intelligence tools by local authorities, privacy advocates like Williams want departments to be upfront about their contracts with Flock. To him, this means local governments that respond to records requests and allow public discussions about the technology at local meetings.
“Some municipalities and state entities have responded extremely quickly and been very transparent; others have not provided any information whatsoever,” Williams said. “The range is stark.”
Williams said he has found that most of the searches in the North Carolina network are done by law enforcement agencies in Texas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky and the federal government. Williams has sent demand letters to local governments, state agencies and UNC System schools. He sent one to the Madison County Sheriff’s Office on behalf of Madison for Privacy’s records requests.
Federal government agencies are stalling records in unforeseen precedent because of personnel cuts in privacy departments, according to recent reporting from ProPublica. In North Carolina, Chapter 132 of the General Statutes says agencies must respond to records requests as promptly as possible without unreasonable delay.
Last week was the ‘National Week of Action Against ALPRs’ for DeFlock, a group that has created a national database for Flock cameras across the country. Madison for Privacy held two social events called “Popsicles for Privacy” last week, which were intended to inform community members about the technology. Stanis said County Commissioner Alan Wyatt expressed interest in learning more about the technology.
“We, the people in Madison County, do not want Flock here,” Stanis said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Humanities takes over National History Day program
description: Indiana students will continue competing in National History Day under a new statewide sponsor after the Indiana Historical Society abruptly dropped the longstanding program in July. Indiana Humanities announced Thursday that it will become the state affiliate for the national academic program, which engages middle- and high-school students in historical res[...]
text:
National History Day students research historical topics and present their work through papers, performances, exhibits, documentaries or websites. (Courtesy photo)Indiana students will continue competing in National History Day under a new statewide sponsor after the Indiana Historical Society abruptly dropped the longstanding program in July.
Indiana Humanities announced Thursday that it will become the state affiliate for the national academic program, which engages middle- and high-school students in historical research and competitions.
The move comes about a month after the Indiana Historical Society terminated its sponsorship amid budget cuts and layoffs.
National History Day officials said at the time that they were searching for a new institutional partner to preserve the Indiana program, which serves more than 5,000 students each year.
“National History Day offers students essential life skills and experiences that will only benefit them in their future endeavors, and it was important to us to make sure that this opportunity remained available,” said Megan Telligman, director of programs at Indiana Humanities. “With experience facilitating conversations about history through the years, we feel well-positioned to take this on and are excited to connect with the students, teachers, and volunteers who really make NHD possible.”
Indiana Historical Society terminates history contest sponsorship

The Historical Society ended its sponsorship on the same day it laid off 11 employees from departments overseeing exhibits, education and library services.
The cuts followed a 2025 state budget deal that gave the Historical Society ownership of the land beneath its Indianapolis headquarters but ended approximately $1 million in annual state support for maintenance and operations. Historical Society officials denied that state funding cuts prompted the layoffs and withdrawal from National History Day, instead describing the moves as part of an organizational restructuring.
Indiana was the second state to join National History Day and has participated for nearly 50 years. The program now operates nationwide, engaging more than half a million students globally.
Participating students research historical subjects and present their findings as documentaries, exhibits, papers, performances or websites. Winners advance through local and regional competitions to state and national contests.
The program also provides teachers with curriculum materials, training and other support.
“We are grateful to partner with Indiana Humanities to ensure Indiana students and educators have continued access to the National History Day program in their state,” said National History Day Executive Director Cathy Gorn. “It is uplifting to see the Indiana historical community unite to support this cause. We are excited to continue the NHD program in Indiana and see how Indiana Humanities’ expertise will allow the program to grow and thrive across the state.”
Information about the 2026-27 contest season will be released as it becomes available.

title: Canada excludes seafood from tariffs, sparing Maine’s lobster industry
description: Canada reversed course on proposed seafood tariffs, easing concern for the impact on Maine’s lobster industry, which was facing a 25% import tax. “Keeping seafood tariff-free protects our shared supply chain and avoids unnecessary economic harm on both sides of the border,” said Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, in a[...]
text:
Researchers catch lobsters as part of long-term ecosystem survey in Maine. (Photo courtesy of GMRI.org)Canada reversed course on proposed seafood tariffs, easing concern for the impact on Maine’s lobster industry, which was facing a 25% import tax.
“Keeping seafood tariff-free protects our shared supply chain and avoids unnecessary economic harm on both sides of the border,” said Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, in a statement Thursday. 
The association raised concerns about the proposed tariff earlier in the week, and said it would have severely disrupted Maine’s lobster markets at the height of the fall fishing season, in an industry already operating on thin margins. 
“We appreciate Canada’s decision to listen to the concerns raised by the seafood industry and remove seafood from these tariffs,” McCarron said. “We urge both governments to continue protecting the longstanding tariff-free trade in lobster that benefits fishermen, businesses and coastal communities throughout North America.”
Late Wednesday, Canada’s Department of Finance announced the decision to remove seafood and fish products from the country’s list of counter tariffs. The agency said it is continually working with Canadian industries to assess the effectiveness of the tariffs, and made the change after receiving feedback. 
Experts warn future of Maine lobstering marked by increased risks, increased corporatization

In a statement, Canadian Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said it was a targeted adjustment to protect Canada’s economy.
“The fish and seafood sector drives Canada’s coastal economy,” Thompson said. “We will be there to protect Canadian harvesters, and all who rely on the fishery.”
In a statement Tuesday, independent U.S. Sen. Angus King said nearly half of Maine lobster goes to Canada in the fall for processing and that the trade war could “devastate” the industry in Maine. 
“Maine people are not interested in personal, retaliatory politics,” King said. “They are focused on the high cost of goods here at home. The majority party must listen to the industry leaders here in Maine, put pressure on the President, and move forward with an economic policy that works for us and not against us.”
The latest trade disputes with Canada come as the state faces several key elections in November, including a contentious U.S. Senate race for Republican incumbent Susan Collins. 
Democratic candidate Troy Jackson was quick to place the blame on Collins, writing on social media that she failed to stop President Donald Trump from restarting the trade war.
“As always she’s got concerns about what these broad new tariffs will do to Maine, but she’s got no action,” Jackson said. 
Pointing to her multiple votes against Trump’s tariffs, Collins told Maine Public Wednesday that she spoke with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer the day prior and urged him to return to negotiations, stressing the need to make sure the tariffs are removed. 
“This is not China we are dealing with,” Collins said during a brief interview after an event in Kenduskeag. “It is Canada, our best friend, a country with whom our economy is completely intertwined and with whom we have so many families that are linked as well.”

title: Trump has widened scope of anti-immigrant policy in second term
text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Treasury’s recent proposed regulation to limit refunds for certain tax credits based on immigration status is the latest move by the Trump administration to restrict noncitizens’ access to federal benefits.In President Donald Trump’s return to the White House, he has employed a governmentwide approach to fulfilling his immigration agenda that includes not only the central campaign promise of mass deportations, but curtailing what few federal benefits some immigrants had. Those actions include pushing out foreign-born workers from the trucking industry, barring noncitizens from accessing government-subsidized housing even for families that include U.S. citizens, and pressuring banks to restrict immigrants' access to opening accounts or borrowing money.Previous presidents generally restricted management of immigration to the departments of Homeland Security, State or Justice. But in Trump’s second term, several unrelated federal agencies have undertaken initiatives meant to disadvantage immigrants.“What's been unique about this administration is beginning to incorporate agencies that have never before been involved in immigration,” Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an analyst with the immigration think tank Migration Policy Institute, said.In Trump’s second term, the Department of Transportation, Department of Housing and Urban Development, Small Business Administration and Federal Communications Commission are among the agencies that have sought to carry out the president’s immigration crackdown.Administration officials have said the benefits of federal programs should be reserved for U.S. citizens.An executive order Trump signed in February 2025 to limit immigrants from receiving benefits, said it was necessary to “prevent taxpayer resources from acting as a magnet and fueling illegal immigration to the United States, and to ensure, to the maximum extent permitted by law, that no taxpayer-funded benefits go to unqualified aliens.”In an Aug. 26 statement to States Newsroom, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the “Trump Administration is putting Americans first.”“As promised, President Trump secured the border, cracked down on illegal immigration, and put Americans first,” Rogers said.Pace acceleratingTrump’s first administration was partially defined by its aggressive immigration policy, including visa restrictions, a travel ban from certain countries, a higher bar for asylum cases in immigration court, and forcing asylum seekers to remain in Mexico while their asylum cases were pending. But the rate at which the second Trump administration is pursuing immigration-related actions is far surpassing the first, according to an analysis from the Migration Policy Institute. In its first year, the administration took more than 500 immigration actions, including executive orders and regulations, compared to 472 actions in all four years of the first administration, according to MPI’s analysis.Welfare restrictionsFederal public benefits are generally denied to “not qualified” immigrants, under a welfare reform law enacted during the Clinton administration known as the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, or PRWORA.The law limits certain public benefits for individuals who do not meet a specific immigration status or eligibility requirements. Over the years, Congress has expanded certain immigrant categories and federal agencies have interpreted which programs are covered under PRWORA.But Trump reversed that trend.Last February, he signed an executive order directing federal agencies to review any programs that benefit immigrants and reverse any expansions. Following the order, the departments of Health and Human Services, Agriculture, Education, Labor, HUD and the IRS either rescinded notices that clarified eligibility or issued reinterpretations of PRWORA.HHS in July 2025 designated 13 additional programs, including the early-childhood Head Start program, that are subject to PRWORA qualifications. HUD in October restricted certain housing programs and grants based on immigration status. USDA now considers certain licenses, grants, payments and loan programs to fall under the law’s requirements.The Labor Department updated a policy that now forces noncitizens with temporary work authorization to go through reverification every three months in order to participate in a program to help access employment or education.And the Department of Education issued a notice that certain higher education programs, such as Pell grants, loans and workforce programs fall under “federal public benefits.” A preliminary injunction currently prevents the Trump administration's new interpretation of PRWORA from taking effect.The FCC, which is supposed to operate as an independent federal agency but has shown a deference to Trump during his second term, issued a proposed rule in April that would limit the Lifeline program, which provides a discount on phone services for low-income consumers, to U.S. citizens and immigrants with a “qualified” status. That group includes lawful permanent residents, refugees, people granted asylum, certain survivors of trafficking and victims of abuse. All other immigrants, including those with some form of legal status, are considered “not qualified.” Livelihoods at stakeWhile the second Trump administration has expanded efforts to limit benefits, it has also moved to restrict access to the workforce in a couple of policies.The SBA in March banned noncitizens from applying for small business loans. And the DOT issued a rule that limits the types of visas which can be used to obtain a Commercial Driver's License for foreign-born truck drivers while pushing for veterans to fill the void. That approach was novel, David Bier, the director of immigration studies of the libertarian think tank the Cato Institute, said.“There were certainly some benefits that they attempted to restrict more on the welfare side of things,” Bier said of the first Trump administration. “But I can't think of an instance where they attempted to try to use their regulatory authority to prevent people from being able to engage in certain occupations that they would otherwise be eligible for if they were authorized to work.”Restrictions in GOP megabillThe massive tax cuts and spending package that the Republican-controlled Congress passed last year also limits safety net programs for immigrants.The “big, beautiful” law restricted eligibility for immigrants in Medicaid, Medicare, the Children's Health Insurance Program, Affordable Care Act coverage, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.

 






Economic assistance application for SNAP, TANF and Medicaid through the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

The bill struck several categories of non-citizens who were previously eligible for SNAP, such as immigrants with longstanding humanitarian status like refugees, asylees, parolees and those with suspended deportation status. It also implemented tighter proof-of-citizenship or immigration verification requirements for Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, while also discouraging states from covering insurance for immigrants until that status is verified. The law also bars several other groups of immigrants from ACA subsidies. Immigrants with asylum or a pending claim, in the country on a humanitarian basis, who hold Temporary Protected Status or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals status, or who an immigration judge has deemed their home country too dangerous to return are ineligible, under the law.The Trump administration’s focus on limiting safety net programs to noncitizens has produced a chilling effect. An estimated one in ten adult immigrants stopped participating in government benefits for food, housing or healthcare because they were afraid to enroll in benefits they qualified for, according to a report from the Migration Policy Institute.

title: ICE agent Christian Castro, charged in Minneapolis shooting, released from Texas jail
description: Christian Castro, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis in January, was released from a Texas county jail early Thursday morning.  Castro has been the subject of a rare interstate extradition battle between Minnesota and Texas, as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign paperwork facilitating[...]
text:
Christian Castro's mugshot. (Cameron County Sheriff’s Department)Christian Castro, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis in January, was released from a Texas county jail early Thursday morning. 
Castro has been the subject of a rare interstate extradition battle between Minnesota and Texas, as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign paperwork facilitating Castro’s transfer to Minnesota, where he is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. 
U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas paved the way for Castro’s release in a Wednesday decision denying Minnesota’s request to force Abbott to facilitate the extradition, or at least keep Castro in custody until the matter is settled. 
Castro was arrested by the Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, on May 29. A Texas law prevents law enforcement agencies from holding fugitives with pending extradition requests for more than 90 days. 
Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño told the Reformer Castro was released at 6:59 a.m. Thursday.
Castro is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg. Castro accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison submitted affidavits to the court showing that Castro was in a romantic relationship with a woman in Mexico, and owns property there, presenting a possible flight risk. Cameron County, where Castro was jailed, is on the U.S.-Mexico border. 
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who charged Castro, said in a Wednesday press conference that the next steps in the legal process become much more complicated if Castro flees the country.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Four years after Tennessee “trigger law,” poll shows Tennesseans favor abortion ban exceptions
description: Tuesday marked the anniversary of Tennessee’s so-called “trigger ban,” the extreme anti-abortion legislation that went into effect in 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to an abortion through 1972’s Roe v. Wade.  Tennessee law makes abortion a felony except in circumstances where the life of the mother is in danger or […]
text:
Four years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to an abortion, polls show Tennesseans of all political stripes favor more exceptions to Tennessee's abortion ban. Photo taken of protests in Nashville on the June 2022 day of the Court's ruling. (Photo:John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tuesday marked the anniversary of Tennessee’s so-called “trigger ban,” the extreme anti-abortion legislation that went into effect in 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to an abortion through 1972’s Roe v. Wade. 
Tennessee law makes abortion a felony except in circumstances where the life of the mother is in danger or she faces serious bodily injury. That means no exceptions for rape, incest or the mental health of the mother and none for life-limiting fetal diagnosis. In other words, if your baby is sure to die, you are still barred from abortion.
Tennessee’s law is one of the most draconian in the country. Four years later, it seems reasonable to ask how Tennesseans are feeling about it.
In January of this year, the Tennessee Freedom Circle administered the first statewide poll measuring Tennesseans’ views on reproductive health policy since the end of Roe. 
We polled 600 likely 2026 general election voters, a population that closely mirrors the 2024 presidential vote in Tennessee, with 64% of respondents identifying as Republican and 73% identifying with the Make America Great Again movement. The most surprising revelation from that poll was how little the majority of Tennesseans actually know about abortion law in our state. 
Many of our respondents were astonished to learn that our abortion law has so few exceptions. Seventy two percent of them told us that they support exceptions for rape and incest and 71% support an exception when the fetus cannot live outside the womb. When we initially asked them how they felt about Tennessee’s abortion law, 49% said they supported it. Once they learned how restrictive it was, 55% opposed it. These statistics tell us that Tennesseans want common sense, not extremist, reproductive health policies. 
Tennesseans also understand that reproductive freedom is about more than abortion. Our respondents overwhelmingly support keeping in vitro fertilization, IVF, legal: 73% of voters, including majorities of Republicans and voters who identify as pro-life, believe IVF should remain legal. Two-thirds of voters oppose new restrictions on genetic testing that could threaten access to IVF. 
Four years after Tennessee enacted one of the most restrictive abortion laws in the nation, these polling results demonstrated that we don’t have to understand reproductive health care policy as a purely partisan issue. And our lawmakers are starting to understand that. 
Last year, the Tennessee General Assembly passed the Fertility and Contraception Protection Act that protects contraception and IVF, becoming the first state in the South to do so. This year, our legislators expanded access to contraception by passing legislation allowing patients covered by applicable health plans to obtain a 12-month supply of prescription contraception at one time. 
At the same time, Tennessee Freedom Circle and its partners worked to successfully oppose extreme proposals, including HB 1528, which would have expanded Tennessee’s wrongful death statute by redefining “person” to include an unborn child beginning at fertilization. Why were we successful? We think it’s because everyone — Democrats and Republicans — are realizing that Tennesseans want a more compassionate, medically grounded approach to reproductive healthcare than is represented by the extremist law triggered by the Dobbs decision. We may have learned a lot in four years.

title: Missouri power grid faces costly upgrades as AI data centers drive electricity demand
description: A new federal report shows the electric grid across much of the country is strained, requiring thousands of miles of new power lines and billions of dollars in investments. The National Transmission Needs Study shows that approximately 4,000 miles of powerlines will need to be replaced each year for the next few decades. The federal […]
text:
(Getty Images)A new federal report shows the electric grid across much of the country is strained, requiring thousands of miles of new power lines and billions of dollars in investments.
The National Transmission Needs Study shows that approximately 4,000 miles of powerlines will need to be replaced each year for the next few decades.
The federal report notes that most of the country’s transmission infrastructure was built in the 1960s and ’70s and is now reaching the end of its useful life and that currently, “operational challenges of the electric grid are evolving in complexity and magnitude.”
Threats from severe weather, increasing demand for electricity and additional wind and solar generation coming online all compound the need for new powerlines nationwide.
“Significant transmission investment is needed to cost-effectively meet future demand through 2050,” the report states.
The federal analysis points to projections that show U.S. electricity consumption rising 16% to 25% by 2034.
Increasing electricity demand is due in large part to the rapid development of data centers needed to support artificial intelligence technologies.
During a visit to Jefferson City on Monday, Department of Energy leaders said they believe operators of forthcoming AI data centers will pay their fair share.
Katie Jereza is the assistant secretary of the federal Department of Energy’s Office of Electricity. She pointed to President Donald Trump’s voluntary ratepayer protection pledge that’s been signed by tech companies, utilities and governors.
“The whole principle is that the data centers will pay for the infrastructure upgrades for their generation, not the families,” Jereza said.
Jereza said the federal government will soon announce funding for what’s called “reconductoring.”
“Which is basically … restringing the lines,” Jereza said. “So you’ve got old conductors, and now we’re going to put in new ones that can carry more electrons through from generation to delivery.”
As technology companies build AI data centers across the state, Missouri lawmakers have passed legislation with new consumer protections in an attempt to ensure the company’s large energy needs don’t increase residents’ utility bills.
“We feel like the transmission element is something that largely gets glossed over, but it’s a huge cost that ultimately is borne by ratepayers,” said Geoff Marke, chief economist with the Missouri Office of Public Counsel, the state’s consumer advocacy department.
He said he’s concerned the cost for the vast infrastructure upgrades needed will fall to the average energy consumers.
“If the proper cost allocation is not in place there, then yes, I do think residential customers will be exposed more than they otherwise would be,” Marke said.
The national study of powerlines comes as a group of nine electric transmission utilities, including Ameren and Evergy, are asking federal energy regulators for the right of first refusal to build and operate new multi-state, large-scale powerlines. The energy companies say pausing the competitive bidding process will speed up needed grid upgrades.
But Marke said competition reigns in overspending.
“Incumbent utilities have the vast majority of the transmission investment,” Marke said. “Opening that up to requests for proposals or just competitive bidding will just force everybody to be more professional and curb those costs.”
Jezera said whether competition brings the cost of new transmission lines down depends on a variety of factors, including location.
“There are parts of the country where it has worked really well. It has gone faster and reduced the cost, and then in other areas it hasn’t worked as well,” she said.
This story was originally produced by KBIA.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming school finance committee moves toward funding solutions
description:
Lawmakers continued work this week to address funding for Wyoming’s K-12 public education system after a judge ruled that the state failed to provide sufficient resources for key areas.
The post Wyoming school finance committee moves toward funding solutions appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CHEYENNE—State lawmakers continued work this week to address funding for Wyoming’s K-12 public education system, attempting to close shortfalls identified by courts in critical areas, including school safety, nutrition and technology.
The Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration heard testimony and public comment on how to tackle these issues.
In February 2025, Laramie County District Court Judge Peter Froelicher issued a 186-page order finding that the Wyoming Legislature had unconstitutionally underfunded public schools. The judge ruled that the state failed to provide sufficient resources for key areas, such as nutritional programs, school resource officers and technology.
The state appealed the decision to the Wyoming Supreme Court, which issued a stay pausing the lower court’s mandate while the state’s appeal proceeds. When the committee began its work, the stay had not yet been issued, and no final ruling has been made to date.
Co-Chair Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, expects the court to pay attention to the committee’s actions in the coming months.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the committee heard from consultants with Picus Odden and Associates, who presented proposals to ensure these programs are funded in compliance with the state Constitution.
School safety
The court order determined that “all Wyoming public school students are entitled to the benefit of SROs.” Not every school is required to have its own full-time school resource officer, but the order does require students to have access to SRO services.
Picus Odden estimated that 172.5 SRO positions are necessary to meet the requirements, at a cost of $15.8 million annually for personnel alone, and $17.1 million annually in total, including professional development, equipment and supplies.
The model, based on the recommendations provided by Picus Odden, proposed one SRO for each high school, one for every two middle schools and one for every three elementary schools.
During interviews, school district personnel emphasized how professional development allows SROs to work effectively and the necessary equipment allows them to perform their responsibilities.
Currently, school districts contract with local sheriff’s offices or police departments to provide SRO services.
Teton County Sheriff’s Office School Resource Officer Andrew Roundy lets Jackson Hole High School seniors back into school during the lunch hour in March 2018. As a resource officer, Roundy was present at the school whenever students were in the building, as well as during special local events. (Ryan Dorgan/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
Manny Fardella, a Cheyenne Police Department officer and president of the Wyoming School Resource Officers Association, spoke on behalf of SROs in the state and about his experience in Laramie County. He disagreed with the notion that SROs are simply there to be security.
“Our school resource officers are more than a security guard. We become part of a school family. To many, we become members, trusted people,” he said.
Jeremy Smith, the business manager for Sheridan District 1, spoke about making sure this funding would not be categorical, meaning that it could only be spent on SROs. Smith stressed that this funding could also be put toward additional district-specific safety needs.
The committee requested that a bill be drafted based on Picus Odden’s recommendations, but did not include professional development or equipment.
Food service programs
The court’s ruling determined that the school funding model not including a nutrition component was unconstitutional because “nutrition is an essential component of a quality education.”
To remedy this, Picus Odden’s proposed options would ensure all students have adequate access to food by covering the difference between food service revenues and expenditures. The consultant’s research estimated the difference during the 2024-25 school year was $17.8 million.
The first proposed option was to provide employee benefits such as health insurance and retirement contributions to food service staff, as they are currently excluded from both. This option would cover about $9 million in district food service costs.
This option would only cover about half of the current statewide difference and would provide limited or no support to districts that contract for food services, meaning it would have to be combined with another option.
The second option would reimburse districts a fixed percentage of food service expenditures; reimbursement rates vary from 10% to 30%. The state could set the rate to reflect the difference between revenues and expenditures statewide.
However, due to the difference varying widely by district, this approach would not cover the difference for 29 of the state’s 48 districts.
The combination of options one and two would leave shortfalls in 25 districts uncovered, according to Picus Odden.
Fort Washakie School second grader Dale Siers eats corn at lunchtime on Farm to School Day. The corn came from 1890 Farms in nearby Riverton. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
The final option would fund food services using the same general approach used to determine funding for other school resources. Under this approach, the Legislature would determine the variables used to calculate the appropriate level of funding. Under Picus Odden’s recommended assumptions, $17.1 million would be provided for food service worker staffing and $5.8 million to food service director staffing, for a total of $22.9 million.
Option three would leave 12 districts with shortfalls uncovered, Picus Odden officials said.
Public comment on the subject was divided, with some preferring the combination of options one and two, and others exclusively preferring option two because their districts contract for meals.
Brian Farmer, the executive director of the Wyoming School Boards Association, explained why there is no perfect fix for this issue.
“There is wide variability, and it’s really challenging because you can come up with something that works great for parts of the state but not necessarily others,” he said.
The committee unanimously requested a bill draft using option two, at a reimbursement rate of 30%, which equates to $17.5 million.
Technology
Judge Froelicher’s order also stated that a computer must be provided for every student, though there has been concern from local communities and parents regarding the amount of screen time students experience. Picus Odden took those concerns into account and provided eight different choices to address them.
The options ranged from the recommended 1:1 ratio for all grades to a 1:3 ratio for all grades and included options five and six, which provide no computers to students in kindergarten through second grade.
The recommendation from Picus Odden is a comprehensive estimate to provide computers at a 1:1 ratio for students and school staff at $208.95 per Average Daily Membership. Also known as ADM, this is the state’s way of calculating student enrollment. Additional operational costs for networks and learning management systems are estimated at $235 per ADM, for a total of $443.95 per ADM, leading to a $16.7 million total cost statewide. The options provided variability concerning the ratio and whether computers would be given to students in kindergarten through third grade.
Kalie Bocek, a senior at Tongue River High School, does school work on the computer. (Sheridan School District #1)
Sheridan County’s Smith noted how this funding could be best used for each district.
“I think having a tech director position in every district would help solidify how we actually operate in real life,” he said.
The committee agreed to request a bill draft with no computers for grades K-2, and a 1:1 ratio for grades 3-12, at a cost of $395 per ADM. State Sen. Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie, also asked that the bill draft include a minimum of one tech director and a part-time tech specialist for every district, based on testimony provided.
Next steps
The recalibration committee will meet Oct. 21 and 22 in Casper to continue discussions and make changes to the bill drafts as necessary.
Sen. Salazar expressed optimism about progress the committee had made, but acknowledged the primary task was ensuring compliance with the judge’s order.
“I think it’s important to go forward because I want to give the third branch of the government the understanding that we are trying to do the right thing in regard to the order,” he said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico psilocybin program opens permitting applications for psychedelic mushroom producers
description: New Mexico’s Medical Psilocybin Program recently opened up applications for producers of the psychedelic mushroom, marking a significant step toward the therapeutic program becoming fully operational.
text:
he New Mexico Department of Health Center for Medical Cannabis and Psilocybin on Aug. 17, 2026, began accepting applications from potential producers to grow mushrooms for the program. (Photo provided by Rudick Law Group)New Mexico’s Medical Psilocybin Program recently opened up applications for producers of the psychedelic mushroom, marking a significant step toward the therapeutic program becoming fully operational.
“We’re no longer talking about a piece of legislation and some rulemaking. This is real, this is happening and it’s being operationalized right now,” Santa Fe-based psychedelic attorney Victoria Cvitanovic told Source NM. 
The program was created last year with the signing of Senate Bill 219, which created the medical psilocybin program, an advisory board and legalized use of the psychedelic in controlled, therapeutic settings. Qualifying conditions currently include major treatment-resistant depression, post traumatic stress disorder, substance use disorders and end-of-life care. 
The New Mexico Department of Health Center for Medical Cannabis and Psilocybin began accepting applications last week from potential producers to grow the mushrooms for future program participants. Cvitanovic told Source that the application is intended to ensure the psilocybin “produced for this program in New Mexico is both safe and medically beneficial for patients, as well as that this doesn’t cause safety issues for people in New Mexico generally.”
According to the permit requirements, applicants must provide a state business license; proof of registration with the New Mexico Secretary of State and the Taxation and Revenue Department; facility safety documents; proof of ownership of the facility or a signed statement from the landowner; proof of compliance with city and county zoning requirements; and verification that psilocybin products will only be produced and tested in New Mexico.
“I think it’s notable that the application balances both the safety of the patients who will be receiving the end product and the safety of people who may live in areas of the state where someone is granted a license to produce psilocybin,” Cvitanovic said. “These applications are open to anyone, but they are fairly extensive because of the high stakes of producing a controlled substance, specifically for very limited medical use.”
She said she believes that most applicants will have an agricultural and entrepreneurial background, but likely only a small number of “highly qualified” applications will meet the requirements. A DOH spokesperson told Source NM in an email that there is currently no deadline for applications and that they will be reviewed in order of submission.
Cvitanovic said she recommends those considering applying to be a producer confer with a lawyer and accountant and get documentation together to submit the most complete and compliant application as possible. However, they should also consider whether their plans are operational if a permit is granted.
SB219 set a deadline of Dec. 31, 2027 for the psilocybin program to be implemented; however, the state committed to expediting the timeline by a year, aiming to open the program to its first patients by the end of 2026.
“The state is working really hard to operationalize this program as quickly as possible,” Cvitanovic said. “People are suffering and they want to address that suffering.”
She added that the program’s rulemaking process is not complete and more permit applications will open up down the line for testing and for qualified clinicians. A “buildout and inspection period” will also likely follow before treatment begins with patients. She encouraged people interested in participating in the program to speak with their behavioral health providers about becoming certified to facilitate the treatment.
“Programs like this are only as strong as the clinicians and therapists and other people who choose to participate in them. This is hard work, and it is not risk free, but it has the ability to change the lives of thousands of New Mexicans who are suffering,” Cvitanovic said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Federal agencies threaten to punish two Kansas school districts over gender-inclusive policies
description: LAWRENCE — The U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Education announced a plan for increased enforcement measures against two Kansas school districts for their gender-inclusive policies.  In April, the department found four public school districts — Olathe, Shawnee Mission, Topeka and Kansas City, Kansas — were in violation of federal Title IX civil[...]
text:
The Lyndon Baines Johnson Department of Education Building in Washington, D.C., stands on Nov. 25, 2024. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)LAWRENCE — The U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Education announced a plan for increased enforcement measures against two Kansas school districts for their gender-inclusive policies. 
In April, the department found four public school districts — Olathe, Shawnee Mission, Topeka and Kansas City, Kansas — were in violation of federal Title IX civil rights protections. Reasons included allowing students to change their name or pronouns used at school without clear communication to parents and allowing transgender students to use the restroom, locker room and changing room that aligns with their gender identity.
On Tuesday, the Education Department announced it would work alongside the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division to take “enforcement measures” against the Olathe and Shawnee Mission school districts for failing to comply with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, or FERPA.
The Education Department said that failure to comply could lead to legal action and potential loss of federal funding.
“These policies encourage schools to conceal from parents whether their child uses different pronouns and even permits schools to print a different name on students’ diplomas without parental knowledge or consent,” the release said. “Withholding such sensitive information from parents when they request their children’s records is a clear violation of FERPA.”
The Education Department issued letters Wednesday to local and state education agencies with reminders about FERPA guidelines as a new school year begins. A news release from the department said the reminder comes amid “rampant reports” of schools withholding records related to a child’s gender or gender transition from parents. 
The Education Department said it proposed resolution agreements with Olathe and Shawnee Mission school districts earlier this year, and that the Shawnee Mission district never agreed to a resolution. 
In a letter addressed to the Education Department’s Student Privacy Policy Office, the Shawnee Mission school district’s legal representation said the office’s findings did not violate FERPA. The letter also said the office’s findings ignored that the district requires proof of parental involvement in official student name change requests.
“Nothing about SMSD’s approach to student names, pronouns, or gender violates or even implicates FERPA,” the letter said. “SMSD has been and remains in compliance with FERPA.”
The Olathe district signed a “voluntary resolution agreement” in May outlining the district’s commitment to giving students access to gender-specific facilities “strictly on the basis of sex.” The agreement was rejected by the Education Department. 
The Olathe district has said throughout the department’s investigation there have been no Title IX or FERPA violations in its schools, and outlined district communication with the department as well as any legal correspondence on its website.
“The unfortunate continuation of this drawn-out political display continues to rob time and resources from the work that matters most as a public school system: educating our children,” said a district press release. “Olathe Public Schools will continue to defend the integrity of its people and practices, and remains committed to serving students, supporting families, and complying with all applicable federal and state laws.”
The Education Department announced Tuesday that its Student Privacy Policy Office entered a resolution agreement with the Topeka school district to uphold parental rights and come into compliance with federal law. 
The agreement’s guidelines include not creating gender support plans, allowing any gender support plans on file to be reviewed by parents, adding FERPA content into staff training and revoking any guidance that prevents schools from keeping parents informed about their students.
