name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Longtime Utah homeless cleanup nonprofit on brink of bankruptcy, issues ‘urgent’ call for help
description: Before Max Loveridge started working for Advantage Services about two years ago, he was homeless, living in and out of homeless shelters in Salt Lake City.  He said he first came to Utah from Wyoming after the restaurant and hotel he was working for went out of business. He was not only out of a […]
text:
Advantage Services employees Trevor Howell, Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) 


Key points

Advantage Services has been struggling financially due to unexpected operating cost increases, higher insurance premiums, and its largest contract, with Salt Lake City’s Urban Services Division, being cut roughly in half.
If emergency fundraising is unsuccessful, by October the nonprofit could fail to pay its 120 employees, who have experienced homelessness and other struggles.
Homeless service providers that rely on Advantage Services for cleanup, work on their properties, shuttle services and more fear what will happen if the company closes.




Before Max Loveridge started working for Advantage Services about two years ago, he was homeless, living in and out of homeless shelters in Salt Lake City. 
He said he first came to Utah from Wyoming after the restaurant and hotel he was working for went out of business. He was not only out of a job, but also a place to live. So to avoid freezing to death on Wyoming streets during its frigid winter, he moved to Utah — also in search of work so he could get back on his feet. 
After spending about six months homeless in Utah, Loveridge said he first heard about job opportunities with Advantage Services, a “social enterprise” nonprofit that goes out of its way to employ people who need it most.
Since it was formed more than 34 years ago in 1992, Advantage Services has employed people who are disadvantaged, whether they have disabilities, are currently or formerly homeless, leaving jail or prison, are refugees, or are living in poverty. 
The nonprofit doesn’t function like a typical employer, but rather provides “supportive employment,” offering job coaching, mentoring, and other resources to help meet employees’ needs so they can not only work, but thrive.
But that work is now under threat as the organization struggles financially, in large part due to a contract dispute with its biggest customer, Salt Lake City.
Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge and Trevor Howell, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Loveridge started out with the nonprofit as a part-time worker, picking up garbage around the Gail Miller Homeless Resource Center. Now he works 40 hours a week earning $10 an hour, fielding calls to help clean up trash, abandoned belongings, encampments or whatever else they come across day-to-day in between trips to the dump. 
Today, Loveridge is no longer homeless, renting a room from a family member. To him, Advantage Services has given him a second chance — in more ways than one. 
“They helped me get my (driver’s) license. I even wrecked one of their trucks, and I’m still working for them,” he said. 
That’s one example of how Advantage Services helps people on a better life path, Loveridge told Utah News Dispatch on Tuesday from the backseat of a pickup truck as he and two of his fellow crew members, Trevor Howell and Anothony Tarchick, headed to the dump to empty their trailer. 
“They’re highly acclaimed in the homeless community,” Loveridge said. “Everybody knows they’ll basically give anybody a chance. And if you do good work for them, they’ll keep giving you opportunities. … It means a chance of turning your life around, and an opportunity that’s there for people that don’t have opportunities anywhere else.” 
But like Loveridge’s past employer in Wyoming, Advantage Services is in financial trouble, threatening jobs for its about 120 employees that remain after the nonprofit was forced to layoff about 40 workers in November. 
Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick, Max Loveridge and Trevor Howell, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Also at risk are the services it provides, including operation of Salt Lake City’s Transitional Storage Program, which has more than 500 bins where people experiencing homelessness can store their belongings, as well as contracts to clean up state highways and provide shuttle services for homeless resource centers. 
The threat to Advantage Services comes during a time when state Republican leaders have put heavier emphasis on “accountability” within the state’s homeless system while embracing models that push people toward “self sufficiency.” 
Financial woes
Advantage Services has been struggling financially, its CEO Rob Ferris told Utah News Dispatch, due to unexpected operating cost increases, higher insurance premiums and scaled back contracts from various customers. One of the biggest reasons is a dispute over Advantage Services’ largest contract with Salt Lake City’s Urban Services Division that was slashed in half from roughly $2 million to less than $1 million. 
Ferris said he even personally took out a loan so he could lend $50,000 to Advantage Services so it could make payroll in June in hopes that the dispute over the Salt Lake City contract would be resolved. But that hasn’t happened, and money is running dry.
Now he’s worried there won’t be enough to pay employees in mid to late October. That could mean filing for bankruptcy or closing down Advantage Services altogether. 
Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge and Anthony Tarchick, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A camcorder is among abandoned property being cleaned up by Advantage Services employees in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employee Anthony Tarchick drops off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Trevor Howell, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Between now and then, if Ferris doesn’t find a way to expand Advantage Services’ contracts or merge with other nonprofits to preserve jobs, he’s worried the nonprofit’s remaining 120 employees will be out of work. 
“We want to diversify our business. We want to have more contracts that pay more so that we can keep working,” Ferris said. “In the short term, we have run out of cash flow, and the only thing that’s really going to be able to save us right now would be an emergency fundraiser where we can fill the coffers.”
This week, Advantage Services issued an “urgent call for community support” as it works to “prevent closure at the end of October.” As part of that effort, Advantage Services is fundraising — a new venture for the nonprofit, which has historically gained the vast majority of its revenue through contract work. 
“Advantage Services must raise $750,000 through an emergency fundraising campaign in September to offset its current operating loss and meet required insurance renewal payments due by December 1,” the nonprofit said in a news release. “Without immediate support, the organization’s ability to continue serving employees, customers and community partners is at serious risk.” 
In addition to the slashed Salt Lake City contract, insurance costs alone rose by about 250% this year, from $177,000 to more than $400,000, Ferris said, noting that’s another challenge that comes from “the population we hire.” 
“There are issues. Higher workers’ (compensation) claims, more automobile accidents,” he said, adding that their previous insurer declined to renew their policy, and “we had to enter into the high-risk market.” 
Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge, Anthony Tarchick and Trevor Howell, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Ferris, also a member of the Salt Lake Valley Coalition to End Homelessness, has made no secret of Advantage Services’ money woes while he’s been working to find a solution to preserve the nonprofit’s jobs. He and his team have been exploring opportunities for new contracts with other cities, service providers and other potential new customers. 
“However, immediate support is needed to stabilize operations and continue serving employees and the broader community through the end of the year,” Advantage Services said in its news release. 
Contract dispute with Salt Lake City 
Though funding for contracts with other partners have also been reduced due to budget constraints or reduced work, a major hit to Advantage Service’s roughly $3.5 million annual budget came from its halved contract with the Urban Services Division under Salt Lake City’s Public Service’s Department, Ferris said. 
He pointed to a long history with Salt Lake City, which since 2011 has partnered with Advantage Services for clean up services related to homelessness issues. Over the years, in response to requests from city leaders, Ferris said, Advantage Services has grown both its workforce and its equipment to provide a variety of different types of services, including pressure washing streets of urine, feces and other biohazards.
But after the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020 and the city started having more problems with homeless encampments, city leaders created the city’s own Rapid Intervention Team to help clean them up. Then last year — under pressure from Republican state leaders to crack down on drugs and camping — Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall created a “public safety plan” that, among many other measures, expanded that Rapid Intervention Team to more quickly respond. 
‘Fed up’: SLC mayor answers Utah leaders’ call for plan to ‘restore public safety’

Advantage Services’ contracts were also reorganized under the new Urban Services Division, created by the Salt Lake City Council last spring.
Ferris said even though city leaders previously approved about $2 million for Advantage Service’s contracts, the Urban Services Division “chose not to utilize all of our services” this year, and the division cut the nonprofit’s contract in favor of doing the work internally, now with a team called the Clean City Program. 
In response to an interview request seeking more information about why the division scaled back Advantage Services’ contract, the Public Services Department issued a prepared statement saying it was a decision to help save taxpayer money. 
“Being good stewards of taxpayers’ dollars is a core value of the Public Services Department. Every year, in a continued effort towards that goal and as an important part of the budget process the department analyzes its internal procedures, explores consolidating services and evaluates external contracts,” the department said. 
“Through this process, an internal solution was discovered that reduced external contract needs for cleaning up trash and debris in public spaces,” the department continued. “The Public Services Department proposed a restructuring of staff’s responsibilities from the external contract to that of a new division.”
The Urban Services Division’s Clean City team cleans up trash and debris in public spaces during their regular work hours, the department said, while also noting that requests for clean ups have gone down as part of city officials’ larger efforts to address homelessness issues. 
“Through the consolidation of teams and creation of the Urban Services Division, along with the concerted effort and investment from the city and the Salt Lake City Police Department to ensure impacts around homelessness are addressed promptly, has reduced the volume of clean-up requests,” the department said. 
Ferris, however, questioned whether the decision to hire more full-time city employees with benefits and purchase new vehicles and equipment for the team will actually save taxpayer money. He argued that Advantage Services already provides the same type of service at lower costs. 
Rob Ferris, CEO of Advantage Services, Inc., poses for a photograph at their facility in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employee Trevor Howell drops off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
He also said the decision to cut Advantage Services’ contract felt like a reversal of the city’s longstanding partnership and investment in the mission of the nonprofit, which he again noted expanded its workforce and fleet in order to respond to growing requests from Salt Lake City ever since they first started working together in 2011. 
“It ignores the history that we have where the mission was ideal to the City Council,” he said. “They loved the idea that we were hiring the homeless to clean up homeless areas … that they were playing a part in giving people back their lives.” 
Now what’s at stake, he said, “is the loss of a community partner that provides employment” to disadvantaged people, including people experiencing homelessness. 
“We are helping give them back their lives, and that’s a big investment the city has put into us over the years,” Ferris said. “And it’s not just the city, but our other community partners who rely on us for the shuttle program, for landscaping and janitorial, and giving the people that they serve employment as well. And so what could be lost is a cornerstone to the community that’s helping (those) most at risk.”
A ‘crucial’ part of Salt Lake’s homeless system
Homeless service providers including Shelter the Homeless, which owns six homeless resource centers in Salt Lake County, worry about what could happen if Advantage Services goes under. 
Ever since Shelter the Homeless’ resource centers opened seven years ago, they’ve contracted with Advantage Services for a variety of types work, including snow removal around shelters and van shuttle services to and from homeless resource centers for employment, healthcare, legal support and other needs, said Laurie Hopkins, executive director of Shelter the Homeless. 
Trevor Howell drives a truck to a cleanup site while working for Advantage Services in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“The (Advantage Services) employment model has been the main source of training and employment for many of our shelter clients exiting homelessness, offering jobs and resources to get people on their feet,” Hopkins said. “Those individuals are driving the shuttles, removing snow and keeping the areas around our facilities and in neighborhoods adjacent to our programs clean and garbage free.”
If Advantage Services were to go out of business, Shelter the Homeless would not only lose its shuttle drivers, but also the Salt Lake Valley’s homeless system would lose a key employer that has acted as a first step for many people needing a chance to build work experience. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I can’t emphasize enough how crucial they have been to our system,” Hopkins said, noting that many other Salt Lake County homeless providers have contracts with them. 
However, she said “the most crucial role they have played has been offering training and jobs” for the homeless population. 
“We have always valued them as a key community partner and it would be very challenging if they exited the system,” she said. “We encourage the community to support this organization.”
Back on the job, after taking a load of garbage to the dump, Loveridge contemplated what it would mean to not just him, but others if Advantage Services were to shut down.
“That would be horrible,” he said. “They’re deep rooted in the homeless community … it would change them overnight. It would immediately make the whole community a lot worse.” 
Tarchick, Loveridge’s co-worker, added, “the city would be a lot dirtier.” 
“You would see a lot more garbage all over the streets,” he said. “It would build up and build up, and nobody would pick it up.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Judge rules Strong Town’s Charles Marohn can legally call himself a professional engineer
description: Charles Marohn, founder of the urban planning advocacy organization Strong Towns, can legally call himself a “professional engineer” despite the objections of the state of Minnesota, a federal judge ruled. The ruling from earlier this month could be a decisive victory for Marohn, who’s been embroiled in a yearslong battle with the Minnesota Board of […]
text:
Charles Marohn (Photo courtesy of Strong Towns)Charles Marohn, founder of the urban planning advocacy organization Strong Towns, can legally call himself a “professional engineer” despite the objections of the state of Minnesota, a federal judge ruled.
The ruling from earlier this month could be a decisive victory for Marohn, who’s been embroiled in a yearslong battle with the Minnesota Board of Architecture, Engineering, Land Surveying, Landscape Architecture, Geoscience and Interior Design — known as AELSLAGID.
It may also set a precedent that restrains state boards from overzealously regulating the use of professional titles.
Marohn says he believes he was targeted because of Strong Towns’ sharp criticism of expensive, car-centric suburban sprawl, and the engineers who promote it.
“That this board has expanded their mandate to go after people for what they say, when that speech is not comfortable to other engineers, is just an abuse of power,” Marohn said.
Kate Van Etta-Olson, executive director of AELSLAGID, declined to comment on the case given pending litigation but signaled that the fight is not over. She said in an email that more would be shared publicly “as the matter moves forward.”
Marohn’s trouble with AELSLAGID began in 2020 after a fellow engineer reported him for calling himself a licensed professional engineer in his speaking engagements and published works after his state license had expired.
Professional engineers — like doctors and lawyers — must be licensed by the state to perform certain engineering work, which requires graduating from an accredited program, passing a state exam and completing professional training.
The state enforces these standards in the interest of public safety. Just like the person performing open heart surgery needs to understand human anatomy, the person designing bridges needs to be able to calculate load capacity.
Marohn, who was first licensed in Minnesota in 2000, says he accidentally let his license lapse in 2018 after missing a renewal notice. When he realized his mistake, he renewed it. A month later, in July 2020, the board told him he was under investigation because of the complaint.
By then, Marohn hadn’t been practicing engineering for years and was focused full-time on his advocacy with Strong Towns. He had written half a dozen books, traveled around the country promoting his vision of economically sustainable development and coined the term “stroad” — a multi-lane road design despised by many urbanists for being expensive for cities, inefficient for cars and unsafe for pedestrians.
He explained to the board that while he called himself a professional engineer in his talks and author biographies, he hadn’t solicited or performed any technical engineering work during the time his license was expired.
The board was unmoved and proposed a $1,500 fine and additional ethics education. Marohn initially tried to settle with them but said the members seemed hostile toward him and his work.
“All their questions were about my speech,” Marohn said. “They were not, ‘What plans did you sign? What projects did you work on?’ Because there were none.”
Over the next several years, Marohn fought the board in federal court, state court and before an administrative law judge.
He argued that the board only had the authority to regulate his use of the title for the purposes of engineering work. The board held that under state law anyone who holds themselves out as being able to perform professional engineering must have a license. They also accused him of lying on his license renewal application when he said he hadn’t represented himself as a professional engineer while unlicensed.
Marohn was unsuccessful, but after failing to overturn the board’s decision at the state Court of Appeals, he filed a lawsuit in federal court in 2023 asserting his First Amendment rights.
U.S. District Judge Nancy Brasel ruled in his favor on Aug. 19, finding the state overstepped its regulatory authority by policing his speech outside of the professional practice of engineering.
It is a bit of a hollow victory in that the court didn’t side with Marohn because of his substantial experience working as a professional engineer. Rather, the First Amendment guaranteed him the right to call himself a professional engineer even if it wasn’t true so long as he wasn’t practicing engineering.
The engineer who reported Marohn to the board in 2020, David Dixon, said in an interview he actually agrees with the court’s ruling affirming Marohn’s First Amendment rights.
His complaint centered on Marohn explicitly calling himself a licensed engineer to elevate his opinions and solicit paid speaking engagements. (State law doesn’t distinguish between the terms professional and licensed.) Dixon said he also didn’t know why Marohn’s license lapsed — believing it could be for misconduct — and felt he had an ethical obligation to report it to the board.
“My complaint wasn’t based on the substance of his talks,” Dixon said, adding he even agrees with some of Marohn’s ideas though he wouldn’t call himself a fan.
Marohn, who has moved his license into retirement status, said the entire ordeal has shattered his trust in the state to appropriately police professional titles.
“It never occurred to me that a state board would look at the advocacy I was doing and say, ‘We can regulate that,’” Marohn said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Why on Earth are so many data centers being built?
description: The topic of new ‘data centers’ is emerging as a major issue in the current election cycle, including most recently in the U.S. Senate campaign in Michigan. Many very legitimate concerns have been raised about the rush to construct these huge AI data centers, including environmental impacts from their enormous energy and water use; their […]
text:
Construction underway on Related Digital's hyperscale data center in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceThe topic of new ‘data centers’ is emerging as a major issue in the current election cycle, including most recently in the U.S. Senate campaign in Michigan.
Many very legitimate concerns have been raised about the rush to construct these huge AI data centers, including environmental impacts from their enormous energy and water use; their impact on raising utility costs; local noise pollution; and even the potential threat of AI displacing existing jobs.  My personal concern is especially based on the fact that their huge need for additional electricity generation could very well ruin our ability to reduce carbon emissions and avoid a climate crisis.
Each of those negative aspects have received at least some media coverage and public discussion.  But there is one other aspect of all this that I have not really seen publicly discussed, and that is: What is the actual business case for all these big new data centers?  Why are so many of these being pursued in such a rush?
These new data centers are enormously expensive.  Construction costs alone for a typical 100 MW data center would be in the neighborhood of $1 billion or more.  The cost of servers, networking gear, and the thousands of specialized AI chips can easily add another $2.5 billion to $4 billion or more.  At the high end, reported costs for the huge 1.4 GW data center recently approved for DTE in Michigan are estimated to be $7 billion.
Sign for Related Digital’s hyperscale data center, known as “The Barn”, in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance
In addition, the operating costs of a major data center are also enormous.  A typical 100 MW data center is estimated to use nearly 900 million kWh per year, which at typical electricity rates, would result in an annual operating cost of about $120 million.  Add to that a few more tens of millions of dollars for various other equipment maintenance and operating costs. Note, however, that the estimated costs for all staffing and human resources for the data center operation are relatively tiny (perhaps $5-10 million/yr.), indicating that these huge projects actually produce very few permanent jobs.
The bottom line is that these new large data centers are extremely expensive, which leads to this fundamental question: Why the heck is such an enormous amount of money being invested into this effort?
A common explanation is that there is a fierce competition between three tech giants (Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) to achieve dominance in this industry.  But that still leaves the crucial question of how does the winner intend to recoup that massive investment (not to mention, what happens to all those huge data centers built by the “losers”)?
More specifically: What are the projected products/services from these data centers that are expected to provide the revenue to cover those enormous costs?
If you Google the question: What products and services will these new data centers provide? … you frankly get a bunch of nebulous buzzwords like “cloud computing”; “artificial intelligence”; “high-performance computing”; and “edge services”.
Given the huge direct costs of these new data centers, not to mention the previously cited important social costs (e.g., energy use and costs, water use, noise, etc.), it would seem appropriate to ask a few more specific questions about the actual intended ‘business model’ for any proposed new data center.
What exactly are the intended products/services that will be sold to provide the revenue to pay the costs of this data center?  Will there really be enough demand for those products/services to pay all those enormous costs?
To what extent will this revenue be from new and unique products/services not currently being offered elsewhere, versus funds that previously went elsewhere to acquire products/services that will no longer be purchased there?  (e.g., one example of the latter might be that the data center would offer AI services that replace existing actual employees in the community)
It is certainly true that the tech bros at the top of the pyramid are making additional fortunes with this rush to build data centers.  There is a lot of circular financing (buying from and between themselves) among the tech titans, and certainly a stock market bubble.  But for the small investors at the bottom, one has to wonder whether this is a 21st Century ‘tulip mania’.  What is the fundamental driving business model behind all of this? Inquiring minds want to know.
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer stands alongside business leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (second from left) at a groundbreaking ceremony in Saline Township. June 1, 2026 | Photo courtesy of Colin Jackson/MPRN
We’ll leave aside for now the fact that this huge buildout of datacenter infrastructure would also be crucial to meeting the immense computing power needed for enabling the mass AI surveillance ambitions by tech giants like Palantir Technologies.  So some of the underlying motivation may go beyond just direct economic returns.  If it turns out that there is more to the motivation for these data centers than just economic return, then further action is urgently warranted.
The essential issue here is that before local communities (and indeed, we as a society) grant approval for construction of these huge new data centers…with all of their associated direct and societal costs… it should behoove us to learn more about what benefits we will be receiving in exchange.  At present, that seems to all be just the proverbial ‘black box’… being foisted upon us by the titans of tech.
There are over 2,000 new data centers planned or under construction nationally, with nearly 1,300 major facilities already in operation.  The costs for this are simply staggering, running into the trillions of dollars.  This has the potential to have profound impacts on our economy, and ultimately on how our society functions.
Given all of the above, there have been many efforts to put a moratorium on the approval of new data centers.  At the national level, we have the proposal by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez (D-New York) and others to create a moratorium, and there are numerous state and local efforts underway.  The National Conference on State Legislatures (NCSL) is tracking state efforts for moratoriums, which currently identifies 15 states working on the issue.  In Michigan, a statewide moratorium was proposed in the Legislature earlier this year (HB5594 and HB5596), and over 50 communities have adopted local moratoriums on new data centers.
The consequences of continuing on the current path of massive and unfettered development of these huge data centers could be tragic…for the environment, the economy, and perhaps our personal liberty.  It would seem indeed prudent to support efforts to put a moratorium on the approval of new data centers until some of these essential questions can be explored and satisfactorily answered.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA Republican Party leader sued for defamation by citizen activist
description: Arthur West is a prolific filer of legal complaints in pursuit of greater government transparency and a fairer political system in Washington.  Typically, he represents himself and targets the structures of power and their occupants. But Tuesday, the open government activist turned his attention to Jim Walsh, suing the state lawmaker and chair of the […]
text:
Washington State Republican Party Chairman Jim Walsh announces initial results of the presidential race at a GOP election night watch party in Bellevue, Wash. Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Washington State Standard)
Arthur West is a prolific filer of legal complaints in pursuit of greater government transparency and a fairer political system in Washington. 
Typically, he represents himself and targets the structures of power and their occupants.
But Tuesday, the open government activist turned his attention to Jim Walsh, suing the state lawmaker and chair of the Washington State Republican Party for defaming him in social media posts after West’s recent setback in Thurston County Superior Court. 
On Aug. 7, Superior Court Judge Chris Lanese denied West’s request to amend or remove a statement set to appear on ballots describing the budgetary consequences of an initiative to repeal Washington’s new income tax on high earners. 
Lanese’s ruling led to the cancellation of a separate legal challenge over the wording backed by the Republican Party that was scheduled for later that day.
In the wake of the decision, Walsh took to Facebook, where he lambasted Lanese and insisted West was “tricked” into making “procedural errors” that killed the other case against the public investment impact disclosure for Initiative 645, according to West’s complaint.
Those assertions were repeated in a similarly toned post on the state Republican Party’s Facebook page under the headline of “Call to Action” that urged “concerned voters” to file a complaint against Lanese. 
West, in his lawsuit, said that second post “repeated and amplified” false claims made by Walsh and added a new “false factual assertion — that Judge Lanese ‘set a trap’ for West that ‘tricked’ West into stating he was also representing Let’s Go Washington’s case — which he was not.’”
Let’s Go Washington is the sponsor of the income tax initiative and it was the political committee’s challenge of the disclosure statement content that was canceled.
“These statements are false statements of fact, not opinion or rhetorical hyperbole. West did not in any way state, represent, or imply to the court that he represented Let’s Go Washington’s case, and was not ‘tricked’ into doing so,” West wrote in his complaint.
West, on Aug. 21, sent Walsh an email demanding a “correction, clarification, or a clear ringing retraction and apology.” None came. 
But the posts disappeared, West said.
Walsh, in a text exchange, said the “call to action” was about Lanese and “had nothing to do with Arthur West.” It came down because it was “time sensitive,” he said.
“West was not defamed by me over his unsuccessful arguments in Lanese’s court during the hearing,” Walsh said Tuesday.
While there is no longer a post on his personal Facebook page, Walsh’s X account has an Aug. 8 post decrying Lanese as a “terrible judge” who “set a trap for a gullible nonlawyer.”
West, in his lawsuit, is seeking punitive damages and an “unambiguous retraction and correction of the defamatory statements” from Walsh and the party. 
The lawsuit, known as West v. Walsh, was assigned to Lanese.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri lawmakers press child welfare leaders on foster care deaths, staff turnover
description: A bipartisan group of Missouri lawmakers pressed Children’s Division Director Sara Smith on Wednesday to explain how the agency ensures children with elevated medical or behavioral needs get appropriate foster placements. The questions came after what state Sen. Mary Elizabeth Coleman, an Arnold Republican and chair of the legislature’s Joint Committee on Go[...]
text:
Teddy Papadopoulos, father of Korbin Papadopoulos, wipes his eyes Wednesday after finishing prepared testimony about the death of his son while in the care of the Missouri Childrens Division (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).A bipartisan group of Missouri lawmakers pressed Children’s Division Director Sara Smith on Wednesday to explain how the agency ensures children with elevated medical or behavioral needs get appropriate foster placements.
The questions came after what state Sen. Mary Elizabeth Coleman, an Arnold Republican and chair of the legislature’s Joint Committee on Government Accountability who called the hearing, described as “a number of fatalities” this summer involving children in the agency’s care. 
Among them was Korbin Papadopoulos, a 17-year-old with type 1 diabetes and autism who died June 6 after Macon County division workers placed him nearly 300 miles away in southwest Missouri. 
Police records reviewed by The Independent show the foster parent was licensed only to care for relatives and later told law enforcement he had not been trained to manage diabetes. An autopsy listed Korbin’s cause of death as diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening buildup of toxins in the blood caused by uncontrolled diabetes. 
Korbin’s father, Teddy Papadopoulos, told lawmakers on Wednesday that his son’s death was the result of failures by the division.
“Our family had to bury our son,” he said, “because of negligence on Children’s Division’s part.”
Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican representing the district where Korbin’s parents live, asked about the agency’s procedures to keep kids safe “when an appropriate placement can’t be found.”
Smith said that “it’s all hands on deck” when a child with elevated medical or behavioral needs must be placed on an emergency basis.
“Everybody needs to be helping to look to find a placement for this child,” Smith said. “Whichever child it is, it is something that (the division’s) central office needs to be involved in. It’s something that our regional leadership needs to be involved in.”
Missouri Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin questions Missouri Children’s Division leaders on Wednesday about the safety of children placed in the foster care system. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
When there is no appropriate placement, Smith told the committee, standard practice is for division workers to stay with kids in hotels because “at the end of the day, Children’s Division is who is charged with keeping that child.”
But state Rep. Ian Mackey, a St. Louis Democrat serving on the committee, said Smith’s description raised questions about whether anyone has clear responsibility for making sure a high-needs child ends up somewhere safe. 
Smith described a centralized residential screening team and regional “level of need specialists” who help find placements. But she also described staff at multiple levels of the department joining the search.
“You said it’s a centralized system, and then you described an all-hands-on-deck approach, which is actually the opposite of a centralized system,” Mackey said. “Having anybody and everybody who’s got their fingerprints on the case or who works at any level of the department ultimately being responsible for finding qualified placements or specialized placement is an incredibly chaotic and unsustainable system.”
  Assessing safety and risk

The scrutiny comes as the division prepares to restructure the teams that investigate allegations of child abuse and neglect, placing workers under more centralized state supervision and creating specialized career pathways. 
Less than 24 hours before Wednesday’s hearing, Gov. Mike Kehoe signed an executive order establishing a child welfare task force to develop “unified standards of safety” for shared use by division staff, juvenile offices, courts and private contractors.
Coleman, who told The Independent she did not learn of the executive order before it was issued, said the governor’s action was a reaction to the legislature’s decision to hold a hearing. 
State Sen. Mary Elizabeth Coleman, center, opens Wednesday’s hearing into issues at the Missouri Childrens Division. Also shown, from left, are state Reps. Wendy Hausman and Melissa Schmidt, and Karen Roach, legislative aide to Coleman (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
Smith said the push for greater consistency grew partly out of an “internal assessment” conducted over the past year through meetings with division staff, courts, juvenile officers, law enforcement and community members across the state.  
This assessment, Smith said, uncovered instances in which division workers did not respond to hotline reports of potential abuse or neglect before law enforcement became involved, did not refer alleged victims of abuse to child advocacy centers and refused to cooperate with juvenile officers.
“This indicated to our leadership team that our workforce did not understand how to assess safety and risk,” Smith said.
After the restructuring goes into effect, workers will report to regional leaders of teams with specialities such as newborn assessments and sexual abuse allegations, instead of local supervisors who oversee all assessments and investigations within a smaller area.
But frontline workers told The Independent in recent months that new requirements and prescriptive policies introduced in the past year and a half have limited their discretion to help children and families and made it harder to close cases. 
Ashley Allen, an investigator who quit the division in April, said those additional demands can have consequences at both ends of the system — delaying responses to children who may be in danger while prolonging investigations involving families whose children are safe.
“You’ve got kids to see that may or may not be unsafe, but you don’t get around to seeing them because of all the other things that you have to do, and it puts some families on the backburner,” Allen told The Independent. “And there are kids that are safe where we’re pestering their families.”
Smith said the restructuring is also intended to reduce turnover among workers who investigate reports of potential child abuse or neglect. 
Current turnover among the division’s frontline workers is about 40%, Smith said. Turnover reached 55% in fiscal year 2022, after then-Gov. Mike Parson cut almost 100 jobs in the division in 2020, citing COVID-19 budget constraints. 
While it’s an improvement, Smith said, the current turnover rate still means that the division lost more than a third of its frontline staff in a year.
In a January email to The Independent, the Department of Social Services, which oversees the Children’s Division, described the creation of specialized teams as a way to build up a more tenured workforce and maximize “efficiency within currently allocated funding levels.”
The division has already expanded a specialized team serving older foster youth and launched a critical investigations unit in January focused on child fatalities and near-fatalities related to alleged abuse or neglect. Smith said those two teams have had no turnover so far.
“One of the clearest lessons was that we cannot continue asking frontline team members to be experts in everything,” Smith said. “That’s just not sustainable.”
Lawmakers had mixed reactions to the restructuring and Kehoe’s announced task force. 
State Rep. Raychel Proudie, a Democrat from St. Louis, cautioned against attempting to write a rigid definition of child safety into state law. 
“The mission is to include keeping kids safe, and we can have a conversation on what that means in particular,” Proudie said. “But obviously free from harm, injury or death seems pretty standard. That seems like a good framework on which to start.”
State Rep. Melissa Schmidt, a Republican from Eldridge, asked for “uniformity of practices across the state, rather than some decisions being made county by county,” which she said could include “the definition of safe practices.”
  ‘Somewhere the buck has to stop’ 

Police records reviewed by The Independent show Macon County workers did not verify that the foster parent who agreed to take Korbin was licensed to care for him. And when workers realized six days after dropping Korbin off in southwest Missouri that they had mistakenly placed him with a foster parent who was only licensed to care for his relatives, they didn’t send someone to pick him up.
One worker involved in Korbin’s placement told police that a circuit manager was part of discussions about whether workers needed to bring the teen back to Macon County. The supervisor said workers had been calling emergency residentials, foster homes and therapeutic foster homes but could not find an appropriate placement for him.
The day Korbin died, according to police records, the supervisor tried to arrange immediate transportation of the teen back to the Macon County division office. 
When no one was available, the supervisor told an on-call worker to drive to southwest Missouri and bring Korbin back to the office. But the worker said the foster parent had agreed to keep Korbin in his care for a few more days, until Monday. 
Korbin died that day.
Jessica Bax, director of the Missouri Department of Social Services, testifies Wednesday to the Joint Committee on Government Accountability about issues within the Missouri Childrens Division. Bax is joined by Sara Smith, director of the Children’s Division (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
Mackey said cases involving children with significant medical or behavioral needs should have a clear line of authority at the state level. 
“I think you want it to be centralized,” Mackey said. “But it sounds like right now it absolutely is not.”
O’Laughlin said the system Smith described left her unsure who ultimately bears responsibility for making sure a child is placed safely.
“If that many people get notified when you’re having a problem placing someone,” she added, “somewhere the buck has to stop.”
When Coleman asked Smith how many children had died while in foster care since she became director in March 2025, Smith said she didn’t have that number but would find out.
Papadopoulos, who told lawmakers he testified “for Korbin and every other kid in foster care now and in the future,” told The Independent time will tell whether the hearing was worthwhile.
“The long term will determine how I feel about today,” Papadopoulos said. “If nothing gets done at all, nothing changes, no policies or no change, nothing at all, then it’s just a waste of time. I’m here to hopefully change something for somebody, to help somebody — between protocols that are in place that weren’t necessarily followed and protocols that should be in place.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: How the car used in the slayings of two MSU students wound up in a deputy’s hands
description: A Toyota MR2 that belonged to Tiffany Miller at the time of her murder in 1992 now belongs to George Carrithers, a retired Oktibbeha County chief deputy sheriff, in Starkville, Miss., on Monday, July 20, 2026.
text:
STARKVILLE — During Mississippi Today’s investigation into the case against death row inmate Willie Manning, reporters interviewed retired Oktibbeha County Sheriff Dolph Bryan.
The former sheriff investigated the 1992 killings of Jon Steckler and Tiffany Miller. He believes Manning, convicted in 1994 in the murders, took the couple in her two-seat Toyota MR2 from a fraternity house at Mississippi State University to the site where he killed them.
Bryan mentioned that the 1986 MR2 was now in the possession of retired Chief Deputy Sheriff George Carrithers, who investigated the murders with the sheriff.
Carrithers told Mississippi Today that Manning deserves to die for what he did. “I don’t know why Mississippi waits so long,” he said in a July interview. “The family doesn’t see any justice out of the system at all.”
He said when the 1986 Toyota MR2 arrived at the sheriff’s office, deputies opened all the doors, built a tent over it and “put Super Glue in” to develop any fingerprints. They also removed the steering wheel and windshield to test for fingerprints.
Deputies found dozens of fingerprints. Sixteen of them belonged to Steckler and Miller. None belonged to Manning, who was sentenced to death for the killings.
Carrithers said he had to clean under the car with a power washer because the killer used the MR2 to run over Steckler.
After the students’ slayings, an insurance inspector showed up every month, wanting to look at the car, which the sheriff’s office had custody of, Carrithers said.
“Hell, you just looked at it last month,” he said he told the inspector.
“Yeah, but I gotta look at it every month,” he said the man replied.
That continued for some time until Carrithers tired of the interruptions. The next time the inspector came in, he said he told the inspector, “Look, to keep you from bothering me, what the hell will you take for that damn car?”
“I don’t know. What will you give me?” he said the inspector asked.
“I’ll give you $300 for it just to get you to where you ain’t gonna bother me,” Carrithers said he replied.
“That’s too cheap,” the inspector replied. “I can’t do that.” 
“Well, what do you want me to do?”
“You give me six.” 
He wrote the inspector a $600 check, he said. “The only reason the insurance company totaled it was because it was going to have to have a new interior.”
It’s impossible to get instant glue out of fabric, he said, “but you can get it off the plastic and vinyl.”
The MR2 sat on the sheriff’s lot for two years after Manning’s trial. When Carithers finally took it home, he replaced the windshield, upholstery, carpet and headliner. He also cleaned it inside and out.
He said his daughter drove the car until she graduated from high school and got her own car, and his grandson drives it now.
He sold the car to a man at one point for $2,500, only to have him call back. The man said he told his wife about the car’s history, and she told him, “You get rid of that damn thing.”
The man insisted on giving him back the car for free, but Carrithers refused and paid $2,000. “I made 500 bucks out of it,” he said.
At one point, Miller’s mother visited the sheriff’s office. “She came into my office and told me she was glad I got it,” Carithers said. “She was proud that it was going somewhere where it meant something.”
When showing the car to Mississippi Today journalists, Carrithers opened the trunk and pointed to smudges on the inside of the lid. “This black stuff you see here? That’s all the fingerprint powder we put on there to dust,” he said. “Of course, this thing had prints all over it.”
He pointed at the sportscar’s small interior, “Can you believe three people got in this thing?”


Claudia Amendoeira is at Mississippi Today on a fellowship from the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism. This story was published with the support of a grant from Columbia University’s Ira A. Lipman Center for Journalism and Civil and Human Rights, in conjunction with Arnold Ventures.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Gov. Sam Ford built a big tent. Current Republicans are building a small table.
description: Montana Republican Party Chairman Art Wittich created a purity test for the GOP. It’s like seventh grade all over. It was horrible the first time. Wittich’s redux isn’t any better. Think of it as a chastity ring for Republican politicians. Sit with a Democrat at lunch, and you are out of the club. Gone. Talk […]
text:
A campaign poster for Sam Ford, a Republican, who served as Montana Governor from 1941 through 1949. (Photo courtesy of the Montana Historical Society Archives; used with permission)Montana Republican Party Chairman Art Wittich created a purity test for the GOP.
It’s like seventh grade all over.
It was horrible the first time. Wittich’s redux isn’t any better.
Think of it as a chastity ring for Republican politicians.
Sit with a Democrat at lunch, and you are out of the club. Gone.
Talk to a Democrat. Agree with one. Ruined for life. You lose your “Republican” pin.
Meet the adolescent purity police.
Wittich’s theology is toxic.  If you aren’t at his table,  you are the problem.  Evil incarnate. A threat to America.  A woke, liberal extremist. Supersized hate.
It is seventh-grade politics. What’s missing?  Adult supervision.
These are small-tent Republicans. Small thinking. They can’t see or think beyond their lunch trays.
It’s not about Montana. Or governance. It’s about power, ego, vanity.  You know, all seventh-grade stuff.
Wittich is no role model, but we have many in our history.
Remember our Constitutional Convention. 100 delegates. They realized that drafting a new constitution was too important for juvenile politics.They voted to sit in alphabetical order. Not by party. Smart. Refreshing. A lesson for our Legislature —  delegates who valued compromise and coalitions.
Sam C. Ford, Montana’s Republican Governor from 1941 to 1949.  The war years.  Before that, he was Attorney General and a Supreme Court Justice. He built coalitions. He was a big-tent Republican. He believed in a really big tent,  big enough to hold people who disagreed.  He was also my grandfather.
His youngest daughter married a Democrat and a member of the United Mine Workers Union.  His son-in-law, Ted James, became a Republican, but remained a proud union member.
The Republican tent had enough room then for a union member, former coal miner, and former Democrat.  James served two terms as a Republican County Attorney in Cascade County and as Lieutenant Governor from 1964-1968.  He was also my father.
Wittich’s “purity” pledge is in sharp contrast to Gov. Ford’s Big Tent.
Ford was close friends with U.S. Sen. Burton K. Wheeler.
“BK,” to his friends, “Bolshevik Burt,” to his enemies,  he served nearly 24 years in the U.S. Senate.  He was a Vice Presidential candidate in 1924.
Wheeler was liberal and, like Montana, independent. He inspired a movie, “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington.”  Watch it.  You will be inspired.
When Franklin Delano Roosevelt tried to pack the Supreme Court, Wheeler stopped him.
Pause for a minute. A liberal Democrat stopped a liberal Democratic President from expanding the Supreme Court. Wheeler opposed his party and his President. Wow!
Today, Sens. Steve Daines and Tim Sheehy won’t even speak truth to Trump’s lies. I can’t imagine them ever opposing Trump or their party.  It hasn’t happened. It won’t happen. They are rubber stamps.  Lapdogs.
These Senators wear the title, but don’t do the work.
Wheeler did the work.
Despite different politics, Ford and Wheeler respected each other.  They actually liked each other.  They shared meals together with their wives.  They wrote personal letters.
They were real friends.
Imagine:  A Republican and a Democrat. They disagreed. They argued. They remained close friends. When Ford ran for reelection, Wheeler supported him over a Democrat.  Really:  A Democratic senator supported a Republican governor’s reelection.
Politics then wasn’t tribal. It was intellectual.
As Governor, Ford appointed Wheeler team members to important government positions.  The test was not one of political ideology, but effective and responsible governance.
It was who could best do the job, not who will always agree with me.  That is a radical concept for today.
Wittich’s “chastity” pledge is different.
No deals with Democrats. Don’t talk to Democrats. Don’t vote with Democrats.
Wittich’s pledge doesn’t make anyone conservative. There is nothing conservative about being obdurate. It is just tribalism enshrined as middle-school cafeteria rules. And it is destructive. It’s hatred wearing a cowboy hat.
Many of my friends and family are Republicans. I agree with them about 95% of the time.  I respect them. I want them at my table, not because they agree with me.  They don’t always.  That is the point:  I learn things from people who disagree with me.  Sometimes, I learn that they are right.
What makes Wittich’s purity pledge insanely dangerous?  Republicans want judges to wear team colors and pick a table. Red or blue.  They want to expand their partisan brand to our courts.  No more independent justice.  Imagine a judge who rules against the Wittich clan.  That judge will be banned. Shunned.  They will take away their “Republican” pin.
Adolescent lunchroom politics has no place in our courts.  We expect our judges to be impartial, to decide cases based upon facts and the law, not based upon a political party’s agenda or purity pledge.
Wittich’s political party purity rules have no place in our justice system.  Let’s keep politics out of our courts and out of our judicial races.

name: WyoFile
title: How did data center skepticism impact elections in southeastern Wyoming?
description:
In Wyoming hot spot for data center development, many candidates who touted tough positions against the boom fell to those with more moderate positions.
The post How did data center skepticism impact elections in southeastern Wyoming? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A growing concern throughout the state, proliferating AI computing and data center development is especially prominent in and around Cheyenne. Whether to accommodate or heavily regulate — even place a moratorium — on what some estimate could be 40 to 70 new facilities in the southeast region of the state was a prominent campaign issue in the lead-up to last week’s primary election.
Granted, there are multiple reasons candidates win or lose elections, but the results suggest that anti-data center positions did not win the day.
None of the top two vote-getters in each of three city council seats up for grabs were expressly against data center development, according to WyoFile’s analysis, while several candidates who favored a moratorium — including Travis French and J.C. Manalo — fell short of the votes needed to advance to the general election in November.
In a field of 10 GOP candidates vying for three open seats on the Laramie County Board of Commissioners, incumbents Troy Thompson and Gunnar Malm, and challenger Jess Ketcham, advanced to the general election to face two Democratic candidates. None of the GOP finalists were seen as anti-data center development. Moses Hasenauer, a candidate adamantly opposed to data centers, got the fifth-most votes — not enough to advance.
People vote on new voting machines during the 2026 Wyoming primary elections on Tuesday, Aug. 18, at the Cheyenne Kiwanis Community Center. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
Among legislative races in the region, Cheyenne Republican Rep. Steve Johnson (House District 8), Cheyenne Republican Rep. Gary Brown (House District 41), Cheyenne Republican Rep. Ann Lucas (House District 43) and Cheyenne Republican Rep. Daniel Singh (House District 61) all lost their bids for the GOP nomination. All were either opposed to or in favor of tighter regulations for data centers. 
“You could certainly make an argument that being opposed to data centers was not a winning position,” Cheyenne Councilman Larry Wolfe, who is not seeking reelection, told WyoFile. Although every campaign and every race was full of nuance beyond being for, against or somewhere in between on data centers, he added, “I can’t point to any of the races where being opposed to data centers was a productive view.”
Zooming out to statewide and congressional primary results, the picture becomes less clear. 
Gubernatorial candidates Brent Bein, who promised to place a moratorium on data centers, and Reid Rasner, who upped the ante with a 5-year moratorium, lost their bids for the GOP nomination. Conversely, Secretary of State Chuck Gray, who railed against AI and data centers during his bid for Wyoming’s lone U.S. House seat, won in the crowded GOP race.
Jacob Trujillo votes during the 2026 Wyoming primary elections on Tuesday, Aug. 18, at the Cheyenne Kiwanis Community Center. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
Beyond data centers, hot-button industrial developments like wind farms and nuclear energy manufacturing were also a big part of the primary campaign discussion in certain regions of the state. Midwest Republican Rep. Bill Allemand, for example, narrowly defeated challenger Peter Boyer for the GOP nomination in House District 58. The two spent the past year clashing over Radiant Industries’ plan to build a nuclear microreactor manufacturing facility outside Bar Nunn, which Allemand adamantly opposed.
And despite fueling community contention throughout central- and southeast Wyoming for years, there was precious little indication of how wind development might have tipped the scales in primary races, according to Cheyenne-area resident Wendy Volk, who has advocated for more intentional planning and oversight over the industry.
“It produced some mixed signals,” she told WyoFile. “I think, depending on the community, the results just showed that voters might be willing to support essential public infrastructure, but they’re starting to be more skeptical about government spending priorities and whether development is moving faster than our public planning.”
There’s certainly a message from voters — not just in southeast Wyoming — to be read in the primary election results, said Betsey Hale, CEO of the economic development group Cheyenne LEADS.
A data center in Casper, June 2025. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Not only did anti-data center campaigns not win the day, but voters passed tax initiatives to support local infrastructure and services, including a 0.75% optional sales tax in Fremont County. In Laramie County, voters approved 13 of 14 “sixth-penny” sales and use tax initiatives.
“I think it’s a broader picture. I think it’s actually [pro-] economic development,” Hale said. “I don’t think the outcomes of the primary were solely focused on wind or solar or data centers — some of the hot issues. I think it was fundamentally, in Wyoming, ‘Are we open for business? And if we are, how are we going to do that?'”
Data center, and industrial development sentiment
Attitudes toward AI computing and data center buildout in the U.S. — along with its perceived associations with negative human health and natural resource implications, replacing jobs, spiking electric rates and enabling surveillance — are increasingly sour. Seventy percent of Americans oppose data centers in their communities, a Gallup poll published in May suggests. Only 7% were strongly in favor.
An Annenberg Public Policy Center report published this month suggests opposition is quickly growing.
Though he wouldn’t speculate on what primary election results in Wyoming might say about how voters here feel about data centers, Jacob Hochard said it’s likely less rooted in political ideology and more about whether they can trust there will be tangible protections and benefits in their communities.
“I can’t point to any of the races where being opposed to data centers was a productive view.”Larry Wolfe, Cheyenne City Council
That comes down to whether communities can assure robust regulatory sideboards and negotiate for significant company investments in local resources — investments that meet specific needs beyond promised job numbers and built-in tax revenue, said Hochard, the Knobloch Associate Professor of Conservation Economics at the University of Wyoming.
“I think there are a lot of small towns in America that were a little starstruck by, you know, one of the top-seven largest companies in the world knocking on their door and saying, ‘We’d like to invest $10 billion, $50 billion in your community,'” he told WyoFile.
Hochard recently co-authored an article in Issues in Science and Technology examining public attitudes toward the industry and suggesting public policy approaches that communities might use to respond.
Instead of responding with intuitive offers like, “How do we make this happen?,” and, “What incentives do you need?,” he said, the smarter approach that’s likely to gain more buy-in from residents is for local officials to use their authority to advocate for what their constituents want and don’t want. After all, he said, Wyoming is not outrightly opposed to economic development. 
Plus, Hochard added, local officials in Wyoming have more negotiating power than they might think.
“We’re a really attractive place for data center investment,” he said. “We have a cool climate that reduces cooling costs. We have a history of siting industrial projects. We have fiber. We have an energy heritage that can support these data centers and support energy expansion. So we’re a pretty desirable place.”
There’s a growing frustration among residents, Volk said, that elected officials are not driving a bargain for their constituents when it comes to industrial development.
“I heard voters saying they believe industry should be required to pay for its fair share of its costs — and they want to have a meaningful voice before [local] decisions become irreversible,” she said. “When these industrial players come to look at Wyoming as a prospective site, I would hope that our elected officials — who are wooing them to come — are also saying, ‘By the way, we could use some help in these 10 areas.'”
That’s what astute tech companies — which are increasingly anxious about negative public sentiment — are looking for, according to Hochard.
“They’re not looking for the community that’s just going to roll out the red carpet and offer them everything,” he said. “They want a community that’s going to negotiate a durable bargain. They want a community that’s intentional with their asks and their needs, because it’s going to increase that community sentiment and support for the data center being there.”
Ideally, Hochard added, “It should be a nonpartisan issue.”

name: WyoFile
title: Judge OKs cattle grazing on controversial Bridger-Teton allotments, for now
authors: Christina MacIntosh, Jackson Hole News & Guide
description:
Judge rebuffs claim of insufficient environmental analysis of the Elk Ridge allotments, which haven’t been studied since 1978.
The post Judge OKs cattle grazing on controversial Bridger-Teton allotments, for now appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Cattle are poised to graze on a controversial, 30,500-acre swath of land near Bondurant and the Gros Ventre Range this fall, pending an ongoing legal dispute.
A federal judge on Tuesday denied an environmental nonprofit’s request for a temporary restraining order to prevent grazing on the allotments, which are on the Pinedale District of the Bridger-Teton National Forest and have not seen livestock in the past decade. The organization also sought a prohibition on grazing while its case is adjudicated.
The suit, filed by Western Watersheds Project, stemmed from concerns about conflicts with large carnivores, including grizzly bears and wolves, and a review process that relied on an environmental assessment from 1978. Kelly Rankin, chief judge for the U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming, found that the organization did not prove that it was likely to prevail in court on its claims of an inadequate review process, or that the grazing pending the legal tussle would cause irreparable harm.
“Consequently, the balance of equities and public interest factors weigh in favor of denying the request,” Rankin wrote.
At issue is whether 500 to 550 cow-calf pairs should graze this fall in four livestock grazing allotments known as the Elk Ridge Complex. The land, nestled in the Green River Basin between the Gros Ventre Range and Wind River Range, has not seen livestock grazing since 2016, when Western Watersheds Project and other conservation organizations bought out the existing permit for grazing sheep. The buyout aimed to prevent the spread of disease between domestic and bighorn sheep, as well as to reduce conflicts between livestock and large carnivores.
The Bridger-Teton National Forest compiled this map showing the Elk Ridge complex allotments in relation to adjacent Upper Green allotments during an Endangered Species Act compliance process because the area is a hotbed for conflicts with “threatened” grizzly bears. (U.S. Forest Service)
The allotments sat vacant until last year, when the Dollar Lake Fire burned about 19,500 acres in the Upper Green, including 15,000 acres permitted for grazing. Because of the fire, forest officials allowed grazing in the complex last year, said Coke Landers, president of the Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association.
This year, as part of the annual operating instructions for the Pinedale District, forest officials permitted grazing on the allotments between mid-August and mid-October of 2026 and 2027.
CJ Adams, a Bridger-Teton spokesperson, declined to comment on the decision because of pending litigation. The decision, signed by Pinedale District Ranger Kate Olsen on June 8, came days before the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which oversees the Forest Service, announced plans to “restore grazing” on national forests.
Western Watersheds Project cried foul on the Elk Ridge decision, arguing that reintroducing livestock to the allotments would have a significant impact to the land, vegetation and wildlife and, as such, warranted a full environmental review, said Erik Molvar, the group’s executive director. The organization filed a lawsuit earlier this month.
“The Forest Service has been very dismissive of their obligations to do the environmental assessment,” he said.
In the time since the environmental assessment, grizzly bears were listed as threatened, wolves have expanded their range, and the Bridger-Teton published its 1990 forest plan.
“A lot has changed in the last 50 years,” Molvar said. “You can’t just reach back 50 years in the past and grab an analysis.”
Attorneys representing the forest argued that the review process — which included a 1978 environmental assessment on grazing in the complex, an updated consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and 2026 environmental compliance review — constituted a proper evaluation. The Fish and Wildlife Service found that the anticipated effects of grazing in the complex fell within the “permissible scope,” including effects on grizzly bears and other protected species, according to court documents.
The court heard arguments on the temporary restraining order on Aug. 19. At this stage in the legal proceedings, the court did not find that the forest’s reliance on the 1978 document was improper, Rankin wrote. Because Western Watersheds Project did not demonstrate that forest officials “shirked their environmental duties,” the court could not conclude that “irreparable harm” would result from grazing this season. Prohibiting grazing would also harm permit holders, the court found.
“We’re glad [Rankin] ruled the way he did, that’s for dang sure,” Landers said.
Ranchers will move their cattle onto the allotments in the next two to three weeks, he said.
Western Watersheds Project was still deciding whether to appeal the ruling by press time. If the organization doesn’t appeal, there will be cattle on the complex this fall. The case still could move forward to adjudication, but that would take more time, Molvar said.

name: WyoFile
title: Democracy in my county
description:
Until the GOP stands up to Trump, columnist David Romtvedt writes, no Republican candidate will get his support. 
The post Democracy in my county appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

After Donald Trump’s first presidential term and now nearly halfway through the second, I have come to feel that I cannot vote for anyone who runs for office as a Republican. I say this as a result of living through Mr. Trump’s attempts to dismantle democracy; his use of his office to enrich himself, his family and his political supporters; his misogyny, xenophobia and islamophobia; his demands that Greenland and Canada become part of the United States; his use of the justice department as a vehicle for revenge against those who disagree with him; his attempts to stifle the press; his cynically imperialistic military actions in the Middle East and in Venezuela where he condoned the murder of people he called drug dealers without any charges or proceedings being brought against them; his construction of prison camps where the undocumented, often refugees and exiles, live and sometimes die under dangerous and unhealthy conditions; his illegal separation and deportation of parents and children; his use of ICE as an agency of state terror; his refusal to allocate federal funds for basic scientific research or for the maintenance of social service programs in Democraticled states; his childish need to see his name and image everywhere; and his pretense of representing Christian values while behaving in the least Christian of ways.
Mostly, I’m tired of his lies.
But the real reason I can’t vote Republican even at the local level where the candidates are often my friends and neighbors, people I know who would do their best, is that over the last decade the Republican Party has not stood up and said no to Mr. Trump’s excesses. The party’s most influential members have refused to condemn what they know is wrong. In the face of what they know is graft and self-aggrandizement, they have remained silent.
Perhaps I feel so strongly about this because I, too, have sometimes remained silent in the face of obvious wrongs and I regret that silence.
But here’s the hangup with my sense that I can’t vote Republican — where I live, only Republicans hold office. My county has 5,058 registered voters; 229 are Democrats. That’s about 4.5% of the total. If we remove the 324 voters registered as neither Republican nor Democratic — Libertarians, Constitution Party members, unaffiliated voters and the 28 voters listed simply as other — there are 4,734 registered voters, with the 229 Democrats making up just over 4.8% of the total. 
All this came home to me in our recent primary elections. The Democratic primary election ballot was, as it has been for the 40 years I’ve lived in Wyoming, a very short one. While there were Democratic candidates for the U.S. Senate and House as well as for the statewide offices of governor, secretary of state, and superintendent of public instruction, there were no Democratic candidates for auditor or treasurer, none for my Wyoming House district, and none for the countywide offices of commissioner, coroner, attorney, sheriff, clerk, treasurer, assessor, clerk of district court, precinct committeeman or precinct committeewoman.
Some years back I was asked to go through the county election records to see how many people had won local office in the past several decades running as Democrats. None. It’s the primary that counts. As the Buffalo Bulletin wrote in an Aug. 13 editorial, “This year, every countywide race will be decided in the primary.” It’s pretty much the same at the state and federal level. Even when there’s a Democratic candidate, the winner of the Republican primary is the de facto winner of the general election. In my county, the choice is not to vote for a Democrat, a Republican, or some other party’s candidate, but for one of various Republican candidates.
But since I’ve decided that at this point in American history I can’t vote for a Republican, what am I to do? I could stay at home on voting day — not vote at all. Or I guess I could run for office even though I’d certainly lose.
Maybe I’m asking too much. I certainly don’t agree with every policy of the national Democratic Party and I have respect for the public records of many Republican officeholders. Still, watching the Trump administration’s efforts to slowly unravel democracy while most Republicans remain quiet is awfully disheartening. So this year, following the primary, I’m going to withhold my vote from all Republicans. It’s not a rational or logical stance, but going with my gut, it’s the one I’ve decided to take.
