name: Daily Montanan
title: Sheehy pushes federal support for passenger rail plans in Montana
description: HELENA — As airports grow more crowded, U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy told Montana residents on Wednesday that passenger rail could help fuel more tourism and economic growth in the Big Sky state. Sheehy, a Republican speaking at the Greater Northwest Rail Summit, also gave an update on legislation that would remove federal match requirements by […]
text:
Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Montana, speaks during the Greater Northwest Rail Summit on Wednesday, August, 26, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)HELENA — As airports grow more crowded, U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy told Montana residents on Wednesday that passenger rail could help fuel more tourism and economic growth in the Big Sky state.
Sheehy, a Republican speaking at the Greater Northwest Rail Summit, also gave an update on legislation that would remove federal match requirements by local governments for long-distance passenger rail corridors during the planning and development phases of those projects. Planning phases, and the resulting improvement projects, would be expensive — and the legislation, introduced earlier this year, would shift the responsibility for funding to the federal government.
Sheehy said that legislation likely would be attached to a larger federal bill.
“I think we have a good shot of that passing,” Sheehy said.
That legislation would matter for the Big Sky Passenger Rail Authority, a multi-jurisdictional Montana government group that’s dedicated to bringing back increased passenger rail service from Chicago to Seattle or Portland. The Great Northwest Rail Summit, a three-day event, has brought over a hundred people from multiple states and countries to discuss railroad issues.
That route, called the Big Sky North Coast Corridor, would go through seven states, including all the way across Montana, with much of the proposed service running through rural areas with small tax bases. The route has locally been called the “southern route” as passenger rail does hit much of the Hi-Line through the Empire Builder train.
Sheehy pointed to the potential economic benefits of the service during a conversation with Missoula County Commissioner Dave Strohmaier, who leads the Big Sky Passenger Rail Authority.
Members of the rail authority have pointed to the potential benefits for Montanans, such as moving from city to city for medical appointments, shopping, recreation and even employment. It’s also being looked at by Sheehy as a potential massive boon for tourism, with the senator joking some Montanans may prefer to see the state’s borders closed.
“The reality is, it’s a huge industry,” Sheehy said. “It’s good for the state economy, and then they’re not going to stop coming. I mean, look out the window. Everyone wants to come here, as they should.
Out-of-state visitors to Montana spent roughly $5.6 billion in 2025. About 1-in-11 Montanans have jobs directly supported by tourist dollars.
But Sheehy also pointed to another industry he’s heavily involved in — aviation. Airports are overcrowded, and the demand for air travel is only increasing, he said.
Cars are one solution, Sheehy said, but so is rail — existing easements and railway infrastructure are already in place, which is how the Big Sky Passenger Rail Authority has approached expanding train service.
“We’re not trying to build a new railroad, we’re not trying to blow new tunnels through mountains, we’re not trying to create a new ecosystem,” Sheehy said. “What we’re saying is we already have the route here. The route exists. The authorities are there. Let’s utilize the existing infrastructure we have. Obviously, some investment will be needed, but this could be a model for helping to do it around the country.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: $17 billion Meta settlement lands in hotbed of debate over social media regulations in Mass.
description: A landmark agreement both reshapes Instagram and Facebook for teenagers, and adds fuel to legislative debate about permanent reforms.
text:
TEENAGERS ACROSS THE COUNTRY will soon have a significantly different experience on Instagram and Facebook, and lawmakers in Massachusetts just got a nine-figure incentive to wrap up their work on a social media bill.
In the midst of a nationwide reckoning over the addictiveness of social media platforms, and with Bay State legislation regulating the industry in negotiations, a coalition of attorneys general announced a massive settlement with tech giant Meta that could inform Bay State debates over how companies can verify the ages of their users without tripping into intrusive data collection.
Meta — which owns social media platforms Facebook and Instagram — is settling a landmark case targeting its design features, Attorney General Andrea Campbell announced Wednesday morning. It will pay $17.1 billion altogether to 47 states and enact major reforms to how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram under the terms of the deal awaiting court approval.
Massachusetts is set to receive up to $516 million through the settlement, according to Campbell’s office, including approximately $366 million guaranteed to be paid over the next 10 years.
With the exception of the landmark Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s, Campbell’s office said this is the largest state consumer protection settlement in history.
“The size of the settlement is not what matters most to me or this team,” Campbell said at a press conference Wednesday. “What matters is that this agreement changes what young people will experience when they open their apps. And I want to be clear that today is not the end of this work. It’s just the beginning.”
The deal between Meta and attorneys general across the country landed as Massachusetts lawmakers continue to deliberate about whether to enshrine permanent restrictions on youth social media use in state law.
Under the settlement, users under 13 will be completely banned from using on Instagram or Facebook. For 13- to 18-year-old users, the platforms will need to implement new protections and keep them in place for at least five years.
These teen users will only be able to access Instagram and Facebook for up to two hours per day, and will be completely blocked between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m. Notifications would also be throttled — shut off entirely between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m., and silenced during standard school hours of 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Along with mandatory breaks while using the site for teens, Facebook and Instagram will introduce options to disable “autoplay” and algorithmic feed features, which prosecutors have argued contribute to increased time on the platform. The settlement also eliminates some metrics that can create comparison and unhealthy competition between young users, like publicly visible counts of likes and other reactions on teen users’ posts. It would disable filters that mimic cosmetic surgery, in a gesture to the detrimental effects of young people being constantly exposed to idealized faces and bodies.
“These are not simply promises to do better,” Campbell said. “These are changes to the products themselves to start to make things safer for our kids online.”
But the settlement only binds Meta, not other industry giants like Google or TikTok. And the new protections are guaranteed for a limited period of time, unless the parties agree to continue the terms.
Campbell noted that a lawsuit against TikTok is pending. That company is facing similar allegations that it designed its platform to addict young users and exploit their vulnerabilities.
Meta explicitly called for other social media companies to join in its new commitments, rolling out an “open letter” to TikTok and YouTube. (Neither TikTok nor Google, which owns YouTube, responded to CommonWealth Beacon inquiries Wednesday.)
Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the limits on nighttime and school hour alerts “will only work if all our peers join us.”
“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement.
Wednesday’s settlement resolves a 2023 lawsuit in Massachusetts arguing that Meta violated state consumer protection laws and caused a public nuisance by purposefully designing its Instagram app to addict young users. The tech giant unsuccessfully argued before the state Supreme Judicial Court that it was shielded from suit by a federal law that protects publishers from being liable for things that third-party users might post.
“That groundbreaking ruling allowed our case to move forward, and Massachusetts leadership helped create the leverage needed to pave the way for today’s agreement,” Campbell said.
She made clear that she still wants state lawmakers to put permanent, industry-wide restrictions on the books, using Wednesday’s press conference to urge the Legislature to finish its work on youth social media bills as well as an effort to ban student cellphone use during the school day.
“We view the settlement as a floor, and we now see these protections as a floor for other tech companies to begin to redesign their platforms to protect our kids,” Campbell said. “We also see it as an opportunity for the Legislature not only to adopt these provisions as the floor, but to go beyond them.”
Attorney General Andrea Campbell (right) and Rep. Alice Pesich (left), who is co-leading legislative negotiations over social media limits for minors, field questions from reporters at an August 26, 2026 press conference about a multi-state settlement with Meta. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
Both the House and Senate support taking action to limit social media risks for children and teenagers, but so far, Democrats in the two branches have not yet been able to agree on an approach.
Legislative leaders signaled they will continue to pursue action even with the Meta settlement in place. Senate President Karen Spilka on Wednesday pledged to “build on AG Campbell’s victory and keep working to finalize a comprehensive youth social media protections bill so we can expand upon and implement these protections across the board.”
Sen. Brendan Crighton, who’s leading negotiations over the bills alongside Rep. Alice Peisch, an assistant majority leader on House Speaker Ron Mariano’s leadership team, said the new settlement “bolsters the argument” for legislators to act.
“We were company-neutral in looking at the overall issue around social media in our bill,” Crighton told CommonWealth Beacon. “That was done intentionally, to not go after one company or another.”
“So I don’t think [the settlement] changes our approach,” he added. “Our goal was to create regulations across all platforms, and that remains the goal.”
There’s an unusual clause baked into the agreement that could expand what Meta owes Massachusetts. If other major social media platforms that are not covered by the terms of the settlement, like TikTok and YouTube, implement similar protections for young users and pay the Bay State $150 million, Meta would match that additional funding.
The logic may appear somewhat counterintuitive. But if Meta were the only platform to change its policies, officials said, it would be willing to pay less than it would if the entire industry embraced similar reforms, which minimizes any risk of one company being at a disadvantage. As an AG spokesperson put it, the provision“levels the playing field.”
The requirement could be triggered either by TikTok and YouTube’s voluntary participation, or by legislative action to force every company to play by the same rules.
State lawmakers are already weighing bills that would implement major limits on youth social media use. Now, they could win Massachusetts hundreds of millions of dollars more simply by coming to agreement with each other.
In the meantime, Meta has one year to implement systems to identify users under 13 and users between 13 and 18 with a “high level of accuracy.” The settlement mandates that whatever age verification system is implemented cannot require users to submit government identification or other sensitive information to verify their age, but it does not specify a particular mechanism.
That drops the settlement squarely into an international imbroglio over data privacy and youth safety online.
Online privacy and LGBTQ advocates have criticized similar language in House and Senate social media regulation proposals. Advocacy group Fight for the Future has been calling for lawmakers to strike language requiring social media companies to implement an age assurance system when new accounts are created. This, they say, “would create a substantial barrier for adults to speak anonymously online, raising constitutional and free speech concerns.”
In the Bay State, money paid by Meta will go toward “efforts to remediate the harms caused by social media to Massachusetts young people” as well as to the state’s General Fund. The harm-reduction options may include youth crisis intervention and mental health services; after-school, summer, and outdoor programs; advancing digital wellness and literacy; phone-free school initiatives; and training medical providers on interactive media use and body dysmorphia.
The attorney general also touted agreements to create “enhanced parental supervision tools” allowing parents to turn on protective settings and receive notifications on their teens’ usage, content searches, and contact with adults.
These tools, her office said, would be tied to a unique mechanism. Teen accounts by default would have the strict new limitations, but if they were tethered to a parent’s account, they could have more lenient default protections with the tradeoff of more parental oversight.
In a statement, Mahoney said the negotiated framework “will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms.”
The one-company limitation echoes a settlement in 2024 between Campbell’s office and ride-share tech companies Uber and Lyft, which killed a potential ballot measure to treat drivers for multiple apps – not just Uber and Lyft – as independent contractors in exchange for ending a lawsuit charging the companies with violating state labor law.
While the major industry players Uber and Lyft are bound by the settlement setting new wage and benefit standards, other gig-work companies relying on drivers, like DoorDash and Instacart, were left to operate as usual.
For now, the attorney general’s office and the Legislature are traveling on individual tracks toward similar ends. But the coming months of lawmakers weighing data privacy, social media, and cell phone bills offer plenty of opportunities for policy collisions.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Tribal leaders, clean water advocates rally in Lansing as Line 5 fight intensifies
description: Following a flurry of developments surrounding Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project, tribal citizens and environmental advocates gathered in Lansing to share concerns about the project and lay out the next steps in their yearslong fight to have the pipeline decommissioned.  The controversial Line 5 pipeline runs from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, with[...]
text:
Clean Water Action Michigan Water Justice Organizer Nichole Keway Biber, Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition Deputy Director of Programming Andrea Pierce and Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians Chairperson Winnay Wemigwase at a rally opposing Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline held at the Michigan State Capitol on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Following a flurry of developments surrounding Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project, tribal citizens and environmental advocates gathered in Lansing to share concerns about the project and lay out the next steps in their yearslong fight to have the pipeline decommissioned. 
The controversial Line 5 pipeline runs from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario, with a 4.5-mile segment of dual pipelines running through the Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet.
Organized by the Anishinaabe Friendship Center, Wednesday’s rally welcomed leaders from the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians and the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe, along with environmentalists and state officials calling for Line 5 to be shut down. 
“This is not just a Native issue, and let me repeat that: it’s not just a Native issue,” said Winnay Wemigwase, the chairperson of the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. “It is not just an environmental issue. It is a Michigan issue. It is a human issue.”
The pipeline transports up to 23 million gallons of crude oil and natural gas liquids per day, with opponents raising concerns about the consequences of a spill into the waterway.
Protest signs at a rally agains Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline in Lansing on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo By Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Sonja Ballew, a member of the Bay Mills Indian Community, helps lead a water ceremony at the start of a rally against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline on the steps of the Michigan state capitol on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians Chairperson Winnay Wemigwase discusses the harms that could come from a Line 5 oil spill during rally at the Michigan State Capitol on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians Chairperson Winnay Wemigwase stresses the statewide impacts of a potential Line 5 oil spill during a rally at the Michigan State Capitol on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Nichole Keway Biber, Michigan water justice organizer for Clean Water Action helps lead a water ceremony at the start of a rally against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline on the steps of the Michigan state capitol on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Nichole Keway Biber, Michigan water justice organizer for Clean Water Action helps lead a water ceremony at the start of a rally against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline on the steps of the Michigan state capitol on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Luke Sprague, chief of the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe, at rally opposing Enbridge's Line 5 tunnel project on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)More than 100 individuals gathered on the Michigan Capitol lawn for a rally against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Nichole Keway Biber, Michigan water justice organizer for Clean Water Action, speaks out against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline at a rally on the steps of the Michigan state capitol on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)More than 100 individuals gathered on the Michigan Capitol lawn for a rally against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Flow Water Advocates Executive Director Liz Kirkwood lays out the next steps in the fight against Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline at a rally in Lansing on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Opponents of the pipeline have pointed to the 2010 Kalamazoo River oil spill stemming from Enbridge’s Line 6B and a 2018 anchor strike which dented Line 5 in places as proof of their concerns. Several speakers at Wednesday’s rally also pointed to research from the University of Michigan, which determined that the Straits of Mackinac are the ”worst possible place” for a Great Lakes oil spill, with more than 700 miles of shoreline facing contamination if the pipeline were to rupture.
While Enbridge is working to construct a utility tunnel beneath the lakebed in hope of mitigating concerns of further anchor strikes and a Great Lakes oil spill, environmental advocates and tribal citizens have raised further concerns around the company’s proposed solution and its impact on natural and cultural resources.
“Their answer is to blast a tunnel through four miles of sacred bedrock directly beneath the straits,” Wemigwase said. “They want us to give them permission to drill through thousands of years of Anishinaabe sacred sites, excavate hundreds of thousands of cubic yards of ancient stone, and lock in fossil fuel infrastructure for another half century. All to protect a pipeline that acts primarily as a shortcut to ship Canadian oil right back into freaking Canada.”
Wemigwase explained that the Straits of Mackinac hold immense spiritual significance for the Anishinaabe, likening tunneling through the straits to running an industrial pipeline beneath the floor of the Vatican.
Andrea Pierce, a tribal citizen of the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians and the deputy director of programming for the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition, said if the tunnel project moves forward, they will need to dig up the remains of their ancestors on both sides of the straits. 
“They were put there to last for eternity, not to be moved at the whims of a pipeline from other countries or any country,” Pierce said. 
In an email to Michigan Advance, Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy said that site surveys have found “no confirmed Tribal ancestral burial grounds within the proposed construction areas,” and that the company would be implementing a strict artifact recovery protocol in coordination with Tribal experts “to ensure any findings are handled appropriately and respectfully.”

@michiganadvance State Rep. Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City) speaks at an anti-Line 5 rally at the Michigan Capitol with a message for Gov. Whitmer. @BigGretchWhitmer ♬ original sound – Michigan Advance


In a recently reissued permit for the tunnel project, the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy states “This project will have adverse effects on known historic and cultural resources, including their destruction and/or removal. These resources are unique and highly significant to the Anishinaabek communities, as well as the State of Michigan. The permittee shall, as a primary condition of this permit, mitigate the loss of historic, archaeological, and cultural resources.”
Enbridge is required to submit a Cultural Resources Mitigation and Monitoring Plan to EGLE by Dec. 31, 2026.
Wemigwase also highlighted the impact that a Great Lakes oil spill would have on the waters, noting that 40 million people rely on the lakes as a source of drinking water.
“A catastrophic spill in the Straits would poison municipal water intakes across Michigan, Ontario, and in downstream communities,” Wemigwase said. “You cannot drink oil. You cannot wash your dishes with crude.”
Nichole Keway Biber, Michigan water justice organizer for Clean Water Action, discussed the pipeline’s impact outside of the Great Lakes, noting that 12 miles of Line 5 run through the Bad River Band of the Lake Superior Tribe of Chippewa Indians’ reservation in Wisconsin. 
Enbridge is currently working to reroute that segment after a federal judge determined the company was trespassing on the Bad River Band’s sovereign lands. Keway Biber noted that Enbridge has already released 1,900 gallons of drilling fluid as part of the reroute. 
On Tuesday, Enbridge and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources confirmed to the Wisconsin Examiner that a segment of the pipeline had leaked natural gas after a truck rolled over a natural gas transmission line at an open excavation site for a Line 5 valve project.
“Near U.S. Route 2, Line 5 runs along the north shore of Lake Michigan, where it crosses 16 tributaries within nine miles of the lake, 11 of which are less than four miles from both shores,” Keway Biber said going on to note that south of the Straits, the pipeline runs across the Indian River, Little Sturgeon River, Pigeon River, Upper Black River, and sits within a few miles of several inland lakes.
While EGLE and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers recently granted permits for the project, the Michigan Supreme Court struck down a critical permit from the Michigan Public Service Commission after determining the regulatory board did not properly consider the environmental harms that could come from extending the pipeline’s operations.
Amid these developments, Liz Kirkwood, the executive director of Flow Water Advocates, urged Line 5 opponents to do three things. 
The first is to tell Governor Gretchen Whitmer, who pledged to take action against Line 5 during her 2018 campaign, to “finish the job” she started when she revoked Line 5’s easement to operate on the Great Lake’s bottomlands in 2020. 
“Our ask is simple: implement the Michigan Supreme Court’s ruling, withdraw EGLE’s recent permit for the tunnel, and finish the job you started in 2020, and shut down this pipeline before you leave office,” Kirkwood said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kirkwood’s second request was for the public to show up to the Michigan Public Service Commission when they open tunnel project proceedings to the public.
“When it does, the public needs to be there,” Kirkwood said. “Ask the hard questions. Would a tunnel extend Line 5’s life for decades? What would that mean for the waters held in public trust for us as beneficiaries for future generations? The Great Lakes are not the only route, they’re just the route Enbridge already occupies.”
Kirkwood’s final request was to question every candidate up for election in November on their stance toward Line 5.
“Our job between now and Nov. 3 is to make sure no one gets elected to statewide office in Michigan without telling the people of Michigan on their record where they stand on oil in the Great Lakes,” Kirkwood said, noting that the state is set to select a new governor and a new attorney general, two positions with significant power over the pipeline’s future.
State Rep. Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City) was even more direct in her message to the governor.
“The flag of this state says Tuebor. That is Latin for ‘I defend,’” Coffia told the crowd. “Gretchen Whitmer, your job when you leave this office is to defend the Great Lakes, to honor the treaties, to remember that water is life, and to use your considerable power to shut down Line 5. Make sure, governor, that your legacy is not one covered in oil and lies.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: ‘Sad period in Nebraska history’: AG Hilgers speaks on ongoing petition fraud investigations
description: LINCOLN — As law enforcement continues to investigate thousands of possibly fraudulent signatures on at least eight different Nebraska petitions this year, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers is speaking out on the historic situation for the first time. The ongoing criminal investigation has already led to the arrest of six out-of-state circulators, and p[...]
text:
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State's Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office's Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — As law enforcement continues to investigate thousands of possibly fraudulent signatures on at least eight different Nebraska petitions this year, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers is speaking out on the historic situation for the first time.
The ongoing criminal investigation has already led to the arrest of six out-of-state circulators, and prosecutors have filed an arrest warrant for a seventh, the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office said this month. Petitions for all four statewide ballot measures, three proposed amendments to the Lincoln City Charter and one nonpartisan bid for Nebraska governor are under investigation.
“It is a sad period in Nebraska history that we’ve had this much fraud in our petition process,” Hilgers told reporters at an unrelated news conference Wednesday.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers hosts a news conference in his office in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Two congressional candidate petitions — one statewide and one in the 3rd Congressional District — plus two statewide petitions to establish new political parties have not been implicated. Another Lincoln petition, related to police staffing, has also not been implicated.
Said Hilgers: “We will apply the same standard and the same rules, and we’ll have the same energy and the same fervor to enforce the laws in the State of Nebraska, no matter who.”
Lancaster County takes the lead
The Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office and Lancaster County Attorney’s Office have taken the lead in the fraud case, which Hilgers said isn’t unusual.
If fraud is suspected in Nebraska, Hilgers said, the state Attorney General’s Office is often involved “in some form or fashion.” Usually, the office leads for statewide issues or in smaller counties, but it takes a coordinating, assisting role with larger counties, such as Lancaster.
Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon, left, and Lancaster County Sheriff Chief Deputy Ben Houchin announce criminal charges and arrests of five out-of-state individuals who helped circulate petitions for three petitions in Nebraska’s capital city at a news briefing Aug. 7, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
When law enforcement announced the arrest of five out-of-state circulators on Aug. 7, Hilgers’ office was not present. That’s in contrast to two years ago when Hilgers and Hall County Attorney Marty Klein announced one arrest related to two medical cannabis petitions. A month later, Klein and Hilgers announced the arrest of a notary for the medical cannabis petitions.
Hilgers said it would be an “outlier,” by contrast, for his office to be at such news conferences in the three most populous counties: Douglas, Lancaster or Sarpy. 
He said he couldn’t recall any such instances — civil, criminal or otherwise.
“The big three drive the bus for themselves,” Hilgers said. “We help where they want us to help.”
‘Operational control’
It was in mid-July that Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen first reported signatures suspected to be fraudulent on three Lincoln City Charter petitions to authorities.
In total, election officials rejected more than 65% of the 30,000 signatures that Good Government Lincoln submitted in an initial batch of signatures seeking to qualify three measures.
Those three petitions seek to limit future Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms, move the dates of city elections from odd years to even years and let certain residents within a 3-mile buffer around Lincoln city limits vote in municipal elections, excluding bond votes.
Each of the three had fallen short of the 4,981 valid signatures needed to qualify for the ballot.
Lincoln City Council Chair Brodey Weber hosts a news conference in Lincoln on Aug. 13, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
At the outset of the investigation, Hilgers said, he gave “operational control” to his chief deputy and criminal prosecution chief “in an abundance of caution.” The top prosecutors still retain control. 
Axiom Strategies, a multistate consulting firm, is assisting the petition effort. Hilgers is among the most powerful Nebraska Republicans among the firm’s clients, including this year.
Hilgers acknowledged he is “absolutely” a supporter of the Lincoln petition campaign. He is not a Lincoln voter — he lives in the 3-mile “extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction” that would be able to vote in Lincoln municipal elections if passed — but he has encouraged support of the measures.
Democratic challenger fires back
Jocelyn Brasher of Omaha, Hilgers’ Democratic opponent this fall, previously worked as an assistant attorney general for five years. She had some overlap with Hilgers, who took over in 2023.
The 2026 candidates for Nebraska attorney general: Republican Attorney General Mike Hilgers, left, and Democrat Jocelyn Brasher of Omaha. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Brasher said Hilgers “went to war” over alleged fraud regarding medical cannabis in 2024. But once allegations reached Hilgers’ “political circle,” she said, “Nebraskans aren’t seeing that same aggressive pursuit of the truth or a full, independent investigation.”
“If Mike Hilgers truly believes, as he said today, that ‘you do not mess’ with the integrity of criminal investigations, then he should step aside and allow a truly independent investigation,” Brasher said in a Wednesday statement.
She said Nebraskans should never have to wonder whether “political connections” influence enforcement. However, Hilgers said he does not see a reason to recuse himself, but if it did rise to that level, he said he would let the public know.
“If there is a time at which I do not think that I can follow the law and discharge my duties, of course, the only thing for me to do is to recuse myself,” Hilgers said.
Brasher said if she faced similar political overlap, she would recuse herself “so Nebraskans can trust that the law is always being enforced fairly and impartially.”
Jocelyn Brasher, the 2026 Democratic nominee for Nebraska attorney general, hosts a small town hall with about a dozen attendees in Lincoln on June 22, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Though not criticizing Brasher by name, Hilgers said former employees of his office, who “should know better,” tried to suggest that the timing of news conferences or announcements suggested different treatment.
“Every case has their own life. Every case has their own set of facts. Every case is a little bit different,” Hilgers said.
Lincoln City Council Chair Brodey Weber and Randall Ritnour, a Democrat challenging Republican Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon this November, have called for a special prosecutor to take over the case. Ritnour is a former county attorney in Gage and Johnson counties. Weber, a Democrat, ran against Hilgers for Legislature in 2020.
Condon has refused to pursue a special prosecutor, citing politics and the cost to taxpayers. 
Hilgers described the special prosecutor request as a “political ploy” with “no basis” in how criminal offices run in this circumstance.
Lincoln faces looming deadline
Good Government Lincoln restarted signature gathering the same day Wiltgen said they didn’t have enough signatures. Former state Sen. Tony Fulton and other sponsors turned in a second set of signatures Aug. 19. Fulton served as tax commissioner under former Gov. Pete Ricketts.
Then-state Sen. Tony Fulton of Lincoln. (Photo courtesy of Unicameral Information Office)
As of Wednesday, election officials have confirmed enough valid signatures for the petitions seeking to enact city council term limits and move the timing of the election. Signature verification is ongoing, and all three measures appear likely to have enough signatures.
Compared to the first set, about 70% of signatures have been validated this time.
However, signature-gathering is the first step, and Lincoln officials must take action to certify items for the ballot. The last day to do so, under state law, is Tuesday.
Hilgers said there’s a “disturbing trend” of Lincoln officials acting “contrary” to the Nebraska Constitution. He noted efforts to enforce a local minimum wage, an ordinance that is, for now, blocked in court. But Hilgers said there are “some other instances, maybe we’ll announce in the coming weeks, where they also have violated the Constitution.” He did not give further details.
Of whether Lincoln officials must put qualifying city charter amendments on the Nov. 3 ballot, Hilgers said it’s a “non-negotiable, non-discretionary requirement.”
Hilgers confirmed he has sent a letter to city officials asking them to confirm by 5 p.m. Thursday whether they’ll forward qualifying amendments to voters.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
If officials refuse or indicate they won’t comply, Hilgers gave a warning: “We will be prepared.”
Hilgers acknowledged the Nebraska Constitution may give a later certification deadline, in early October, but he hopes that isn’t needed.
Weber told the Nebraska Examiner that the role of a city councilor is to work with the City Attorney’s Office and ensure “we follow the right steps and we have an appropriate procedure.” 
“Just because they [Good Government Lincoln] did not handle this situation with the level of care that it required doesn’t mean that the city has to act in a similar fashion,” Weber said Tuesday. “We are going to do the right thing, and we’re going to follow the process to make sure that we’re upholding the law.”
Campaign sponsors have said they were unaware of any alleged criminal activity and that they support investigation and prosecution of all actors, at every level, who may have been involved.
‘Cheating doesn’t win’
Hilgers said a message that “cheating doesn’t win” needs to resonate at the top of petition campaigns. He hearkened back to the Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana campaign from 2024 — its third attempt to reach voters, which voters overwhelmingly supported — and how his office’s investigation went all the way up to the sponsors behind the issue.
Hall County Attorney Marty Klein, standing, speaks to the jury during the first day of trial before Hall County Judge Alfred Corey, center, against a former notary public, Jacy Todd of York, at left, who was connected to two 2024 statewide medical cannabis ballot measures in Grand Island on Feb. 23, 2026. (Photo by Kasey Mintz-Pool/KSNB Local 4)
One sponsor was among campaign supporters who pleaded their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in 2024. That was, in part, because of possible criminal charges in addition to a civil lawsuit from Hilgers and Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen to disqualify the effort.
“We treated them the way we treated them based on where the facts went,” Hilgers said.
One Grand Island circulator pleaded guilty to attempting to falsify his circulator’s oath. He had used a phone book to forge signatures. A jury convicted a York notary for improper notarizations on that circulator’s petitions. That notary is now appealing his convictions.
No other prosecutions came as a result of the medical cannabis investigation, but Hilgers and Evnen implicated multiple circulators and notaries in the civil lawsuit.
The Hilgers-Evnen lawsuit is now in front of the Nebraska Supreme Court. A lower court judge ruled against assertions of widespread fraud. If the justices reverse, it could lead to invalidation of the 2024 voter-approved laws for legalization and regulation of medical cannabis.
If there is evidence implicating any ballot sponsors this year, Hilgers said, his team will go in that direction “100%, full stop.”
‘Nowhere to be found’
In a Wednesday statement, the Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana campaign said Hilgers reminded Nebraskans “exactly who he is: an attorney general who is ruthless when attacking ordinance people, but when scrutiny reaches his own political allies, he’s nowhere to be found.”
Nebraska advocates for medical cannabis have worked for more than 12 years, and continue to wait, for a safe, regulated system in Nebraska, after winning voter approval in November. Pictured are many longtime advocates for the effort. (Photos courtesy of Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana)
The unsigned campaign statement said Hilgers waged a “taxpayer-funded vendetta” that dragged patients and families “through the mud.” They also criticized Hilgers’ claim Wednesday that the campaign was “top to bottom the most corrupt, the worst run, poorly executed, most disrespectful to voters in the State of Nebraska petition I’ve ever seen.”
Campaign supporters have continued to stand by their campaign and pointed to the Lancaster County District Court judge’s rejection of claims alleging widespread fraud or malfeasance.
“When patients and volunteers were involved, Hilgers was happy to use every tool at his disposal. Mistakes became scandals. Allegations became press conferences. Petition integrity became one of his favorite talking points,” the campaign said.
“These were not political operatives sitting in a boardroom. These were parents of sick children.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: New challenges to Trump mail-in voting order arrive after US Supreme Court ruling
text: Democrat-led states and voting rights groups re-filed lawsuits Wednesday to block the Trump administration from executing a new regulation to restrict mail-in voting, while a federal judge lifted a nationwide pause on the policy in line with this week’s U.S. Supreme Court decision that handed the administration a procedural win.Democratic officials in 24 states and the District of Columbia launched a new federal lawsuit challenging a U.S. Postal Service rule establishing federal vote-by-mail standards as unconstitutional and a coalition of voting rights advocates filed a supplemental complaint against the USPS rule after the Supreme Court struck down a similar suit as premature.The rule establishes new ballot-design requirements and mandates states collect information from voters and voting-age citizens and transmit that information to the federal government. It forbids the Postal Service from delivering or collecting mail-in ballots from people who have not been confirmed as eligible voters.The Supreme Court’s decision Monday, with the three liberals dissenting, said states had not had the right to challenge President Donald Trump’s March 31 executive order because there was no corresponding enforceable final rule. The new filings largely incorporated earlier arguments, but updated the procedural history to reflect that the USPS rule is now final, and presumably open to legal challenge.“As recently as August 12, 2026, USPS told the Supreme Court that there was significant ‘uncertainty concerning the government’s future actions,’” the voting rights groups wrote. “That uncertainty is now gone.”In fact, the final rule published Aug. 21 hewed closely to the March executive order, the groups said.“The Final Rule now makes concrete what Defendants previously called speculative,” they wrote. States’ responsibilityThe voting rights groups said the rule would create a significant burden for voters.The Democratic officials added that the requirements would place a significant strain on their resources, forcing them to scramble to overhaul their vote-by-mail systems less than three months before midterm elections.And the rule impedes on a power that the U.S. Constitution expressly gives to states: election administration.While Congress can make laws related to voting, the president and Postal Service have virtually no role, the state officials said.“Whether a qualified voter may vote by mail is a question of state law, as is the question of whether a ballot will be accepted for processing and tabulation,” the states’ complaint reads. “Congress has not afforded USPS any authority whatsoever to set rules for federal elections or mail voting, even though Americans have cast ballots by mail for generations.”The states also noted that Trump has objected to mail in voting for political purposes.“One need not look further than the White House to explain USPS’s unprecedented and unlawful conduct,” they wrote. “President Trump has long opposed mail voting, expressing that it would ‘LEAD TO THE END OF OUR GREAT REPUBLICAN PARTY.’ Since reassuming office,the President has aimed to—in his words— ‘get rid of MAIL-IN BALLOTS.’”The states that brought the suit are: Massachusetts, Virginia, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon,  Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin. Decision coming soonAlso Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Indiria Talwani removed her nationwide preliminary injunction blocking the administration from implementing the executive order that directed the USPS to create new restrictions and standards for mail-in ballots. She dissolved her order only to comply with the Supreme Court decision, which she suggested might be different if the court considers a complaint filed after the USPS final rule.“While Plaintiff Organizations have substantial arguments that might persuade the Supreme Court to reach a different result if Plaintiff Organizations have an opportunity to present them, this court is compelled by the Supreme Court’s ruling” to lift the injunction, she wrote Talwani also set a quick briefing schedule for both cases Wednesday, with the final brief before a decision on a request for a new temporary injunction due Aug. 31.That decision is likely to see an appeal.White House responseTrump and administration officials have largely framed the order as an election security measure.In a statement Wednesday, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis repeated that defense and blasted Democrats for seeking to undermine the rule.“The Supreme Court ruling was a major win for the security of American elections,” Bis wrote. “Radical Democrats continue to oppose commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders. The Trump Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Alternative media pioneer Nat Winthrop on a half-century of covering Vermont
description:
Winthrop’s new book, “On the Record,” collects his cover stories over the years, from his reporting on a controversial Randolph physician in the 1970s to his stories about Bernie Sanders and ice cream icons Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield as they rose to national fame.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Alternative media pioneer Nat Wint[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Nat Winthrop. Photo Credit: Martha Winthrop
Journalist Nat Winthrop has been covering Vermont for a half-century, reporting stories that have surprised, infuriated and enlightened readers. 
From 1978 to 1990, Winthrop was publisher of the pioneering alternative weekly the Vanguard Press, and later the Vermont Times. These publications were launching pads for many journalists and were forerunners to Seven Days, the Vermont weekly that is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year. He was also executive producer of “Freedom & Unity,” a six-part documentary film about Vermont that was led by Nora Jacobson. In 1987, he co-founded the online alternative news service AlterNet.
Winthrop explained the niche filled by Vermont’s early alternative weeklies. “There’s the myth of objectivity in the media,” he told me. But “the Vanguard, in particular, wore our opinions on our sleeves or on the editorial page.”
The weeklies differ from newspapers with their “narrative style of storytelling, so that all of the important information isn’t necessarily right up at the top of the article.”

“On the Record” by Nat Winthrop. Courtesy photo

Winthrop, 74, has a new book, “On the Record,” a collection of 17 of his cover stories. The topics vary widely, from his reporting on a controversial physician at Gifford Hospital in Randolph who championed in vitro fertilization in the 1970s, to his coverage of Iranian cadets at Norwich University just after the 1979 Iranian revolution, to his stories about Bernie Sanders and ice cream icons Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield as they rose from obscurity to national fame. The book has many contemporary echoes and includes updates on what has happened with the subjects of each story.
Filmmaker Jay Craven wrote in a foreword, “A newspaper in tune with its readers creates common ground and lets us know where we live in ways that are specific to ourselves, our towns, and our neighbors. Nat’s work strengthened our links to each other and helped move our state forward.”
Winthrop earned a bachelor’s degree from Harvard and came to Vermont to attend Goddard College, where he received a master’s degree in media education in 1977. He lives in Montpelier.
“Print media across most of the country are a lot smaller in numbers and some say a dying breed,” conceded Vermont’s alternative media pioneer. But he pointed to VTDigger, Seven Days and Vermont Public as indications that media “are actually doing quite a bit better in Vermont than in most states.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Alternative media pioneer Nat Winthrop on a half-century of covering Vermont.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota wins $214M settlement from Meta in teen addiction case
description: Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, has agreed to pay $214 million to Minnesota over 10 years to settle a lawsuit brought by dozens of states alleging it knowingly made its apps addictive for children. The proposed settlement, which must be approved by a judge, includes payments of as much as $17.1 billion […]
text:
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison holds a press conference after Meta and dozens of states agreed to settle in a landmark teen addiction case, Wednesday Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, has agreed to pay $214 million to Minnesota over 10 years to settle a lawsuit brought by dozens of states alleging it knowingly made its apps addictive for children.
The proposed settlement, which must be approved by a judge, includes payments of as much as $17.1 billion across 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories as well as changes to its social media apps.
The settlement could prove to be a watershed moment for Big Tech, which has historically been adept at avoiding regulation even when it comes to the safety of children.
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

“Meta knew its platforms were harming kids,” said Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison at a Wednesday press conference announcing the settlement.
Meta does not admit to any wrongdoing as part of the settlement, which comes just a week after a trial began in the case in Oakland, Calif.
Former Meta employees testified in the trial that Meta knew its teen safety tools were ineffective and that several internal Meta studies had highlighted the risks for teens on its apps while the company continued to prioritize usership over safety.
The payments are among the largest Big Tech settlements with states to date. Meta will pay at least $12 billion over the next decade, plus $5 billion more if Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube reach similar settlements.
The product changes Meta agreed to implement as default safety features include a two-hour time limit; a block on Meta apps between midnight and 6 a.m.; options to make their social media feeds less personalized; and a block on beauty filters. The safety features can be overridden by a supervising parent.
The settlement also includes requirements that Meta improve its age-identification algorithms to identify teen accounts and catch accounts of kids under 13, who are not supposed to use Meta apps under the company’s policy. Kids often bypass age restrictions by lying about their birth date, which isn’t verified. The company instead uses artificial intelligence to analyze an account’s photos, posts, comments and other content for clues on their age, such as birthday wishes.
Most of the new safety features are required for a decade. Ellison said he thinks “it would be great” if the settlement terms were “nailed into state law” by the Legislature.
The settlement includes examples of how states can use the funds, such as spending on crisis hotlines like 988, after school programs and public health advertising, but Minnesota’s share of the settlement will just go into the state’s general fund until the Legislature decides how to allocate it.
Minnesota’s payout has the potential of reaching $307 million depending on whether other industry giants — TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube — agree to similar terms in possible future settlements. On Wednesday, Meta published an “open letter” to TikTok and YouTube to adopt the new standards set by the settlement.
Minnesota sued TikTok last year in state court, alleging that the infinite scroll short-form video platform preys on young users with addictive algorithms. That case is currently in discovery, with a trial date set for October to November of 2027.
A 2024 Pew Research survey found that 90% of teens use YouTube, 63% are on TikTok, and 61% use Instagram. More than 1 in 10 teens said they use YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat “almost constantly.”
In 2025, 90% of Minnesota high school students reported using social media every day, and a large portion — over 1 in 3 eighth graders and juniors — suspect they have a social media problem. Over 1 in 6 students, including those in fifth grade, said they use technology between midnight and 5 a.m. on all five school nights.
States that have brought suits against social media companies are using a similar playbook that led to billions in damages levied against Big Tobacco in the 1990s and helped drive down American nicotine use until vapes and pouches brought about a revival. Ellison acknowledged the comparison.
“For years, it was like, you can’t beat Big Tobacco, and then suddenly, you know, Minnesota took on Big Tobacco,” Ellison said.
On social media litigation, he said, “I see this as an industry sweep, but we’re at the front end of it.”

title: Four Iowa nurses are accused of putting patients at risk
description: State regulators have charged four Iowa nurses with incompetence or acting in a manner that put patients at risk. The Iowa Board of Nursing has charged Trisha M. Davis of Holstein with a lack of knowledge, skill, or ability to discharge her professional obligations; deviation from the standards of learning, education, or skill ordinarily possessed […]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing is responsible for overseeing Iowa's licensing boards and nursing homes. (Main image via Canva; logo courtesy of Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing)State regulators have charged four Iowa nurses with incompetence or acting in a manner that put patients at risk.
The Iowa Board of Nursing has charged Trisha M. Davis of Holstein with a lack of knowledge, skill, or ability to discharge her professional obligations; deviation from the standards of learning, education, or skill ordinarily possessed by other nurses; willful or repeated failure to practice nursing with reasonable skill and safety; committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; and failing to assess or accurately the status of a patient or client.
The board has disclosed no information related to the circumstances that gave rise to the charges other than to say they occurred when Davis was practicing in Cherokee. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Oct. 16, 2026.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Davis for comment.
Other Iowa nurses recently charged with incompetence include:
Melanie Hall of Sioux City — The board alleges Hall entered incorrect information regarding a patient’s medical condition into record or a device after misreading a lab report. According to the board, she also failed to follow proper isolation procedures, potentially exposing patients to cross contamination, and failed to follow proper disinfection protocols following the treatment of a patient. The board charged Hall with one count of committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare.
To settle the case without a hearing, the board agreed to issue Hall a warning that any such future conduct might result in sanctions. As part of the settlement, Hall has agreed to complete 30 hours of educational training on the nursing profession’s standard of practice.
Erica Roethler of Riceville — The board alleges Roethler was working as a registered nurse at MercyOne Medical Center in New Hampton on July 16, 2025, when she failed to adequately respond to a patient whose condition was rapidly deteriorating. Roethler also failed to transfer the patient to a higher level of care in a timely manner, the board alleged. The patient subsequently required emergency intubation and was in critical condition, according to the board. The board charged Roethler with failing to assess the status of a patient or client, committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare and failing to accurately document the status of a patient.
To settle the case without a hearing, Roethler has agreed to complete 60 hours of educational training related to patient assessments, documentation, professional accountability and ethics. As part of the settlement agreement, Roethler’s license will be placed on probation for two years, during which she will be subject to monitoring.
Billie Munson of Hills — The board alleges Munson incorrectly entered information for a patient into some unspecified record or device and then “ignored warnings” she was given. The board has not disclosed where or when the alleged conduct occurred, other than to say it transpired while she was working in Iowa City.
The board recently charged Munson with professional incompetence, failing to assess or document the status of a patient and committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare. To settle the matter without a hearing, Munson has agreed to a one-month suspension of her license and to complete 30 hours of educational training on the subject of medication administration.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Stitt move creating Oklahoma ballot measure is illegal, critics say
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Gov. Kevin Stitt acted outside his authority when he ordered a state question pertaining to a constitutional convention be placed on a future ballot, a former Oklahoma attorney general said Wednesday. Stitt on Tuesday issued an executive proclamation ordering a special statewide election on April 6, 2027 to consider State Question 848. […]
text:
Gov. Kevin Stitt speaks during a forum with Jenks High School students at the Jenks Public Schools Math and Science Center on Nov. 13, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Gov. Kevin Stitt acted outside his authority when he ordered a state question pertaining to a constitutional convention be placed on a future ballot, a former Oklahoma attorney general said Wednesday.
Stitt on Tuesday issued an executive proclamation ordering a special statewide election on April 6, 2027 to consider State Question 848. Stitt’s state question asks voters to determine if they want legislators to hold a constitutional convention that would give them the power to “to propose alterations, revisions, or amendments” or even propose a new constitution.
But former Oklahoma Attorney General Drew Edmondson said state law does not give the governor the power to place items on the ballot. That authority rests with either the Legislature or the people.
“There should not be anything on the ballot as a result of this order,” said Edmondson, who made a failed bid for governor as a Democrat against Stitt.
Stitt, in a press release, said his ballot measure  enforces a state law which requires voters to have the opportunity every 20 years to request a constitutional convention.
“The Oklahoma Constitution is clear,” Stitt said. “At least every 20 years, Oklahomans have the right to decide whether it’s time to call a constitutional convention. It’s been 56 years since the question was sent to the people. This action puts the question to the people and ensures Oklahomans finally get the opportunity their Constitution guarantees.”
Stitt is correct in saying he is required to enforce state laws, but that doesn’t mean he gets to put something on the ballot, said Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Del City.
“He’s acting unilaterally, outside, frankly, of his authority,” Fugate said.
Stitt’s recourse is to seek a court order to force lawmakers to put the issue to a vote, Fugate said.
“It’s just the latest example of this governor demonstrating just how little he’s learned in his eight years about the separation of powers that is the basis of American government,” Fugate said.
Last session, a proposed state question about holding a constitutional convention passed the House, but House Joint Resolution 1089 failed to secure approval in the Senate. 
Supporters proposed creating a commission that included the governor, Oklahoma’s chief Supreme Court justice, the leaders of the House and the Senate and two members appointed by each legislative chamber. The plan faced criticism that it excluded tribal leaders, Oklahomans not represented by Republicans and did not adequately provide for representation for those outside of government. 
Sen. Shane Jett, R-Shawnee, speaks in favor of his amendment to Senate Joint Resolution 22 on May 13, 2025, in the Senate chamber of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Sen. Shane Jett, R-Shawnee, said Wednesday that a constitutional convention is long overdue.
Jett said the Constitution has a lot of outdated items and needs to reflect today’s values, including banning abortion.
“Protecting Oklahomans from murder absolutely should be step one,” Jett said.
Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, said his team will review the order and determine the next steps. He said that the upper chamber has always been willing to seriously discuss the issue.
“It’s disappointing the governor would issue an executive order of this magnitude without first having a conversation with legislative leadership,” he said.
Numerous other legislative efforts to call a constitutional convention over the years have failed.
Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Oklahoma City, speaks during a special legislative session on Jan. 31, 2024, in the House chamber of the Oklahoma State Capitol. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)
Edmondson said if lawmakers obtain the power to hold one a, they could make major alterations to the state Constitution. Those could include removing the protections of the voter-approved Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust, which is enshrined in the Oklahoma Constitution. 
TSET, which manages billions in public dollars, takes the funds from a settlement  with tobacco companies and invests them. The interest is used for programs, such as tobacco cessation, cancer prevention, physical fitness and healthy lifestyles.
For years lawmakers have attempted to control TSET funds and failed because TSET is in the Constitution, said Edmondson, who is considered the architect of the program.
In addition, the Constitution prohibits lawmakers from passing bills that have multiple subjects. That provision exists so that
lawmakers, who might like one item in a bill but not another, won’t be put in a precarious position of voting for something they don’t like to get something they support in exchange.
The Oklahoma Supreme Court has tossed out numerous bills because they contained more than one subject and were deemed unconstitutional.
“Just to be protective of what we have, I would say that this is a bad idea,” Edmondson said.
Stitt is finishing his final year in office. A new governor could nullify his decision to put the matter to a vote of the people if it doesn’t wind up in litigation.
Stitt and lawmakers over the years have clashed in court over which entity has the power to do what.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: House Armed Services chair urges defense industry at Arkansas summit to rebuild stockpile
description: The U.S. House Armed Services Committee chairman called on the defense industry to help rebuild the country’s military stockpile Wednesday at a summit of aerospace and defense firms that’s drawn protests over Arkansas’ role in supplying deadly weapons to overseas conflicts. Alabama Republican Rep. Mike Rogers joined Arkansas Republican Rep. Steve Womack for[...]
text:
Republican Congressman Mike Rogers (left) and Steve Womack (right) participate in a fireside chat on Aug. 26, 2026 during the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate) The U.S. House Armed Services Committee chairman called on the defense industry to help rebuild the country’s military stockpile Wednesday at a summit of aerospace and defense firms that’s drawn protests over Arkansas’ role in supplying deadly weapons to overseas conflicts.
Alabama Republican Rep. Mike Rogers joined Arkansas Republican Rep. Steve Womack for a discussion on the nation’s defense program during the 2026 Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville Wednesday morning. 
The United States’ defense industry and spending shrank in the decades following the end of the Cold War, Rogers said. But that could change if Congress approves the Trump administration’s request for a $1.5 trillion Defense Department budget, a $445 billion increase over its current funding level.  
“So we’re out now trying to make sure that industry knows there’s opportunity for them to grow and be a part of this buildup that we hope will get us back to a point of peace through strength, where we don’t have to worry about a conflict with China because our capabilities will be such that they don’t want to mess with this country or our allies,” Rogers told reporters.
Hegseth touts Arkansas missile industry in speech at arms factory expansion site

Increased defense spending could benefit Arkansas, where aerospace and defense is the state’s leading export by revenue with more than 150 industrial facilities and operations around the state, according to the Arkansas Economic Development Commission. Aircraft and aircraft parts were Arkansas’ largest category of export in 2024 with more than $950 million in goods exported. 
South Arkansas is a hub for defense contracting with Lockheed Martin, L3Harris and Raytheon facilities all located in the Camden area. 
“Camden, Arkansas is a critical player in our munitions production, and there’s some really neat things going on down there to grow their capabilities,” Rogers said. 
The summit occurs as the Pentagon has been pushing the defense industry to replenish military stockpiles depleted by the war in Iran.
Womack, who represents Arkansas’ 3rd Congressional District, said it will likely take some time for lawmakers to approve a budget. A former House Budget Committee chairman, Womack said Congress should approve a continuing resolution when it returns to work next week that would fund the government into early December. Lawmakers could then work on approving a dozen appropriations bills after the midterm elections. 
A longtime critic of Congress’ budgeting process, Womack this month called the national debt surpassing $40 trillion a national security threat. Womack also agreed with Rogers’ “peace through strength” philosophy, and said squaring the two is problematic. 
“That means if this country wants to be safe, wants to be secure, and if we’re going to meet like a 5% (gross domestic product) to the national security apparatus, then we’re going to have to find the savings or find the resources with which to be able to make that happen without complicating an already difficult deficit and debt situation,” Womack said. 
Participants who attended the summit’s opening reception Tuesday night were greeted by more than three dozen protesters who expressed their displeasure with the state’s connection to the defense industry by holding signs, chanting and waving a Palestinian flag.
The event was organized by Friends of Palestine NWA, a community group founded after the start of the Israel-Hamas war in 2023 who have hosted events to raise awareness about the overseas conflict.
Protestors rally outside the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda)Larry Meyer of Rogers holds protest sign at a demonstration held outside the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Protestors rally outside the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda)Protestors rally outside the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda)Protestors rally outside the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda)Protestors rally outside the Mid-America Aerospace and Defense Summit in Bentonville on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda)
Larry Meyer held a sign that read “Stop Profiting from Genocide” while sitting quitely on a stool with a cane leaning against his leg. Meyer said he wore his black Vietnam Veteran ballcap to signal to veterans there are other veterans who also disapprove of Arkansas’ ties to the defense industry.
“You’ve been in the military, you know what it’s about,” Meyer said. “You don’t want that for your neighbor. You don’t want it in your neighborhood.”
One business Meyer said he doesn’t want in his community is Swarm Aero, a California-based company that manufactures large unmanned drones. Despite pushback from local residents, Swarm Aero opened a facility in south Fayetteville earlier this year, and announced it secured more than $10 million in contracts with the Air Force Research Laboratory this month. 
Tammra Fields with Indivisible NWA, another local advocacy group that supports Arkansans participating in democracy together, said she hoped summit attendees and elected leaders like Womack would take a moment to listen to their concerns.
Camden-made rocket launcher and missiles changing Ukraine conflict

Fields said she realistically didn’t expect any major changes, but she hoped they could plant the seed that “human life is worth more than money.”
“You can’t put a price on it,” Fields said. “Right now that’s what they’re doing is putting a price on human life.” 
Meyer said Arkansas doesn’t need to be courting the military or building bombs and drones. The long-term solution will require a change in administration, someone who listens to the people, said Meyer, who noted the Iran War is unpopular and elected officials, like Womack and Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, aren’t listening. 
Only 31% of Americans support the Iran war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.
Because he’s felt unheard, Meyer, who considers himself an independent, said he’s started to support Hallie Shoffner, a Democrat challenging Cotton. Libertarian Jeff Wadlin is also running for the seat.
“I’ve asked her about these things and she really believes in peace and believes in the American people and not in the American dollar,” he said.
Ultimately, Meyer said protestors like himself and his wife are fighting for their family’s future.
“We’ve been married for 57 years, so we’re going to do this together,” he said. “We want our grandbabies — not so much babies anymore — but we want them to have a better world.”

title: North Dakota regulators approve short-term electric rate increase for MDU
description: The North Dakota Public Service Commission on Wednesday approved a short-term increase in electric rates for customers of Montana-Dakota Utilities while the agency considers a larger increase.  Under the interim rate increase, a typical residential customer will see an increase of about $12.90 per month, or 12.3% over current rates. The rates kick in Tuesday[...]
text:
An electric transmission substation operated by Montana-Dakota Utilities in Bismarck on April 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Public Service Commission on Wednesday approved a short-term increase in electric rates for customers of Montana-Dakota Utilities while the agency considers a larger increase. 
Under the interim rate increase, a typical residential customer will see an increase of about $12.90 per month, or 12.3% over current rates. The rates kick in Tuesday. MDU’s revenue increases by $26.3 million annually with the change.
Commissioner Jill Kringstad said MDU customers should note that the 12.3% increase is not on their entire bill, but only to the basic service charge, the demand charge, and the energy charge — not to other riders customers may see on their bill. 
The company filed for a 14.5% rate increase on June 30. If approved, it would increase revenues by $34.5 million annually. 
Commissioner Sheri Haugen-Hoffart said Wednesday that hearings in the rate case will likely not take place until 2027. 
MDU says the proposed rate increase will cover electric infrastructure improvements and address rising business costs. The company last filed for an increase in 2022.
Travis Jacobson, vice president for regulatory affairs for MDU, told North Dakota lawmakers last month that the rate increase request is not related to data centers it serves or data center projects.
