By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE DOVER — A capacity crowd of 400 caregivers gathered Wednesday at the Rollins Center at Bally’s Dover for the 16th a[...]
text:
Photos taken by George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
The free statewide gathering connected caregivers with 50 service providers while emphasizing that those caring for others also need support, practical resources and time to protect their own health.
By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE
DOVER — A capacity crowd of 400 caregivers gathered Wednesday at the Rollins Center at Bally’s Dover for the 16th annual “Taking Care of YOU” Caregiver Conference.
Registration for the free conference closed after all available spaces were reserved, reflecting the growing demand for caregiver support and resources across Delaware.
Hosted by Easterseals Delaware & Maryland’s Eastern Shore and co-sponsored by the Delaware Division of Services for Aging and Adults with Physical Disabilities, the conference connected caregivers with 50 companies and community organizations providing respite care, health services, assistive technology, legal guidance, education and other resources.
The strong attendance reinforced Easterseals’ position as one of Delaware’s leading sources of support for families caring for seniors and people with disabilities.
Caregivers turn out for help and connections
Jen Batog, director of marketing for Easterseals Delaware & Maryland’s Eastern Shore, said the turnout demonstrated that caregivers are eager to find assistance and connect with people who understand their experiences.
“We were thrilled to see caregivers so excited to seek help, discover new resources and spend the day talking with other caregivers,” Batog said. “This event shows that the number of Delawareans caring for a senior or a loved one with special needs continues to grow, and we are grateful that Easterseals can be there to help.”
Batog thanked the state of Delaware, participating vendors, community partners and Easterseals staff members who worked together to organize the conference and make its resources available to caregivers.
The exhibitors reflected the wide range of services caregivers may need during different stages of their journey. Participants included the newly reorganized Delaware chapter of the Alzheimer’s Association, MeadowWood Behavioral Health Hospital, AARP Delaware, Delaware NeuroRehab, PWW Law, PACE Your LIFE and WeCare at the Milford Wellness Village.
Technology innovator Wisdom and its partner, Griswold Home Care, also participated, along with many other organizations offering health care, in-home assistance, education and community resources.
Taking care of the caregiver
The conference’s “Taking Care of YOU” theme focused on caregiver well-being, balance and self-care — concerns that often receive less attention than the needs of the person receiving care.
The program included a caregiver panel titled “What I Do to Take Care of ME!,” opportunities to meet service providers and a session focused on kindness and self-compassion. The combination of education, peer discussion and access to providers gave caregivers an opportunity to find practical assistance while connecting with others facing similar challenges.
The conference also reflected Easterseals’ broader role in Delaware. Rather than providing a single service, the organization helps families navigate a complicated network of health, disability, aging and community resources.
Its caregiver programs include case management, support groups, educational workshops, respite assistance and demonstrations of technology designed to improve safety and independence.
Burnout is more than being busy
Keynote speaker Heather Volkema, client success manager at Trualta, told caregivers that burnout is not simply the result of having too much to do.
Volkema has more than a decade of health care experience. She began her career working with hospice patients and their families, later developed caregiver-education programs and served as operating director of an in-home care organization before joining Trualta.
She said caregivers frequently balance emotional and physical demands with jobs, family responsibilities and circumstances they cannot control. Those pressures can lead to exhaustion, anxiety, irritability, isolation and feelings of being overwhelmed or taken for granted.
Volkema’s central message was that caregivers must protect their own health if they are going to continue caring effectively for someone else. Many hesitate to seek assistance because they feel guilty, fear rejection or believe they should be able to manage everything alone.
Asking for help, she said, is “a sign of strength and self-awareness,” not an admission of failure.
Practical ways to reduce the pressure
Volkema encouraged caregivers to identify the responsibilities creating the greatest stress and make specific requests of relatives or friends.
Instead of simply asking someone to help, a caregiver could ask a family member to provide transportation to an appointment, purchase groceries or take responsibility for a particular personal-care task.
She also recommended that caregivers establish boundaries, schedule personal time and take even brief breaks when longer periods of respite are unavailable. Support groups, community organizations, professional assistance and online resources can reduce isolation and make difficult responsibilities more manageable.
Caregivers should begin with small steps, share responsibilities whenever possible and recognize that protecting their own health is an essential part of caring for another person, Volkema said.
Support continues throughout the year
Easterseals’ work with caregivers continues beyond the annual conference through its Caregiver Resource Centers in New Castle and at the Milford Wellness Village. Caregivers can speak with case managers, obtain educational materials and receive referrals to programs addressing their particular circumstances.
The organization also offers monthly support groups, free educational workshops and virtual office hours. Its Resource and Technology Demonstration Centers contain hundreds of assistive devices that caregivers can examine before deciding whether a product could make a home safer or help a loved one remain more independent.
Respite programs can give caregivers time away from their daily responsibilities while ensuring that a family member continues receiving appropriate care. Easterseals’ adult day programs and Camp Fairlee also provide structured activities for participants while giving caregivers time to rest, work or handle other responsibilities.
In 2024, Easterseals reported serving more than 7,970 people directly through programs including children’s therapy, adult day services and supported employment. Another 44,280 people were reached through education, training, information and referrals.
The conference’s capacity attendance illustrated why that network matters. Caregivers may perform much of their work privately in homes across Delaware, but Wednesday’s gathering showed that they constitute a large community with shared challenges.
Supporting that community requires more than encouragement. It requires education, respite, practical tools and a trusted organization capable of connecting families with the right assistance at the right time.

name: VTDigger
title: Manchester Selectboard discusses future of Flock cameras
description:
Some town officials and residents are questioning the use of the cameras, which have been in place in Manchester since 2023, concerned about the potential creation of a surveillance-state infrastructure.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Manchester Selectboard discusses future of Flock cameras.
text:
A license plate reader camera on Main Street in Manchester Center seen in June 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Ryan Pacheco was first published in the Manchester Journal on Aug. 25, 2026.
MANCHESTER — The future of Manchester’s controversial use of Flock cameras was discussed but ultimately not resolved at a public selectboard meeting at the Manchester Town Hall on Aug. 18.
Manchester currently has five Flock cameras. According to the surveillance watchdog project deflock.org, they are located on Bonnet Street, Depot Street and three on Main Street: one at the Manchester Center roundabout, one near the intersection of Main and Union streets, and one near the intersection of Main Street and Barnumville Road. 
The cameras have been in place since 2023 and have been used by local law enforcement to assist in previous investigations.
Flock cameras have drawn criticism both locally and nationally for concerns regarding privacy, potential misuse and the creation of surveillance-state infrastructure. Critics point to documented cases where law enforcement officers in other states, with access to the camera data, were able to use the camera’s artificial intelligence-powered license plate tracking to surveil romantic interests for personal reasons. The use of AI further concerns critics, who cite documented cases of people being falsely flagged by the technology and arrested in communities across the country that have implemented it.
Proponents of the technology claim that Flock cameras serve as a valuable tool that law enforcement can use to identify, track and arrest suspects, streamlining enforcement operations and making the job safer.
During the Manchester meeting’s Flock discussion, Manchester Police Chief James Blanchard discussed the positive impacts of the cameras but made clear that he was not there to defend Flock. The meeting concluded with members of the selectboard agreeing to table the issue until an upcoming visit to the police station, intended to further inform their perspectives about the nature of the cameras and their data collection specifics, and look into the possibility of implementing less privacy-invasive options. 
After the meeting the Manchester Journal caught up with Blanchard, who said the town is taking measures to limit data-sharing features and attempting to balance the public safety benefits with avoiding possibly intrusive features.
“My focus is less on the company itself and more on how we use the technology here in Manchester,” said Blanchard. “We control our own data, we decide who has access to it, we’ve intentionally limited the sharing features, and we have policies in place that govern how it can be used. Those are the things we can control. I don’t think any technology should ever be above scrutiny. It’s important to keep evaluating it, and making sure the safeguards are working.” 
Blanchard said the tool is helpful but not particularly necessary.
“No investigative tool is absolutely necessary by itself. Police departments have investigated crimes for decades without automated license plate readers, and if the cameras were no longer available, we would continue to do our job using traditional investigative methods.That said, the cameras have proven to be a valuable investigative tool. They can significantly reduce the time it takes to determine whether a suspect vehicle entered or left the area, allowing officers to focus investigative efforts more efficiently. As for alternatives, there are other companies that offer similar automated license plate reader technology. I think it’s reasonable to evaluate different vendors and determine which product best fits the needs and values of the community,” said Blanchard.
“My support isn’t about Flock in particular, it’s about having an effective investigative tool that helps us investigate crimes, recover stolen vehicles, locate missing or endangered people, and respond to critical incidents where every minute matters, such as child abductions or locating a vulnerable adult with dementia, while respecting privacy and operating under clear policies and oversight,” added Blanchard.
The current contract with Flock, which has been paid through March 2027 at $15,000 this year, cost $12,500 for the first three years of operation and a camera cost of $2,500. During the meeting, it was suggested that the prospect of removing the cameras could wait until the upcoming budget season, rather than prematurely pulling the plug on a service that has already been paid for through the contract year.
Manchester Town Manager Scott Murphy cited his support for the cameras, before stating his preference that removal efforts remain tabled until budget season.
“If I could just interject for a moment, we have talked about data and civil liberties, but not public safety. We have had circumstances in the last few weeks where this system helped us. We don’t want to turn into a Brown University shooting. That is how that person was caught. Our system right now helps us find, and gets notified if there is someone who threatens a town or school official, which has happened within the last two months,” said Murphy.
“We are paid through until the end of March. When we get to budget time in the fall, that would be the time where the selectboard could defund this at that time. We have already paid town money, taxpayer money for this, and I would like to see us stick to the budget season,” added Murphy.
Community members had the opportunity to voice their feelings and concerns during the meeting, with many stating a desire to move away from Flock. Selectboard member Ivan Beattie later stated that he does not believe it would be realistic for a selectboard to expect to make any decision that did not have negative, unforeseen consequences or disappoint some voters.
“I just want to be clear that almost every decision we make at this table causes harm or discomfort for somebody, somewhere. It could be anything from land use regulations, to taxes, to everything we make a decision on. There’s always somebody who if not hurt by it, will at least be made uncomfortable by it. Some have even more major impacts. We have made decisions here at this table that cause people enough harm that they can’t afford to live here or be able to continue to run their business,” said Beattie.
“There is no way to have a no-harm policy. You would never be able to make any decision on any subject. You have to weigh the risk versus the reward. I understand that there is a lot of risk here, in many ways that I do not understand,” added Beattie.
Selectboard member Jonathan West, citing privacy, data and civil liberty concerns — echoed by many of the critics and concerned community members who voiced their concerns at the meeting — brought the issue to the table with hopes of opening a dialogue about rethinking the use of Flock cameras.
West told the Manchester Journal that there was no way to anticipate how advanced and concerning the technology would become when the town decided to install the cameras in 2023.
“I understand why the technology was purchased at the time, but the decision we made four years ago was in a very different technological environment. What began as a very straightforward license plate reading tool has evolved into a much larger, cloud-based network capable surveillance platform. For me, that really changes the question,” said West.
“It is not about whether or not we trust our own police department here in Manchester, which I do, but it is about whether or not Manchester should participate in a system where sensitive information about people traveling through our community is stored through infrastructure that we do not control, using technology that we do not control. We have no idea where this is going to be in a year. I want technology where Manchester can establish boundaries and guardrails that can maintain meaningful control. Right now, what we have with these Flock cameras is not, and it is susceptible,” added West.
West encouraged community members to speak up and voice their opinions regarding the issue at upcoming selectboard meetings, which can be found on the town website.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Like other Florida universities, UNF gets one presidential candidate to consider
description: One finalist has emerged for the University of North Florida presidency, following a trend of state institutions relying on an “exceptional circumstances” carveout to state policy that otherwise requires three or more finalists. The university received 152 applications, search committee chair and trustee Jack Boyle said, calling it a “clear reflection of UNF[...]
text:
University of North Florida students move through the campus in Jacksonville on Oct. 30, 2025. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)One finalist has emerged for the University of North Florida presidency, following a trend of state institutions relying on an “exceptional circumstances” carveout to state policy that otherwise requires three or more finalists.
The university received 152 applications, search committee chair and trustee Jack Boyle said, calling it a “clear reflection of UNF’s momentum and growing national reputation.”
Michael Shannon, now president of University of North Georgia, is the finalist, subject to approval by UNF trustees and the Florida Board of Governors. 
“Dr. Shannon is a strong leader with an impressive background in higher education and military service,” Boyle said. “He is passionate about student success, community engagement and the future of UNF.”
Board of Governors policy requires a presidential search committee “to submit more than two qualified applicants” to the board of trustees “other than in exceptional circumstances.” Additionally, trustees must be notified about the reason why fewer than three candidates are being presented to them.
According to Boyle, in an email sent Tuesday to trustees and forwarded to the Phoenix Wednesday, the search committee selected four finalists and only one was willing to be publicly announced as such. Boyle said the committee returned to the candidate pool but an additional candidate declined to be publicly named, leaving only Shannon.
“While the outcome is a sole finalist, I want to emphasize that this result followed a broad, competitive and deliberative search. The committee considered a deep applicant pool, evaluated semifinalists through a rigorous interview process and took additional steps to determine whether other candidates were willing and able to continue into the next phase,” Boyle wrote to trustees.
The news release announcing Shannon says the institution “reviewed candidates in accordance with” Board of Governors rules and state statute.
“While I understand the hesitancy of some to move forward in the absence of a guarantee, it shows that Dr. Shannon has demonstrated a high level of respect for the public nature of our presidencies in Florida, and a healthy respect for our process,” Board of Governors Chair Alan Levine said in an email response to Boyle, also forwarded to the Phoenix.
Among other institutions to name a sole finalist:

University of West Florida in naming former Education Commissioner Manny Diaz Jr.
Florida International University in naming former Lt. Gov. Jeanette Nuñez.
University of South Florida in naming former UNF President Moez Limayem.
University of Florida in naming former U.S. Sen. Ben Sasse, former University of Michigan President Santa Ono, and former University of Alabama President Stuart Bell.

Florida university applicants for president were previously subject to the state’s “sunshine” laws, meaning their names were not exempt from public disclosure. In 2022, lawmakers and Gov. Ron DeSantis approved keeping applicants’ names private until the final stages.
The fear voiced at that time, and as was the case at least in FIU’s search, was that finalists not named president don’t want their current employer to know they are seeking a new job.
“I congratulate you on attracting such a high-quality candidate, and I find that he is both qualified to serve as President of the University of North Florida, and that he would be an exceptional addition to our cadre of 11 of America’s best university presidents!” Levine wrote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
About Shannon
Shannon has served at UNG since 2023. His background is in aerospace, nuclear, and radiological engineering. 
He earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in 1995 and 1999 and a doctoral degree from Georgia Institute of Technology in 2009.
UNF Presidential Finalist Michael Shannon. (Photo via University of North Florida)
“Jessica and I are excited for the opportunity to spend time with the UNF community, to listen and learn, and to better understand its aspirations for the future,” he said. “There is tremendous momentum here, and I am inspired by what UNF can become and the impact it can continue to make for its students and this region,” Shannon said in a news release.
He spent 20 years in the U.S. Army and later was a faculty member and executive at Georgia Tech. 
The UNF news release highlights a period of growing enrollment and retention at UNG under Shannon’s leadership. 
UNG, a public institution, calls itself “The Military College of Georgia.”
The presidency opened when Limayem left the Jacksonville university to return to University of South Florida as president, where he once served as a dean. The search committee was established in March and a listening session happened in April. 
Former Polk State College President Angela Garcia Falconetti has been serving as interim UNF president.
UNF trustees will interview Shannon and vote on his presidency in mid-September.

name: VTDigger
title: What ‘coal rolling’ at protests tells us about this moment
description:
The practice of belching black smoke while passing protesters mirrors the administration they're demonstrating against.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  What ‘coal rolling’ at protests tells us about this moment.
text:
Dear Editor,
Since Donald Trump was elected for the second time, I have been protesting a great deal, largely in Chittenden County. We get many honks and waves and thumbs-up, as well as the occasional thumbs-down — and, rarely, people flipping the bird. 
I can imagine flipping the bird to protesters with whom I disagree, and I can deal with receiving that gesture, though I don’t think I would do it myself. What bothers me far more is the loud revving of trucks, speeding through intersections and blowing black smoke from their tailpipes, known as coal rolling. This is the practice of modifying a diesel truck so that it belches thick black exhaust on demand. 
It’s jarring and dangerous, and definitely activates a fear response in me and others. Anecdotally, this happens at least once at most protests and sometimes more than that. 
This past weekend, I was at a protest, and there were three incidents of coal rolling, perhaps perpetrated by the same person; I am not sure.
What type of person does this? What type of person wants to scare people and put them in danger? We are peaceful protesters, standing with signs, waving our hands at times to motorists passing by. 
Then I realized this is the type of person Trump is. He does not care that he is putting people in danger. He does not care that he is disruptive and scaring people. I suddenly saw this coal rolling as a metaphor for the current administration. And sadly, I no longer believe the type of person doing the coal rolling is open to facts, reason or compassion. 

READ MORE

What would stop one of these trucks from doing this? Maybe they would respond to law enforcement. Maybe not. 
Just like our president.
Krista Reincke
Shelburne, Vt.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Supreme Court clears the way for two new Nebraska political parties
description: The next step for the new political parties, once certified, is to nominate candidates for Nebraska races.
text:
The seal of the Nebraska Supreme Court. May 4, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party will become official parties in Nebraska after the state Supreme Court unanimously affirmed a Lancaster District Court judge’s decision dismissing objections from the state’s two major parties.
The new parties have submitted their constitutions and leadership to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office. Secretary of State Bob Evnen has informed the Supreme Court that he plans to certify the parties later this week — shortly after the ruling, Evnen certified the parties Wednesday afternoon.
In the case involving the Nebraska Working People Party, Lancaster District Court Judge Darla Ideus had said the Nebraska Democratic Party and National Working Families Party filed their objections too late. In the other case, Ideus ruled that state law doesn’t address the “confusion” that the Republican Party claimed the America First Party’s name would cause for voters.
GOP lawyers sought to give the state’s top election official authority to reject a party or candidate. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“In the absence of any language in the statutory text giving the Secretary of State the broad authority for which the Republican Party argues, we will not recognize such authority,” part of the high court ruling reads. 
The Supreme Court’s order also reaffirms that the Democratic Party filed their objection to the secretary of state past the seven-day window, saying the court found “no merit” to the Democratic Party’s argument that “they are being subjected to an ‘ex post facto objection deadline.’”
Attorneys for the Nebraska Democratic Party and the national Working Families Party had sought to compel Evnen to remove the Nebraska Working People Party because its name is too similar to the Working Families Party.
The next step for the new parties is to nominate candidates for races.
It’s unclear which races will have candidates from these two new parties, but the deadline to file names for the Nov. 3 general election is Sept. 1. Former 2nd Congressional District candidate Kishla Askins told the Omaha World-Herald that she won’t run in Nebraska’s U.S. Senate race on the Working People Party ballot line.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Judge allows independent candidate to remain on ballot in Bucks County state House race
description: The challenge was brought by two local voters who were represented by Adam Bonin, a prominent attorney who primarily works with Democrats on election-related issues.
text:
A voter deposits a mail-in ballot at the drop box outside the Chester County, Pennsylvania, Government Center on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Pennsylvania Capital-Star/Peter Hall)Chris Gambino, an independent candidate who is running in the 143rd state House District in Bucks County, will be allowed to stay on the ballot after a challenge to his nomination papers.
Commonwealth Court Judge Lori Dumas issued the ruling on Tuesday, but did not provide a detailed explanation.
“The judge’s ruling was welcomed news. It confirmed what we knew to be true, real people signed to get an independent on the ballot,” Gambino said. “Now, we can get back to what matters most, spreading the word. People in this district need to know they have a real option this November.”
The challenge was brought by two local voters who were represented by Adam Bonin, a prominent attorney who primarily works with Democrats on election-related issues. Their objection took issue with the signatures Gambino collected, and with the name of the political body Gambino affiliated himself with when filing to run.
In his nomination papers, Gambino listed “Forward Independent” as his political body.
Chris Gambino, independent candidate in the 143rd state House District in Bucks County. (Photo provided by Gambino)
Gambino told the Capital-Star that’s because he views himself as an independent, but consulted with and is endorsed by the state Forward Party.
The center-left organization endorses candidates and officer holders from both major parties, as well as independents who they refer to on their website as “Forward Independents.” 
The objection to Gambino’s nomination papers took issue because Pennsylvania law prohibits political parties from adopting names too similar to one another. It also noted another candidate had already filed as a member of the “Independent Party” in an adjacent district. 
The objection stated, “Gambino could not lawfully include ‘Independent’ as part of the name of his political body.”
“The risk of voter confusion in these adjacent districts is considerable if Gambino is permitted to employ a political body name which he is not legally permitted to use,” it continued.
Gambino called the objection political, and alleged it had little to do with election integrity or the quality of his nomination papers. He has accused the filers of aiming to knock a candidate off the ballot they feared could siphon votes from a Democrat.
The state Forward Party echoed the sentiment.
“The political establishment often succeeds in bullying new voices with the threat of legal fees or personal pressure,” Brian McMurray,” a member of the state party’s executive committee, said in a statement. “Chris Gambino stood up and fought for his rightful place on the ballot and for all those constituents who signed his petition. We’re proud to continue to support Chris’s candidacy as he continues to shine a light on these issues and look forward to more people working to take our ballot back from major parties.”
The Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee lists the 143rd Legislative District as one of its “target races,” backing Democrat Tim Hayes. The District is currently represented by Republican Rep. Shelby Labs.
Bonin, the Democrat-affiliated lawyer who filed the objection, declined to comment on the ruling until a more detailed opinion is issued. He said he had “no interest in getting involved in a tit-for-tat” when asked about Gambino’s allegations his motives were political.
Gambino is not the only third party candidate to have their attempts to appear on the ballot in competitive districts challenged.
In eastern Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, Both Democrats and the progressive Green Party of Pennsylvania have filed petitions to boot Andrew Tupone, who has filed to represent the Green Party, off the ballot.
The Democratic challenge is on technical grounds. But the Green Party warns Tupone is attempting to trick voters by claiming their mantle. Tupone was a registered Republican until earlier this year. PoliticsPA also reported he’s being represented in court by lawyer Wally Zimolong, who has worked with Republicans — including President Donald Trump and Pennsylvania Senator Dave McCormick — in election-related matters in Pennsylvania.
Both major parties view the 7th Congressional District race as potentially decisive in determining control of the U.S. House. It’s currently represented by Republican Ryan Mackenzie, and believed to be among the most competitive House districts in the country.
In Western Pennsylvania’s 60th Legislative District, Libertarian Brian John Peltier requested to remove his name from the ballot after a challenge to some of the signatures he collected.
Bonin was also involved in a successful effort to remove Green Party candidates for governor and lieutenant governor from November’s ballot on the grounds that gubernatorial candidate Tony Dastra did not collect enough valid signatures.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire is one of a kind — and that cuts both ways
description: There are a lot of things that make New Hampshire special, and many who call the Granite State home wouldn’t have it any other way. It begins with our geography, which includes New England’s tallest mountain, its third-largest lake (or second, behind only Maine’s Moosehead Lake if you don’t count the border-crossing Lake Champlain), a […]
text:
Why do so many people love New Hampshire? Just look around. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)There are a lot of things that make New Hampshire special, and many who call the Granite State home wouldn’t have it any other way.
It begins with our geography, which includes New England’s tallest mountain, its third-largest lake (or second, behind only Maine’s Moosehead Lake if you don’t count the border-crossing Lake Champlain), a petite stretch of coastline, and centrality that allows easy access to the natural treasures of neighboring Maine to the east and Vermont to the west, and the cultural treasures of Boston to the south and Montreal to the north. There’s no sales tax here, which is a good thing if you’re not a fan of regressive taxes, and no state income tax, which makes New Hampshire a little piece of heaven for those opposed to public services and supports, and fiscal equity.
Our form of government is unique, too. No other state has an Executive Council quite like New Hampshire’s, which hasn’t really changed since the 18th century, and we have the third-largest legislative body in the English-speaking world. New Hampshire is one of only two states whose governor serves for two years rather than four (the other is Vermont). And, up until recently, New Hampshire held the first presidential primary elections for both the Democratic and Republican contests.
But there are plenty of outlier positions that give this purple state its deep-red tint, and elicit intended insults like “New Hampshire is the Texas (or Mississippi, or Alabama) of New England.”
We’re the only state in the region, for example, that defaults to the $7.25 pittance that is the federal minimum wage (along with, you guessed it, Texas, Mississippi, and Alabama, among others). The common defense for the position is twofold: raising the wage would hurt small businesses and nobody pays the federal minimum wage anyway. I wonder though, if everybody is already paying more than $7.25, how would raising the wage harm small businesses?
And when 10 Northeastern states banded together last year as a counterweight to the Trump administration’s assault on vaccines, which continues to this day, New Hampshire said, “No thanks, we’re good.” The Granite State was, however, happy to be the only New England state to join another coalition: President Donald Trump’s not-so-united “Great American State Fair.”
Despite New Hampshire’s full embrace of booze and gambling (and the sin tax revenue they generate), it remains the only New England state that hasn’t legalized cannabis for recreational use. So much for “Live Free or Die” — and that goes for the state ban on true bars, too.
New Hampshire is also the only state in New England without a state or federally recognized Native American tribe, despite the 12,000-year presence of Abenaki people, but it does recognize ICE: We’re the only state in the region, according to the ACLU, “where local police have entered formal agreements to engage in immigration enforcement.”
Despite the state’s love for and reliance on the natural environment, New Hampshire is also the only New England state without a moratorium on nuclear energy development or a 100% clean energy goal. To punctuate that aversion to clean energy, it is also the only coastal New England state to stand in opposition to offshore wind.
With its state-run school voucher program now free of income limits, New Hampshire has also become the only New England state to opt into the Trump administration’s new voucher program, which provides a $1,700 federal tax break for “individuals who donate to organizations that provide private and religious school scholarships.” While some blue states outside of New England have recently opted in, citing what they see as a potential boon for public schools in addition to private and religious schools, the ultimate aim of the tax credit is not lost on many public school advocates, like New York teachers union leader Melinda Person.
“I expect that public school kids are going to get crumbs, and the biggest winners are going to be those that are trying to privatize public education,” she told Education Week.
Many of these outlier positions are likely cause for celebration for the state’s right-leaning residents — a testament to that “Live Free or Die” spirit of living — but others are primarily reflective of self-inflicted revenue limitations.
For example, I’m not sure how being one of only six states in the country, and the only one in the Northeast, without publicly funded preschool can be touted as credit to the New Hampshire Way. This month, Florida International University published the results of a 20-year study that found, in short, that “students who attended public school pre-K performed better on standardized tests and earned higher grades throughout their academic careers, and that these benefits persisted into adolescence.” 
For years, study after study has reached the same conclusion.
But New Hampshire remains an island, in part because the state’s overreliance on property taxes to fund public education means we can’t even cover the cost of an adequate education for the students we do have, never mind the pre-K kids. That, and all of the other ways New Hampshire resists investing in its future, make the New Hampshire Way read as “I’ve got mine, so you’re on your own.” 
Despite all of this, and I know the list could be much longer, New Hampshire is the place I want to be. It’s where my grandparents wanted to be, my mom, dad, and siblings, too. It’s where my children want to be, if the state will have them, but their generation is getting priced out. Whatever the “New Hampshire Advantage” once promised to its people, the only ones with an advantage now are high-income transplants (including the seasonal variety) drawn to this place because of its natural beauty, great location, and, it seems, the “every man for himself” philosophy reflected in its policies.
What you can feel in the air now, though, is perhaps the dawning realization that too many full-time and longtime New Hampshire residents, regardless of political affiliation, are being left behind or financially chased to more affordable states. “Good riddance” doesn’t seem quite as fashionable on the right as it did even a year or two ago, and that shift was evident during this month’s Veto Day: Lawmakers in both parties overruled Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s rejection of toll and state park fee increases for out-of-state visitors. 
Maybe a stubborn fiscal fog is lifting, slowly.  
And when enough of the people who call New Hampshire home stop buying the cynical political argument that we don’t owe each other anything, watch out.

title: Amazon challenge of data centers’ value could reduce tax payments to Madison County by millions
description: Gov. Tate Reeves signs an Amazon beam during an announcement about an Amazon data center planned for Ridgeland on Thursday, April 9, 2026.
text:
Madison County residents were told that Amazon’s data centers would pay significant property taxes that would boost school and government budgets. But the actual amount may be lower than was projected, with Amazon challenging the tax valuation of its properties.
Amazon Web Services recently challenged the Madison County tax assessor’s valuation of its data centers in Canton claiming that the county’s assessment is too high. The lower assessment Amazon is claiming would mean $5 million to $6 million less in tax dollars next year for schools and the county, according to the tax assessor’s office, down from an estimated payment of over $28 million. 
At an August county Board of Supervisors meeting, the company argued that each of its five buildings is worth $69 million, while the assessor put the value at $292 million per building. 
The board upheld the tax assessor’s valuation but Amazon could appeal the decision to Circuit Court.
In the next few years, Amazon plans to build 34 data centers in Madison County, expected to bring in tens of millions of new tax dollars each year.
READ MORE: Canton and Madison County schools anticipate millions of dollars from Amazon data center fees
Amazon representative James Polianski said the company’s valuation came from industry standards. But Madison County Tax Assessor Norman Cannady, argued that Amazon’s buildings are unique and should be evaluated as such. 
“They’re highly specialized data centers,” Cannady told the board. “And this is not simply a conventional building or shell. The real property includes specialized building systems that are integral to the facility. And their construction involves significant electrical, specialized structural requirements, mechanical cooling, redundancy, and supporting infrastructure. ” 
Cannady said that when calculating the value of a building, Amazon used replacement costs  but his office estimated the actual costs associated with constructing the building. 
Cannady added that Amazon had refused to share data about the actual construction costs with his office. Polianski said that it was company policy not to share those documents as it “may put Amazon at a competitive disadvantage.”

text:
Clouds are shown over the Rhode Island State House early in the evening on Thursday, June 11, 2026, the last night of the legislative session. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)About one in four applicants seeking to be Rhode Island’s first inspector general has the certification required for the job, the commission tasked with selecting finalists revealed Wednesday.
Only eight of the 33 applicants had certification from the Association of Inspectors General, but the panel narrowed the candidates down to six names during a 45-minute meeting at the State House. The six will be invited to be interviewed in public by the Inspector General Advisory Commission in the next few weeks.
The five-member panel has until Sept. 28 to forward three names to Gov. Dan McKee. The commission is made up of Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, Secretary of State Gregg Amore, General Treasurer James Diossa, Ethics Commission Executive Director Jason Gramitt and Will Fletcher, president of the New York-based Association of Inspectors General.
Resumes of the six candidates were not immediately made available. They are:

Stuart Robinson, director of investigations for the Palm Beach County, Florida Office of Inspector General
David Harper, an inspector general for the United States Capitol Police  
Mark Priebe, the acting inspector general for the U.S. Department of Education
Jim Kirdar, an assistant inspector general for investigations for the United States Capitol Police
Steven Kreuger, 1st assistant inspector general for the city of New Orleans
Thomas Whetstone, an analyst for the office of inspector general in Louisville, Kentucky

Background checks on each of the candidates by the Rhode Island State Police will take six to eight weeks, which means they won’t be finished before the Sept. 28 deadline. Commissioners voted to allow the governor to hold off on making a nomination from the finalists until the background checks are complete.
“I’m not going to lose any sleep,” Neronha said.
Once McKee receives the list of three finalists, he has 90 days to pick his nominee and forward the name to the Senate for confirmation.
The new statewide office — tasked with rooting out fraud, waste, abuse, and mismanagement by government agencies — was created in this year’s budget, alongside the commission charged with conducting a nationwide search.
The inspector general may serve for five years and be eligible for reappointment for one term of the same duration. The annual salary range for the position is between $175,000 and $225,000.

title: Staff of two suppressed University of Alabama student magazines go to federal appeals court
description: Attorneys representing student staff at two University of Alabama magazines shut down by the school late last year appealed a lower court ruling to the U.S. 11th Circuit Court of Appeals Wednesday. A U.S. district court in May refused to issue a permanent injunction to halt the suspension of Alice, a magazine that focused on issues […]
text:
The Denny Chimes at the University of Alabama as seen on March 28, 2026.  Student staff of two magazines filed an appeal with the 11th Circuit seeking a preliminary injunction to stop the university from terminating the publications.(Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Attorneys representing student staff at two University of Alabama magazines shut down by the school late last year appealed a lower court ruling to the U.S. 11th Circuit Court of Appeals Wednesday.
A U.S. district court in May refused to issue a permanent injunction to halt the suspension of Alice, a magazine that focused on issues related to women, and Nineteen Fifty-Six, that highlighted subject matters that dealt with the Black student community on campus. The school claimed that continued publication of the magazines could violate federal guidance on diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
“Closing these magazines because of their editorial perspectives related to race and gender perpetuates discrimination, rather than fighting it as the university claims,” said Sam Boyd, senior supervising attorney with the Southern Poverty Law Center, in a astatement. “We urge the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit to protect the First Amendment rights of the students and editors at these magazines and stand up for all students at the University of Alabama and beyond.”
A message was sent to the Alabama Attorney General’s Office and the University of Alabama on Wednesday seeking comment.
The students’ lawsuit alleges that suspending the two student-led publications amounts to viewpoint discrimination and violates their First Amendment protections in the U.S. Constitution.
The university cited a memo sent by the former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi that provided recommendations to remain compliant with policies ordered by President Donald Trump that targeted diversity, equity and inclusion.
U.S. District Judge Edmund LaCour Jr., a former Alabama solicitor general, ruled against the students in May, writing that UA has the authority to regulate content so long as it is not a pretext for viewpoint discrimination and that the university made the selections based on content and not viewpoint.
“A decision to exclude either of them from board affiliation would be a decision based ‘on specific topics … not a decision to discriminate against a ‘sports viewpoint’ or ‘historical viewpoint,’” LaCour wrote in his ruling.
Attorneys representing the student staff said in the appeal that UA terminated support for the publications because of the “missions and perceived demographics of the magazines’ respective audience, relying on its flawed interpretation of the Bondi Memorandum as justification for the suspension.”
The magazines were created to publish the views of people who were aligned with the stated purpose for the creation of the publications.
“It is, in part, these viewpoints communicated through the magazines’ editorial choices that attracted readers to Alice’s and Nineteen Fifty-Six’s content and that the University finds unwelcoming,” the appeal states. “But ‘the government may not insulate a law from charges of viewpoint discrimination by tying censorship to the reaction of the speaker’s audience.”’
Emily Waugh, a student plaintiff in the case, said that Alice provides students with a platform to tell their stories.
“Students should be able to write, create and express themselves without fear that their publications will be silenced simply because a university dislikes a publication’s focus on topics related to gender, sexuality and race,” she said in a news release.
Jermaine Ball, a student plaintiff in the case, said students filed the lawsuit for future students.
“We are fighting not just for us, but for the students who will come after us — because student-operated publications give students the vital opportunity to shape the conversations happening around them while ensuring that a diversity of experiences and perspectives are represented,” he said in a news release. “Protecting student publications means protecting our constitutional right to be heard.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘These are your people.’ Mississippians reflect on their special connection with Dolly Parton
description: A billboard outside of Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium in Jackson honors Dolly Parton on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026.
text:
Even in his first conversation with Dolly Parton in the early 1980s, Sam Haskell leaned on his Mississippi roots to connect with the country music icon.
Haskell’s job, working with the Beverly Hills talent group William Morris Agency, didn’t seem to interest her much. What piqued Parton’s interest, Haskell said, was when he told her he was from a small town called Amory and went to the University of Mississippi.
“She said, ‘Ole Miss, that’s my husband’s favorite football team. Sit down here,’” Haskell recounted to Mississippi Today. “And that’s how our relationship began.”
Years later, Haskell became Parton’s agent as she continued to write and record some of the most famous country songs of the 20th century. The duo expanded their ambition, producing television movies and winning multiple Emmy awards together.
Haskell said their professional success was grounded in their deep friendship, and that friendship was natural from their first meeting because of their shared small-town Southern roots.
“That instant connection brought trust, and brought respect, and brought friendship,” Haskell said. “And that’s what Dolly’s about.”
Sam Haskell, from left, Debbie Allen, Maria S. Schlatter, Hudson Hickman, and Joe Lazarov accept the Emmy for outstanding television movie for “Dolly Parton’s Christmas on the Square” during the third ceremony of the Television Academy’s 2021 Creative Arts Emmy Awards at the L.A. LIVE Event Deck on Sunday, Sept. 12, 2021, in Los Angeles.  Credit: Phil McCarten/Invision/AP
Parton’s fans from the nation’s capital to the Appalachian hollers near where she grew up are mourning her death Tuesday at age 80. Haskell and other Mississippians are reflecting on the connection she had with this state — both her appreciation of the place and the deep admiration she garnered from its people.
Haskell saw Parton’s admiration for Mississippi constantly, especially during the 2000 edition of “Stars Over Mississippi”. It was a biannual Amory charity concert series Haskell hosted to raise money for local college scholarships. Haskell asked Parton to be the headliner of the October concert that year, and she agreed.
Long before the event, Haskell got a call from Parton. She had dialed him up from the landline phone at an ice cream shop in Amory.
“I said, ‘Dolly you don’t have to come to Amory until October,’” Haskell said. “She said, ‘I’m just here to check it out and see where you’re born.’”
Parton gave the phone to the woman working at the ice cream shop, who told Haskell about all the times he would order a double dip chocolate cone from her as a kid. As she handed the phone back to Parton, Haskell realized the woman didn’t recognize the country music icon.
“I go, ‘Dolly, does she not know who you are?’ And she went ‘uh uh,’” Haskell said. “I said, ‘How is that possible? These are your people.’ She said, ‘Oh Sam, I just take off my wig and wear a baggy shirt. Nobody knows who I am. I’ve been up in Walmart all morning.’”
But that October, 10,000 people came out to watch Parton in the “Stars Over Mississippi” concert, according to Haskell.
Amory native Dee Monaghan Howard was one of them. She wasn’t a big country music fan, but she  braved the cold autumn day to watch Parton perform.
“Any time a star comes to Mississippi, it’s a big deal,” Howard said. “Especially a small town like Amory.”
And of the stars Haskell brought to Amory, Howard said Parton was the one she was most excited about.
Dolly Parton performs on NBC’s “Today” show in New York on May 13, 2014.  Credit: AP Photo/Charles Sykes
Hudson Hickman, a New Albany native and producer who worked on television hits such as “The Love Boat” and “MacGyver,” met Parton through Haskell, a longtime friend, 11 years ago. The two approached Hickman about making short movies based on her songs, starting with “Coat of Many Colors.”
Parton always wanted to make more movies, Hickman recalled, and saw her music as a vehicle for that ambition.
“ I was just kind of taken aback because I just thought, here I am, this boy from Mississippi sitting in a room with Dolly Parton, and she’s telling me that the work we’re going to be doing is going to be a dream come true for her,” he said. 
Hickman remembered the legend’s glowing presence on the set of productions including “Dolly Parton’s Mountain Magic Christmas” and “Dolly Parton’s Heartstrings,” dishing out hugs to crew members and knowing everyone by name.
During one “magical” meeting he and Haskell had with Parton, Hickman said she jokingly broke into song mid-conversation. 
“I don’t remember what the song was because I was just sitting there looking into her blue eyes about two feet away from me, thinking: Dolly Parton is singing a song to me,” the producer said. “I said, ‘It is the voice of an angel.'”
Despite the somber moment, Hickman conveyed an overwhelming sense of fortune. 
“Of course I’m sad at her passing, but I’m just struck with a feeling of being grateful,” he said. “I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to work with her and observe up close her genius.
“She spread love wherever she went.”
Dolly Parton performs benefit concert at Marty Stuart’s Congress of Country Music on Aug. 26, 2023, in Philadelphia, Miss.  Credit: Curtis Hilbun
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves ordered flags to be flown at half-staff in honor of Parton.
“An American music icon. An even better person,” Reeves said on social media. “Mississippi is praying for Dolly Parton’s entire family.”
Her renowned philanthropic legacy has had direct benefits for Mississippians. Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library sends books to children across the country, coordinating with dozens of organizations in Mississippi. The Ole Miss Women’s Council for Philanthropy chose Parton for its 2020 Legacy Award, an honor reserved for those who embody the values of philanthropy, leadership and mentorship.
The COVID-19 pandemic delayed Parton from accepting the award until 2022, an event at which she surprised the audience by playing two songs. Elizabeth Randall, chair of the women’s council at the time, told Mississippi Today in an email Wednesday that Parton’s values represented the very best of what the award aims to recognize.
“Even Dolly’s willingness to come to Ole Miss was an act of philanthropy,” Randall said, adding that it was a testament to the friendship between her and Haskell and his wife, Mary. “That was so characteristic of Dolly.  She showed up for people she loved.”
Parton directly lent her public image to others’ charitable efforts as well, including many directed to help Mississippi. Haskell said that when he co-chaired fundraising campaigns for different colleges, including the University of Mississippi, Parton offered to help out in a way only she could.
“She would always tell me, ‘Just auction off a dinner with me,'” Haskell said. “‘Just tell them you can have dinner with Dolly, and see how much you can get.'”
Haskell said those “Dinners with Dolly” would be auctioned for up to $75,000, all of which would go straight to the fundraisers.
Her music made a strong impression on Mississippians across the state, as well. In the fall of 1972, long before Malcolm White started booking artists at Hal & Mal’s restaurant in Jackson, he drove up to Nashville to see a Grateful Dead concert at Vanderbilt’s campus. White hung around the stage after the show, until he had a chance to speak to lead guitarist Jerry Garcia.
White asked Garcia what music he’d been listening to lately. The guitarist told him about a country artist and an album White had never heard of.
“He didn’t miss a beat,” White said. “He turned and said, ‘You got to get Dolly Parton’s ‘Coat of Many Colors.’”
White, who later led the Mississippi Arts Commission, said he bought the album as soon as he got back to Mississippi, and he still has that same copy over 50 years later. “Coat of Many Colors” has since become one of his all-time favorite records. It helped him realize that a lot of the rock music he loved listening to — from the Grateful Dead to Jimi Hendrix — had country roots from artists like Parton.
Country singer Dolly Parton appears at a rehearsal session in Nashville, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 1982.  Credit: AP Photo/Mark Humphrey
The album’s tile song tells the story of Parton as a young girl, when her mother stitched together a coat made of rags. Parton recounts feeling pride despite other schoolchildren mocking her — a message White said resonated with what he saw growing up in rural Stone County.
“It just reminded me of kind of where I came from,” he said. “I think everybody connected with her in their own unique way, because she lived so long and had so many lives and so many careers.”
Parton maintained her Mississippi connections in recent years. On Aug. 26, 2023, she performed a benefit concert at the Congress of Country Music, developed by her friend and country music icon Marty Stuart, in the east Mississippi town of Philadelphia. The venue was smaller than those where Parton normally played, but she felt it was important to do the concert as a favor for Stuart and his wife, country music singer and songwriter Connie Smith.
“The Congress of Country Music benefited greatly from the concert she performed inside our hallowed walls in Philadelphia, Mississippi,” the venue said in a statement. “She did it out of her love for Marty and Connie, with a smile on her face and a song in her heart to help support the cause of preserving the history of country music. We will always love you, Dolly.”
For Haskell, the connection runs deeper than most. Parton was close with much of his family, and Haskell said she would dote on his three young grandchildren. When they were moving from California to Mississippi, she would speak to each of them separately to see how they were handling the big transition.
Just before Parton performed for a 2023 NFL Thanksgiving halftime game dressed as a Dallas Cowboys cheerleader, Haskell said she called him up with a message.
“‘Get those boys in front of the television, because they’re about to see Aunt Dolly like they’ve never seen before,’” Haskell recalled.
Whether reflecting on Parton’s nationally televised performances or the small moments of laughter and wisdom she shared with his family, Haskell is working to figure out how best to mourn his friend of nearly five decades.
“It’s just devastating to our whole family. She was part of our family.”
Dolly Parton speaks to a audience gathered to celebrate the expansion of the Imagination Library of Kentucky at the Lyric Theatre in Lexington, Ky., on Aug. 27, 2024.  Credit: AP Photo/Timothy D. Easley

description: PIERRE — A committee of South Dakota lawmakers endorsed budget increases Wednesday for the Legislative Research Council to cover the anticipated rise in legislator pay. The council manages the Legislature’s day-to-day operations, helps lawmakers draft bills and is responsible for updating the state’s code of laws. Interim Director Jeff Mehlhaff asked for a $[...]
text:
Interim Legislative Research Council Director Jeff Mehlhaff speaks to South Dakota lawmakers during a meeting of the Legislature's Executive Board on Aug. 26, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)PIERRE — A committee of South Dakota lawmakers endorsed budget increases Wednesday for the Legislative Research Council to cover the anticipated rise in legislator pay.
The council manages the Legislature’s day-to-day operations, helps lawmakers draft bills and is responsible for updating the state’s code of laws. Interim Director Jeff Mehlhaff asked for a $29,479 addition to the council’s fiscal year 2027 budget to cover rising lawmaker salaries, and a $96,872 increase in the council’s fiscal year 2028 budget to cover rising lawmaker salaries and “per diem” payments — Latin for “per day” —which help cover lawmakers’ daily living expenses during the annual legislative sessions.
The salary for legislators is 20% of the South Dakota median household income as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau, according to state law. The number is reported in September, Mehlhaff said. He told lawmakers their salary could increase from $15,970 to $16,608 for the legislative session that begins in January — a 4% increase.
The per diem, which lawmakers earn on top of their salary during the session and for committee meetings outside of the session, is tied to rates set by the federal government. The council’s existing budget is based on a per diem of $161.95, but the current per diem is $178. During this year’s 38-day legislative session, the total per diem paid to each lawmaker was $6,764.
Legislators also receive mileage at a rate set by the Bureau of Finance and Management, which is currently 70 cents per mile.
The council’s total anticipated budget for legislator pay during the 2028 fiscal year is about $2.8 million.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: In Tampa, RFK Jr. questions accuracy of report of measles deaths in Pennsylvania
description: TAMPA — U.S. Health & Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. defended the Trump administration’s stances on childhood vaccinations Wednesday, questioning the accuracy of a report that that two unvaccinated Pennsylvania residents have died amid a global measles outbreak. Kennedy is in the middle of series of public events with Florida Republican elect[...]
text:
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Florida U.S. Republican Sen. Ashley Moody at Tampa Bay Boulevard School in Tampa on Aug.26, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — U.S. Health & Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. defended the Trump administration’s stances on childhood vaccinations Wednesday, questioning the accuracy of a report that that two unvaccinated Pennsylvania residents have died amid a global measles outbreak.
Kennedy is in the middle of series of public events with Florida Republican elected officials ahead of November’s midterm elections. He visited Tampa Bay Boulevard Elementary School in Tampa Wednesday with U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody to announce $32.5 million to help schools offer nutritious foods to students and strengthen evidence for nutrition interventions.
Before his media availability with reporters in Tampa, an aide told reporters to ask only about the initiative being introduced.
The Phoenix instead asked about the reported measles deaths in Pennsylvania, which led Gov. Josh Shapiro to say Tuesday that Kennedy’s history of casting doubt on the effectiveness of vaccines “is having a negative impact on communities across America.”
Kennedy responded by questioning whether those two deaths were connected to the measles.
“We’re trying to get information about those two casualties,” he said. “According to a statement that was released by the Lancaster County Commission today, they do not find any measles status in Lancaster County. And they complained that the governor will not give them that information.”
He went on to say that he has sent officials from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to cooperate with state health agencies whenever there’s been a notable measles outbreak, “and the only state that won’t cooperate with us is Pennsylvania and we can’t get any information.”
“The press is all covering this [as] if those measles deaths actually happened, and nobody is doing any critical inquiry to find out – we’re trying to find out whether those deaths actually happened, and we can’t figure that out.”
The Phoenix was unable to contact officials with Lancaster County.
Shapiro did respond, however, and he took exception to Kennedy’s comments.
“According to doctors and medical experts, the MMR vaccine is the best way to protect yourself, your kids, and your community against measles. But we have seen vaccination rates decline on RFK’s watch,” he said in a written statement also posted on X. 
“The correlation is clear: Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others — and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases.”
He did not respond to the assertion the deaths may not be attributable to measles.
‘Anti-vax evangelist’
The group 314 Action, which works to recruit, train, and elect Democratic scientists across all levels of government, responded to Kennedy’s remarks.
“As an anti-vax evangelist and the nation’s alchemist-in-chief, he can’t have it both ways,” said 314 Action President Shaughnessy Naughton.
“Two more Americans are dead because RFK Jr. has spent his career promoting discredited claims, dangerous conspiracies, and quack cures. Instead of using his position as HHS secretary to provide clear advice to Americans on how to keep their children safe from the measles, he has used his megaphone to spread confusion and chaos — with deadly consequences.”
The CDC posted a message Tuesday afternoon on X. “HHS and CDC extend their condolences to the families and communities affected by two measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania.”
Kennedy asserted that the United States is doing a better job in controlling the measles outbreak than any other country. (The U.S. does not make the top 10 list of countries with measles outbreaks, according to the CDC). He attributed the outbreak to the lockdowns that took place during COVID-19.
“We are actually restoring faith in the public health agencies so people will take our advice, and our advice is that people should get the measles vaccination,” he said. “They’re certain communities and certain religious communities that don’t want to do that, and we want to take care of those kids as well.”
The CDC recently released the latest data on national kindergartner vaccination rates. Non-medical exemptions for vaccinations for kindergarteners grew by 17% last year. However, the overwhelming number of parents still vaccinate their children, with vaccination rates at 94.2 % for measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) and polio vaccines.
Florida has 142 reported measles cases, according to the CDC. That ranks the state fifth behind South Carolina (670), Utah (526), Pennsylvania (321), and Virginia (176). A total of 88.9% of Florida students have been vaccinated.
Immigrants blamed
Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor, told CBS’ Face the Nation last weekend that a measles outbreak in Southwest Florida might be happening because of people who have entered the country without documentation.
“If you’re going to go back to the illegal immigration point I made on Face the Nation — there was an illegal immigrant detention facility in Chicago that had a measles outbreak,” he told a Phoenix reporter Tuesday night in St. Petersburg.
“The one in El Paso, Texas, had a measles outbreak. So, you can pretty quickly see for people who’ve come into the country illegally, with no vaccination history at all, it has created flareups in the United States.”
Kennedy’s visit comes the same week the DeSantis administration released a proposed regulation that would eliminate four specific vaccines for public and private K-12 school enrollment in Florida. The HHS secretary said he “wasn’t familiar with the precise proposal.”
He added, “Vaccines are medical interventions … intended to permanently alter your immune system, and so parents ought to have a say in that, and the decision should be between the parents and the physician and not the state.”
Kennedy’s Florida visit will continue Thursday, when he will meet with U.S. Rep. Laurel Lee at a Tampa high school to discuss the recently restored Presidential Fitness Test to encourage young people to stay active and build healthy habits.

title: NC Attorney General Jackson sues to stop Postal Service ballot control
description: State Attorney General Jeff Jackson and other state attorneys general are suing to stop the U.S. Postal Service from controlling who receives absentee ballots.  The lawsuit stems from President Donald Trump’s executive order that would have the US Postal Service block delivery of some absentee ballots.  Under the Postal Service rules, it would direct the […]
text:
Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)State Attorney General Jeff Jackson and other state attorneys general are suing to stop the U.S. Postal Service from controlling who receives absentee ballots. 
The lawsuit stems from President Donald Trump’s executive order that would have the US Postal Service block delivery of some absentee ballots. 
Under the Postal Service rules, it would direct the design of absentee ballot envelopes to include barcodes and require states to compile lists of eligible voters. People not on those lists would not receive absentee ballots. 
The U.S. Supreme Court gave Trump a procedural victory on Monday when the majority issued an emergency opinion that the administration could proceed with plans described in the executive order while lower courts consider legal challenges. 
In the lawsuit filed Wednesday, 24 attorneys general and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro challenged the Postal Service rule as unconstitutional and unlawful. 
The Constitution is clear that states regulate and administer elections, unless Congress says otherwise, the lawsuit says. 
North Carolina is set to start mailing out absentee ballots on Sept. 4. 
Implementation of these rules for the midterm elections means that eligible voters won’t receive their ballots in time for them to be mailed and returned in time to be counted, Jackson’s office said in a news release. 
“The Constitution is clear on this: The states have the authority over elections, not the Postal Service,” Jackson said in a statement. “Not only is this last-minute rule change against the law, but it threatens North Carolinians’ voting rights and imposes a whole new process right before an election. We’re taking the Postal Service to court to stop it.”
The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts.

name: WyoFile
title: Gov. Gordon concerned by ‘aggressive’ DOJ election observers during Wyoming’s primary election
description:
Wyoming’s chief executive has asked the attorney general to look into the nature of the visits. 
The post Gov. Gordon concerned by ‘aggressive’ DOJ election observers during Wyoming’s primary election appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
As the state canvassing board met Wednesday in Cheyenne to certify the results of Wyoming’s primary elections, Gov. Mark Gordon raised concerns about what he described as “aggressive” and “irregular” conduct by federal officials observing last week’s primary elections. 
Two Department of Justice attorneys were dispatched to Laramie County as part of a “monitoring initiative,” according to a department press release published on Aug. 18, Wyoming’s primary election day. 
“This monitoring initiative is aimed at promoting transparency and an open flow of communication between poll observers and election monitors,” the release stated. 
Federal election observers aren’t new to Wyoming, or other states across the country. However, the Trump administration says it’s ramping up those efforts and planning to dispatch about 1,000 staff members across the country in November, when voters will decide who controls Congress. The monitoring follows the Justice Department’s efforts to obtain states’ voter data, which it successfully procured from Wyoming in 2025 with the assistance of Secretary of State Chuck Gray. 
Last week, however, local and state officials were not made aware of federal observers, Gordon said at Wednesday’s meeting, pointing to the Wyoming Office of Homeland Security, the Wyoming Attorney General and the Laramie County Clerk’s Office as being out of the loop. 
“To my knowledge, the U.S. Attorney was unaware of it, and it sounded like the behavior of the observers was a bit aggressive,” Gordon said at Wednesday’s meeting. 
“It just was irregular, and I have asked the attorney general to start looking into, you know, kind of the nature of the visits and all that sort of stuff,” Gordon said. 
Gray disputed the governor’s assertions, pointing to news reports which featured a statement from U.S. Attorney for Wyoming Darin Smith. Several hours after the Justice Department announced its plans to monitor elections in Laramie County, Smith’s office released a separate statement. 
“Voters deserve absolute confidence that their ballots are secure and their voices are heard without interference,” Smith wrote. “We are working alongside local officials to ensure every lawful vote is protected.”
When Gordon asked if the federal government had notified the secretary of state’s office ahead of election day, Elections Division Director Paul Raines said, “our office had received an email, but that’s the extent of communications I’m aware of.” 
Gray also pointed to state law, arguing that it “provides for observation of the election process.” 
Gordon said he wasn’t “objecting to the observers,” but “their behavior seemed to exceed what the authority that Congress had given them was.” That behavior, he said, is why he’s asked the attorney general to “examine that.” 
“I’m not saying anything went wrong or anything else, and I certainly think the conduct of this election was phenomenal,” Gordon said. 
“I feel very strongly about federal government coming in and taking our guns,” he said. “I don’t like that. And I don’t like federal government coming in and taking our voters either.” 
The Department of Justice did not respond to WyoFile’s request for comment by publishing time, nor did the Laramie County Clerk’s Office. 
This is a breaking news story and may be updated.
