text:
(Photo by skynesher/Getty Images)Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson has been traveling the state to build support for his forthcoming legislation to ban cellphones in public schools.
On Wednesday, Ferguson promoted his “away for the day” plan at Pasco High School, where a phone ban is already in place.
“We find it hard to believe that we ever allowed smoking on airplanes, right?” Ferguson said. “That’s how we’ll view cellphones being available in classrooms.”
Under the proposal, cellphones would be banned at public schools from the first bell of the day to the last. The governor expects to release more details on the proposal Sept. 15 and pre-file a governor-requested bill on Dec. 7, the day that prefiling opens for the next legislative session. 
If passed during the session, which begins in January, school districts would be required to implement the policy in September 2027. 
“This is not a punishment, but a way to help us connect with the real world,” said Tais Borge, student board representative at Pasco High School. 
When Borge was a new student, she said it was easy “to pretend I was doing something important on my phone instead of facing the discomfort of talking to people I didn’t know.” 
“When I finally had enough courage to put my phone away and approach people, I discovered that it actually wasn’t as scary as it seemed,” Borge added. 
Washington is behind the curve on restricting cellphones in the classroom. At least 29 other states have implemented some kind of ban, according to Education Week. One national report gave Washington an F grade for its efforts in this area, or lack thereof.
“This is a thing we can do that essentially costs no money that can really improve student learning and achievement all across our state,” Ferguson said. 
When asked why it’s taken Washington so long to pass a statewide cellphone ban, Ferguson said “change is hard” and “getting any bill through the Legislature is hard.”
“I’m not really too focused on the past,” Ferguson said. He expressed optimism his bill will get across the finish line next year. 
The idea isn’t new in Olympia. In fact, lawmakers have proposed it in the Legislature for the past three years. 
Earlier this year, Sen. Marko Liias, D-Edmonds, passed a bill that would have banned cellphones, but it was slimmed down into a study from the superintendent’s office, with a deadline to submit policy recommendations by December 2027.  
Rep. Stephanie McClintock, R-Battleground, has sponsored, but failed to pass, a cellphone ban for the last three sessions. During the past two, her bill did not receive a hearing in the House Education Committee, the first step in passing this kind of legislation. 
And in 2024, state Superintendent Chris Reykdal challenged school districts to enact cellphone bans, and about 75% complied. 
Reykdal has called for a statewide policy, voicing concern that a patchwork of cellphone policies has emerged. He endorsed the governor’s proposal when it was announced in June. 
“Educators, students, and families whose schools have cellphone restrictions report the positive effects on student engagement and learning,” said Katy Payne, chief strategy officer for the superintendent’s office. “A statewide policy … is an important and necessary step.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Rep. Paulino pleads not guilty, due back in court October 7
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: Paulino faces eight counts of wire fraud and three counts of unlawful monetary transactions.
text:
METHUEN REP. FRANCISCO PAULINO was arraigned in federal court Wednesday afternoon, where he pleaded not guilty to all 11 counts brought against him for pandemic benefit fraud.
Paulino faces eight counts of wire fraud and three counts of unlawful monetary transactions. He was indicted Tuesday by a grand jury, arrested Wednesday morning in Lawrence, and arraigned Wednesday afternoon at Moakley Courthouse in Boston.
A federal public defender stood beside Paulino in court Wednesday, Judge David Hennessy notes, since the second-term Democrat’s counsel is based in Washington, DC. The defense attorney listed on Paulino’s indictment could not immediately be reached Wednesday and did not respond to a request for comment.
Hennessy presided, but said that it would be “Cabell’s case,” referencing U.S. Magistrate Judge Donald Cabell.
Paulino is due back in court October 7. He faces Democrat Celina Reyes of Lawrence in the September 1 primary for the 16th Essex District seat he holds.
Some conditions of Paulino’s release include that he only travel within Massachusetts and New Hampshire and get permission to travel anywhere else; that he cannot change his address; that he surrender his passport, which Hennessy confirmed was already seized; and that his remaining business, Madison Tax, temporarily suspend operations and that his clients be notified of the suspension.
US attorneys Kristina Barclay and Christine Wichers requested that the conditions include that Paulino have no access to client accounts or records. Paulino’s counsel agreed. 
To every count read by the judge, Paulino replied, “Not guilty.” 
Paulino exited the front doors of the Moakley Courthouse at about 2:47 p.m., and was met by members of the press. He walked to a nearby parking garage and did not reply to any questions from reporters as he walked.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Crowley says he’s ‘befuddled’ by decision not to charge Musk with election bribery
description: David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin, said at an event Tuesday in Madison that he’s “kind of befuddled” by the decision of the La Crosse County district attorney not to charge Elon Musk with election bribery over the two $1 million checks he gave to voters during Wisconsin’s 2025 state Supreme Court […]
text:
Billionaire businessman Elon Musk at the KI Convention Center on March 30, 2025, in Green Bay, Wisconsin, where he handed out checks to voters as part of his advocacy for Brad Schimel's state Supreme Court race. A local prosecutor assigned to investigate whether Musk violated Wisconsin law with the stunt said this week he would not prosecute Musk. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin, said at an event Tuesday in Madison that he’s “kind of befuddled” by the decision of the La Crosse County district attorney not to charge Elon Musk with election bribery over the two $1 million checks he gave to voters during Wisconsin’s 2025 state Supreme Court race. 
In July, the Wisconsin Elections Commission voted 5-1 to refer two complaints to the Brown County District Attorney’s office, alleging that Musk’s handouts — which he announced went to people who could prove they had already voted in the election — amounted to bribery. 
During the 2025 election, Musk pumped more than $20 million into the race on behalf of conservative Brad Schimel. Schimel lost to Justice Susan Crawford partially because of backlash to Musk’s involvement at the peak of opposition to his DOGE effort to cut federal government spending for President Donald Trump.
La Crosse County DA Tim Gruenke was appointed as a special prosecutor to decide if charges should be brought against Musk, the world’s richest man. 
In a letter released Tuesday, Gruenke said that while Musk posted on X, the platform he owns, that the checks he handed out at a political rally in Green Bay would go to people who had cast absentee ballots, he said in a later post that entrance to the rally was limited to people who had signed a petition opposing “activist judges.” 
“In this case, without the famous name attached and the large dollar amounts involved, it is a simple case of a poorly worded statement that was corrected and brought into compliance with the law,” Gruenke wrote. “Because the original post was poorly worded and ambiguous about who would receive money, and the second post corrected the problem relatively quickly, I do not believe a jury would convict Elon Musk of a crime.” 
At the Tuesday event, Crowley said he hadn’t read Gruenke’s reasoning but that Musk had “publicly talked about giving a million dollars to folks to actually go vote, which is absolutely against the law in Wisconsin.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: New tariffs on Canada heighten Michigan Democrats’ affordability attacks on Trump, GOP
description: Michigan Democrats are taking aim at a new round of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump on Canada as talks between the two nations failed, with Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel saying the tariffs will “throw Michigan’s economy into chaos.” “Donald Trump has once again escalated his reckless trade war with Canada, allowing trade […]
text:
A truck celebrating Gordie Howe completes the first processing through the Canadian Border Services Agency at the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Michigan Democrats are taking aim at a new round of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump on Canada as talks between the two nations failed, with Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel saying the tariffs will “throw Michigan’s economy into chaos.”
“Donald Trump has once again escalated his reckless trade war with Canada, allowing trade talks to collapse while imposing sweeping 50% tariffs on Michigan’s largest trading partner,” Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), the running mate for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson, said in a press conference on Wednesday. “These tariffs will have real consequences for people across Michigan. They will drive up costs at a time when families are already struggling with the costs of groceries, gas, and housing, and they will put even more pressure on Michigan’s manufacturers and small businesses that depend on strong trade with Canada.”
This week, Trump said that the United States would impose 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods — about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors, the Associated Press reports. 
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would retaliate beginning on Sept. 8, according to the AP, with measures affecting the steel, dairy, appliance and agricultural equipment sectors. 
“These reckless tariffs on Canada threaten to spike costs even higher and will kill more jobs and wreak even greater havoc on our manufacturing industry,” Hertel said. 
Processing lanes at the Canadian border entry at the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Similarly, Christina Hines, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, emphasized her district’s proximity to Ontario and border crossings in the Detroit and Sarnia areas and the importance of strong business relationships with Canada. 
“When politicians make decisions that hurt these industries, it literally impacts our ability to put food on the table, to buy back-to-school supplies to cover our medical bills, and yeah, to pay for gas,” Hines said. “We have already been seeing the fallout from these tariffs on Michigan families, on workers, and on businesses. Prices are up, profit sharing is down, and the auto industry is facing record losses. Our small businesses are fighting just to stay open.”
Criticism coming from Michigan Democrats goes beyond Trump himself, as Democratic candidates around the state are using the tariffs to attack their counterparts for supporting the policies of the head of their party. 
“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price. Michiganders were already paying over $3,200 a year for tariffs—over 50% more than the rest of the country because we share a border with Canada—and we have a president who cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis,” U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said in a press release. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long. Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber stamp them.”
Trump holds a chart while speaking during an event in the Rose Garden at the White House on April 2, 2025. Touting the event as “Liberation Day,” Trump announced sweeping tariffs on imported goods. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
El-Sayed’s U.S. Senate opponent, Mike Rogers, has stood by the Trump administration’s policies, including on tariffs, throughout his campaign, and has not commented to multiple reporters on the most recent round of tariffs. A spokesperson for Rogers’ campaign didn’t provide a direct comment on the new tariffs, but instead pointed the Advance to previous statements made by the former congressman on Michigan manufacturing and prescription drug prices.
Brinks similarly sought to implicate U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), the Republican nominee for governor, citing his past votes in Congress supporting other tariffs proposed by Trump.
“John James has enthusiastically supported Trump’s trade war. In February, James voted in favor of tariffs on Canada,” Brinks said. “He had a chance to stand up for Michigan families, workers, and business, but instead he chose to support Trump’s tariff agenda. And now, as these new 50% tariffs take effect, John James has not said a single word, and that silence matters.”
In response to Democrats’ criticism of the tariffs, James campaign spokesperson Alyvia Bailey said affordability concerns should be more tied to Democratic leadership at the state-level rather than the Trump administration. 
“Michigan ranks 46th in the nation overall — 45 states are doing better than we are on education, on the economy, on infrastructure and we all have the same President. We have lost over 20,000 manufacturing jobs. Energy costs are crushing families and small businesses across this state,” Bailey said. “This is the result of eight years of failed Democrat leadership that Michiganders simply cannot afford anymore.”
Tariffs were also a sticking point in the July opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, with the threat of tariffs leading Canadian officials to cancel a joint ceremony between the two countries and host one of their own in Windsor, without any American government officials present.
Doug Ford, the Premier of Ontario, speaks at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the Gordie Howe International Bridge. July 24, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford emphasized in his speech at that event the importance of a cooperative relationship between Canada and the United States — and explicitly said that Trump has challenged that relationship through his overall foreign policy, including tariffs.  
“Team Canada has never been more united,” Ford said. “Ontario will be ready to respond to any new American tariffs, will not back down, and will negotiate from a position of strength as a top trading partner.”
Meanwhile, Trump has defended his decision to levy the tariffs — while also suggesting renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in the wake of crumbling trade negotiations between the two nations.


4:55 pmThis story has been updated with additional information from the Rogers' campaign.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico immigrant advocates warn of ‘uptick’ in ICE arrests in Albuquerque
description: Members of New Mexico immigration advocacy groups and local elected officials warned Wednesday that they’ve seen a sharp increase in federal immigration arrests in Albuquerque in recent days.
text:
Albuquerque City Councilor Stephanie Telles joined immigration advocacy group El Centro de Igualdad y Derechos at a news conference Aug. 26, 2026, to warn of a reported increase in federal immigration arrests in the city in recent days. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Members of New Mexico immigration advocacy groups and local elected officials warned Wednesday that they’ve seen a sharp increase in federal immigration arrests in Albuquerque in recent days.
Within the last week or so, group leaders said they’ve received far more phone calls than usual from relatives of Albuquerque residents arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At a news conference Wednesday, members of one such organization, El Centro de Igualdad y Derechos, read anonymous testimonials from four Albuquerque residents recounting the impacts of ICE arrests of their family members Aug. 21. 
Leaders of El Centro and New Mexico Immigrant Law Center told Source NM on Wednesday that they do not have an estimate of exactly how many people ICE may have arrested in the city in recent days, but they’re certain ICE has stepped up arrests based on the increase in calls to their respective organizations. 
El Centro’s Fabiola Landeros, an immigrant rights organizer, told Source NM her organization has heard from approximately eight family members in the last week; Immigration attorney Emily Alvarez at the Immigrant Law Center said her organization has heard from approximately six family members recently.  
“It’s a huge uptick,” Alvarez told Source NM. “We’re dealing with fuzzy numbers, like I’m not able to say exactly, but I think it’s probably the biggest surge in enforcement we’ve seen in our state” since President Donald Trump began his second term in January 2025. 
An ICE spokesperson did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Wednesday. 
ICE periodically releases detention data that gives some insight into its arrest activity, including snapshots of detainee populations at facilities in New Mexico and elsewhere. The agency’s most recent data release regarding its July activities shows the agency detained 51,000 people, the highest monthly total during Trump’s second term. 
Albuquerque resident Marisol Meyer-DrioVínto shared a video of what she said was one such ICE arrest Sunday morning in Albuquerque, in which ICE officers in unmarked vehicles and masks pulled over a man driving a work truck around 8:30 a.m. in a tree-lined neighborhood. 
Albuquerque resident Marisol Meyer-DrioVínto provided Source NM a video of what she said was a federal immigration arrest of a man in a work truck Aug. 23, 2026, in her neighborhood. (Screenshot of video, courtesy Marisol Meyer-DrioVínto)
The reported ICE activity in Albuquerque in recent days follows reports of increased arrests last week in Santa Fe, where advocates said ICE arrested as many as 16 people over the course of several days. Those arrests prompted outcry from local and federal elected officials, as well as a local protest. 
During the news conference Wednesday, Albuquerque City Councilor Stephanie Telles touted the city’s ordinance aimed at protecting immigrants from being arrested in sensitive places like clinics or hospitals and ICE from using city resources to make arrests. She said she has also heard from constituents about an uptick in ICE activity. 
“We’re not seeing big raids throughout the city, but we are hearing again and again about cars with blackened windows following our family members throughout the city, with the intent to intimidate and to strike fear,” she said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: As $2.7B interchange project advances, federal officials praise SC for clearing up congestion
description: Work to replace bridges near "malfunction junction," a snarled interchange near Columbia, is underway, state transportation officials said.
text:
Construction on a new bridge over the Saluda River is underway beside Interstate 20 in Lexington, S.C., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)LEXINGTON — A major Columbia-area interchange project to unsnarl a notorious bottleneck is a prime example of the work states should be doing to improve roadways, a federal highway official said Wednesday.
Known among locals as “malfunction junction,” Carolina Crossroads is one of the biggest road projects in state history, said Secretary of Transportation Justin Powell. The $2.7 billion improvements are expected to wrap up in 2034, according to the transportation agency.
Sean McMaster, administrator of the Federal Highway Administration, and Justin Powell, state secretary of transportation, talk to reporters about the Carolina Crossroads project in Lexington, S.C., on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
Roughly 90% of that money will come from the federal government, Powell said. The remaining 10% will come from the state’s coffers.
Focused on increasing safety and decreasing traffic, the project is what President Donald Trump wants to see under the Freedom to Drive Initiative launched in April, said Sean McMaster, who oversees the Federal Highway Administration (and is no relation to South Carolina’s governor).
“This is the exact type of project that we want to help and support and invest in,” McMaster said.
The program doesn’t come with specific funding. Rather, the federal Department of Transportation asked governors to pick out the worst chokepoints for congestion in their states and outline what they’re doing to fix it.
The federal agency then offers solutions to high-traffic areas, as well as technical support in getting projects done, McMaster said. The idea is that extra expertise will allow states to finish improvements that may seem daunting, especially in places that get federal funding, he said.
“Where you have that federal work, you should have federal support,” McMaster said.
Completing the Carolina Crossroads construction is vital not just to local commuters who take that route to work or school every day but to national companies that drive shipments across South Carolina, McMaster said. An estimated 134,000 people drive through the corridor every day, according to the Department of Transportation.
Price increases in construction across the country have caused the cost of the project to increase by about $1 billion. Facing delays, the agency changed the order of construction to speed up the process, Powell said.
Federal and state help will “continue to make it a priority for us” to finish the crossroads and ensure everything gets done, he said.
“We have been able to make tremendous progress,” Powell said.
What is the project?
The Carolina Crossroads project long predates the federal program. Construction began in 2021, and the project is on the third of five phases.
The first phase involved building a new interchange where Interstate 126 meets Colonial Life Boulevard, removing the Interstate 26 interchange and Bush River Road and lengthening the exit ramp off I-26 onto Sunset Boulevard.
The next step was to make improvements to interchanges on Interstate 20 and remove an unnecessary ramp, making it easier for drivers to get on and off the interstate.
A project meant to reduce traffic and improve safety on interstate interchanges near Columbia, S.C., is undergoing the third of five phases. (Graphic courtesy of the South Carolina Department of Transportation)
Workers are in the process of replacing two interstate bridges, where I-20 crosses the Saluda River and a railroad track. This week, work will begin to construct new bridges on I-26 over the river and railroad, along with replacing parts of I-126.
The “big boy” of the project is a complete overhaul of the interchange where I-20 and I-26 meet, Powell said.
That will involve redoing the roads where drivers get on and off the interstate, ending the need to get across multiple lanes of traffic, which makes the area especially prone to accidents, he said.
By the end of the project, workers will have widened both I-20 and I-26 from three lanes to four for 14 miles and extended the roads’ shoulders, giving emergency vehicles more space to maneuver around traffic when responding to accidents.
Carolina Crossroads is an especially challenging undertaking, Powell said. Not only is it expensive and time-consuming, but the agency must deal with multiple major arteries, railroad crossings, bridges and a large number of utility lines, he said.
The interchange has been a thorn in drivers’ sides for decades, Powell said. He heard complaints about the area when he first got his driver’s license, he said.
Support, both monetary and otherwise, from the federal government and state politicians made the difference in actually getting the work done, he said.
In 2017, state legislators raised the gas tax by 12 cents per gallon over six years, putting the additional money toward fixing deteriorating roads and bridges.
A law passed this year is meant to speed up the construction process by allowing the transportation department to take over environmental permitting from the federal government and build “choice lanes,” where drivers can opt to pay a toll and bypass congestion.
“We are tackling some of the biggest, hardest projects that South Carolina has and making a difference on it right now,” Powell said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Judge denies Minnesota’s extradition request for ICE agent Christian Castro
description: A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday denied the state of Minnesota’s extradition request of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro, who is charged in the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in north Minneapolis in January.  The ruling means Castro is likely to be released from a Texas jail. Hennepin County issued a warrant […]
text:
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison announces a lawsuit on March 24, 2026, against the Trump administration seeking evidence in the shootings of three people by federal immigration agents. On Wednesday, a federal judge denied Minnesota’s extradition request of an ICE agent Christian Castro charged in a Jan. 14 shooting in north Minneapolis. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday denied the state of Minnesota’s extradition request of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro, who is charged in the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in north Minneapolis in January. 
The ruling means Castro is likely to be released from a Texas jail.
Hennepin County issued a warrant for Castro’s arrest on May 18, and he was arrested by Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, on May 29. Since then, Castro has been incarcerated in a county jail and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has declined to sign the paperwork ordering his extradition to Minnesota. 
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison sued Abbott on Aug. 18 under a federal law prohibiting law enforcement agencies from detaining fugitives awaiting extradition for longer than 90 days. Ellison asked the judge to require Abbott to sign the extradition papers, or at least block Castro’s release, ahead of the 90-day deadline on Thursday. 
U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas did neither, denying Ellison’s request outright. 
“This case should concern officials and citizens of every state,” Ellison said in a statement Wednesday. “If a governor can delay extraditions and cherry-pick cases according to their political tastes, then no state will be able to hold fugitive criminals accountable.”
Rodriguez Jr. ruled that Abbott has not violated the Constitution, the Extradition Act or the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act.
“Those statutes prescribe no deadline for a governor of the asylum state to complete an investigation and either sign a rendition warrant or deny the request,” Rodriguez Jr. wrote in his order.
Ellison had argued that governors have no discretion when it comes to facilitating extraditions. 
A unanimous 1987 Supreme Court ruling said “the commands of the Extradition Clause are mandatory, and afford no discretion to the executive officers or courts of the asylum state.”
Rodriguez Jr. cited a section of the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act, a state law in Minnesota and Texas, which authorizes the governor of the asylum state to call on authorities in the demanding state to investigate the circumstances of the subject of the extradition request, and whether he ought to be surrendered.
The Extradition Act also allows governors to consider “whether the petitioner is a fugitive.”
Abbott’s office argued that Castro is not a fugitive because he didn’t flee Minnesota — he was reassigned to Texas by ICE. 
AG Keith Ellison sues Texas governor for failure to extradite ICE agent charged with assault

Castro is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. He is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg. Three other people were inside the house, according to Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, and one of the bullets was found embedded in the wall of a child’s bedroom. 
Castro is also charged with falsely reporting a crime because he accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire. The U.S. Department of Justice charged the two immigrant men with assaulting a federal agent, but the charges were dropped after surveillance footage disproved Castro’s claims.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Judge says western Wisconsin CAFO permit doesn’t do enough to protect groundwater
description: A western Wisconsin factory dairy farm will have to restart its effort to obtain a permit after an administrative law judge found this week that the Department of Natural Resource’s initial approval failed to do enough to protect local groundwater.  The Ridge Breeze Dairy in Pierce County has applied to expand from a 1,700 cow […]
text:
Opponents of the Ridge Breeze Dairy expansion watch the contested case hearing in March against the farm’s permit in Eau Claire. An administrative law judge this week found that the Department of Natural Resources didn't do enough to protect groundwater and sent the permit back to the agency. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)A western Wisconsin factory dairy farm will have to restart its effort to obtain a permit after an administrative law judge found this week that the Department of Natural Resource’s initial approval failed to do enough to protect local groundwater. 
The Ridge Breeze Dairy in Pierce County has applied to expand from a 1,700 cow farm to 6,500 cows. The expansion is expected to generate 78 million gallons of manure per year. Since proposing the expansion, residents in the region have protested against the effects that operating the largest factory farm in western Wisconsin will have on the local water. 
Residents worked to oppose the DNR’s permitting decision along each step and previously raised concerns that the dairy had named properties as sites for planned manure spreading although those property owners were never contacted. 
Last year, the DNR granted a modified permit for the dairy to expand. Pierce County residents and a western Wisconsin-based advocacy group petitioned for a contested case hearing against the DNR decision. That hearing was held in Eau Claire in March.
In a decision issued Monday, Administrative Law Judge Angela Chaput Foy stated that the permit doesn’t do enough to ensure Ridge Breeze’s operations protect the groundwater. 
Communities across western Wisconsin have struggled with nitrate contamination in their groundwater, the source of drinking water for much of rural Wisconsin. Nitrate contamination has been linked to blue-baby syndrome, thyroid disease and colon cancer. 
The driftless region of western Wisconsin is especially vulnerable to groundwater contamination because parts of the bedrock are susceptible to sinkholes and fracturing. 
Residents in the area have pointed to the vulnerability of streams near the Ridge Breeze site and previous manure spills on farms operated by Ridge Breeze’s owner, Breeze Dairy Group. 
“The permit conditions set Ridge Breeze up for anticipated compliance, they also command compliance, but the permit lacks a mechanism to verify compliance,” Foy wrote. “By omitting a mechanism to verify actual compliance, the (DNR) has issued a mandate while simultaneously denying itself the tools or data necessary to know whether that mandate is broken.”
Foy’s order sends the permit back to the DNR, which will now have to include additional conditions in the permit to detect if the state’s groundwater standards are being violated. This could include installing monitoring wells, a step that some farmers and agricultural industry advocates say is too costly. 
“Protecting groundwater requires more than simply telling Ridge Breeze to comply with the law,” said Adam Voskuil, senior staff attorney at Midwest Environmental Advocates. “The DNR must have a way to determine whether those requirements are actually being followed and whether groundwater is being protected. This ruling makes clear that paper promises are not enough.”
Residents who spent years fighting the farm’s expansion celebrated the decision.
“This victory started when a handful of neighbors sat down together in the a garage down the road from Ridge Breeze and decided that we wouldn’t let our health, water, or our farming heritage be treated as an afterthought,” said Ty Fisher, a Pierce County farmer and member of Grassroots Organizing Western Wisconsin. “For more than three years, locals here have organized, testified, and stood together. This decision proves that when we’re organized we can take on corporate ag special interests and win.”
Gregg Wolf, the CEO of Breeze Dairy Group, told Wisconsin Public Radio that the farm has already completed construction on the new buildings for the expansion and currently houses about 6,000 cows. He said the decision will simply require the farm to do more to reassure neighbors that the state’s rules are being followed. 
“Ridge Breeze has always been committed to protecting the environment and all the resources, including groundwater, and doing things properly, and having enough acres to manage nutrients properly,” Wolf said. “This is just another avenue that is going to be added to the permit to reassure the community that’s being achieved.”
Danny Akenson, an organizer with GROWW, said that successfully overturning a DNR permit decision is a sign that residents opposed to the influence of factory farms over state policy can secure wins. 
“This isn’t the end of our fight, but it is proof that our organizing works,” Akenson said. “We’re going to celebrate what Pierce County residents won, and then we’re going to carry that people power to Madison to win the common sense accountability we need over corporate factory farms like these. Communities in Wisconsin shouldn’t have to fight for protections one factory farm and one permit at a time.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Supreme Court to rule on question of bias in ballot measure language
description: The Alaska Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Tuesday on legal challenges brought by two groups on opposing sides of the state’s current ranked choice voting election system. The two groups of plaintiffs brought lawsuits against the Alaska Division of Elections challenging the language of a ballot measure, set to go before voters in November, […]
text:
Voters at Anchorage City Hall wait in line to cast their ballots on Nov. 4, 2024, the day before Election Day. City hall, in downtown Anchorage, was one of the designated early voting sites in the state's largest city. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Tuesday on legal challenges brought by two groups on opposing sides of the state’s current ranked choice voting election system. The two groups of plaintiffs brought lawsuits against the Alaska Division of Elections challenging the language of a ballot measure, set to go before voters in November, abolishing the voting method along with other changes. 
Ballot Measure 2, which will appear on the ballot as 24ESEG, would overhaul the state’s elections system via three major components: repeal ranked choice voting; rescind the nonpartisan, open primary system; and repeal campaign disclosure rules enacted by voters in 2020.
A Superior Court ruled in June that the state’s ballot summary was “true and impartial,” siding with the Alaska Division of Elections, overseen by Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom.
Plaintiffs have appealed that decision to the Alaska Supreme Court, which is expected to issue a fast-tracked ruling before a division deadline of Sept. 2 to print general election ballots.     

The Alaska Supreme Court heard oral arguments in a case challenging the Alaska Division of Elections’ language of a ballot measure that would overhaul state elections on Aug. 25, 2026. (Screenshot of hearing via Gavel Alaska)
 

One group of plaintiffs are represented by attorney Scott Kendall, an author of the 2020 ballot measure implementing Alaska’s ranked choice voting and open primary system. They argued that the current ballot measure language is unclear, partisan and omits serious implications of the repeal effort.
The other group of plaintiffs, drafters of the measure, is called the “Repeal Now” campaign. The measure’s primary sponsors are Republican gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson, along with former Anchorage library director Judy Eledge and former Alaska House Rep. Ken McCarty of Eagle River. 
In court, attorneys representing Repeal Now argued against the lawsuits being combined and for a series of language changes, including changing of the term “repeal,” which they say is not easily understood by voters, and the term “true source” of campaign disclosures as “inflammatory partisan suasion.” 
Under Alaska law, the division is required to prepare a ballot measure with a “true and impartial” summary of the proposed law. It must be “free from misleading tendency, whether the amplification, of omission, or of fallacy, and … must contain no partisan coloring.”
In the June ruling, a Superior Court judge found the division fulfilled its legal obligation and “if ballot summary language is true and impartial, the Court will not invalidate the language just because better language could be written.” 
On Tuesday, the division, represented by attorney Laura Fox with the Alaska Department of Law, argued that the ballot language could be edited thousands of ways, but the division fulfilled its legal duty and prepared the ballot with a “true and impartial” summary and title.  
“This case is not an editing exercise,” Fox argued. “We’re not assembled here as a big team of editors trying to polish a piece of writing by committee, as fun as that might be. Instead, the question here is just whether the summary clears the basic hurdle of being true and impartial. Because it does, the court should affirm.”
The Alaska Supreme Court justices will either uphold the lower court’s decision or order the division to revise the language. They’re expected to issue a ruling before Sept. 2 and then follow sometime later with an extended legal opinion. 
Timeline of ballot measure and legal challenges
Alaska voters narrowly rejected a similar initiative to repeal ranked choice voting in 2024. Proponents quickly restarted the campaign in 2025, collecting more than 34,000 signatures to again place the question on the ballot in 2026. The division first published the ballot language last December. 
A group of plaintiffs represented by Kendall filed a lawsuit challenging the ballot language in January. Plaintiffs include Anchorage Republican Sen. Cathy Giessel, AFL-CIO union president Joelle Hall, and former member of the Juneau Borough Assembly and vice president of Ocean Conservancy ‘Wáahlaal Gidaak Barbara Blake. They argued the ballot language was biased and inaccurate.
The division subsequently revised the ballot language in February with significant changes to the title and summary. The plaintiffs dropped the lawsuit without prejudice, according to court documents. 
In mid-February, the Repeal Now group filed a lawsuit challenging the new language, arguing “opponents got their preferred language” adding the term “repeal” three times, and the summary was not “true and impartial.”
In March, the division again revised the title of the ballot measure, adding the phrase “ending ranked-choice general elections.”
Giessel and fellow plaintiffs filed a new lawsuit, and the two suits were consolidated by the Superior Court judge in April. 
Both groups of plaintiffs filed suggested ballot language with the court, and the state filed a motion defending their ballot language. 
Court arguments
On Tuesday, Kendall argued before the Supreme Court that the ballot language should be a clear map for voters to understand what the measure does.
“But the state’s language here isn’t a map. It’s effectively an obstacle course where a voter can only understand Ballot Measure 2 by doing independent research outside the four corners of the ballot language. The state’s language is unclear, contains partisan suasion, and omits details that would give voters significant pause,” he said.
In particular, Kendall raised concerns the ballot measure does not clarify that if passed, nonpartisan or Independent voters would be excluded from voting in party primaries, unless registered with that party.  
“It fails to make clear that Ballot Measure 2 specifically empowers political parties at the stroke of a pen to make it illegal for undeclared and nonpartisans to vote in the primary election,” he said. “I think voters need to be put on notice, especially the two-thirds of voters that don’t belong to either party, that you may not be able to vote in the primary election at all.”
Kendall also argued the language related to campaign finance disclosure rules was inadequate, and fails to give details of the implications.
If passed, the measure would repeal campaign disclosure rules and limits enacted by the ballot measure passed in 2020, including rules that individuals and entities who contribute more than $2,000 to candidates or campaigns must disclose the true source, as defined by law.
Attorney Julie Pack, representing the group of plaintiffs with the Repeal Now campaign and supporting the ballot measure, argued against the use of the term “repeal” because she said campaigners collecting signatures for the ballot measure found voters were not familiar with the term. 
“Many people do not use that word on a daily basis. It’s not common parlance. It is for lawyers. It’s not for people who are not lawyers, and it’s not a term that is readily understood,” she said.
Justices pushed back, pointing out the term is in the name of their organization.
“My organization named itself before they canvassed, got all the signatures, talked to over 31,000 Alaskans, and understood that repeal is not a word that lots of people understand,” she replied. “So my client named itself before it learned that repeal is a term that’s mildly to moderately sophisticated.”
“There is no need to use words that are sophisticated,” she added. “When ‘redo,’ ‘remove,’ ‘undo,’ ‘get rid of’ are perfectly fine, and they would protect Alaskan voters’ right to know what they’re voting on.”
Pack also raised concerns with the term “true source” related to campaign finance disclosures, and argued the measure would maintain “open primaries.”
Arguing on behalf of the Division of Elections, Fox urged the justices to reject the plaintiffs arguments and affirm the lower court’s decision that the division met its legal obligations and should print the ballot measure as is.



Ballot Measure 2 as currently proposed by the Alaska Division of Elections:
An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked Choice-General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws
This Act would get rid of open primary elections, where all candidates appear on one ballot. It would also get rid of ranked-choice general elections. It would bring back political party primaries and single-choice general elections. It would also repeal certain campaign finance rules that were added by a 2020 ballot measure. 
Elections would occur as they did before open primaries and ranked choice elections. In the primary election, voters would choose a party’s ballot, unless prohibited by the party’s bylaws. They would only vote for candidates on that ballot. The winning candidates from each primary would be the party’s nominee. In the general election, voters would vote for only one candidate in each race. Party petitions, special runoff elections, and other processes would return. 
This act would repeal campaign finance rules that were passed in 2020. It would remove the limits on donations to joint campaigns for governor and lieutenant governor. It would remove limits and disclosure rules under current law, including for digital ads, out-of-state donations, undisclosed donations and the true source of donations. It would change the meaning of a campaign expenditure and remove some fines.
Should this initiative become law?

name: Maine Morning Star
title: More ICE arrests so far this year in Maine than previous two combined, data show
description: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has arrested more people in the state so far in 2026 than in the previous two years combined, and those arrests have overwhelmingly been people who did not have criminal convictions. These are takeaways from the latest data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a Freedom of Information Act […]
text:
FBI agents outside Ocean Seafood Depot during an immigration raid, Newark, NJ, Wednesday, Nov. 19, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has arrested more people in the state so far in 2026 than in the previous two years combined, and those arrests have overwhelmingly been people who did not have criminal convictions.
These are takeaways from the latest data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit, analyzed by Maine Morning Star. 
The new data from March 3 to Aug. 6 provide an updated look at every ICE encounter, detainer request, arrest, book-in to detention, and removal since October 2022, though it has some limitations. For example, around 5% of arrests do not show where they were made.
Of 491 ICE arrests that led to detentions in Maine through Aug. 6 of this year, nearly 89% were people who did not have criminal convictions. 
ICE apprehended 56 people convicted of a crime — but only one person with a violent criminal conviction — and 97 people with pending criminal charges. Comparatively, the agency detained 338 people this year with no criminal conviction or charge.
“When you look at the data, there’s no public safety risk justification that can be found,” said Ruben Torres, advocacy and policy manager for the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition. 
The highest monthly arrests this year was 208 in January, when ICE launched a large-scale operation in the state. There was another spike of 74 arrests in June. 
Most of these arrests were of people originally from Angola, followed by Ecuador, Guatemala and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, respectively. 
On Saturday, ICE arrested a Cumberland County Jail corrections officer originally from Angola. He is at least the fourth jail officer in Maine arrested during President Donald Trump’s second term so far. 
Looking at all arrests, including those that did not result in detention stays, there were 497 in Maine this year. 
The data also confirm ICE’s operations are happening across the state, with apprehensions reported in 50 different towns so far in 2026. 
The Trump administration has indicated that federal operations are expected to ramp up. 
Border czar Tom Homan recently told state Rep. Mike Soboleski, R-Phillips, “You’re going to see a lot more enforcement action in Maine,” which he noted was because of the recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for immigrants from Haiti and Syria. 
Nationally, federal immigration agents arrested nearly 50,000 people in July, higher than any previous month in the Trump administration, according to the data obtained through records requests. That’s slightly lower than the total reported directly by the feds. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, had told Maine Morning Star’s sister site Stateline that it arrested about 51,000 immigrants in July. 
In the latest data ICE shared via the FOIA lawsuit, the agency removed the “apprehension type” field, which had specified whether an arrest was listed as targeted or collateral, so insight into whether those detained by ICE were the subject of targeted field operations cannot be determined.  
According to Lisa Parisio, policy director of the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, the majority of arrests in recent months are “happening as people are leaving their house to go to work, leaving work at the end of the day, and then the more random racial profiling pick ups.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho federal judge narrows abortion ruling to only protect Boise doctor who filed lawsuit
description: An Idaho federal judge has narrowed a previous ruling that had allowed abortions to protect a mother’s health or from self-harm to only apply to the Boise doctor who challenged the law.  The narrowed ruling issued Tuesday means that Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and the Ada County prosecutor may not enforce Idaho’s felony abortion […]
text:
U.S. District Judge B. Lynn Winmill ruled earlier this month that the state of Idaho cannot regulate abortion when a pregnancy threatens a person’s physical or mental health. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the decision, and the judge narrowed the ruling to only apply to the Boise doctor that challenged the law. (Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun)An Idaho federal judge has narrowed a previous ruling that had allowed abortions to protect a mother’s health or from self-harm to only apply to the Boise doctor who challenged the law. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office)
The narrowed ruling issued Tuesday means that Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and the Ada County prosecutor may not enforce Idaho’s felony abortion ban in cases where Dr. Stacy Seyb administered the procedure because of serious risk of harm due to physical health or mental health concerns. 
Other doctors in Idaho will still be subject to Idaho’s near-total ban, which includes an exception to prevent the death of the mother but does not include exceptions to prevent her death from self-harm. Elective abortions are completely banned in Idaho. 
U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill narrowed the ruling at the request of Labrador, who argued in a recent motion that Winmill’s initial decision was too broad. 
Winmill agreed with Labrador, citing recent U.S. Supreme Court cases that ruled federal judges in most situations cannot issue “universal injunctions,” which block laws nationwide or more broadly than against the plaintiffs in the case. 
Winmill wrote “an injunction limited to Dr. Seyb will suffice to address the alleged harm.” 
Seyb was represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice in the case. 
“While we are disappointed in the ruling, it is only one step in the litigation,” Tanya Pellegrini, co-director of litigation at the Lawyering Project said in an emailed statement. “We will continue to stand with providers and their patients to ensure it is safe to be pregnant in Idaho.” 
Seyb is a maternal-fetal medicine physician who specializes in high-risk pregnancies. He challenged Idaho’s laws, testifying in court that he’s sent patients out of state amid health concerns because he did not feel comfortable providing abortions under the limited exceptions in Idaho’s law. 
Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows an abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license.
The judge denied Labrador’s request to fully eliminate the block on enforcement. Winmill remained “persuaded” abortions to protect women against serious health risks or against death from self-harm were constitutionally protected. 
Labrador on Aug. 20 also appealed Winmill’s decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing the block defies the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico could see $924M in ‘new money’ largely due to Iran war driving up oil prices
description: New Mexico Legislative Finance Committee analysts on Aug. 26, 2026, told state lawmakers that rising oil costs from the ongoing Iran war are contributing to the hundreds of millions of dollars of “new money” for the state’s budget.
text:
New Mexico Legislative Finance Committee analysts on Aug. 26, 2026, told state lawmakers that rising oil costs from the ongoing Iran war are contributing to the hundreds of millions of dollars of “new money” for the state’s budget. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico’s coffers could see $924 million in “new money” in the next fiscal year largely from rising oil costs as a result of the war in Iran, economists told state lawmakers Wednesday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state’s total amount of recurring revenue increased from about $14 billion in the last fiscal year to $14.5 billion in the current fiscal year, according to a new Legislative Finance Committee report. It’s expected to grow again to nearly $14.8 billion in the next fiscal year starting next summer, the report said.
While the conflict overseas has been difficult to predict at times, even a small change in the price of oil has significant impacts for New Mexico. A $1 change in the price of a New Mexico barrel of oil has a nearly $56.5 million impact on state revenue, according to the new report.
In addition to high levels of oil and gas revenue, the state’s investments in various trust funds are also behind the revenue growth. In fact, LFC Chief Economist Ismael Torres told lawmakers that nearly 40% of the state’s general fund comes from out-of-state sources such as oil and gas and investments.
“That’s a really incredible thing that New Mexico benefits from that other states don’t get,” Torres said at Wednesday’s interim Legislative Finance Committee hearing in Farmington.
While the Iran war, oil and gas prices and investment dividends are driving huge growth, Torres cautioned lawmakers that those factors could overshadow areas of the state’s economy that are otherwise weak, such as high levels of inflation and low levels of workforce participation.
Torres advised lawmakers to pay close attention to the Early Childhood Trust fund, which Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced in 2020 with a balance of about $320 million. Earlier this year, the fund had grown to more than $11 billion and pays for New Mexico’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program.
Previously, excess revenue from oil and gas taxes and federal mineral leasing went to a number of state trust funds, including the Early Childhood Trust fund. State leaders have expanded the number of trust funds that receive that income now, Torres said, meaning the Early Childhood Trust Fund stands to receive a smaller portion of the excess tax revenue.
In addition to decreasing the trust fund’s share of revenue, state lawmakers have also increasingly made withdrawals from the fund, Torres said.
“I think there was this general thinking that the Early Childhood Trust Fund had an excess of money,” Torres said. “What we’re seeing is with those two changes, that may no longer be the case.”
He added that there is not an immediate risk to the fund’s balance and that lawmakers have several years to improve its revenue stream.
Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces), who chairs the interim Legislative Finance Committee, said he and his fellow lawmakers should expect unique challenges when overseeing something as unique as the state’s universal childcare program.
“The administration deserves very strong recognition for a wide range of initiatives,” he said. “I think this is a very important perhaps strong yellow light for all of us to see that we are, really, one of one in the country.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: In a divided Tennessee, Dollywood – and Dolly – shows us who we could be
description: (This commentary was originally published in Nov. 26, 2025.) We are a nation and state divided — on paper anyway.  The last presidential election was decided by a difference of 1.47%. Here in Tennessee, Republicans have held a supermajority in the state legislature for a little over a decade, but when given a choice statewide […]
text:
Singer, songwriter and state icon Dolly Parton -- and her theme park, Dollywood -- provide something on which politically divided Tennesseans can agree. 
(Photo: Dollywood)(This commentary was originally published in Nov. 26, 2025.)
We are a nation and state divided — on paper anyway. 
The last presidential election was decided by a difference of 1.47%. Here in Tennessee, Republicans have held a supermajority in the state legislature for a little over a decade, but when given a choice statewide and gerrymandering is taken out, our Tennessee values are a lot less divided than our legislature would reflect. 
If you look at polling from Vanderbilt University, Tennesseans in clear majorities support recreational marijuana, red-flag gun safety laws and exceptions to the abortion ban for rape, incest and the life of the mother. Our Republican-dominated legislature may not do anything about it, but Tennesseans agree on a lot more than we disagree. 
Another thing Tennesseans share in wide agreement? Our complete adoration of singer, songwriter and Tennessee icon Dolly Parton.
Dolly Parton is universally beloved. In 2019, the New York Times put out a piece entitled “Is There Anything We Can All Agree On? Yes: Dolly Parton”  She has always been a topic that could be brought up around a dinner table or in mixed company and agreement can be found. 



				We’d be a lot better off if we saw each other the way we all see Dolly: familiar, human and worth a little grace.			


I grew up on the Cumberland Plateau and spent my birthdays as a child at Dollywood. When I came out as gay, she was an affirming fixture. I have always called her the patron saint of the Southern Queer. She was never loud about her politics — what once was a Tennessee tradition — but she always made clear where she stood. On her recent “Rockstar” album, a song called “World on Fire” has a line:
“Greedy politicians, present and past / They wouldn’t know the truth if it bit ’em in the ass.”
If there’s ever been a bipartisan sentiment, that is it. 
I’m so tired of division. Not disagreement, which is healthy and part of a strong democracy, but the division that we’ve been experiencing for so many years. I’m a Tennessean. I have Republican friends. I don’t always understand their lifestyle or reasoning for their beliefs, but they are my neighbors and I’d really like to be able to acknowledge their presence in Kroger without wondering if I’m safe to be around them.
We’d be a lot better off if we saw each other the way we all see Dolly: familiar, human and worth a little grace.
We’re starting to see a crop of gubernatorial candidates pop up. When the Aftyn Behn/Matt Van Epps race for Congressional District 7 winds up in a few days, I expect we’ll see some more. For any of the candidates, considering running, I’d point them to Dollywood.
Writer Eric Patton gets a little Dolly Parton magic — and cinnamon sugar in his beard. (Photo: Submitted)
As someone who holds a Dollywood season pass, I’m there often. I love going, because the experience reminds me of what is still good about my home. On any given trip to Dollywood, you’ll see a church youth group next to a group of gay men decked out in Dolly shirts. Newlyweds on their honeymoon shopping for knicknacks. A rural family on the only vacation they can afford this year waiting patiently for their time on board Wild Eagle. Immigrants and folks here on tourist visas, all excited to share in home-spun fun and down-home goodness. 
We need a governor who will ask themself “What Would Dolly Do?” She’d make sure Tennesseans are fed, educated and breathing clean air. She’d make sure they’re getting along. She’d make sure they have access to cutting edge healthcare they don’t have to go into bankruptcy over. She’d make sure if something bad happened to their community, she’d fight for everything she could to take care of them. 
I know we can’t get Dolly herself, but whoever it’ll be needs to be as close as we can get. 
Our next governor should be someone who understands the job is more than policy. It’s about restoring the basic social adhesive we’ve let disintegrate. We will need someone who can walk through Dollywood and see the same thing you’ll see on any given day there: people worth loving, not voters worth dividing. 
And if we’re in need of something to get us to stick together, I’m pretty sure there’s some cinnamon sugar stuck in my beard from the last trip.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Meta to pay North Carolina up to $645 million dollars in landmark settlement
description: Attorney General Jeff Jackson announced Wednesday that Meta, the owner of Instagram and Facebook, will pay North Carolina up to $645 million and make major safety upgrades in a landmark case involving 47 states. Meta will pay $17.1 billion to the states in the second-largest state consumer protection settlement in history. “My wife and I […]
text:
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson (center) with Superintendent Mo Green and Governor Josh Stein discuss the new safety upgrades Meta will be required to make in a settlement that will secure up to $645 million for North Carolina. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Attorney General Jeff Jackson announced Wednesday that Meta, the owner of Instagram and Facebook, will pay North Carolina up to $645 million and make major safety upgrades in a landmark case involving 47 states. Meta will pay $17.1 billion to the states in the second-largest state consumer protection settlement in history.
“My wife and I have three kids. We know how hard it is to argue with them about screen time,” said Jackson.”Part of the reason that it’s so hard is because parents are up against technology that has been engineered specifically to capture and hold their child’s attention.”
In 2023, under then-Attorney General Josh Stein, the state joined 32 states in suing Meta for violating consumer protection laws with apps designed to increase the amount of time children spent using them, while downplaying the risks. The states also alleged that Meta collected data from minors without the consent of their parents.
Based on Meta’s own internal documents, researchers knew which features hooked children into coming back, and which delivered a dopamine response. They knew millions of children were using Meta’s platforms between midnight and 4 a.m., interrupting their sleep cycle and disrupting their school days. Other documents showed Meta’s own employees warned that face-altering filters could mimic cosmetic surgery and contribute to body-image issues for its teenage users.
Jackson said under the agreement, new measures will be installed to help keep children under 13 off Meta’s platforms. The apps will now have default time limits, giving parents more control over how much screen time their children have.
“The data shows that nearly 80% of teens use social media for over two hours a day and nearly 40% of them use social media for over five hours a day,” said Jackson. “That is why the first provision is a daily limit of two hours.”
Graphic courtesy of the NC Department of Justice
Parents will have the power to change the settings by dialing them up or dialing them down, but that is a decision that will be made by parents, said Jackson. Parents will also be able to get data about their teen’s social media use.
One of the most disruptive ways social media can impact a young person is by interrupting their sleep.
“A significant percentage of young people are using social media after midnight. The new default will be that those feeds will be disabled between midnight and 6 a.m.,” said Jackson.
Meta will be required to establish a new school mode to prevent push notifications from going off during school hours.
Teens won’t see the number of likes and reactions on posts by default. 
There will also be scrolling pauses to prevent hours and hours of mindless scrolling by teens. Under this safety feature, after 15 minutes of continually using an app like Facebook or Instagram, a pop-ad will discourage the young person from scrolling endlessly.
Gov. Stein said as attorney general he spoke with fearful parents worried about video content that encouraged weight loss and glorified eating disorders. Stein said the tech giant knew about those harms and did nothing to protect children from becoming more addicted to the apps.
“Meta did not see children as precious beings to be protected. They saw them as dollar signs to be exploited,” said Stein at Wednesday’s press conference.
In a statement, Meta said that all social media platforms should embrace the changes agreed to in the settlement.
“For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard, to ensure teens use social media in a healthy and responsible way,” said Meta in a press release.
 Settlement money will target youth mental health 
North Carolina is guaranteed at least $451 million from Meta to resolve the claims, with an additional $194 million coming to North Carolina when the states have adopted industry-wide adoption of the protections.
“I look forward to working with the attorney general, with the legislature, Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Public Instruction to figure out how we can best utilize these dollars to make the biggest impact on improving young people’s mental health,” Stein said.
The states alleged that approximately 22 million teens log on to Instagram daily in the U.S.  And teens who exceed three hours a day on social media face double the risk of anxiety and depression, according to the U.S. Surgeon General.
North Carolina Superintendent of Public Instruction Mo Green said the settlement will go a long way toward improving mental health support for students.
“We don’t have nearly enough programs or personnel like school counselors, school social workers, school psychologists, and school nurses,” said Green.
North Carolina high schoolers show improvements in mental health 

The recommended ratio for school social workers is one for every 250 students. In North Carolina, it’s currently one for every 1,055 students. For school psychologists the recommended ratio is one for every 250 students. Last year in North Carolina, the ratio of psychologists was one to every 1,954 students.
“The resources and commitment announced today are essential to closing these gaps,” said Green.
The first payment of $45 million to North Carolina will come 30 days after the settlement is approved by the court. Additional installments will be made every Jan. 15th.
Jackson said the speed of this settlement will mean child safety upgrades are made to Meta’s platforms in months rather than after years of costly litigation.
“It would risk losing another generation, and that’s a risk we cannot take,” said Jackson.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi to get at least $189 million from landmark Meta settlement
description: Attorney General Lynn Fitch speaks during a press conference announcing the distribution of Ring doorbells and outdoor cameras to support domestic violence survivors Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, in Jackson. The initiative is a partnership with Ring, an Amazon company, and the Mississippi Coalition Against Domestic Violence.
text:
Mississippi will receive $189 million over 10 years as a result of a settlement announced on Wednesday between technology giant Meta and 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories that sued claiming the company’s social media platforms harmed children.
The agreement nationwide comes out to $17.1 billion, the largest settlement ever paid by a social media company to states. Mississippi’s share of the payout was announced by Attorney General Lynn Fitch, who said Meta is setting a new standard for the way children engage with social media.
“Big Tech has been conducting a social experiment on our children’s developing brains by making platforms that were purposefully addictive and preyed on children’s greatest vulnerabilities,” Fitch said in a statement. “A generation of children have suffered, but with this settlement we spark transformational changes to protect children from harm.” 
The settlement was reached after a bipartisan, nationwide investigation that nearly every attorney general in the country participated in, starting in 2021. The investigation found that Meta designed Instagram’s features to addict children, documented the resulting mental health harm and showed how the company failed to warn parents, Fitch said.
In 2023, states around the country, including Mississippi, began filing parallel lawsuits and joint federal complaints. This settlement resolves those cases, Fitch said. 
Legal experts said the settlement could be a watershed moment for the social media industry, which has largely escaped regulation in response to how its platforms could harm children.
Under the settlement, Meta will be required to institute a series of safety features on Instagram and Facebook, including daily time limits on platform use by children, blocks restricting children’s access during school hours, age verification and a range of content control.
States could receive more money if other platforms agree to similar settlements. Meta will initially pay about $12 billion, but it will pay an additional $5 billion if fellow tech companies Snap, TikTok and YouTube also agree to financial penalties and changes to make the platforms safer for children. If that happens, Mississippi could receive $270 million over 10 years, Fitch said.
Meta’s legal team said on Wednesday that the company negotiated the terms of its settlement to require the other companies to join Meta in developing industry standards, the New York Times reported. 
Michelle Williams, Fitch’s chief of staff, said Mississippi will next month file a consent decree in Hinds County Circuit Court, where the state lawsuit played out. That filing will contain more information on how the money will be spent in Mississippi.
Compared to other federal settlements such as the one that mandated spending to fight opioid addiction, the Meta settlement gives Mississippi more leeway on how it chooses to spend the money, Williams said. But the settlement does include guidance that the money should be spent on youth mental health and similar initiatives.
Fitch filed a similar suit against TikTok, and litigation in that case is ongoing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT awarded $10 million federal grant to improve K-3 literacy
description: It’s the latest in a string of recent investments CT has made in improving literacy outcomes, set in motion by the Right to Read law in 2021.
text:
Connecticut’s efforts to improve K-3 literacy are getting a boost through a $10 million grant from the U.S. Department of Education. Gov. Ned Lamont and Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker announced the competitive award in a press release this week. 
The money comes through the federal Education Innovation and Research program and will support the CT Research and Innovation in Literacy Intervention project, a five-year effort to bring small group reading intervention to more elementary schools in the state. UConn’s Neag School of Education, Fordham University and the nonprofit HILL for Literacy are also participating.
“We are pleased to have secured this competitive grant, which builds upon the significant investments Connecticut has made to strengthen literacy instruction and support our educators,” Russell-Tucker said.
It’s the latest in a string of recent investments Connecticut has made in improving literacy outcomes, which were set in motion by the landmark Right to Read law in 2021.
That law mandated that districts switch to curricula aligned with the science of reading and changed how teachers screen for literacy delays. School leaders from a range of districts have spoken positively about the changes, but teacher training remains a major bottleneck — one the $10 million grant aims to help address.
The money will train teachers at participating schools on Enhanced Core Reading Instruction, in which small groups of students hone key early literacy skills like identifying sounds and forming them into words. 
According to a spokesperson with the Connecticut State Department of Education, “The approach provides teachers with clear, structured routines for modeling these skills, giving students opportunities to practice, and providing immediate feedback to students to assist in their learning.”
As the name implies, there is a research component, as well. The program will study what happens when teachers pair Enhanced Core Reading Instruction with positive behavioral supports — that is, explicitly teaching certain behaviors and giving affirmation when students demonstrate them. It will also examine how Enhanced Core Reading Instruction compares to “typical small-group reading intervention” and what is needed to scale it effectively across schools.
For now, the state’s focus remains squarely on the K-3 age group. One reason for that: Detecting and addressing reading delays is much easier at younger ages. By the time a child reaches fourth grade, it becomes exponentially harder to catch up, and delayed literacy begins to have a bigger impact on academic performance overall. 
State leaders have expressed the hope that, by catching reading delays earlier, schools can keep more kids in general education settings and out of — often costly and sometimes isolating — special education programs.
According to the press release, Connecticut has spent about $41 million in recent years on K-3 literacy. This latest grant boosts that by about 25%.
There is interest in the state to expand literacy support for students in grades 4-9, as well. A bill to do so drew positive feedback from advocates and education leaders, but the final product scaled the effort back substantially amid concerns about capacity and cost.

title: Colorado to get $615 million in settlement over youth Facebook, Instagram addiction case
description: The tech giant Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, agreed Wednesday to pay over $17 billion in a nationwide settlement in a case centered on youth social media addiction. The deal includes over $615 million over nine years for Colorado, which was one of 51 states and territories to sue the company in 2023. “The […]
text:
Phil Weiser, Colorado attorney general, speaks to supporters in Denver in June. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)The tech giant Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, agreed Wednesday to pay over $17 billion in a nationwide settlement in a case centered on youth social media addiction. The deal includes over $615 million over nine years for Colorado, which was one of 51 states and territories to sue the company in 2023.
“The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order,” Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat, said in a statement. “The focus of this case was to protect our kids — stopping notifications and alerts at night and when they are in school, encouraging them to take breaks from social media, protecting them against harmful features, implementing age assurance technology, and more. Today’s action is an important step forward and I welcome Meta’s decision to accept responsibility and to collaborate with the multistate coalition to protect kids who deserve better.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The action ends a federal trial in the U.S. Northern District of California that began last week, where Colorado and a handful of other states argued that Meta intentionally designed its social media apps to be addictive to children and knew about those risks without telling the public. The states also alleged that Meta routinely collected data on children younger than 13 without their parents’ consent, a violation of the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act. Colorado will get an additional $11.4 million for those data privacy claims.
Meta denies the allegations in the lawsuit.



Quotation







The focus of this case was to protect our kids — stopping notifications and alerts at night and when they are in school, encouraging them to take breaks from social media, protecting them against harmful features, implementing age assurance technology, and more.


– Phil Weiser, Colorado attorney general


The settlement requires Meta to make certain changes to its products, including daily limits for children, limited app notifications during typical school hours and stronger age verification measures. Teens will also be able to opt into a non-algorithmic social media feed and turn off auto-play features. Meta will ban image filters for teens that replicate cosmetic surgery. Likes and reactions to posts will be invisible to younger users.
“The framework we’ve negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away.”
The Colorado money will go “directly to protecting and restoring the mental health and safety of Colorado children,” according to Weiser’s office. The settlement says the money can pay for things like crisis intervention services, after school programs, outdoor activities, digital literacy counselors and youth mental health programming.
The settlement must still be approved by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers.
