name: Colorado Newsline
title: Mail ballots will go out as normal despite Supreme Court ruling, Colorado election officials say
description: Colorado election officials expect the November election to proceed without interruption despite attempts from the Trump administration to change how states use mail ballots.  ​The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed to move forward an executive order from President Donald Trump that would upend mail voting, saying a lower court issued an injunction prematu[...]
text:
Volunteers at the Denver Clerk and Recorder's office atrium check and organize primary ballots on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Colorado election officials expect the November election to proceed without interruption despite attempts from the Trump administration to change how states use mail ballots. 
​The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed to move forward an executive order from President Donald Trump that would upend mail voting, saying a lower court issued an injunction prematurely. The injunction had come in a lawsuit filed by 23 Democratic-led states, including Colorado, and Washington, D.C., but another injunction that blocks implementation of the order ahead of November remains in place. That order, which applies nationwide, stemmed from a lawsuit filed by several voter advocacy organizations.  
Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said the Supreme Court ruling is largely procedural because the lower-court judge issued a ruling before any party was harmed, and it will not result in any immediate changes to Colorado’s election system. 
“The most important thing voters should know is that the decision (Monday) doesn’t change anything for November,” Crane said. “It’s my expectation that the election this year coming up in November will be as it always has been in Colorado with the current model.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat running for attorney general, said in a statement Monday that she’s disappointed with the Supreme Court’s decision but that Colorado and other states will “fight back” when the federal government tries to implement the executive order. Her office did not respond to questions from Newsline Tuesday about what that means or any preparations for possible federal interference with mail ballots in Colorado. 
The Supreme Court’s conservative majority did not rule on the constitutionality of Trump’s executive order. The order called on the Postal Service to create a rule that requires states to notify the agency if they intend to send ballots through the mail. States would have to submit a list of voters planning to vote by mail. The Postal Service would not deliver ballots in states that refuse to submit a list. It would also require that ballot envelopes have a unique barcode that allows the Postal Service to identify which voter mailed the ballot. 
The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani of Massachusetts said in an order that the Postal Service publishing the rule runs contrary to her Aug. 11 nationwide injunction. The rule states that none of its provisions will be implemented for the 2026 election as long as Talwani’s injunction remains in effect. 



Quotation







Colorado voters should know that nothing has changed about their ability to vote in November.


– Steve Schleiker, El Paso County clerk 


Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat running for governor, on Wednesday joined other Democrat states in a new lawsuit challenging the Postal Service rule. 
“States determine the time, place and manner of elections — not the president,” Weiser said in a statement. “And Congress has never given the USPS authority to regulate mail ballots.”
Colorado is one of eight universal mail-in ballot states — every voter receives a ballot in the mail — and the vast majority of residents choose to vote by mail. Implementation of the executive order and the Postal Service rule ahead of the midterm elections would upend Colorado’s ability to conduct elections, but election experts don’t expect that to happen. 
No guidance
El Paso County Clerk Steve Schleiker, a Republican, said counties have received no direction from the secretary of state’s office related to Trump’s order or the Postal Service rule. Guidance from the state has consistently said that state election laws and rules remain in effect and counties should prepare to run their elections under those provisions, Schleiker said. 
The clerk’s office and county attorney staff have been closely monitoring the legal developments around the executive order, Schleiker said, and he anticipates no impact to his county’s administration of the November election. 
“Colorado voters should know that nothing has changed about their ability to vote in November,” Schleiker said in a statement. “Voters do not need to complete any new federal process, enroll with USPS, or take any additional steps. All existing Colorado verification, security, and audit procedures remain unchanged.”
El Paso County’s elections staff have conducted “internal scenario-planning” to determine how the order and the Postal Service rule would affect their ability to conduct elections if implemented. The biggest lift would be the rule’s requirement that election offices upload voter names, mailing addresses and envelope barcodes. 
“For a county our size, that verification step, repeated for every mailing batch, would be a significant operational consideration,” Schleiker said.
Denver Clerk Paul López agreed that the Supreme Court ruling had to do with the timing of the lower court decision and not the legality of Trump’s executive order, which he said is the “latest in a string of baseless claims” intended to undermine confidence in elections, instill fear and confuse voters. 
“I know when you see the headlines and you see people say, ‘Trump is getting closer to his mail in voting restrictions,’ that tends to freak people out, and you know what? That’s what it’s intended to do, is to try to put a chilling effect on people’s participation in an election,” López said. 
Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold and Denver Clerk and Recorder Paul López address members of the news media during a press conference at the Denver Elections Division on Super Tuesday in Denver, March 5, 2024. (Photo by Kevin Mohatt for Colorado Newsline)
Trump’s attacks on mail ballots are “absolutely hypocritical coming from a president who also votes by mail,” López said. Trump voted by mail in Florida’s GOP primary this year. 
Local election officials and other agencies in Denver always come together to consider what they need to prepare for going into an election, considering possible scenarios like a blizzard, a power outage, federal troops showing up at polls and problems with the Postal Service, López said. 
“I can tell you that this team that we run here in my office is more than ready. We’ve been ready. We’re the pros at this,” López said. 
Crane said he expects Trump’s executive order ultimately to be deemed unconstitutional. Election officials in Colorado are focused on preparing for the November election and mailing out ballots in the coming weeks. 
“The expectation that we can change all of these processes and procedures for this election, it’s just nuts to think that we can do that and not have it impact both people’s ability to access the ballot and our ability to secure the process,” Crane said. “Changes like this at the last minute will introduce opportunities for error, and so anybody concerned about election integrity would not want changes like this this close to the election.”
Colorado voters can request mail ballots for the November election from their county clerks starting Sept. 19. That’s also the last day clerks can mail ballots to military and overseas voters. Clerks can begin to mail ballots as early as Oct. 2. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi cattle producers and politicians lament Trump’s imported beef plan
description: U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith smiles at her supporters before speaking during her reelection campaign launch at the Mississippi Agriculture Museum in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 28, 2025.
text:
Mississippi cattle producers and politicians are worried that President Donald Trump’s plan to suspend tariffs and cut a deal to import more cheap beef to the U.S. will hurt the state’s farmers and potentially cause long-term damage to an industry already facing high costs and record low herd numbers. 
“This policy does not help the U.S. herd-rebuilding efforts and could possibly do permanent damage,” the Mississippi Farm Bureau Federation and its president, Mike McCormick, said in a statement. “Instead the Administration should focus its time and energy on reducing fuel and input costs for American agriculture that could result in lower prices for all American consumers.” 
The Trump plan brought rare, if mild, dissention from Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, one of Trump’s staunchest allies who has generally supported Trump’s trade policies. She and her husband are cattle farmers.
Trump recently posted on social media that over the next 90 days he will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of beef to be imported into the U.S with lower tariffs in an effort to bring consumer prices down. According to reporting from Bloomberg and the New York Times, the president is expected to sign an executive order removing the tariffs in the next few weeks. Trump has said he has struck a deal for foreign importers to sell the beef at 25% below current market prices.
Additional beef imports would happen ahead of the November midterm elections, as politicians focus on high consumer costs.
The cattle industry is an important part of Mississippi’s economy, and beef is one of the state’s top five agricultural commodities. It had about a $640-million production value last year according to Josh Maples, an agricultural economist at Mississippi State University Extension Service. 
Maples said the state has over 14,000 cattle farms and most are small farms with about 30 head of cattle each.
“There’s a lot of people involved. Even more so than some other crops or commodities you might think about. They may have a higher value of production but fewer total people involved,” Maples said.
Smaller herds, rising costs
The American cattle herd has been shrinking and is at a 75-year low, in part because of continued droughts and rising operating costs. Maples said that producers were unprofitable for many years and chose to sell their cows for meat instead of expanding their herds, a lengthier process that involves predicting where the market might be in a few years. 
Constrained supply and strong consumer demand has resulted in sky-high prices.
In July, ground beef was $6.89 per pound according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, nearly double what it was 10 years ago and up 10% from July of last year. In his post, Trump wrote that the imported beef will be sold at 25% below current market price. 
Agriculture groups warn that while the infusion of cheaper, imported beef could lower consumer prices, it could prevent the U.S. from rebuilding its herd.
“Higher production costs combined with downward pressure on cattle prices will not encourage producers to retain heifers, expand their herds or invest in additional cattle production,” the Mississippi Cattlemen’s Association wrote.
Maples said the lack of details available right now is causing uncertainty and market volatility which could impact what producers do as they decide whether to sell their heifers or keep them to build up their herds.
“It doesn’t give detail about where they would come from and in particular, what matters is, are these additional imports that we weren’t going to get or is it the same beef just coming in at a lower tariff,” Maples said of Trump’s Truth Social post announcing the lower tariffs. 
This is already a big year for imported beef, but whether the 300,000 metric tons are included in already expected imports or will be new would determine how much of a shock the imports would cause market. Mississippi producers say that even a small amount could have a significant impact on their bottom line. 
The Cattlemen’s Association said producers and consumers need “certainty and a fair marketplace — not government actions that create additional volatility and downward pressure on cattle prices.”
Mississippi politicians weigh in
Livestock is one of Mississippi’s most valuable agricultural commodities. The state’s cattle industry was valued at over $700 million in 2025 according to the Mississippi State University Extension Service. Mississippi politicians took to social media to voice their support for American beef.
Hyde Smith, who serves on the Senate Agriculture Committee, said in a post on social media that she had been to the White House to express concerns about the impact of cheaper imports on farmers. She said she would “promote policies that help farmers and ranchers grow our domestic herd without leaning on foreign beef to paper over the problem.”
Scott Colom, a Democrat challenging Hyde-Smith in the November midterm election, has said she is doing too little to help Mississippi beef producers. “Cindy Hyde-Smith gave away Mississippi’s voice on tariffs,” Colom said.
Statewide officials including state Agriculture Commissioner and gubernatorial candidate Andy Gipson and Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann, a potential gubernatorial candidate, posted on social media that the focus should be on lowering costs and supporting U.S. beef producers.
“We need to double down on supporting and buying American beef, not foreign imports,” Gipson wrote on social media.
Hosemann wrote: “Importing more foreign beef at a lower rate is not the way to significantly lower prices for Mississippi families.”
Hyde-Smith and other Mississippi Republicans did not refer to Trump in their posts nor did they directly mention tariffs. But for Hyde-Smith this represents a rare, if tepid, break from the president. 
In a February interview, when asked about what Republicans would do to get rising beef prices down, Hyde-Smith said that lower fuel prices at the time could help lower overall costs. 
“You have so many proteins to choose from and all commodities go through peaks and valleys,” Hyde-Smith said. “You know it is a global market, but we will be seeing a difference, I truly believe, because of so many things.”
But the U.S. war with Iran has caused fuel and fertilizer costs to increase.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Off-site renewable projects will contribute more to infrastructure costs under latest reform
description: In the latest regulatory reform to Maine’s renewable energy landscape, the Public Utilities Commission has finalized the details of a new fee for larger, off-site renewable energy installations. Last year, the Legislature passed a law to reform the state’s net energy billing program, which is designed to encourage renewable energy projects by offering custom[...]
text:
Solar panels in Damariscotta, Maine. (Photo by Evan Houk/ Maine Morning Star)In the latest regulatory reform to Maine’s renewable energy landscape, the Public Utilities Commission has finalized the details of a new fee for larger, off-site renewable energy installations.
Last year, the Legislature passed a law to reform the state’s net energy billing program, which is designed to encourage renewable energy projects by offering customers credits to offset their power bills.
That law made it so projects that produce energy off-site are no longer eligible for the credit and created a new fee for those so-called front-of-the-meter projects, which typically involve larger scale installations like community solar. After months of discussions, the commission has finalized a formula to determine how any increases or decreases to that new project fee should be calculated. 
Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said in recent years as power transmission and distribution costs have increased, owners of those front-of-the-meter projects have collected more profits, without having to pay for the infrastructure. 
“The Legislature needed to find a mechanism to make sure that those dollars — that weren’t being paid for the distribution and transmission system — were not just going into the pockets of the solar owners, but instead there was a balance there,” Sanborn said. 
The project charge is meant to collect some of that money from installation owners, and put it towards infrastructure maintenance and improvements — costs that would otherwise have to be paid by ratepayers. 
“So it’s directly credited to all the other ratepayers who would otherwise have to pick up that tab on the grid without the contribution from the solar owner,” Sanborn said. 
At their meeting Tuesday, commissioners focused on the question of how to evaluate the value of a given project. All three commissioners said they had closely scrutinized the issue. 
“This was an incredibly close call for me, and I have gone round and round and round and round in my head on this one,” said Commissioner Carolyn Gilbert.
But the commission ultimately sided with the Office of the Public Advocate over the initial recommendation from commission staff. 
The Legislature set the initial levels for the new fee, which are based on how much energy is produced by a project, and project owners began paying the charge earlier this year. The new formula will take effect in January, and will determine if that fee will change.
Because the charge is paid by the project owner, it isn’t something that ratepayers will see on their bills. 
The law also directed the Department of Energy Resources to design a new program to encourage the development of front-of-the-meter projects, now that they are no longer eligible for net energy billing. The department has until the end of September to complete that proposal, which will go before the commission for approval. 
In 2019, net energy billing was expanded to include renewable energy generators located outside of their property but within the same utility service territory, such as a community solar project. But that led to ballooning costs for the program, and prompted the Legislature to amend the program, and ultimately exclude front-of-the-meter projects.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia to receive $353 million in landmark Meta child-safety settlement
description: Virginia is set to receive at least $353 million from Meta Platforms Inc. under a major multistate settlement that would also require the parent company of Facebook and Instagram to adopt new safeguards aimed at protecting children from addictive features and harmful content.  The agreement, announced Wednesday, could reach more than $17 billion nationwide,[...]
text:
Facebook parent company Meta has agreed to pay Virginia at least $353 million and adopt new safeguards for young users under a proposed multistate settlement over allegations that its platforms harmed children. (Photo by Thomas Ulrich/Pixabay)Virginia is set to receive at least $353 million from Meta Platforms Inc. under a major multistate settlement that would also require the parent company of Facebook and Instagram to adopt new safeguards aimed at protecting children from addictive features and harmful content. 
The agreement, announced Wednesday, could reach more than $17 billion nationwide, making it one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in U.S. history outside the Big Tobacco agreements of the 1990s. It remains subject to approval by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, where the case was filed. 
“This is a momentous day for Virginia,” Attorney General Jay Jones said in a Zoom call with reporters Wednesday morning, adding that the changes Meta would be required to make to its social media platforms could ultimately prove more significant than the money. 
“This is historic, this is a shift in how Meta and these companies are going to operate,” he said. 
Jones said that Virginia plans to use the $353 million to pay for a range of initiatives, including “unplugged” programs and activities intended to combat the loneliness and social isolation associated with children’s online lives. The state also wants to support digital literacy programs that help parents better understand social media. 
“We are really excited to put this money into efforts that are going to continue to help protect our kids,” Jones said, adding that he also sometimes struggles to navigate social media as a parent. 
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones on Wednesday announced a proposed multistate settlement that would provide the commonwealth at least $353 million and require Meta to adopt new safeguards for young Facebook and Instagram users. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
The commonwealth could ultimately receive more than $500 million if other social media companies, including TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat, agree to specified settlement terms, Jones said. 
The agreement resolves allegations from 47 other states, Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram with addictive features, knowingly exposed young users to serious mental health risks and misled the public about the safety of its platforms. 
The investigation began in 2021 with a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general from California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, Tennessee and Vermont. Virginia and other states later joined the effort, which continued through several state administrations.
“Democrats and Republicans came together to find a solution to a problem that harmed children across this country,” Jones said. “The size of the settlement is massive and represents a huge victory for kids’ online safety. But I want to be very clear, this is not the end of this effort.”
 Settlement ends closely watched Meta trial

The agreement effectively ends a federal case that grew out of the states’ 2021 investigation and was filed in 2023. A trial began last week in Oakland, California, where the plaintiff states were seeking roughly $200 billion over allegations that Meta’s platforms harmed children. U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers is expected to review the proposed settlement. 
Meta denied wrongdoing during the litigation, arguing that research had not established a clear link between adolescents’ use of social media and diminished well-being. The company has also pointed to protections it introduced for younger users, including teen accounts with tighter privacy, messaging and content restrictions. 
In a statement released Wednesday, Meta said the agreement builds on its efforts to give teenagers a safer experience online and parents more control. 
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” the company said. “We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that’s why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard.”
Meta also encouraged other platforms to adopt similar protections. 
Jones said evidence gathered during the states’ investigation showed Meta designed its platforms to encourage compulsive use among children while putting profits ahead of their safety and mental health. 
“When pressed about the harm that these platforms had caused, Meta repeatedly parroted lies and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms,” Jones said. “We all can tell that Meta is a company with seemingly unlimited monetary resources, which it used at every turn to try to make this case go away.”
 New limits for young users

Under the settlement, children using Instagram and Facebook would be limited to a combined two hours a day. The platforms would have to interrupt continuous use with “productive pauses” after 15 minutes and again at 60 and 90 minutes. 
Access would be blocked between midnight and 6 a.m., while push notifications would be disabled on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year. 
Meta would also have to strengthen its age-assurance systems to prevent children younger than 13 from using the platforms and give parents greater control over their children’s accounts. 
Age-appropriate content protections would be required to reduce exposure to bullying, harassment and material promoting eating disorders, suicide or self-harm. 
The agreement also targets social-comparison features linked to poor mental-health outcomes among children and teenagers. Meta would have to restrict features including beauty filters and visible “like” counts. Jones specifically cited cosmetic surgery filters that can promote unrealistic beauty standards. 
An independent auditor and the states participating in the settlement would regularly evaluate whether Meta has implemented the safeguards and whether they are working. 
Jones said those requirements address design features that have kept young users scrolling and increased their exposure to potentially harmful content. 
“While we know and can tell that the monetary rewards are going to be transformative, I want to focus on the injunctive relief that we obtained as a part of the settlement, because this will help ensure that our young people are protected from addictive and damaging features that have caused tremendous harm to them for years,” he said. 
Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Snap, the owner of Snapchat, still face thousands of lawsuits from states, school districts, parents and young people who allege the companies deliberately designed their products to encourage compulsive use. 
Wednesday’s settlement resolves separate state claims involving Meta’s sharing of nonpublic Facebook user information with third parties, including Cambridge Analytica, before the 2016 presidential election. Virginia will receive another $11 million through that portion of the agreement, according to the attorney general’s office. 
Jones credited attorneys working for the state under two administrations who spent more than five years investigating and prosecuting the case. He said the agreement could also become a model for changes elsewhere in the social media industry. 
“This will help ensure that our young people are protected from addictive and damaging features that have caused tremendous harm to them for years,” he said.

title: New Mexico judges working on statewide guidelines for artificial intelligence use in court
description: Two New Mexico judges told a panel of state lawmakers this week that the underlying theme of the guidelines they’re crafting for artificial intelligence use in the courtroom is, “Please, don’t be dumb.” They pointed to two examples of AI-related fiascos in the courtroom as evidence that guardrails are sorely needed.

New Mexico Sixth Judicial District Judge Jarod Hofacket, left, and Second Judicial District Family Court Judge Jane Levy, right, speak about artificial intelligence use in court before the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee in Albuquerque on Aug. 25, 2026. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Two New Mexico judges told a panel of state lawmakers this week that the underlying theme of the guidelines they’re crafting for artificial intelligence use in the courtroom is, “Please, don’t be dumb.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Second Judicial District Family Court Judge Jane Levy and Sixth Judicial District Judge Jarod Hofacket spoke before the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee in Albuquerque on Tuesday and updated them on their AI-focused efforts. They said they are working on three separate sets of guidelines — one each for self-representing litigants, attorneys and judicial staff.
They pointed to two examples of AI-related fiascos in the courtroom as evidence that guardrails are sorely needed.
An Arizona family last year used AI to recreate their deceased relative, who died in a road rage incident, to deliver his own courtroom statements. And the New Mexico Supreme Court recently found a local attorney in contempt of court for using AI to file a brief that contained fabricated witnesses and testimony.
Levy and Hofacket sit on the state Supreme Court’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts, which also includes academics and state lawmakers, and is set to produce annual recommendations so that anyone interacting with the legal system understands the expectations regarding AI use.
“It’s a tool to be used, like anything else — like spellcheck. But it is just a tool,” Levy said. “How do we make it so every lawyer appearing in the state understands what the rules are in front of every judge?”
State Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez (D-Albuquerque) told Levy and Hofacket that she has encountered problems with AI’s credibility firsthand.
“I asked it a legal question and what was fascinating is it used a bill that was in the Legislature to say what the law is,” she said. “I was like, ‘Oh my God. That’s my bill.’ It didn’t pass.”
Hofacket responded that he believes the “human element” of the courtroom experience remains essential. 
“I think about going to a fast food restaurant. If I order something from a human employee and they make a mistake, I’m not nearly as upset as if I have to use a kiosk to order something and it doesn’t come out that way,” he said. “There’s a human element to judging. Having a human sit and listen to your problems and come up with an answer — even if you don’t like it — is part of the experience.”

title: Maine to receive $56 million in landmark Meta settlement over addictive features
description: Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey announced on Wednesday that he, along with the attorneys general of 50 other states and territories, had reached a settlement agreement with Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, over concerns about the addictive nature of those platforms, especially for children. The settlement totals around $17 billion, with[...]
text:
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, along with 33 other state attorneys general, initially sued Meta in October 2023 in a lawsuit that alleged Meta had received millions of complaints about underage users on Instagram, but never disclosed that fact or made any serious effort to close those accounts. 
(Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey announced on Wednesday that he, along with the attorneys general of 50 other states and territories, had reached a settlement agreement with Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, over concerns about the addictive nature of those platforms, especially for children.
The settlement totals around $17 billion, with Maine to receive at least $56 million under the agreement, which Frey’s office described as “the largest state consumer protection settlement in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.”
It addresses allegations that Meta designed its social media apps, specifically Instagram, with addictive features, that it knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms. 
“This hard-fought settlement provides important protections for children on Meta’s platforms, Instagram and Facebook, and empowers parents with tools to help address the negative impacts of social media use on children,” said Frey. 
Frey, along with 33 other state attorneys general, initially sued Meta in October 2023 in a lawsuit that alleged Meta had received millions of complaints about underage users on Instagram, but never disclosed that fact or made any serious effort to close those accounts. 



The settlement puts in place a number of new limits on Meta’s social media apps for children:

Hard caps on daily time limits and “Productive Pauses” for children: for its two platforms, Instagram and Facebook, a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling. These limits will remain in effect for five years. If Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube adopt comparable terms, the daily limit on each platform will drop to 60 minutes for 10 years.
“Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from midnight to 6 a.m.
Limited school-time access for children, eliminating push notifications on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.
Robust age assurance measures to more effectively verify the age of young users.
Safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying, content that promotes eating disorders, and content related to suicide and self-harm.
Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls.
Limits on social comparison features, including beauty filters and visible “like” counts, that have been linked to poor mental health outcomes in children and teens.




Those changes — both their implementation and how well they are actually working — will be “regularly assessed” by the states in the settlement and an independent auditor.
The settlement also resolves the states’ claims against Meta over its sharing of nonpublic Facebook user information with third parties, including Cambridge Analytica, before the 2016 election, according to Frey’s office.
“While this settlement is an important step, the need to make social media safer for children must extend to the entire industry,” said Frey. “We will continue to work with our multistate partners to push for comprehensive changes that prioritize the safety and welfare of children over profit.” 
Michigan Advance reporter Kathrine Dailey contributed to this reporting.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ to receive $565M+ from Facebook owner over teen addiction claims
description: Facebook owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens.
text:
Facebook owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Facebook’s owner agreed to pay New Jersey more than $565 million as part of a landmark settlement resolving claims by 47 states, the District of Columbia, and some U.S. territories who charged the tech giant violated child privacy and intentionally built addictive features that exposed young users to mental harms.
As part of the settlement agreement, which does not carry an admission of guilt and must still be approved by the courts, tech giant Meta agreed to institute new limits like daily caps on underage users’ social media activity, subject its platforms to independent auditing, and limit the discoverability of teens’ accounts, among other things.
“As a parent, protecting your kids is always your North Star, and this agreement achieves critical protections for our children today,” New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport said in a statement Wednesday.
Meta agreed to pay the states and others who sued a combined $17.1 billion. New Jersey, which was among the first states to sue Meta, will receive between $525 million and $752 from a portion of the settlement covering the firm’s use of addictive features and its minimization of their harms.
New Jersey will also receive $20.3 million over privacy claims related to Cambridge Analytica, the now-defunct firm that improperly acquired access to the private data of millions of Facebook users while aiding President Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
In total, Meta agreed to pay $459.3 million to plaintiffs to resolve claims stemming from Cambridge Analytica, plus $75 million for litigation costs.
The settlement agreement requires Facebook to erect an array of new limits on teens’ social media use.
Those include provisions to block teens’ access to social media platforms between midnight and 6 a.m. and others to limit push notifications from the platforms between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m.
The settlement also requires the tech firm limit teens’ access to its platforms during school hours and regularly present teen users with the option to switch to a non-personalized feed.
The agreement requires Meta to cap teens’ daily use to two hours across all its platforms, which include Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, with periodic notifications to pause after 60 and 90 minutes of cumulative use in a given day.
“Today’s settlement is a major victory for New Jersey families. Big Tech is finally being held accountable for the harm it is causing, especially to our children’s mental health and safety. More important, parents and teens will finally get some relief, including groundbreaking new safety features to protect kids online,” said Gov. Mikie Sherrill. “But here in New Jersey, we won’t stop fighting until all of the Big Tech companies follow suit.”
Many of the settlement’s restrictions mirror New Jersey statute that Sherrill signed into law earlier this month.
In an unsigned statement, Meta said teens’ safety is paramount for its platforms but warned the changes may be less impactful if younger users migrate to other social media platforms not subject to the settlement’s provisions.
“We know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” it said in the statement. “For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard, to ensure teens use social media in a healthy and responsible way.”
Other parts of the settlement require Meta to block teens from seeing like counts, limit unrelated adults’ ability to find their accounts, and step up its own age verification efforts.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska to receive up to $201 million from Meta landmark settlement
description: The tech giant also agrees to implement changes for younger users on its platforms
text:
(Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)LINCOLN — Nebraska will receive up to $201 million from the Meta landmark settlement, Attorney General Mike Hilgers said Wednesday morning.
Nebraska’s sum is part of a larger settlement of $17.1 billion with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories over claims that the company knowingly designed and deployed harmful features on its social media platforms intended to addict children and teens. As part of the settlement, Meta has agreed to implement changes to its platforms for younger users.  
Hilger called Wednesday’s announcement of the settlement “one of the biggest days” in the history of the Nebraska AG office. 
“We have achieved some of the most important relief … both for the state to help abate the impact of social media on kids, but also to empower parents to help protect kids,” he said during his press conference. 
The settlement ends the trial of the case that began in California last week, which had been expected to last six to eight weeks.
The changes for younger users of Facebook and Instagram will include hard-cap daily time limits and “productive pauses” — a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Other changes include:

“Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from midnight to 6 a.m.
Limited school-time access and no push notifications for children on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year. 
Robust age assurance measures to more effectively verify the age of young users.
Safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders, and content related to suicide and self-harm.
Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls. 

Most of these changes will be effective for a decade. 
Hilgers said the funds will go to the state’s consumer protection cash fund; he added that it will be up to the Legislature and the governor how the money will be used. Meta, in a statement, said the fund “can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities.”
Nebraska Attorney General logo on a podium on June 18, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska will also get $5.1 million from Meta for its “sharing of nonpublic information about Facebook users with third parties, like Cambridge Analytica, leading up to the 2016 election.” 
Cambridge Analytica, which had ties to former Trump political strategist Steve Bannon, purchased Facebook data on tens of millions of Americans without their knowledge to target U.S. voters during the 2016 Trump campaign, according to AP. 

In the same statement, Meta called on YouTube and TikTok to implement similar changes on their platforms. 
“For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard, to ensure teens use social media in a healthy and responsible way,” part of the statement reads.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland Republicans take round one in redistricting challenge
description: Maryland Republicans challenging a proposed state constitutional amendment that would set standards for how congressional districts are drawn won an initial courtroom skirmish. The 10-page decision issued Wednesday comes almost 24 hours after the conclusion of a daylong hearing in Annapolis that focused on process and whether or not lawmakers erred as they r[...]
text:
Anne Arundel County Circuit Court in Annapolis. File photo by Bryan P. Sears.Maryland Republicans challenging a proposed state constitutional amendment that would set standards for how congressional districts are drawn won an initial courtroom skirmish.
The 10-page decision issued Wednesday comes almost 24 hours after the conclusion of a daylong hearing in Annapolis that focused on process and whether or not lawmakers erred as they rushed a constitutional amendment to Maryland voters.
In his ruling, Anne Arundel County Circuit Court Judge Robert J. Thompson issued an injunction preventing the question from being placed on the ballot but stayed his order pending an expected appeal to the Supreme Court of Maryland.
“A chamber that holds a supermajority is still a chamber bound by the law,” said Delegate Matt Morgan, chair of the Maryland Freedom Caucus. “Today the court made clear that three-fifths of the vote doesn’t buy you an exemption from the rules you wrote yourself. Maryland doesn’t answer to kings, and it doesn’t answer to a legislature that thinks it’s one.”
An appeal and the pending decision would further tighten an Aug. 31 deadline for the Maryland State Board of Elections to finalize roughly 1,200 different ballot versions that will be used by voters across the state.
The case in Anne Arundel County Circuit court is one of two challenges to the proposed constitutional amendment that would set standards for how the state’s eight congressional districts are drawn.
On Tuesday, Thompson closed the hearing expressing concern about how the Democratic supermajority pushed the bill through during a special session earlier this month.
Should the amendment be approve by the voters, Republicans fear it will open a door to Maryland joining a flurry of hyper-partisan mid-cycle redistricting that has taken place in states controlled by both Democratic and Republican parties.
Currently, Democrats control seven of the state’s eight seats. The lone Republican, U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st), is the likely target of any effort to redraw maps. Some Democrats including Democratic Gov. Wes Moore have called the push for new maps an effort to make the districts “more competitive” but the intent, based on one map approved in February by the House of Delegates, focused on pushing more Democratic voters into the district represented by Harris.
That map stalled in the Senate.
This story will be updated

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA sues again to stop Trump administration mail-in voting requirements
description: SEATTLE — Washington is suing to stop the Trump administration’s latest attempt to restrict mail-in voting, days after the U.S. Supreme Court opened the door for the effort to move forward. Washington and other states had sued over President Donald Trump’s executive order issued in March on the issue. A lower court blocked its implementation, […]
text:
Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs speaks at a press conference announcing a new election-related lawsuit, alongside Attorney General Nick Brown, on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026, in Seattle. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)SEATTLE — Washington is suing to stop the Trump administration’s latest attempt to restrict mail-in voting, days after the U.S. Supreme Court opened the door for the effort to move forward.
Washington and other states had sued over President Donald Trump’s executive order issued in March on the issue. A lower court blocked its implementation, but an emergency ruling from the high court this week lifted that injunction.
The justices, in a split decision along ideological lines, didn’t weigh in on the constitutionality of Trump’s order, only determining the lower court injunction was premature. 
The muddled legal landscape just over two months out from the midterms is stirring confusion as Democrats hope to retake Congress and hold the Trump administration accountable.
The outcome of the court fight is particularly important in Washington, where almost all votes are cast via drop boxes and mail. Washington already requires each voter to sign an attestation that they’re qualified to vote, and a signature verification process ensures each ballot is cast by a registered voter.
Trump’s order, issued in March, would require state election officials to share with the Postal Service a list of mail-in voters. The Postal Service, an independent federal agency, wouldn’t send ballots to voters not included on the lists. 
It also sets new conditions for states to send ballots via mail, including envelope design. Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said county election officials would need to replace five million ballot envelopes to comply. States would bear the cost. Hobbs said this would be impossible for return envelopes, forcing voters to use drop boxes, instead of mailing ballots the Postal Service may not deliver.
Attorney General Nick Brown, a Democrat, said in a press conference Wednesday morning that the proposed federal rules accompanying the executive order “will totally upend how our elections are administered.”
Meanwhile, Hobbs’ office is seeing if extra drop boxes can be added. Nearly 70% of ballots in this month’s primary election were returned via drop box.
The Postal Service says if ballots are compliant with the new federal rules, they won’t be intercepted or delayed, and would move through the mailstream as usual.
Washington officials fear the requirements could result in eligible voters not receiving their ballots due to administrative errors or flaws in the unprecedented procedures.
Proponents of the change say it would help improve integrity and trust in elections. 
Issued Friday, the U.S. Postal Service said its final rule would take effect immediately, arguing that “delaying the effective date would jeopardize implementation of this rule in time for the 2026 general election.” Election Day is Nov. 3. Ballots are mailed out in mid-October. Absentee ballots will be sent sooner.
Twenty-five states are bringing Wednesday’s lawsuit, filed in federal court in Massachusetts. Brown is co-leading the coalition. The complaint argues the Trump administration’s proposal “effectively eliminates mail voting through its onerous administration requirements.”
The states say the order violates the U.S. Constitution, which gives states the power to run elections. They’re seeking a temporary restraining order from a judge blocking its implementation, and hoping for a court hearing as soon as possible.
“This rule was written to satisfy the president’s continued desire to control our vote, but the United States Constitution is clear: states control elections, not the president,” Brown said.
Washington state lawmakers invited Postal Service officials to discuss the sweeping rule change at a public hearing earlier this year, but the federal officials canceled just hours before the meeting.
The Washington Legislature established vote-by-mail as an option for all elections in 2005. By 2011, 38 of the state’s 39 counties had switched to this system, and the Legislature adopted it as a statewide requirement.
The Trump administration previously sued Washington for its voter rolls, arguing it needed them to confirm noncitizens weren’t registered to vote. Earlier this month, a federal judge in Seattle heard the state’s move to toss the case, but hasn’t issued a ruling yet. Courts have dismissed numerous similar cases across the country.

Hobbs has been willing to hand over public information contained in voter rolls, but not voters’ sensitive information, like dates of birth, driver’s license numbers or the last four digits of Social Security numbers.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: What’s next for contentious Tiverton oyster farm proposal? More meetings.
description: The more than six-year saga of an oyster farm proposed for Tiverton’s Sapowet Cove continues with no end in sight, after a state coastal lawyer rejected neighbors’ attempt to scrap the project. A small crowd packed the second-floor state office where the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council met Tuesday, lured by a single line […]
text:
Buoys mark the outline of the 1-acre oyster farm that Patrick and John Bowen want to build in Tiverton's Sapowet Cove in this 2023 photo. (Photo by Jocelyn Jackson/Rhode Island Current)The more than six-year saga of an oyster farm proposed for Tiverton’s Sapowet Cove continues with no end in sight, after a state coastal lawyer rejected neighbors’ attempt to scrap the project.
A small crowd packed the second-floor state office where the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council met Tuesday, lured by a single line in the meeting agenda for a determination by CRMC hearing officer Mark Krieger. None of them knew what Krieger would recommend, having not heard from Krieger since their Sept. 23, 2024, hearing.
Krieger was not there Tuesday night. Instead, a synopsis of his 11-page decision was shared by the agency’s legal counsel and promptly accepted by the seven-member, appointed panel.
His decision rejected opponents’ arguments that a 2024 law limiting development along the Sakonnet River should prevent the 1-acre oyster farm application from being considered. 
The reason: The law was not in place when Little Compton brothers John and Patrick Bowen applied for the aquaculture lease in 2019. Since the language in the law does not state the restrictions apply retroactively, the Bowen brothers’ application is not subject to the limits on water use for anything but “passive outdoor recreation,” Krieger wrote.
“In essence, it was not illegal for the applicants to operate a commercial entity, i.e, an oyster farm within Sapowet Cove,” Krieger said.
Sitting in the last row of folding chairs Tuesday night, the Bowen brothers looked at each other and smiled as they heard the news.
“We feel validated,” Patrick Bowen said in an interview after the meeting.
Patrick Bowen, left, and his friend, Bruce Eddy, look to the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council following its vote to accept its hearing officer’s decision at a meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
The property owners and their attorneys declined to comment. 
An Aug. 24 blog post on the opposition website, Save Seapowet for All, reiterates the legal objections to the project.
“If CRMC ignores the law, then they will be disregarding the General Assembly’s authority,” the anonymous post states. “Allowing the application process to continue through the permitting process wastes the public’s and CRMC resources.”
Krieger’s determination allows debate to continue on the substance of the case — whether the mountain of objections from property owners, fishermen and even the state aquaculture association are enough to warrant denying the project application. 
In the initial, 2021 recommendation, CRMC staff wrote that the proposal for 200 bottom cages a few hundred feet from the shoreline met the technical requirements used to evaluate aquaculture farms. But staffers deferred to the appointed council to consider the many objections over how the project would interfere with fishing, boating and recreational use. 
After multiple delays and postponed meetings, the council punted the decision in late 2023 to Krieger. As the newly appointed hearing officer brought on to adjudicate contested cases, it made sense to let the Lincoln private practice attorney give first review to the proposal, council  members reasoned.
But the rigorous schedule of hearings, involving questioning and cross-examination of both sides, and expert witnesses, was abandoned after three groups of objectors, all of whom own properties nearby, asked Krieger to dismiss the case based on the 2024 law. Their attorneys’ July 2025 joint motion spawned a series of legal filing back and forth with the Bowen brothers, who were representing themselves. The last legal filing was submitted in January 2025.
Since then? “Radio silent,” Patrick Bowen said.
Anthony DeSisto, the CRMC’s legal counsel, referred to Krieger when asked why it took nearly two years since the last in-person meeting on the case for a decision. Krieger did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.
Krieger’s decision is not a final order. Under the state’s Administrative Procedures Act, once a final determination is made — including a vote by the council — on the merits of the project, objectors can appeal administratively and to the Superior Court.
Resumed hearings have not been scheduled. 
The Bowen brothers maintained their commitment to the project despite the yearslong delays and contentious nature.
“My brother and I both farm,” said Patrick Bowen. “We’re both getting older, and it’s something we look forward to doing in the future.”
Patrick Bowen, 56, works as a carpentry teacher at Dighton-Rehobeth Vocational High School and owns an apple orchard in Little Compton. Sean Bowen, 55, works as an aquaculture coordinator for the state of Massachusetts and owns a local garlic farm.
If approved, the duo hope to sell oysters direct-to-consumer and to local restaurants, while offering educational visits to students from grade to graduate school. 
The Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council met on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026 to review the decision of its hearing officer in the contested Tiverton oyster farm case. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
Attorneys and residents filled the folding chairs of the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council meeting, waiting for the scheduled update in the Sapowet Cove oyster farm case. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Dolly Parton showed us a different kind of Southern politics
description: I stared at my phone, waiting for the interview of my life. Dolly Parton was scheduled to call to promote the first national tour of her musical “9 to 5” at Greenville’s Peace Center. This was January 2011, when I was an arts writer at The Greenville News. But Dolly was 10 minutes late. Would […]
text:
Dolly Parton speaks onstage at "Dolly Parton's Threads: My Songs In Symphony" world premiere at Schermerhorn Symphony Center on March 20, 2025, in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Jason Kempin/Getty Images)I stared at my phone, waiting for the interview of my life.
Dolly Parton was scheduled to call to promote the first national tour of her musical “9 to 5” at Greenville’s Peace Center. This was January 2011, when I was an arts writer at The Greenville News.
But Dolly was 10 minutes late. Would she even call?
Then the phone rang. I nervously picked it up.
“Paul?” she said in that famous sparkling voice. “I’m sorry I’m late. I was on another line and I said, ‘I gotta hang up and call Paul!’”
She said my name as if we were the closest of longtime friends — even though we had never spoken before.
I stammered, “It’s really OK, Ms. Parton.”
“C’mon now, Paul, call me Dolly. Everybody does!”
Dolly’s legendary charm reduced me to mush. And I understood why everybody loved her.
Dolly, who died Tuesday at 80, was beloved across cultural boundaries: by conservative Southern Christians, who appreciated her faith; feminists, who admired her independence; country-music traditionalists, who loved her music; and members of the LGBTQ community, who were grateful for her support.
That might seem impossible, but Dolly made it look easy.
She had strong convictions, but she didn’t weaponize them. Her Christianity was deep and unmistakable. She grew up in a Pentecostal family and continued throughout her life to speak openly about God, prayer and faith.
Yet she was remarkably nonjudgmental.
When asked about gay and transgender people, Dolly said she believed everybody should be allowed to be who they are. She supported same-sex marriage, even before the Supreme Court made it the law of the land.
And she didn’t merely talk about accepting transgender people. She wrote “Travelin’ Thru,” an Oscar-nominated song for the 2005 film Transamerica, about a transgender woman’s journey. Dolly said the song reflected her belief that “it’s alright to be who you are.”
This was Dolly’s particular genius: She could be deeply Southern, deeply Christian and deeply inclusive.
And she didn’t seem to regard those qualities as contradictory.
South Carolina roots
South Carolina has a special claim on Dolly.
Her mother, Avie Lee Owens, was born in Lockhart, Union County, and Dolly said the state was “very near and dear” to her heart because of her mother. She considered South Carolina almost a second home.
For 18 years, her Dixie Stampede dinner theatre operated in Myrtle Beach, employing South Carolinians and bringing millions of visitors to the coast.
In 2011, when the attraction became Pirates Voyage, the South Carolina General Assembly declared June 3 “Dolly Parton Day,” honoring her contributions to the state’s economy, tourism industry and charitable causes.
Perhaps her most important South Carolina legacy is quieter: for years, Dolly’s Imagination Library has been putting books into the hands of South Carolina children — tens of thousands of them.
In Charleston County alone, the program has delivered nearly 400,000 books since 2010.
So, Dolly didn’t merely entertain South Carolinians. She left something of herself here — books in the hands of children, jobs along the coast and a living example of a Southern identity spacious enough to include people who didn’t look, worship or love exactly as she did.
That example seems especially worth remembering at a time when some politicians are weaponizing the word “inclusivity” — portraying as a threat what Dolly treated as an invitation.
Inclusivity has become a political battleground. (See, for instance, the recent antics at the S.C. Arts Commission targeting LGBTQ groups.) But Dolly offered a different understanding of the idea.
It didn’t mean that everyone had to think alike. It meant that everyone belonged.
She didn’t require conservative Christians to surrender their faith. She didn’t require LGBTQ people to surrender their identity. She didn’t require liberals or conservatives to pass a political purity test before they could enjoy her music.
She simply treated people as people.
Dolly had political opinions, too. She jumped into the vaccine debates, donating $1 million to COVID-19 vaccine research and publicly received the Moderna vaccine, encouraging others to get the shot.
But Dolly understood something our politics often forgets: disagreement does not have to become dehumanization.
That is a particularly valuable lesson for South Carolina.
We can be Southern, Christian, patriotic and deeply inclusive at the same time.
Perhaps that is part of what it once meant to be Southern at our best: not that everyone belonged to the same tribe, but that there was room at the table for people who were different from us.
Dolly understood that.
Maybe that’s why, in this angry, divided country, so many Americans loved her.
And maybe that’s why, 15 years after our phone conversation, I still remember the feeling of hearing that lilting voice on the other end of the phone.
For a few minutes, Dolly Parton made a nervous newspaper reporter feel like an old friend.
She made millions of people feel the same way.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Appeals court rejects Rep. LaMonica McIver’s bid to avoid trial on assault charges
description: Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) is accused of assaulting federal agents outside a Newark migrant jail last year. McIver argued she cannot be prosecuted.
text:
Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) is accused of assaulting federal agents outside a Newark migrant jail last year. McIver argued she cannot be prosecuted. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)A federal appeals court Wednesday largely rejected Rep. LaMonica McIver’s bid to have criminal charges against her thrown out, ruling that two of the three counts she faces over a confrontation with federal agents outside a Newark immigration detention center are not shielded by congressional immunity.
In a 49-page filing, a divided three-judge U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals panel affirmed a lower court’s decision that allowed prosecutors to proceed on the first two counts of the indictment, which accuse McIver of striking and grabbing federal agents outside Delaney Hall in May 2025. The court sent the third count back to the lower court for further review.
McIver, a freshman Democrat who represents the 10th District, had argued the Constitution’s speech or debate clause, which shields lawmakers from prosecution for legislative acts, protected her conduct that day. But the majority’s ruling says McIver’s physical contact with agents was “unambiguously non-legislative.”
“In sum, Count One neither charges Congresswoman McIver for an act that is legislative in nature nor requires that she answer for any legislative act,” it says.
Two of the judges on the panel — one a Donald Trump appointee, the other named by Joe Biden — agreed that McIver is also not shielded from prosecution for the second count of her indictment. The third judge, named by Bill Clinton, disagreed and said he would have returned that count to the lower court for further review.
All three judges agreed that the third count should be reviewed again by a lower-court judge because he did not properly assess its claims against McIver.
The charges stem from a chaotic scene outside Delaney Hall on May 9, 2025, when Newark Mayor Ras Baraka (D) was arrested by federal agents as McIver and two other members of Congress were on site to conduct an oversight inspection of the facility. A melee occurred as federal agents moved to arrest Baraka, and body camera footage from the episode shows McIver pushing agents during the scuffle. Agents did not arrest McIver that day.
Days later, federal prosecutors announced they were dropping the trespassing charge against Baraka but filing assault charges against McIver. She was soon indicted, and she has argued that the Trump administration targeted her because she is a vocal critic of its policies. She has pleaded not guilty.
McIver faces up to 17 years in prison if convicted.
Paul Fishman, McIver’s attorney, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Michigan Advance
title: In Her Honor brings stories of Black mothers lost to maternal mortality to Detroit
description: A national art movement is in Detroit this week, calling attention to the maternal health crisis Black women face by honoring those who have lost their lives to pregnancy-related complications. On Aug. 26-28, Detroit’s Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation will host In Her Honor, a series of events including a film screening, gala […]
text:
Portraits included as part of the "In Her Honor" exhibition and gala sponsored by Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation. (Photo courtesy of Mothering Justice)A national art movement is in Detroit this week, calling attention to the maternal health crisis Black women face by honoring those who have lost their lives to pregnancy-related complications.
On Aug. 26-28, Detroit’s Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation will host In Her Honor, a series of events including a film screening, gala and art exhibition. In Her Honor aims to shine a light on the fact that Black women are three times more likely to die from a pregnancy-related cause than white women, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The series of events is intended to go beyond that statistic, Mothering Justice founder and Executive Director Danielle Atkinson said, to humanize those stories by elevating them through art.
“We know the numbers, but it’s different when we are talking about a particular individual and that’s what the portraits and the honorees do for the issue,” Atkinson said. “They really put a face with the statistic. They put a story to a face, and when we do that, it humanizes the problem and it gives us all something to relate to.”
Through film, art, and community dialogue, In Her Honor’s seventh stop on its nationwide tour will elevate the stories of families impacted by maternal mortality and highlight the advocates, birth workers and organizers working to improve outcomes for Black mothers. In the United States, 80% of pregnancy-related deaths are preventable, according to the CDC.
A portrait included as part of the "In Her Honor" exhibition and gala sponsored by Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation. (Photo courtesy of Mothering Justice)A portrait included as part of the "In Her Honor" exhibition and gala sponsored by Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation. (Photo courtesy of Mothering Justice)A portrait included as part of the "In Her Honor" exhibition and gala sponsored by Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation. (Photo courtesy of Mothering Justice)A portrait included as part of the "In Her Honor" exhibition and gala sponsored by Mothering Justice and the national ARIAH Foundation. (Photo courtesy of Mothering Justice)
The national art movement also aims to bring attention to how the maternal health crisis impacts Michigan, where 15 counties have little to no hospitals or birth centers providing pregnancy and childbirth care, Atkinson said. Additionally, policy rollbacks, the recent closure of three Michigan Planned Parenthood clinics and federal Medicaid funding cuts, highlight the urgency of the Black maternal health crisis.
Racism is a “huge factor” in contributing to this lack of access to care, Atkinson said, with Black women reporting that they are being treated differently or ignored when they say they’re in pain or lacking postpartum support.
“The abortion bans have a real effect on the safety of women,” she said. “When we are closing a huge provider like Planned Parenthood, we are only putting more people at risk for a variety of diseases. So, when we’re not thinking about women’s health in totality, we’re not thinking about outcomes for birth. We have to be making policy accordingly.”
Atkinson said the state’s efforts to provide resources to new mothers through initiatives like the Rx Kids cash assistance program and passage of the “Momnibus” legislative package, which works to improve accountability in Michigan’s maternal health care system, are steps in the right direction toward providing mothers with equitable opportunities to experience a healthy pregnancy and birth.
The “Momnibus” bills helped Michigan set up and license freestanding birth centers. Still, Atkinson said more needs to be done to offset a presidential administration that does not invest in prenatal care and postnatal support, Atkinson said.
“We’ve seen some things pass that we know are scientifically based to create better outcomes, but we obviously still have work to do,” she said. “We pass paid sick days, but we need paid family medical leave. We need access to affordable childcare, because caregivers, birthing people and mothers live a whole life, which means they are caring for a lot of people, which means they have stressors on their life that prevent them from being able to get to the services that they need, and those services need to be extremely accessible.”
During In Her Honor, Mothering Justice’s partner in the event, the ARIAH Foundation, will host a screening Wednesday night at the Detroit Institute of Arts of the award-winning documentary “Aftershock,” along with a community discussion, with speakers and attendees sharing personal stories of pregnancy, motherhood, and tragedy. The evening will explore the ongoing Black maternal health crisis, the systemic barriers contributing to maternal mortality and the community-led solutions advancing maternal health equity. 

“Aftershock” tells the story of 30-year-old Shamony Gibson, who died 13 days after the birth of her son. Following Gibson’s death, her mother, ARIAH Foundation co-founder Shawnee Benton Gibson, turned her grief into a movement supporting families facing similar losses.
Benton Gibson, who had already been working in reproductive health justice prior to her daughter’s birth-related pulmonary embolism, said the “silent fourth trimester” that led to her daughter’s death brings to light how this issue can be overlooked.
“When she transitioned, it was a shock that she died from something that we had been working on together for years,” she said.
“You need to be listening to them when they have something to say about what’s happening with their body or not happening with their body after they give birth, and you need to take action because of the statistical data that proves that we’re three times more likely to experience maternal mortality than our white counterparts.”
In addition to the film screening, In Her Honor will host its signature gala on Thursday, Aug. 27 and a “public exhibition day” on Friday, Aug. 28 that features portraits, personal stories and educational installations honoring Black mothers whose lives were lost to pregnancy-related complications. 
The exhibition, which takes place from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. at the Mothering Justice National Movement Home at 1948 Division St, Suite 101 in Detroit, highlights the experiences of impacted families while examining the racial disparities that continue to shape maternal health outcomes in the United States.
From left to right: Mothering Justice Executive Director Danielle Atkinson, ARIAH co-founder Omari Maynard and ARIAH co-founder Shawnee Benton Gibson. (Photo provided)
Artist and ARIAH co-founder Omari Maynard said he began painting portraits following the death of Shamony Gibson, his partner who he had two children with, as a way to communicate with her through art.
More than five years later, he has painted around 60 portraits of other Black women who have lost their lives to tell their stories around reproductive health, gifting them to their families. Many of those portraits will be on display during the exhibition.
“Art is a universal language — one that all people understand and speak — and what makes us human,” he said. “I think that it creates a different entry point of having more of a listening ear and more of a spiritual and and physical experience of not just understanding what the statistics are, but understanding the human side of what maternal health looks like and how it affects families in a traumatic way, but also in a healing way.”
For more information on In Her Honor, including how to RSVP for events, visit its website.

title: Vermont Progressive Party chair resigns after less than a year on the job
description:
Bill Hunsinger stepped down Tuesday but will stay involved with the party, its executive director said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Progressive Party chair resigns after less than a year on the job.
text:
Bill Hunsinger, who has resigned from his position as chair of the Vermont Progressive Party. Photo courtesy of Bill Hunsinger
The chair of Vermont’s Progressive Party, Bill Hunsinger, has resigned from his post. 
Hunsinger stepped down Tuesday after less than a year in the job as the leader of the state’s third largest political party, according to Heather Thomas, the party’s executive director. The chair is the party’s public-facing leader, while the executive director manages its day-to-day operations and is the organization’s only full-time staffer.
According to Thomas, Hunsinger’s decision was a result of the challenges of balancing the job’s significant workload with his full-time job, raising a young daughter and serving on the selectboard in his hometown of Ripton.
“It takes an incredible amount of time and energy to work within structures that are designed by and for the wealthy,” Thomas said in an interview Wednesday. “We’re very grateful for his time and all the ways that he’s helped advance our mission.”
Hunsinger’s resignation leaves one of the state’s major political parties without a figurehead in the middle of an election cycle with just weeks until voters start receiving their ballots in the mail. The Progressive Party is the third-largest in Vermont by a wide margin, with just a handful of elected officials in its state House and Senate caucuses and far fewer voters taking part in its statewide primary elections than the number who participate in the Democratic and Republican contests.
Thomas said she is confident in the party’s organizational capacity around the state regardless of any turnover at the top, pointing to its “strong group of members who are deeply committed to the movement.” 
The party will meet soon to choose an interim chair, she said, and then formally elect a new one at its state convention the week after the Nov. 3 election.
Hunsinger will stay involved with the party, including as chair of its Addison County committee, Thomas said.
Hunsinger did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday morning.

title: University of Iowa partnership to expand healthcare education pathways
description: The University of Iowa is partnering with a graduate healthcare institution to provide UI graduates more opportunities to further their education in different areas of medicine. Midwestern University, a graduate health sciences institution with locations in Arizona and Illinois, announced in a news release Tuesday it has signed an articulation agreement with[...]
text:
The University of Iowa and Midwestern University have partnered to offer qualified UI students guaranteed interviews and admission to certain programs. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The University of Iowa is partnering with a graduate healthcare institution to provide UI graduates more opportunities to further their education in different areas of medicine.
Midwestern University, a graduate health sciences institution with locations in Arizona and Illinois, announced in a news release Tuesday it has signed an articulation agreement with the UI to provide guaranteed interviews and acceptance into certain programs.

“The University of Iowa has long been recognized for excellence in the health sciences, and this partnership builds on that strength by creating additional opportunities for our students to pursue advanced professional education,” said UI Executive Vice President and Provost Kevin Kregel in the release. “By expanding pathways to graduate study, we’re helping more students access high-quality educational opportunities that prepare them for meaningful careers in healthcare.”
Starting with students set to enroll at Midwestern University in fall 2027, the release stated qualifying UI students will have guaranteed admission interviews for Midwestern programs including osteopathic, podiatric, veterinary and dental medicine, as well as pharmacy, optometry and other areas.
Students who “meet specified academic criteria” could also receive guaranteed acceptance into certain Midwestern programs through the institution’s college of graduate studies and its college of health sciences nurse anesthesia program, according to the release. Both Midwestern campuses are included in the agreement.
This articulation agreement provides a smoother, more transparent path from undergraduate to graduate study, the release stated, allowing students to more easily achieve their academic and professional goals.
“Midwestern University is proud to partner with the University of Iowa, an institution renowned for its rigorous academic standards and dedication to student excellence,” said Midwestern University Provost Y. Gloria Yueh in the release. “This agreement reflects our shared commitment to creating seamless pathways for high-achieving students as they prepare to become leaders in human and animal healthcare.”
