name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming GOP lost power, credibility with wasted Bien endorsement
description:
Governor nominee Barlow doesn’t need to listen to state party leaders who didn’t support him, opines columnist Kerry Drake.
The post Wyoming GOP lost power, credibility with wasted Bien endorsement appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
With much fanfare and at the risk of violating state law, the Wyoming Republican Party broke with decades of tradition and endorsed candidates in last week’s primary election instead of remaining neutral.

Opinion

It picked the losing candidates in all four of the competitive races for statewide offices. The most embarrassing misfire was Brent Bien for governor, who finished third.
The far-right retired Marine colonel has never won a political race. He finished a distant second to Gov. Mark Gordon in the 2022 GOP primary.
What was it about Bien that convinced party leaders to bypass two Republicans with real governing experience?
State Sen. Eric Barlow, R-Gillette, has served in the Legislature for 14 years, including a term as House speaker. He won by 20,000 votes over Megan Degenfelder, state superintendent of public instruction.
The Wyoming Republican Party was never going to give Barlow a pat on the back and tell him he’s their man. 
Barlow’s agenda — keeping public land in public hands, improving healthcare affordability and accessibility, and properly funding education — is what party executive officers deride as the goals of Democrats and RINOs (Republicans in name only).
Degenfelder served only one term before seeking the state’s top job. One of her most touted accomplishments on the campaign trail, as strange as it sounds for the state’s public school chief, was her support for a bill that gave state public education dollars to pay tuition for private and religious schools.
And Degenfelder was on the far-right side of all of the political wedge issues that state GOP leaders embrace.
She backed banning a handful of transgender athletes from competing in girls’ sports events. Degenfelder pretended that it’s necessary to ban pornographic books and materials from public and school libraries that don’t have pornography on their shelves.
Plus, Degenfelder had the most prized political possession in this ultra-red state: President Donald Trump’s endorsement. It was the most prominent feature in almost all of her campaign advertisements and yard signs, as if the connection to Trump would automatically give her the kind of landslide win Rep. Harriet Hageman had over Liz Cheney in 2022.
To top it off, Degenfelder had the ringing endorsement of Hageman herself. If the golden girl of her state party can’t persuade the GOP to back her friend unconditionally, what in the heck drove the Bien endorsement?
Perhaps it was Bien’s push for “the people’s initiative” to cut residential property taxes by a massive 50% that will be on November’s general election ballot.
Republican lawmakers, especially Freedom Caucus members, have promoted chopping property taxes — or getting rid of them for good — in the past several sessions. They’ve viewed it as a winning issue, even though their own legislative efforts at such huge cuts have failed.
But I just don’t buy that’s the reason the state party gave Bien its blessing. I submit it was looking for a far-right conservative Christian male to carry its banner, and Bien was the only one in the race. Only he was “qualified.”
Imagine that, in the Equality State.
But think about it. Wyoming has only had one woman governor, Democrat Nellie Tayloe Ross, in the state’s 136-year history. She won a special 1924 election to fill the unexpired term of her late husband, Gov. William Ross.
While several Wyoming women have run for the GOP gubernatorial nomination, none have been successful.
Wyoming voters are used to putting women in congressional seats, and also into the offices of secretary of state, state treasurer, state auditor and superintendent of public instruction.
The Wyoming Republican Party had no problem giving its secretary of state endorsement to Rep. Rachel Rodriguez-Williams of Cody, chair of the Freedom Caucus.
But like the other two Freedom Caucus members who chose to leave the House — Rep. Scott Smith to challenge State Treasurer Curt Meier, and Rep. Tom Kelly, who vied for Degenfelder’s open superintendent’s seat — she lost.
Now, I do think there’s one woman that the Wyoming Republican Party would have endorsed for governor, and that’s Hageman. She reportedly considered running to become the state’s chief executive before deciding to try for retiring Sen. Cynthia Lummis’ open seat last December.
Republican gubernatorial candidate for Wyoming Eric Barlow speaks during a primary election candidate forum with fellow contender Megan Degenfelder organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming at Casper College on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Barlow announced his run for governor more than a year ago. While I believe a Barlow-Hageman race would have been a barnburner, and Hageman would have come closer than Degenfelder, I think Barlow still would have won.
Hageman would undoubtedly have had Trump’s endorsement, but that didn’t turn the tide for Degenfelder, did it?
A Trump endorsement is no longer the golden ticket that it was for Hageman four years ago. Degenfelder’s loss marked the fifth losing gubernatorial candidacy that the president has backed this year.
Hageman ran for governor in 2018 against Trump’s pick, Foster Friess, and both lost the primary to then-State Treasurer Mark Gordon. Wyomingites like their governors to be moderates compared to ideologues like Hageman, Degenfelder and Bien. 
No matter who his opponents were, in a year when the Freedom Caucus was blown out of the water in state government, Barlow was seen by voters as the right man for the job.
And despite the absurd claim of Bien’s camp that Barlow is really a Democrat, he won the primary because Republicans chose him.
The far-right has been flooding social media to falsely charge that Democrats made Barlow the GOP nominee, even after Republican legislators changed state election laws to ban changes in party affiliation before candidates even file for office. It was statistically impossible, given the relatively low numbers of Democrats who switched.
The best thing about the Wyoming GOP trying to stick it to the man who is now the nominee is that Barlow never has to worry about party leaders threatening him if he doesn’t toe their line.
They have no more power. What little they did have was wasted on backing Bien, and it backfired big time.

title: States take the wheel in grizzly recovery
description:
Many species could benefit from the new management rule enacted for grizzly bears, which incentivizes states, landowners and conservation groups to invest in recovery, writes guest columnist Jonathan Wood.
The post States take the wheel in grizzly recovery appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In mid July, the Secretary of the Interior and three governors gathered near Yellowstone National Park to celebrate the remarkable recovery of grizzly bears. Rather than declaring their work done, they announced an innovative approach to implementing the Endangered Species Act — one that allows states to earn greater management authority by demonstrating a species’ recovery.

Opinion

To this point, grizzlies have embodied both the best and worst of the Endangered Species Act. The positive is that the bears, especially around Yellowstone and Glacier national parks, have achieved an impressive recovery spurred by clear goals. For 30 years, those goals have motivated federal agencies, states, ranchers and conservation groups to collaborate on conservation.
And they have. When the species was listed in the 1970s, only 136 grizzly bears roamed the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service set recovery at 500 bears in the region. Thanks to decades of effort, there are more than 1,000 bears in the area today.
The negative is that grizzly recovery has been mired in conflict. The Yellowstone population reached its recovery goals in the early 2000s. But successive efforts to delist the population — first during the Bush administration, and again during the Obama and first Trump administrations — have been blocked by courts demanding more analysis.
One reason for that conflict is that the stakes of delisting are enormous. One day, a species is fully controlled by the federal government. The next, the species is delisted and control moves to individual states. Such dramatic shifts create unnecessary uncertainty and fear. To an environmental activist who has spent decades fighting for a species, this can feel like jumping straight from a toddler taking her first steps to giving her the car keys. 
Of course, states are not toddlers. They are the nation’s primary wildlife managers and have proven effective at sustaining the recovery of formerly endangered species. The federal government has delisted 73 species in the U.S. following successful recoveries. None has been relisted due to backsliding under state management. But, given the stakes, there’s a persistent fear that the next species will prove the exception to this rule. 
For that reason, the Endangered Species Act has long needed a more gradual and predictable off-ramp. The government’s new approach would provide it. 
In 2020, during a species status review, my organization, the Property and Environment Research Center, urged the Fish and Wildlife Service to let states earn expanded management authority as grizzly populations meet recovery goals. Last year, we partnered with the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Boone & Crockett Club and Wyoming Wildlife Federation in a comment proposing how the Fish and Wildlife Service could put this idea into practice. The proposed rule takes that path, giving states substantial authority to manage bears while they remain listed and the federal government retains some control, including a hunting prohibition. This breaks the all-or-nothing pattern and makes state authority dependent on achieving and maintaining recovery goals. 
Some areas already exceed their recovery goals and could see expanded state management soon; others are close, giving states extra incentive to clear the bar. And accountability is built in through the use of objective criteria that would trigger a shift back to federal management.
This approach wouldn’t end conflict over the bear’s status. But it would give the federal government and the states something like an insurance policy against future conflict, locking in greater flexibility now rather than conditioning everything on delisting.
While the agency deserves credit for embracing this novel solution, the proposal could be improved. Rather than setting recovery goals in the regulation, the proposed rule creates a new bureaucratic process for the federal government and states to negotiate key details later. That decision has caused environmental groups to speculate that standards will be set too low. It could equally let a future administration withdraw states’ authority regardless of their success. But this uncertainty can be easily fixed by incorporating clear, objective standards into the rule.
Many other species would benefit from this model. Shifting authority to states gradually as species progress toward recovery goals would create the needed incentives for states, landowners and conservation groups to invest in the recovery of struggling species. It would also allow states to build trust with the conservation community by allowing them to demonstrate they can effectively manage a species in advance of a delisting. 
For more than 50 years, the Fish and Wildlife Service has had the flexibility to condition regulatory relief on recovery progress — but hasn’t used it. Instead, the agency has reflexively regulated threatened species the same as endangered species, ignoring opportunities to tailor regulations to spur and reward recovery. Its recent decision to rescind this policy opens the door to more thoughtful and creative approaches, like the grizzly bear proposal, informed by science rather than lazy one-size-fits-all presumptions.
That’s critical to improving the Endangered Species Act’s performance. Examining every species for which the Fish and Wildlife Service has set a projected recovery date, my organization found that, of the 300 species projected to recover by 2023, only 11 actually did. Flexibility and incentives are essential to close this recovery gap. Ultimately, the goal is to get every species to follow the grizzly’s lead to recovery.

title: Montana GOP is the victim of political eugenics
description: An important part of the political movement in Germany before and during World War Two was the belief that the “Aryan race” was superior to any other and that it was possible to create a “master race” through eugenics; that is, through selective breeding. That would mean that people having the ideal blonde-haired, blue-eyed features […]
text:
GOP Chair Art Wittich, left, Rep. Terry Falk, center, and Sen. Greg Hertz discuss property tax legislation at the GOP Winter Kickoff event at the Heritage Inn on Feb. 7 in Great Falls, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)An important part of the political movement in Germany before and during World War Two was the belief that the “Aryan race” was superior to any other and that it was possible to create a “master race” through eugenics; that is, through selective breeding. That would mean that people having the ideal blonde-haired, blue-eyed features of the Aryan would be encouraged to breed and that other people with less desirable physical characteristics would be sterilized or killed. 
It didn’t work out well.
Neither will the attempt of the Montana Republican Party to demand absolute purity within its ranks have good results. 
The latest attempt of party leaders to remove two political gadflies from the November ballot has resulted in a defeat for the party leadership and an increase in bad blood between the party purists and the more moderate party members under attack. The latest defeat was begun by Senate President Matt Regier, R- Kalispell, asking Republican Attorney General Austin Knudsen for a new legal opinion on the law of term limits. 
Term limits restricting a person to no more than eight years in one elected office were enacted by the Montana electorate in 1992. The first time the eight-year limit was reached was 2000, and since then legislators had been legally jumping between House and Senate chambers every eight years. Why Regier waited until after the primary election to ask the question was pretty obvious, the Republican Party’s attempt to take out Senate candidate Llew Jones, R-Conrad, in a primary failed. Another method had to be looked at which the Attorney General was able to provide; create a legal obstacle to Jones being on the ballot. Knudsen found that a person who had spent eight consecutive years in the Senate and then another eight consecutive years in the House would have to sit out an election cycle before being eligible to run for the Senate again. This fit Llew Jones perfectly, and to make the idea even sweeter, it applied to Senator Steve Fitzpatrick, R-Great Falls, another important Republican who didn’t follow orders meekly. Knudsen released his opinion less than two weeks before the Montana Secretary of State’s Aug. 20 deadline to certify the November ballot.
Jones and Fitzpatrick filed for a court injunction against the ruling which was granted by a Lewis and Clark County District judge. Knudsen then appealed to the Supreme Court to block the injunction. The state’s highest court said in effect, “a lack of planning on your part does not constitute an emergency on our part” and refused to take the case. So, Jones and Fitzpatrick will still be on the November ballot.
The worst of this began a few years ago when the Republican Party decided to breed for purity. Their first failure was to attempt to punish several Senate members by not giving them the committee assignments they had requested because their purity as true Republicans was in question. Understandably, they were peeved and they managed to form a block of votes which amended the rules to give the affected Senators the committee assignments of their choice. These nine Republicans then began voting with the Democratic minority to defeat many of the agendas of the Republican leadership. Moral: If you are going to kill a snake, make sure it’s dead. 
Several of the dissenting Republican senators had just been elected to the Senate, meaning they would be back in 2027 and back with bad memories. Others would face opponents in the primaries and be subjected to defeat, as some were. In the 2026 Republican Convention the nine dissenting Senators were not allowed to vote, aggravating the situation further.
It is not wise to make enemies of people on your own side, whether or not they disagree on issues. Whatever the proposed agenda of the Republican Party is in the 2027 Legislature it has the potential to be stymied by Republican members who have been mistreated by party leadership. 
There is a better way to run a Legislature than by making enemies out of allies.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Twin Falls ICE flight observers record more than 500 detainees flown out of Magic Valley airport
description: Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal.  Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around […]
text:
Maureen Newton waves as she uses binoculars to watch U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees board a plane on Aug. 11, 2026, at the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes. 
One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van. 
According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle. 
Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport.
Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel record the entire boarding process for each ICE flight that operates out of the airport near Twin Falls. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun)
Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April. 
An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.”
“ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email.  
The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.” 
The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed. 
The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data. 
Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation. 
“We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said. 
 ‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’ 

Maureen Newton, left, and Karen Stroder, observe an ICE flight on Aug. 11, 2026, out of the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun)
Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization. 
“I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. I think everybody deserves their day in court.”  
Twin Falls resident Heather Muth, who helped found the local Indivisible group, learned from an Indiana chapter member that these flights were happening and that various groups tracked and recorded them. She and other members connected with these groups to learn about monitoring the flights. 
Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April. 
“What’s new in the last couple of years is just the fact that … these people aren’t getting their due process,” Muth said. 
Maureen Newton of the Burley/Rupert area recently went to the airport to watch a flight for the first time. She said she’d read about the flights and had concerns about it. 
“This is my taxpaying dollars here I’m watching go down the garbage can,” she said, keeping her eyes on the plane as detainees with their hands bound in front of them boarded the plane one at a time. 
Shelly McDaniel records a video of the boarding process for each flight and later takes a screenshot of each person who boards. She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch. The goal is to make the information available to attorneys so they can find their clients. 
McDaniel and her husband told the Sun they are supportive of people with criminal convictions being deported, but their concern is that the detentions and deportations happen too quickly for the court process to finish. Shelly McDaniel said she 
“I know of people that have been taken on a Sunday, and on Tuesday they’re on a plane,” Shelly McDaniel said.  “… there’s just no way they’re even able to present their case in court.”
State Rep. Clint Hostetler, R-Twin Falls, asks a question during the March 16, 2026, Idaho House Local Government Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Twin Falls Republican state Rep. Clint Hostetler told the Sun in an email he’s supportive of the flights and argued that due process is being followed.
He said he supports “the rule of law, and that includes enforcing our nation’s immigration laws.”
“My understanding is these operations prioritize individuals who have already gone through the legal process and received a final order of removal, it also includes people with criminal convictions, public safety concerns, or no valid legal status to remain in the country,” Hostetler said. “This isn’t a new or extraordinary policy, it’s the law being applied.”
He said he understood that the flights could be “unsettling to some in our community, but failing to enforce the law isn’t fair to the people who came here the right way, or to Idaho taxpayers.”
“My focus as a representative is on what’s best for Idaho families and communities,” he said, “and that includes a secure, lawfully enforced immigration system.”
An ICE detainee climbs a ramp onto a plane on Aug. 11, 2026, at the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun)
 Attorneys must file a Habeas petition in court with jurisdiction before detainee is moved 

If an attorney is going to be able to stop a detention before someone is deported and get a chance to argue their client’s case in court, they often must obtain what is called a habeas corpus petition. 
Habeas petitions allow people to challenge their detention in court. 
Twin Falls attorney Brian Tanner said attorneys for detainees must file for a habeas in a court with jurisdiction over where the detainee is located. 
“You have to know immediately where they are, because you have to provide notice to the district court that you are filing habeas so that they don’t send them out, or you have to get them before they leave,” Tanner said. 
If the petition is filed in time and someone is flown out anyway, that person has to be returned, Tanner said. 
Shelly McDaniel said she’s seen at least one person leave on a plane and return later. 
ICE detainees climb a ramp onto a plane on Aug. 11, 2026, at the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun)
Prior to 2025, those who were apprehended by federal immigration authorities in the interior of the United States and who hadn’t committed a separate crime typically had the ability to get a bond hearing and avoid detention. 
Tanner said before the flights began, a bus with the area’s detainees would leave on Wednesdays and eventually take them to an immigration court in Utah. Tanner could often secure his clients’ release before they left. 
However, the U.S. Department of Justice under the Trump administration has changed its policy and began using a federal law typically only used for people who are caught while crossing the border or who just crossed the border, which allows them to be held without bond. 
He said the no-bond policy reinterprets how immigration has been enforced for “decades and decades and decades.” 
This new policy has been challenged and, at the end of July, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel of judges ruled that the government couldn’t withhold bail. Other circuit courts in other regions have had mixed rulings regarding this policy, with some upholding it and others blocking it, Stateline reported. 
Tanner’s frustration with the recent major changes in the system have led him to limit how many immigration cases he’s taken. He’d previously practiced immigration law for nearly 20 years. 
“Immigration is constantly changing in so many different ways. The president has an influence. The courts are basically interpreting laws in different ways. It’s always moving,” Tanner said. “So we get a different president, but I’ve never seen anything like this.” 
 ICE flight observers helped someone find detained family member, hope to help more

McDaniel said she recently saw a post on social media about someone trying to find their family member after he was detained in Idaho Falls. McDaniel reached out to ask her what he was wearing when he was detained and shared some photos with the person that matched the description. 
McDaniel used the screenshots of detainees boarding flights and was able to help to find the family member near Tacoma. The person who posted was then able to try and find a lawyer in the area. 
“It was very nice to know we were able to help them,” McDaniel said. 
Muth, the Indivisible leader, said the plan is to try and keep monitoring and let people know what’s happening at their local airport. 
“I think it’s always good to hear what everyone thinks about them, and to be able to have civil discourse, to talk about it,” Muth said. “… we do notice people are either one way or another. So they’re either for the flights and they’re happy that it’s happening, or they’re just extremely upset. And there can be a lot of emotion on both sides.”

title: Tennessee Transportation finds no “red flags” in toll-land bidder despite past problems
description: Tennessee Department of Transportation officials picked a road-building group to take on the state’s first toll project despite a series of bumps the consortium’s companies hit over the past decade-plus, ranging from bankruptcies to price-gouging accusations. DriveTN’s winning bid included a $9.2 billion construction plan to build toll lanes in Nashville’s s[...]
text:
DriveTN, the consortium picked to build Tennessee's toll roads, known as "choice lanes," was accused of price-gouging in a 2025 lawsuit. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Department of Transportation officials picked a road-building group to take on the state’s first toll project despite a series of bumps the consortium’s companies hit over the past decade-plus, ranging from bankruptcies to price-gouging accusations.
DriveTN’s winning bid included a $9.2 billion construction plan to build toll lanes in Nashville’s southeast interstate corridor, mainly along I-24 to Murfreesboro, with the promise to pay the state nearly $25 billion over the life of a 50-year contract. 
No other bidder came close to DriveTN, which, along with its large long term payout, offered $1.5 billion up front.
Two other bidders offered about $7 billion in payment “concessions” to the state, and a fourth asked for a state subsidy to complete the project.
Transportation Commissioner Will Reid said the companies that make up DriveTN had to meet basic requirements to move on to a second phase of pre-qualifications entailing everything from financial information to the ability to deliver such a large project. In the process, the state turned up no major problems, he said.
“We would not have short-listed them had we found red flags,” Reid said.
Yet the group’s companies, which are based in Australia, Spain, France and the United States, ran into operating and financial problems over the last 10 to 20 years.
Tennessee taps road-building group for $9B toll lanes project

Australia-based Transurban’s tolls hit $40 in 2017 on the second day of collections on Interstate 66 from Virginia inside the Beltway of D.C. before dropping back to $24.75, then $5 before they ended that morning, according to a report on Patch.
Reid said I-66 was one of the interstates he visited as Tennessee studied toll lanes and the concept of dynamic pricing, which is based on traffic and the need to keep motorists moving when they pay a fee.
Tennessee’s toll lanes will use the same type of pricing, based mainly on the number of vehicles paying to take express lanes.
In 2025, Virginia motorists filed a class-action lawsuit against Transurban claiming it wrongfully hit them with thousands of dollars in penalties, according to an ABC News report. One couple was charged $11,000 in accumulated fees after replacing a credit card and failing to notify E-Z Pass, which handles fees.
Ferrovial’s toll-road affiliate Cintra Holding also hit a bump in 2006 when the joint venture Cintra-Macquarie took over the Indiana Toll Road, doubled rates, then filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy because of heavy debt, according to a U.S. Department of Transportation report. The venture, which had paid the state of Indiana $3.8 billion for 75 years of operating rights, raised questions about revenue projections and whether plans should be made for setbacks such as recessions.
North Carolina officials found themselves taking a fresh look at Spain-based Cintra after choosing it to build and run toll lanes on I-77 as one of its subsidiaries filed for bankruptcy in 2016, according to a report.
Another member of the consortium, AECOM Technical Services, paid $201 million in a court settlement because of “improper disclosure” to investors dealing with inaccurate traffic projections, another report shows.
Asked about these problems, Department of Transportation spokesperson Beth Emmons declined to address them, saying that even though Drive TN was selected as the “proposer” for the project, the department remains in an “active procurement process” and can’t give more details.
“This milestone reflects TDOT’s extensive planning, strong community engagement, and significant private sector interest. Our current focus is on verifying commitments, completing required reviews, and finalizing the agreement to ensure long-term benefits for Tennesseans,” Emmons said in a statement.
Speaking to reporters after the Tennessee Transportation Modernization Board approved the top proposal, Reid said DriveTN’s dollar figures draw the most attention because “they’re eye-popping.”

“But what is really critical about their proposal is it was also the best technically,” he said.
DriveTN’s “concession fee” is not related to the rates it will charge motorists to use the lanes but will be based on demand and the group’s 50-year revenue projections, Reid said.
Most of the toll lanes will be elevated, and DriveTN came up with ways to avoid areas such as the Pan-Asia Supermarket in the Bell Road area, Noble Place Townhomes, in addition to eliminating reconstruction of the Hickory Hollow Parkway bridge. 
State officials did not give an estimate of how many homes could be affected. But the proposal gained points for reducing the impact on public rights of way.
The group also committed to incorporating park-and-ride facilities into the project and increasing connections to the toll lanes.
In addition to stretching to a point near Murfreesboro, the toll-lane project will run out I-40 East toward Nashville’s airport and along I-440.
Construction is expected to start in 2027 and take eight years to complete, though portions of the toll lanes will be ready for motorists sooner, state officials said.
Long-term, toll lanes could run through downtown Nashville, then along I-24 and I-65 toward Goodlettsville as well as farther out I-40 East toward Lebanon and through Murfreesboro.
Public hearings are set for Sept. 8 from 12:30 to 6 p.m. at Nashville Public Library Pruitt Branch and Sept. 9 from 12:30 to 6 p.m. at Smyrna Event Center.

title: Rural health grants aimed at offsetting Medicaid cuts go to 80 unique institutions
description: The first round of federal grants in a program aimed to partially offset Medicaid cuts were awarded Monday afternoon to over 80 unique healthcare and educational institutions across the state. The grants are awarded through the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program (ARHTP), which is funded by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). It distributes […]
text:
Vaughan Regional Medical Center in Selma, AL, on Tuesday, Sep. 3, 2024 in Selma, Ala. The hospital was one of many to receive a grant in the first round of awards in the Rural Health Transformation Program on Monday. (Will McLelland for Alabama Reflector)The first round of federal grants in a program aimed to partially offset Medicaid cuts were awarded Monday afternoon to over 80 unique healthcare and educational institutions across the state.
The grants are awarded through the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program (ARHTP), which is funded by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). It distributes $50 billion in grants through the U.S. Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services (CMS) to the states over five years for rural health care. 
“Alabama is serious about creating systematic changes through the ARHTP to ensure every citizen has access to quality care,” Gov. Kay Ivey said in a statement. “This program is enabling institutions covering every part of the state to improve healthcare for Alabamians through projects that are both innovative and sustainable.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alabama was awarded $203.4 million in December based on its application for 11 initiatives: Collaborative Electronic Health Record (EHR), IT and Cybersecurity; Rural Health; Maternal and Fetal Health; Rural Workforce; Cancer Digital Regionalization; Simulation Training; Statewide EMS Trauma and Stroke; EMS Treat-In-Place; Mental Health; Rural Health Practice and Community Medicine – which will not receive funding until year three of the program.
Monday’s grants were distributed to the applicants who applied under the Rural Health, Rural Workforce, Mental Health, Rural Health Practice and Collaborative Electronic Health Record, or IT and Cybersecurity initiatives, according to a press release. Ivey announced 138 grants were awarded, totalling more than $144 million. 
The program is administered through the Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). Applicants had to show that they could sustainably transform rural health.
“To say that there is great interest in improving rural healthcare in Alabama is an understatement,” Kenneth Boswell, director of ADECA, said in a statement. “This announcement comes at the end of a process that included six packed-house informational meetings in different locations throughout the state, five grant application workshops and hundreds of grant applications.”
U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, said in a statement that the grants will give hospitals the resources they need to serve their communities. Aderholt represents Alabama’s 4th Congressional District, which covers the northwestern corner of the state and the foot of the Appalachian Mountains.
“Representing one of the more rural congressional districts in America has taught me that where a person lives should never determine the quality of healthcare they receive or the opportunities available to them,” he said.
But experts say one-time grants might not be enough to save rural hospitals.
According to a brief from KFF, a national health policy research organization, the fund could offset just over a third (37%) of the estimated federal Medicaid spending cuts in rural areas, which are projected to be $137 billion over ten years.
According to the University of North Carolina’s Sheps Center, nine rural hospitals have closed in Alabama since 2009. Only 30% of the state’s rural hospitals have labor and delivery units, leaving many expectant parents to drive long distances for care. Alabama is one of ten states that has not expanded Medicaid. 
Alabama’s hospitals have long pushed for expansion, saying it would help hospitals on the brink of collapse survive, but Republican leaders have resisted it. 
While Alabama House leaders have signaled openness to a public-private hybrid approach to expansion, the Senate has been hostile, and removed a provision from a 2024 gambling bill that could have provided money for the program.  
U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Selma, said in a statement Tuesday that while the grant money is helpful, it is “like putting a Band-Aid on an open wound.” Sewell’s 7th Congressional District covers rural west Alabama and part of Birmingham. Many of the hospitals that have closed in the state have been in that region. 
“They will not stop the bleeding caused by (President Donald) Trump’s healthcare cuts,” she said. “As I have said from the beginning, the best way for state officials to support our rural hospitals is by expanding Medicaid, which they refuse to do for political reasons. Alabama’s rural communities deserve better, and I will continue fighting to protect access to quality health care across our state.”
U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise – who is also the party’s nominee for U.S. Senate – said in a statement that the grants will help rural Alabamians get access to care that those in urban areas have. Moore currently represents the 1st Congressional District, which covers the Wiregrass region of the state to Mobile and Baldwin Counties. 
“Too many families in rural Alabama have had to travel too far or waited too long to get the care they need,” he said. “By strengthening our rural healthcare workforce, expanding mental health and emergency services, and giving local providers the tools they need to modernize, we are investing in the people and communities that make Alabama strong.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Water is a missing element in the grand plan to build up the Idaho National Laboratory
description: Editor’s note: This is the second in a series of three op-eds written by columnist Jim Jones that will discuss Idaho’s application to become the host of one of three Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses in the U.S. The first column, “With lifecycle campus plan, is Idaho getting ready to buy a nuclear waste pig in […]
text:
The Snake River flows alongside the Idaho Falls greenbelt. (Photo courtesy of Hyo Lee/U.S. Department of Energy)Editor’s note: This is the second in a series of three op-eds written by columnist Jim Jones that will discuss Idaho’s application to become the host of one of three Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses in the U.S. The first column, “With lifecycle campus plan, is Idaho getting ready to buy a nuclear waste pig in a poke?” ran Tuesday, and the third will run Wednesday.
The recently announced proposal to greatly expand the Idaho National Laboratory is exciting. In order to become a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Center, Idaho merely needs to agree to take and store one-third of the nuclear waste generated across the country.  
The documents released by Idaho Gov. Brad Little extoll the virtues of the plan, but I was unable to find a significant element in the sheaf of papers. There is no mention of where the water will come from to fuel the fantastic growth of the INL.
The governor does say at page 14 of his plan: “Idaho is prepared to identify sources of readily accessible on-site water supplies capable of meeting industrial-scale needs, including cooling systems for reactors and reprocessing facilities.” 
However, it is not clear to many who are familiar with the water demands currently being made upon the East Snake River Plain Aquifer, where those sources might be. The wording — “industrial-scale needs” — implies a lot of water. The governor should identify those “readily accessible” water supplies to ease the concerns of Idaho water users.
‘This year is different’: The water reality Idaho can no longer ignore

Most water observers understand that the East Snake River Plain Aquifer is greatly overburdened already, creating bitter conflicts over its declining water supplies. 
As Dan Davidson, a career water manager, succinctly put it, “Idaho does not have enough water.” He correctly says that the aquifer “remains at historic lows” and that this year’s “record water demand, drought conditions and depleted water availability are red flag warnings.” 
Water users are continually fighting over allocation and usage of Snake River waters, resulting in numerous curtailments of water for many users.
The U.S. Department of Energy entered into a Water Right Agreement with the state of Idaho in 1990. As Idaho attorney general at the time, I signed that agreement along with former Gov. Cecil Andrus. The agreement set the terms and quantity of the INL’s water rights. The agreement was approved by the adjudication court. 
In order to increase its water usage, as contemplated by Gov. Little’s plan, INL must acquire a new water right, which would come at the expense of existing uses. That might cause the agricultural community to rise up in righteous anger. 
Many Snake River water right holders have had their water usage curtailed in recent water shortage years, but the Department of Energy has asserted that the state does not have “any right to curtail or otherwise administer DOE’s adjudicated water rights” at the INL. A recent decision by the director of the Idaho Department of Water Resources found that this was a matter to be decided by the adjudication court. 
The state planned against such a claim years ago, so INL is likely to lose the claim that it should have its full water right while all other water users have their water curtailed.
Page 39 of the governor’s plan throws another fly into the ointment. It says: “While water rights on-site are sufficient for current operations, precise management will be critical as NLIC activities increase water demand. The state anticipates significant adoption of sustainable water practices such as recycling and non-water cooling technologies for data centers to mitigate demand on the aquifer.”
With lifecycle campus plan, is Idaho getting ready to buy a nuclear waste pig in a poke?

So, despite the uncontested fact that the aquifer is already significantly over-appropriated, there are plans for data centers? The governor did state it in the plural. 
One does not have to be an expert to understand that data centers require massive amounts of electricity and water to operate. The public is starting to awaken to the fact, as shown by two laws enacted by the Legislature this year. 
Rep. Stephanie Mickelsen’s House Bill 911 protects electric ratepayers from higher bills resulting from large electricity users like data centers. Britt Raybould’s House Bill 895 protects against excessive water grabs by data centers. 
We can’t allow data centers to cause electric rates to skyrocket for the general public or to impinge on the water rights of farmers, businesses and consumers. There must be clearcut requirements for data centers to be wholly responsible for their own electric and water usage.
The unfortunate thing is that data centers at the INL may not be subject to state and local control under the governor’s plan. The Trump administration has been pushing to locate data centers on federally controlled property for this very reason.
The upshot is that the state should not rush headlong into signing a binding agreement to take one-third of the nuclear waste in the country unless and until there is a clear and binding agreement as to how the INL will obtain the supplies of water and electricity to fill its substantial and increasing needs, without jeopardizing the rights of existing water users and ratepayers.
It would not be asking too much for the Department of Energy to commit in writing that it will not use a declaration of national security necessity to get around existing state laws.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: What climate science tells us about the causes of the Colorado River crisis
description: Elected officials from across Colorado’s political spectrum continued a 68-year-old tradition last week when they took to the stage at the annual summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs. First convened by Gov. Steve McNichols in 1958, the Water Congress brings together experts, policymakers, agricultural producers and other inte[...]
text:
The Colorado River flows through Palisade on June 9, 2023. (William Woody for Colorado Newsline)Elected officials from across Colorado’s political spectrum continued a 68-year-old tradition last week when they took to the stage at the annual summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs.
 
Connecting the news in Colorado to the big picture.

First convened by Gov. Steve McNichols in 1958, the Water Congress brings together experts, policymakers, agricultural producers and other interest groups to negotiate and strategize in a state where water has always been a scarce and carefully managed resource.
That’s never been more true than it is today, at a time of extreme drought and escalating political conflict over the future of the Colorado River. The river’s cumulative flow at Cameo, just upstream of Palisade and Grand Junction, is at a record low this year, and Colorado and six other states that depend on its water are likely headed for an extended, high-stakes court battle over how to apportion the cuts forced on them by more than two decades of persistently dry conditions.
Addressing the Water Congress, Colorado leaders said the way forward for water users is through, as Attorney General Phil Weiser, the Democratic nominee for governor, put it, “collaboration and innovation.” They talked about storage and diversion projects, conservation measures and drought-resistant crops. They promised to defend farmers and ranchers from so-called “buy and dry” purchases of their water rights by municipal utilities, and to fight off efforts by the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California and Nevada to force mandatory cuts on upstream users in Colorado.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Notably absent, however, from the event’s three days of speeches on water policy — from politicians on both sides of the aisle — was the predominant reason why the situation on the Colorado River is bad and getting worse: human-caused climate change.
Neither Weiser nor Victor Marx, the Republican candidate for governor, made any mention of the threat posed to Western water supplies by rising global temperatures. It was missing, too, from speeches by both GOP U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a longtime fossil-fuel industry booster, and Democratic U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse, a former member of the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis.
Dwayne Romero, the Democratic nominee in Colorado’s drought-ravaged 3rd Congressional District, went so far as to say that “the climate is putting new pressure on” water management issues, but no further.
The lack of acknowledgment of the causes of the Colorado River Basin’s post-2000 megadrought comes as Colorado Republicans largely continue to ignore or deny the science of climate change — and as Democrats have been pressured by some party consultants to deemphasize the issue in the wake of their defeat in the 2024 election.
Clockwise from top left: U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a Windsor Republican; Democratic congressional nominee Dwayne Romero; U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse, a Lafayette Democrat; and GOP governor nominee Victor Marx spoke at the summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs from Aug. 18 to 19, 2026. (Photos by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
But even as this “climate hushing,” as Rhode Island Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse dubbed it earlier this year, appears to have taken hold in the Democratic Party, hydrologists and climatologists have grown increasingly confident in identifying human emissions, rather than natural variability, as the overwhelming factor driving the West’s water woes.
Whether or not it’s politically expedient for either party to say so, the scientific consensus is that rising levels of greenhouse gases in the Earth’s atmosphere — mostly the result of burning oil, gas and coal — have pushed the Colorado River system to the brink, and that drought conditions are likely to continue to worsen as long as those emissions continue to push global temperatures higher.
‘Hot drought’ and beyond
As of 2024, average global temperatures had risen by more than 2.3 degrees Fahrenheit over pre-industrial levels, according to NOAA data, and climate scientists have concluded that virtually all of that observed warming is due to greenhouse gas emissions from human activity. Parts of Colorado, including much of the Western Slope, are among the areas in the U.S. where average temperature increases have been most severe.
As litigation looms and drought takes its toll, state officials defiant over Colorado River’s future

Even in the absence of any other changes to global climate patterns, this higher heat alone can lead to drier conditions on the ground, by increasing the rate at which moisture evaporates — sometimes called evaporative demand, a measure of the atmosphere’s “thirst.” In a 2024 report for the Colorado Water Conservation Board, state climatologists found that evaporative demand had risen by 5% statewide between 1980 and 2022, and was projected to increase by 8% to 17% by 2050.
Within about a decade of the onset of the Colorado River megadrought in the 2000s, researchers began to conclude that rising temperatures were a major factor, making the drought more severe than it otherwise would’ve been. In an influential paper published in 2017, hydrologists Brad Udall and Jonathan Overpeck used the term “hot drought” to describe the basin’s current conditions, distinguishing it it from previous 20th-century “dry droughts,” caused largely by lower precipitation.
Further research has only solidified those conclusions. Using historical soil-moisture data and tree-ring records, one 2022 study found that the current megadrought is the worst dry spell the Southwest has experienced in at least 1,200 years. Studies generally agree that about 40% to 50% of the Colorado River’s declining flows can be attributed to higher temperatures alone.
This chart showing rising average temperatures was published in state climatologists’ 2024 report on climate change for the Colorado Water Conservation Board. (Colorado Climate Center)
Still, scientists were cautious about the other half of the hydrological equation — whether, and to what extent, climate change was influencing rainfall and snowfall, too. Modeling global warming’s precise impacts on precipitation patterns proved more complicated than identifying what state climatologists called the “basic physical relationship” between heat and evaporation.
“Compared to the 20th century, the 21st century has indeed been drier, but only by about 2.5%,” hydrologists with the Colorado River Research Group wrote in 2016. “Whether or not this is the leading edge of a trend, or merely a part of normal variability, is unknown.”
In just the last two years, however, new research has begun to dispel that uncertainty — and the findings, wrote Udall and Overpeck last year, “translate to mostly bad news.”
It’s precipitation, too
Overall precipitation in the Upper Colorado River Basin has continued to decline since 2000, with multi-year averages about 7% lower than previous levels as of 2025. Colorado was one of nine states in the West to have experienced their warmest winter on record in 2025-26, and statewide snowpack fell to its lowest level in more than 40 years, setting the stage for this summer’s extreme conditions.
Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder found last year that global warming is reducing precipitation in the West by stalling a key oceanic climate cycle known as the Pacific decadal oscillation, indicating that the region’s persistently dry conditions are being driven by human emissions “more intensely — and more directly — than previously understood.” Another 2025 paper by a different group of researchers echoed their findings.
“What’s important here is that we’re showing that rainfall has also been influenced by humans, in addition to just evaporation,” Pedro DiNezio, one of the CU Boulder study’s co-authors, told Newsline last year. “Both contribute to drought.”
A final key takeaway from climatological research on the Colorado River is that the higher global temperatures get, the worse things will be for river flows, which are not likely to ever return to their previous “normal.” Udall and others have encouraged the use of the term “aridification,” rather than drought or megadrought, to more accurately describe what’s happening to the river basin. But it’s also why he and Overpeck wrote last year that there’s a “silver lining” to the better understanding of river’s hydrology that researchers have gained over the last decade.
“We can say with confidence that human-caused emissions of greenhouse gases are having an increasingly negative impact on the flows of the Colorado River,” they wrote. “This climate change impact will continue to worsen, but because humans cause it, humans can halt it.”



The Trendline offers analysis on public policy in Colorado. Articles explore ways to think about the news based on research, history and other important context, helping Coloradans connect the headlines to the big picture.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Columbia water pipeline project gains key state financial approval amid ongoing opposition
description: A project to expand water utility capacity in fast-growing Southern Middle Tennessee by building a new $520 million intake on the Duck River and a new water treatment plant advanced Monday after obtaining key financing approval from the state’s local development authority. The controversial undertaking — which will be funded in part by rate hikes […]
text:
Land along the Duck River is among thousands of acres conserved in Tennessee in 2025 by private landowners and conservation organizations. Kayakers paddle in the river on July 6, 2025. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson)A project to expand water utility capacity in fast-growing Southern Middle Tennessee by building a new $520 million intake on the Duck River and a new water treatment plant advanced Monday after obtaining key financing approval from the state’s local development authority.
The controversial undertaking — which will be funded in part by rate hikes of up to 20% per year over the next five years — was first approved in January after weeks of intense debate.
The Tennessee Local Development Authority previously approved the project’s State Revolving Fund loan, and on Monday unanimously approved Columbia’s request to issue $315 million in WIFIA debt on parity — or equal priority — with the state loan. If the city’s request had been denied, the project would have been unable to use the lower-interest State Revolving Fund loan, which would raise the cost of the project by around $50 million in additional interest over the project’s life. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“We at the TLDA cannot stop this project, as some have asked,” Comptroller Jason Mumpower said Monday before the vote. “In fact, the local government in Columbia has made it very clear, regardless of what we do, they plan to move forward … even if it’s going to cost the citizens $50 million more in interest.”
Mumpower said he favored saving that money.
The rate increase will affect Columbia Power and Water Systems’ 27,000 customers in addition to 35,000 customers who are served by other water systems that purchase water from Columbia Power and Water. Customers who rely on the utility’s water but live outside of Columbia city limits have said they felt disenfranchised by the decision-making process. Because Columbia Power and Water Systems is a city utility, rate changes are approved solely by the Columbia City Council.
“The way that they have elected to pay for this is by raising rates by 20% across the board … The county ratepayers are already paying a higher rate (than city ratepayers),” said Dustin Kittle, a Maury County resident and an agricultural and environmental attorney who represents multiple property owners along the pipeline route. “It’s logical the county ratepayers will be paying more for this pipeline than what people inside the city will, and the ironic part of that is the county ratepayers won’t have any stake in that at all. This will be an asset that will belong to the city.”
The council also approved an increase to the water impact fee, a fee paid by developers to help cover costs associated with higher demand. The increased rate and impact fee are being used to secure federal and state long-term, low-interest loans to finance the project. That includes loans from the State Revolving Fund program and the federal Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act, WIFIA.
Columbia Power and Water Systems’ WIFIA loan has not yet closed, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s loan tracker.
Columbia Council approves water rate hike of up to 150% over next 5 years for new infrastructure

“I think we, in delaying this, gave an opportunity for more local dialogue, and I hope that has been constructive to some degree, but … what this board is faced with is a situation where we know there’s a need for more water resources in this community, and a path has been chosen by locally elected leaders,” Mumpower said. “That’s where the credit and the blame lie. And it’s for this board, really, to just look at the financing options available.”
State Treasurer David Lillard, Jr., who sits on the Tennessee Local Development Authority, said Tennessee should expect to see this issue arise more and more as the state’s population grows. 
“This is a good example of a situation where further input and the opportunity of gathering views from the ratepayers that are outside the city would have been very, very helpful here,” Lillard said. “I hope that in the future the General Assembly will take some action to look at this issue across the state.”
The Duck River Watershed Planning Partnership, an advisory group created by Gov. Bill Lee in February 2025 to identify ways to balance preservation, drought management and utility uses on the Duck River, also recently affirmed the plan for the new intake, pipeline and water treatment plant. The partnership ultimately approved the project 12-2, with three members abstaining.
A pending regionalization study did not consider alternatives to this water intake, so the outcome of the study would not affect the project, Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation Director of Water Resources April Grippo said Monday.

name: VTDigger
title: Vital Communities enters talks to save town listservs from shutdown
description:
A group of Upper Valley residents aims to launch UV Lists to take over 38 town listservs from Vital Communities this fall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vital Communities enters talks to save town listservs from shutdown.
text:
David Beane Jr., left, and Kate Harrison hike along the Appalachian Trail in Hanover, N.H., in Nov. 2023. Harrison donated a kidney to Beane in 2021 after seeing a listserv post from his mother seeking a donor for her son. Photo by Alex Driehaus / Valley News and Report For America

This story by Liz Sauchelli was first published in the Valley News on Aug. 25, 2026.Talks have started between Vital Communities and a group of Upper Valley residents about preserving town-specific listservs before the nonprofit pulls the plug.
“Vital Communities has been approached by a group of current and past listserv managers and community members interested in continuing the town-based listserv service as an independently organized entity,” Ellen Hender, executive director of the White River Junction-based organization, wrote in a Monday announcement posted to multiple listservs. “We are open to this idea and will continue to host the town-based listservs to allow time for the group to organize.”
The organization’s announcement came after it announced last week that it would no longer support the 38 town-specific listservs — where people share town news, business deals and information about lost pets, among other topics — that it has overseen since 2014. Originally, the listservs were scheduled to end last Friday, but after community feedback Vital Communities delayed their demise.
“I am surprised that Vital Communities did not recognize the value to the community and decided to shut them down in such an abrupt manner,” said Stan Williams, a Norwich resident whose history with the listservs extends back to their founding by ValleyNet around 2004. “To me it should be an easy decision to move it to a newly formed nonprofit and cooperate.”
Williams is a member of a group that is in the process of establishing a Vermont-based nonprofit organization called UV Lists to take the town-specific listservs. Group members are working on a memorandum of understanding with Vital Communities, which will detail the roles of each organization throughout the transition process, he said.
“It is important to us that any process of sharing listserv subscriber data be handled responsibly and legally. We are seeking legal counsel to determine what this would need to entail,” Hender wrote in Monday’s announcement. “We hope to have more details to share on the timeline soon.”
Williams said the group hopes to have the transition completed this fall. Thousands of listserv subscribers would “receive exactly the same emails” as they do now, he said, except with a new domain name that matches the new nonprofit organization. 
He estimated it would cost around $10,000 a year to pay for the technology to operate the listservs. The group is working on calculating other expenses, including how much money it needs to establish the new nonprofit organization. Group members will post more information to the listservs, which will include information about how to get involved with the new nonprofit and how to donate money.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Federal judge dismisses Trump administration lawsuit against Washtenaw County’s sanctuary policies
description: A federal judge in the Eastern District of Michigan on Friday dismissed a lawsuit alleging that Washtenaw County’s “sanctuary policies” were illegal. In her opinion, Judge F. Kay Behm stated that “neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will,” adding that “the government cannot otherwise compel localiti[...]
text:
Washtenaw County Courthouse (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)A federal judge in the Eastern District of Michigan on Friday dismissed a lawsuit alleging that Washtenaw County’s “sanctuary policies” were illegal.
In her opinion, Judge F. Kay Behm stated that “neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will,” adding that “the government cannot otherwise compel localities to enforce the President’s priorities in the manner it wishes.”
She wrote that the federal government cannot compel states or local governments to enact or administer a federal program, and cannot “conscript state or local officers directly.”
Three county policies were at issue in the lawsuit, Behm laid out in her decision. First, the county prosecutor’s office directed prosecutors to consider immigration consequences when making charging decisions, as well as not to share information with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement beyond what would be required by federal law. Second, the county sheriff’s office instructed officers not to ask about immigration status and determined that the office would not detain individuals for ICE without a judicial warrant or court order. Finally, the county’s Board of Commissioners decided not to allow federal immigration officers onto county property if they did not have a judicial warrant or court order. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The federal government’s initial complaint alleged that the county “insists on obstructing federal immigration enforcement operations and shielding criminal offenders from apprehension by federal law enforcement. Washtenaw County’s policies aim to obstruct federal law enforcement and celebrate thwarting the constitutional obligation of the President of the United States to take care that federal immigration law be faithfully executed.”
The supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution has complicated local and state level responses to federal immigration enforcement for communities around the country that do not want ICE to have a presence. 
One aspect of that legal doctrine is ‘obstacle preemption,” when state law serves as an obstacle to the purposes and objectives embodied in a federal law. The federal government argued Washtenaw County’s policies fit that definition. However, a high threshold must be met to prove that preemption.
Behm wrote that a refusal to cooperate with immigration enforcement “does not constitute discrimination against the federal government,” and therefore is not constitutionally prohibited. 
Quoting from another court ruling, Behm added that a “healthy balance of power between the States and the Federal Government [reduces] the risk of tyranny and abuse from either front,” concluding that Washtenaw County had done nothing more than “exercise its constitutional authority under the Tenth Amendment.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: After lawsuit, Kentucky updates rule to match voter registration with out-of-state records
description: Kentucky election officials have created a new regulation to match Kentucky voter registration against out-of-state records following a lawsuit from Kentuckians For The Commonwealth.  KFTC withdrew the case in federal court Monday after the emergency regulation was issued. The group filed the lawsuit in 2024 against Republican Secretary of State Michael Adam[...]
text:
Voters should check the "write-in candidate" bubble and need not worry about remembering their chosen candidate's first name, says a spokesperson for the Kentucky secretary of state. (Austin Anthony for The Kentucky Lantern)Kentucky election officials have created a new regulation to match Kentucky voter registration against out-of-state records following a lawsuit from Kentuckians For The Commonwealth. 
KFTC withdrew the case in federal court Monday after the emergency regulation was issued. The group filed the lawsuit in 2024 against Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams and the State Board of Elections, which includes Republican and Democratic members. KFTC argued state election law, changed in response to the coronavirus pandemic and made permanent in 2021, violated the federal rules requiring registered voters who have moved to receive notice in writing to confirm their address and have time to respond before they are removed from voter rolls.
“Protecting the voting rights of Kentuckians is vital as we strive to build democracy,” Lynne Anderson, a KFTC leader from Shelby County, said in a statement. “This requirement to verify voting registrations accurately is a big win for all of us.”
A spokesperson for Adams told the Kentucky Lantern that while the regulation is new, the policy is not. The policy codifies how election officials verify ineligible voters before removing them from rolls. 
“We are pleased this lawsuit was dismissed, but it never should have been brought in the first place,” Adams said. “On my watch, we require photo ID to vote and we keep our voter rolls clean.”
Taylor Brown, the general counsel for the State Board of Elections, also said the regulation reflects “the process the Board was already undertaking to comply with the existing state law.” 
“The Board is pleased that Kentuckians for the Commonwealth saw the promulgation of these procedures as an efficient way to resolve their concerns,” Brown added. 
KFTC was represented in the lawsuit by Jackson Cooper Law and the Fair Elections Center. 
Jon Sherman, litigation director at Fair Elections Center, told the Lantern state officials “were not in compliance” with the National Voter Registration Act when it came to removing a voter to maintain voter rolls. The new regulation “will make it much much less likely that there be a false match” between Kentucky registration records and out-of-state records from when a voter has moved to another state. 
Sherman said the emergency regulation, signed by Gov. Andy Beshear and State Board of Elections Executive Director Karen Sellers, immediately went into effect. Through an upcoming public comment period next month, a permanent rule mirroring this regulation would be established. 
“We hope this serves as a template for resolving these issues in other states. We brought a challenge that said this law was not violating the National Voter Registration Act on its face, but as applied by Kentucky election officials,” Sherman said. “So, there are likely other states that are applying similar laws in a way that would violate the NVRA.”
Kansas recently passed a law designed to remove ineligible voters, Sherman noted. The Kansas Reflector, a sister outlet to the Lantern reported some advocates there warn could conflict with the NVRA. 
“Hopefully Kansas election officials enforce it in a way that is compliant with the NVRA, but my suspicion is that they might need to be sued for the same reasons we brought suit in Kentucky,” he said.

title: National monuments drive economic growth and unite diverse interests
description: Colorado’s public lands encompass four national parks and nine national monuments, including the 210,844-acre Dinosaur National Monument in Moffatt County, home to some of the most stunning canyons on the continent, including the jaw-dropping Lodore Canyon and Echo Park. text:
A view of Echo Park Road snaking through the canyons of Dinosaur National Monument in 2015. (Peter K./NPS)Colorado’s public lands encompass four national parks and nine national monuments, including the 210,844-acre Dinosaur National Monument in Moffatt County, home to some of the most stunning canyons on the continent, including the jaw-dropping Lodore Canyon and Echo Park.
During August, I joined a group of public lands and national monument proponents — hunters and anglers, banking and mining executives, a local rancher, small business owners, marketing professionals, economic development specialists, public lands and waters stewards — for a four-day float down the Green River through Dinosaur.
Sponsored by Visit Moffatt County and the National Park Service, we were tasked with discussing the diverse and sometimes conflicting interests intertwined with public lands and waters management along with considering the economics of communities that are sustained by these public resources in Northwest Colorado and beyond.
The common denominator among all of us is a desire to help ensure that public lands are managed sustainably for everyone: communities and wildlife. Unfortunately, threats to public lands have increased significantly during recent years. From proposed sell-offs to rapidly accelerated oil and gas leasing with limited opportunity for public input to growing year-round recreation, our shared estate is experiencing unprecedented pressures.

Earlier this year I joined a group of public lands advocates visiting Colorado congressional delegation offices in Washington, D.C. Tom Kleinschnitz, Moffat County director of tourism, was among them and he explained to our U.S. senators and representatives that his county has a population of about 13,000 people, but Dinosaur National Monument attracted over 315,700 visitors in 2025.
A January 2026 report from Headwaters Economics called “Economic performance of communities near national monuments” documents the vital role national monuments play in local economies. The report emphasizes that Colorado’s national monuments and other public lands are sustainable economic engines that power rural economies and support our great hunting, angling and outdoor recreation heritage.
Nationwide, outdoor recreation — from hunting, fishing and camping to cycling, boating and more — accounts for $788 billion in annual gross economic output and generates 5.2 million American jobs. The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis calculates the economic output of outdoor recreation in Colorado to be $13.9 billion, surpassing industries such as mining, utilities, farming and ranching.
“Recent lease sale proposals in areas such as North Park, Moffat County, and Routt County have generated concerns from landowners, sportsmen, conservation organizations, and state wildlife managers regarding potential impacts to wildlife migration corridors, outdoor recreation, and local economies that depend on healthy public lands,” an Aug. 21 Grand Junction Daily Sentinel editorial explained. “But, under current law, the Bureau of Land Management has no authority to respond to those concerns.”
Eighty-four percent of Western voters say that “rollbacks of laws that protect our land, water and wildlife” are a serious problem, up from 68% eight years ago, according to a 2026 poll by Colorado College’s State of the Rockies project. “Whether one supports or opposes additional oil and gas development, Coloradans should be able to participate in decisions that affect the lands and resources they own collectively,” the Daily Sentinel editorial added. “That’s the American way.”
“I’ve hunted elk on Colorado’s public lands for some 20 years, on ground that belongs to all of us — truck drivers, ranchers, schoolteachers, and veterans back home on leave,” I explained in an Aug. 7 Colorado Times Recorder op-ed. “That’s the quiet miracle of public land: you don’t have to be rich to have somewhere to hunt, fish, or otherwise recreate in the outdoors.”
And as the old saying goes, “All of us are smarter than any of us.” But if that collaborative process gets short-circuited by Washington, D.C., politicians favoring one industry or interest group without giving the rest of us a seat at the table, then “we the people” will, at best, be an afterthought.
Former U.S. President (and Medal of Honor recipient) Theodore Roosevelt said, “Of all the questions which can come before this nation, short of the actual preservation of its existence in a great war, there is none which compares in importance with the great central task of leaving this land even a better land for our descendants than it is for us.”
During our four days rafting the Green River in Dinosaur National Monument through the Gates of Lodore, Lodore Canyon, Echo Park and beyond, we all seemed to agree with both Roosevelt’s sentiment and the Daily Sentinel: “Public lands belong to all of us and we should all have the opportunity to have a say in how they’re managed.”
