name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger orders state agencies to prepare for Medicaid, SNAP changes
description: Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday ordered Virginia agencies to step up efforts to prevent eligible residents from losing Medicaid and food assistance as sweeping federal changes are set to take effect next year.  The governor announced Executive Order 20 to boost the state’s implementation efforts of H.R.1, a reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer.[...]
text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger speaks during a roundtable with healthcare organizations on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday ordered Virginia agencies to step up efforts to prevent eligible residents from losing Medicaid and food assistance as sweeping federal changes are set to take effect next year. 
The governor announced Executive Order 20 to boost the state’s implementation efforts of H.R.1, a reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer. 
The move comes as the state faces approaching effective dates for changes to Medicaid access and food stamp eligibility and payment mechanisms. 
Of Virginia’s nearly 2 million Medicaid enrollees, more than 500,000 will be subject to new work requirements and additional verification paperwork each year, while about 5,800 lawful immigrants will lose coverage. Roughly 749,000 Virginians receive food stamps through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to help purchase groceries. 
With the eligibility requirements set to change Jan. 1, Virginia’s social services departments are working to streamline processes to keep as many eligible people as possible from losing their health insurance or benefits. 
On a Zoom call with reporters Tuesday morning, Spanberger said keeping people covered is paramount to preventing healthcare cost burdens from growing further. 
“We are lessening the risk that individuals may walk into a hospital with an emergency need because they haven’t previously sought medical care,” she said. 
Key aspects of the order include providing “plain-language outreach” for beneficiaries subject to new eligibility requirements, strengthening collaboration between state agencies to direct certain populations to a new state-level subsidy to purchase Affordable Care Act insurance, and enhanced public-private partnerships and regional communications to help with outreach to vulnerable populations. 
Dropped your ACA insurance due to spiking premiums? You could qualify for a state subsidy this fall

The order also directs state agencies to expand and improve connections to employment, volunteer, apprenticeship, job training and educational opportunities to help ensure people meet the new eligibility requirements.
To further help Virginians navigate the changes, the state also created a dashboard to track health and social services data and connect people to resources. 
Health and Human Resources Secretary Marvin Figueroa said that while the state can’t promise to keep everyone covered because some people may fail to meet the new requirements, it can help reduce unnecessary coverage losses. 
“Some will lose coverage because federal law changes who qualifies.” he said. “Others may still be eligible but lose coverage because a form was missed, a notice was misunderstood, or the process became too difficult to navigate. That distinction matters. A paperwork failure should not become a healthcare crisis.” 
Because uninsured people are more likely to put off preventative care, eventual emergency room visits when crises arise can strain hospital budgets and lead to higher private-market insurance rates for others. Safety net providers such as free clinics and Federally Qualified Health Centers are bracing to absorb more uninsured patients, which will strain their resources as well. 
Figueroa noted that the administration remains in touch with providers and regional social service workers. 
Despite state budget allocations for H.R. 1 implementation, support for safety net providers and a state-level program to make up for ACA subsidies Congress allowed to expire this year, Figueroa said preparing has been tricky. 
“The changes are layered, so it makes it hard to plan. Many changes come on Jan. 1, after the midterms,” he said. “But the world is not waiting for us to plan.” 
Figueroa and Spanberger noted that some clinics have closed or hospitals have trimmed services in the past year, citing H.R.1 as a factor. A recent state watchdog report found that 13 rural hospitals in Virginia may be at higher risk of closure over time. 
The state has also had to invest not only in implementing the federal law, but also in covering other costs the law has shifted to states. 
For instance, SNAP, which was once split evenly between state and federal coffers, will move to states handling 75% of the share starting this October. H.R. 1 will also scale down what’s known as a provider tax, a funding mechanism hospitals use to support some of Virginia’s Medicaid coverage.
Spanberger noted that on its face, H.R. 1 was meant as legislation to cut taxes because it extended a set of tax cuts from President Donald Trump’s first term, but how it is made possible by the sweeping changes to Medicaid and SNAP. 
“Cutting a tax sounds like a good idea,” Spanberger said. But she said that the provider tax change is “pulling back dollars that had gone to hospitals” and is one additional way that this bill is “negatively impacting the basic operations of hospitals across Virginia.”
Va. hospitals predict $31B reduction in state’s Medicaid funding if proposed CMS rule passes 

Virginia hospitals also predict billions in reductions in the state’s Medicaid funding if proposed Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service rules stemming from H.R. 1 are adopted. 
Virginia Hospital and Healthcare Association spokesman Julian Walker said in an interview last month that the proposed rules “go well beyond” what was prescribed in H.R. 1. 
Despite Figueroa’s noted challenges in planning for the fallout, he emphasized that the administration would do its best to triage matters. 
“What we can promise is disciplined execution. We will communicate early,” he said. “We will tell the truth of what we can and can’t do. We will publish the data, and we will listen when the process is not working and try to fix it.”

title: Amazon changes course on water use for King George data center campus
description: Amazon Web Services is changing course on how a King George data center project will get its water after an application to renew a groundwater permit allowing withdrawals of up to 6.4 million gallons annually from the Potomac aquifer raised concerns. The tech giant is set to construct a major data center campus in the […]
text:
The Robert O. Norris Bridge is located over the Rappahannock River. (Courtesy of the Virginia Department of Transportation)Amazon Web Services is changing course on how a King George data center project will get its water after an application to renew a groundwater permit allowing withdrawals of up to 6.4 million gallons annually from the Potomac aquifer raised concerns.
The tech giant is set to construct a major data center campus in the county at the Birchwood Drive tech campus that could host more than a dozen data centers across the 869-acre property. 
While some of the project is currently tied up in court proceedings, an application to renew a water permit already in place for the tech campus led Sen. Richard Stuart, R-King George, to urge the Department of Environmental Quality to deny the application. 
The permit would have allowed the facility to withdraw water from the aquifer that would not be used for cooling the data centers, but rather for employee use, grounds management and other purposes.
However, the application came on the heels of a DEQ report that laid out a stark warning that groundwater east of Interstate 95 is “declining (in) availability in the near future,” and that the aquifer would not be able to handle any major new permits for water withdrawals.
“They do not need to drill a well into the aquifer, particularly since we finally got my water study released, which shows us… that we’re in a critical stage with regard to the Potomac aquifer,” Stuart told The Mercury last week.
The report has led to policy discussions over how the commonwealth can preserve the Potomac aquifer, a critical water source for the eastern portion of the state. 
Following the release of the eastern groundwater availability report, a group of lawmakers has called on Gov. Abigail Spanberger to convene a special session to pass legislation aimed at protecting the resource ahead of the General Assembly’s regular session in January. The governor has not publicly responded to this request.
Stuart wrote a scathing letter to DEQ noting that the department has directed the county to reduce its reliance on the aquifer and switch to surface water from the Rappahannock River as its primary source of drinking water. Stuart said allowing a massive company like Amazon to use the water instead of preserving it for human consumption should not be allowed. 
“The (Virginia) Constitution guarantees the natural resources for the benefit and enjoyment of the citizens. We do not have any extra water,” Stuart said. “Why in the world would they allow Amazon to withdraw water from the aquifer and force a county of 29,000 people, a small rural county, to spend $70 to $100 million to get water from the river and require treatment?”
While 6.4 million gallons over the course of one year may seem like a lot, the permit would not have come close to cracking the top five industrial water users from the Potomac aquifer. The top two users, according to DEQ records, are the two paper mills: Global Cellulose Fibers in Franklin, which is permitted to withdraw 6.4 billion gallons annually, and WestRock CP LLC, which may use up to 6.3 billion gallons. 
However, Stuart said that it did not matter that the Amazon permit would be dwarfed by other permits. He said the report shows that new withdrawals should not be considered in order to preserve drinking water for Virginians.
Amazon responded by saying it is looking at alternatives.
“We take concerns of the community seriously and plan to seek alternate water sources as advised by VDEQ and Virginia regulation,” a spokesperson for the tech giant told The Mercury. “We prioritize minimizing water use, and that’s why we invest in infrastructure to utilize reclaimed water across the commonwealth and continuously work to make our data centers more water efficient.”
Amazon is in the process of withdrawing its application for the groundwater withdrawal permit.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Mission impossible? Young progressive takes on Jack Reed in Democratic primary
description: The woman still in her pajamas sized up the man in a black jacket and blue jeans holding a clipboard at her door in Providence’s Smith Hill one rainy Saturday in May. He had just told her he’s running for U.S. Senate. As Connor Burbridge outlined a platform of taxing billionaires and support for universal […]
text:
Connor Burbridge, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Jack Reed, approaches a house in Providence’s Smith Hill neighborhood on May 2, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The woman still in her pajamas sized up the man in a black jacket and blue jeans holding a clipboard at her door in Providence’s Smith Hill one rainy Saturday in May. He had just told her he’s running for U.S. Senate.
As Connor Burbridge outlined a platform of taxing billionaires and support for universal healthcare, she cut him off with one question.
“Who are you kicking out?”
“It would be Sen. Reed in the primary,” the 31-year-old first time office seeker replied.
The woman stepped back and placed her hand over her heart. Then she mouthed the four words that continue to pierce Burbridge’s insurgent campaign in the Sept. 9 Democratic primary.
“I love Jack Reed.”
Recent polls show the majority of Rhode Island voters feel the same way about the state’s senior U.S. senator, who was first elected to his seat in 1996. 
A survey published Aug. 17 by the Pell Center at Salve Regina University showed Reed with 61% of likely primary voters backing the incumbent’s bid for a sixth term. A poll by the University of New Hampshire in July found Reed  “comfortably leads” his competitor with 63% support among likely voters.
Burbridge had support from only 12% of likely voters while a third Democratic contender, Dr. Luis Daniel Muñoz, saw 4% in the Pell Center poll.
“I don’t think this race is likely to turn out in any way other than what we expect,” Adam Myers, an associate professor of political science at Providence College, said in an interview. “Reed would have to have some really bad headlines or make some major snafu for this to change.”
Reed can barely make it through a public event without someone stopping him to take a photo with him, or chat about how his work in Washington D.C. has benefited the community. At 76 years old, he is running for his sixth term and shows no signs of slowing down while racking up endorsements from his party, influential unions, environmental groups and the defense industry. A national poll found Reed’s approval rating put him in the top 10 among the country’s 100 U.S. senators. The son of a Cranston school janitor who went on to graduate from West Point and serve as a U.S. Army paratrooper, Reed has been a leading voice against the war in Iran while continuing to bring in federal dollars for Rhode Island.
Take the recent Wednesday when Reed attended a boat christening in South Kingstown for a new harbor patrol vessel funded almost entirely with $500,000 in federal money.
“They may have the Independent Man on top of the State House, but we have the indispensable man here,” Michael Marran, vice president of the South Kingstown Town Council, told a small crowd gathered at the Ram Point Marina.
Burbridge knows it’s an uphill battle to take down someone with Reed’s political stature. In an election year where progressive insurgencies have led to establishment defeats, however, he sees a chance to bring his perspective to Congress.
It’s the very message Burbridge pitched on the steps of the woman who answered her door.
“I have a lot of respect for Sen. Reed,” he told the woman. “But it’s time for a new generation of leaders to step up.”
Connor Burbridge, far right, speaks with volunteers before canvassing Providence’s Smith Hill neighborhood on May 2, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Progressive plan
Burbridge was born in 1995, the year before Reed first won his U.S. Senate seat with 63% of the vote in the November election. 
A New Jersey native, Burbridge moved to Rhode Island in 2020 after receiving his master’s degree in environmental policy at Lehigh University in eastern Pennsylvania. He paid his way through school by joining the U.S. Army’s Reserve Officers’ Training Corps program. 
Burbridge served five years as a battalion human resources officer in the Army Reserve, helping to plan war game scenarios. These days, he works as a grant writer for a nonprofit nursing home in East Providence, along with co-running a small tree nursery in Smithfield.
He said he was drawn to elder care in part because of a close relationship with his grandparents, particularly his grandfather who served in the Navy during World War II.
“He lived through the Great Depression, and then the New Deal — we talked about that a lot,” Burbridge said.
That connection with his grandfather helped shape Burbridge’s political identity. He describes himself as a New Deal Democrat, viewing the economic programs, public works projects and financial reforms of the 1930s as the blueprint for shaping America’s future.
Burbridge’s own platform calls for sweeping programs such as universal long-term care, a national wealth fund funded by taxes on billionaires, public ownership of electric utilities, corporate limits on housing and a constitutional right to equal education.
“We have an opportunity right now to realign the political landscape in that way that will win the trust of working class voters for a generation, and ultimately build a durable national majority that is long-lasting,” he said.
Burbridge is active on social media, his primary medium of getting his message across when he and his team of volunteers are not out canvassing the state. He points to online political streamers, podcasters and YouTubers — from Hasan Piker to the progressive channel the Majority Report — as the kind of platforms Democrats must use if they want to reach more voters.
“We need strong communicators who are willing to go wherever people are getting their news from,” he said. “It’s not just MSNBC anymore or CNN.”
Muñoz, 41, is a Central Falls native and medical school graduate who has worked as a technology consultant and ran for governor in 2018 and 2022. He said in an emailed statement to Rhode Island Current that he’s running for the U.S. Senate because too many of the issues facing Rhode Islanders — from health care and housing to climate change and corporate power — are shaped at the federal level. 
“The affordability crisis, signs of fascism, genocide in Gaza, war in Iran, and a weakening economy compelled me to stand up, and run for better tomorrows,” Muñoz said. “All children deserve a future, and I am committed to fighting for one that does not include complicity in genocide, endless wars, or fascism.”
A survey published Aug. 17 by the Pell Center at Salve Regina University showed U.S. Sen. Jack Reed with 61% of likely primary voters backing his bid for a sixth term. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Elder statesman
Reed turns 77 nine days after the Nov. 3 general election. He’d be 83 by the time a sixth term ends in 2033. But the longtime senator argues age is less important than his work ethic.
“I try very hard to pay attention to what’s happening in the world and to the new and threatening issues we’re facing,” Reed said during an interview when he stopped at Shanya’s Place in Wickford Village. The interview was interrupted twice, each time one of the cafe’s co-owners greeted him.
Among the threats Reed is most concerned about: artificial intelligence (AI), which he said is “going to reshape the country and the world.” 
In June, Reed and Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware introduced legislation that would establish guidelines on how the Department of Defense acquires, tests and uses AI-enabled autonomous weapon systems. Reed said the U.S. also needs to engage China, Russia, and others to set shared rules on AI, comparing it to Cold War-era negotiations over nuclear weapons.
Reed also pointed to his constant engagement with Rhode Islanders as another reason voters should give him another term in Congress. 
With the Senate on recess until mid-September, his schedule on Aug. 19 started with an 8:30 a.m. breakfast in Jamestown with a candidate for local office. Then he headed to Woonsocket to join Head Start advocates to raise the alarm on proposed Trump administration rules that would transfer many of the federal standards and decision-making governing the early education programs over to the states.
Next Reed was off to South Kingstown for the boat christening, followed by the stop at Shayna’s Place at 2:30 p.m. before returning to his Cranston office. His day ended with a 9:25 p.m. CNN appearance in Providence and finally returning to his home in Jamestown a little after 10 p.m.
And that workload “was probably a lighter day than most,” campaign and Senate office spokesperson Benjamin Craig wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current.  
“Some days it’s 7 a.m. to late at night,” Craig wrote. “Some days it’s a slew of public events into the evening.”
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed speaks with members of the U.S. Coast Guard before a boat christening in South Kingstown on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
The ‘quiet dealmaker,’ outspoken on military affairs
The ever soft-spoken Reed has never been one to seek the spotlight. The New York Times in 2008 called him a “quiet dealmaker” respected by both Democrats and Republicans.
But that same piece notes where he had emerged as one of the Democratic Party’s loudest voices on military affairs, a subject on which Reed has only grown more outspoken during President Donald Trump’s second term. 
As the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Armed Services, Reed has frequently clashed with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over boat strikes in Venezuela, attempts to politicize the military, and the ongoing war against Iran.
“The base wants Democrats to fight right now,” Myers said. “Reed’s just reading the room.”
But Burbridge believes establishment Democrats like Reed have still not met the political moment in standing up to Trump and opposing the Iran War. He pointed to Reed’s support for massive increases in military spending that he argues made it possible for the president to wage the conflict.
“Jack Reed has been hesitant to do what he can to try and gum up the works of this administration,” Burbridge said.
Reed doesn’t see it that way. Trump demanded Reed’s impeachment in a Truth Social post in June following Reed’s criticism of his deal to end the U.S. war with Iran. Reed had called the deal less than what President Barack Obama obtained in his peacetime deal in an interview with Fox News.
“He didn’t pick my name out of the hat,” Reed said.
Burbridge is also critical of Reed’s support for increased military spending and defense contractors that make up some of Rhode Island’s largest employers.
“People have argued that the defense industry is really good for the American worker, because it creates stable, high quality jobs,” Burbridge said. “But do we want all the high quality jobs in our state to be tied to producing weapons of death?”
Reed defends his support for defense contractors as a matter of national security and jobs. He notes he’s backed submarine production in Rhode Island since the 1990s.
“This is about what’s best for the country,” Reed said. “We’ve got much better stuff than the other guys.”
Reed’s support for a robust defense industry is part of a broader foreign policy divide between him and his challengers, particularly over U.S. support for Israel. Both Burbridge and Muñoz describe Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide and are calling for the federal government to cut military aid and halt weapons transfers to the country. 
Reed remains supportive of continued U.S. military aid to Israel, saying “We can’t forget Oct. 7,” referring to the date when Hamas militants launched a surprise attack on the country in 2023. But he has criticized Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for causing “great harm” to Israel’s standing and said the U.S. must press Israel’s government to protect Palestinian civilians and recommit to a two-state solution.
Connor Burbridge opens a door in Providence’s Smith Hill neighborhood with his canvassing clipboard in hand. The poster still notes the original Sept. 8 primary date, which the General Assembly changed to Sept. 9 in late April. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Where’s the insurgent support?
Burbridge’s attempt to unseat Reed comes as the national Democratic party is fighting over what kind of candidates can lead them back to power on Capitol Hill.
Insurgent candidates toppled longtime House incumbents in New York City in June. A week later in Colorado, 29-year-old Democratic Socialist Melat Kiros defeated a nearly 30-year House incumbent.
Myers said those successful campaigns each have a common thread: massive grassroots support from progressive organizations like the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), along with endorsements from prominent national figures.
“It would appear to be the case that the conditions necessary for that kind of an upset victory by a far-left insurgent are not present with regard to the U.S. Senate race,” Myers said.
The state’s chapter of DSA told Rhode Island Current via email the organization “does not participate in any Democratic races,” focusing its support squarely on Brittany Kubicek’s campaign for Providence’s House District 5 seat.
Reclaim Rhode Island, a Providence-based tenant organizing group, has volunteers supporting candidates for local and state office, with much of its focus on David Morales’ bid for mayor of the state’s capital city. That’s not to say the group is supportive of the state’s delegation in Washington D.C. 
“Every single member of our congressional delegation deserves a credible challenge and to be replaced,” Dan Denvir, the group’s co-chair, said in an interview. “But at least so far this cycle, there doesn’t seem to be a credible campaign to take any of them out.”
Even Morales has abstained from endorsing in the U.S. Senate primary. He told Rhode Island Current at one of his campaign events that he was prioritizing state and local races where he would “have the most direct impact” on his own priorities.
Asked whether Reed has earned another six years in Congress, Morales said he looked forward to working with the senator if both are elected in November.
“I believe Jack Reed has delivered for Rhode Island,” he said. 



Quotation







I don’t think this race is likely to turn out in any way other than what we expect. Reed would have to have some really bad headlines or make some major snafu for this to change.


– Adam Myers, an associate professor of political science at Providence College


Reed has racked up the support of the state’s Democratic party, the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, Providence Streets Coalition, and progressive U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.
Burbridge does boast a handful of endorsements from state elected officials and organizations. V.A. Lopes, co-director of Indivisible Southcoast New England, said she supports Burbridge’s call for a new generation of leaders in Congress.
“People get stagnant,” she said. “Connor is living the pain of the younger American people.”
Chris Woods, treasurer for Burbridge’s campaign, said the campaign plans to “aggressively” pursue national endorsements after raising more than $25,000 since launching last year. 
As of Aug. 20, filings with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) show Burbridge’s campaign had $4,130 on hand. Reed’s pre-primary report was unavailable on the FEC’s website. He ended the most recent quarter with over $3.7 million in his campaign account.
Voting is already underway in the state primary election that ends on Sept. 9. The winner of the three-way race will face Republican Ray McKay and independent Michael Bahry in the November general election.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Holding back third graders feels like punishment in Rhode Island. It’s a kindness in Mississippi.
description: The state of Mississippi has long been sick of being the nation’s educational runt. For decades, they’ve scored last among states on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) a.k.a., the Nation’s Report Card. Educators in other lagging states consoled themselves with: “At least we’re not Mississippi.”  Until 2019 when the state wowed the nation’[...]
text:
Western Line School District Assistant Superintendent James Johnson chats with second graders about books the class is reading at Riverside Elementary School in Avon, Miss., on Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today)The state of Mississippi has long been sick of being the nation’s educational runt. For decades, they’ve scored last among states on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) a.k.a., the Nation’s Report Card. Educators in other lagging states consoled themselves with: “At least we’re not Mississippi.” 
Until 2019 when the state wowed the nation’s edusphere with improved fourth-grade reading scores while every other state tanked or stalled. However, most NAEP scores proved disappointing that pre-pandemic year so the success could have been a one-off.
Mississippi was and still is the poorest state in the nation. In Rhode Island, the 17th richest state, some educators blame the lackluster performance of our schools on poverty and bad parenting. Poverty is a massive challenge for any state, but after Mississippi’s fourth grade reading scores stayed steady or improved over time, that excuse dissolved. 
By the 2010s, Mississippi’s districts had already developed pockets of strong reading results by shifting to science-backed curricula. So in 2013, Commissioner Carey Wright and her team at their Department of Education convinced their legislators to pass America’s first “science of reading” law, the Literacy-based Promotion Act. 
The name of the law captures the core of their strategy, which is that any third grader who fails the state’s reading assessment would be retained in grade. But gosh that seemed harsh to me, even believing that the nation’s decade-long retreat from accountability is at the root of the nation’s declining performance. But should we punish 9-year-olds for the system’s failure?
The 2001 No Child Left Behind Act’s version of data-driven accountability initially boosted academic results, but scores soon plateaued while the law’s relentlessly punitive approach poisoned educator culture, leading to cheating scandals and hostility towards any accountability.  
Accountability is not synonymous with punishment. It’s information that only might lead to consequences. Disappointing data might hurt, as failing scores do, but facts are just facts to use for good or ill. 
As I studied “Mississippi Miracle,” the third grade gatekeeper test started to look like the first time a reform strategy took seriously the educational cliche: From kindergarten to third grade, kids learn to read. After that, they read to learn.
Failing 9-year-olds is upsetting, but secondary-age kids who fail tests command far less compassion, even though educators know most of them never learned to read well enough to absorb grade-level content. Bad science or history instruction won’t cripple a kid’s chances to accumulate knowledge independently the way illiteracy will. 
In that light, socially promoting non-readers to the fourth grade began to look like an academic death sentence.
So Mississippi’s law laser-focused on equipping third grade readers fully. 
The state provided teachers with professional development and vetted curricula free of the debunked guessing and non-phonics techniques that had been the kudzu of reading instruction for 50 years, leaving kids unable to sound out words for themselves.  
Developmentally appropriate screenings are administered three times each year, K-3, to keep a close eye on each child’s progress. 
The legislature allocated money for curricula, testing and most importantly, for coaches who could interpret the metrics, troubleshoot and offer solutions. Coaches work directly with teachers, not students, to help them identify struggling kids early, to determine the reasons why, and to shore up teachers’ weak instructional skills when necessary.
Interestingly, Alabama’s early use of a similar strategy put them way ahead of Mississippi until losing funding for their coaches. Coaches are critical. The real Mississippi miracle was that for 15 years, even as leaders themselves changed, the strategy and budget priorities did not. 
Towards the end of third grade, kids take the gatekeeper test, but can try again two more times with intensive interventions at each failure. The law delayed the “retention gate” for two years so the changes could take hold. 
As early as 2015, 85% of the third-graders passed the test on the first try. Over time, the retention rate started hovering around 6%. Mississippi now has one of the highest retention rates in the country.
“Good cause” exemptions are available for students with certain special needs. But mostly, the kids held back really do need more time and reading instruction. 
Here’s a huge kicker: When the Urban Institute disaggregated the 2024 fourth grade NAEP scores by poverty, Mississippi was best in the nation. Ever the leader in high scores, Massachusetts was merely fourth. So, the strategy works well for all kids, but especially for low-income children.
Rhode Island’s per pupil funding is $22,110, 9th highest. Massachusetts is 7th highest at $22,947. Mississippi’s is $12,093, the 5th lowest.
Money does not stand in the way of Rhode Island replicating this strategy so much as the lack of anyone in particular being responsible for academic results. As a right-to-work state, Mississippi’s Department of Education has far more control over their educational landscape than our mishmash of decision-making forces that include a tradition of local control, teachers unions, and powerful politicians. The state does not share a “students first” approach, however much the adults who benefit from the system profess one.
To end on a bright note, in 2019 Rhode Island also passed a good reading law that lit a fire under enough schools to propel the state’s low income children to 15th in the nation, below both Massachusetts and Mississippi, but better than our usual meh performance. 
Research contends that fully 95% of all kids can become proficient readers. Permitting illiteracy with social promotion is a choice we make out of misguided compassion when actually, sending a non-reader into a reading-dependent environment is no kindness at all.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Lawmakers study Indiana’s sexual assault response
description: Crime victim advocates say a backlog of untested rape kits, shortage of trauma-informed investigators and forensic nurses and forthcoming cuts to federal funding is hampering Indiana’s sexual assault response. The Interim Study Committee on Public Health, Behavioral Health and Human Services met in House chambers Tuesday to hear testimony on the topic — the[...]
text:
Beth White, president and CEO of the Indiana Coalition to End Sexual Assault, speaks to the Interim Study Committee on Public Health, Behavioral Health and Human Services on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Crime victim advocates say a backlog of untested rape kits, shortage of trauma-informed investigators and forensic nurses and forthcoming cuts to federal funding is hampering Indiana’s sexual assault response.
The Interim Study Committee on Public Health, Behavioral Health and Human Services met in House chambers Tuesday to hear testimony on the topic — the first hearing of the summer as lawmakers prepare for next year’s budget session.
“Survivors deserve a response that is compassionate, coordinated and consistent,” state Rep. Becky Cash, R-Zionsville, said in a statement.
Gaps in response
Cash requested a study of the state’s sexual assault response workforce after her bill to require Indiana State Police to eliminate its backlog of untested rape kits did not advance earlier this year.
There are zero forensic nurses to examine sexual assault victims in 40 of Indiana’s 92 counties — 16 counties have no hospital at all — forcing victims to travel far from home.
Turnaround for the 815 rape kits submitted to Indiana State Police last year averaged 217 days.
“Those are 217 days when a victim is waiting, when a perpetrator is allowed to reoffend, when we have no criminal case moving forward,” Beth White, president of the Indiana Coalition to End Sexual Assault, testified on Tuesday. “That is unacceptable.”
White said Indiana’s network of rape crisis centers and sexual assault service providers does not cover the entire state, a trend likely to be exacerbated by forthcoming cuts to federal Victims of Crime Act grants.
Meanwhile, few investigators outside major cities are trained in trauma-informed interviewing techniques.
Plainfield Police Chief Kyle Prewitt waits to speak to the Interim Study Committee on Public Health, Behavioral Health and Human Services on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Indiana law requires investigators who regularly investigate sexual assaults to be trained in the neurobiology of trauma, available through the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy and elsewhere.
Still, Plainfield Police Chief Kyle Prewitt said 337 of Indiana’s 664 law enforcement agencies employ 10 or fewer officers, leaving patrol officers to conduct sensitive investigations for which they have little to no training.
“A patrol officer is used to showing up, asking very blunt questions of victims, and not taking a trauma-informed approach with them,” he said.
Rape survivor Samantha McCoy recounted a “confusing” and “dehumanizing” experience — describing her assault to a rotation of officers, submitting to an invasive rape examination in which photographs were taken without explanation, followed by a 30-minute drive to the crime scene and more questioning.
McCoy told the committee she did not receive mental health services nor a victim advocate.
“After months of doing everything that I was asked, it became clear that I was never going to receive criminal justice for what happened to me,” she said.
Still, McCoy said her case likely would have resulted in an arrest had officers been properly trained beforehand — calling on lawmakers to impose consequences for agencies that do not comply with state-mandated training standards.
“At the very least, I would have been treated with dignity throughout the process,” she said.
Calls for funding
Advocates asked for increased state funding to offset the 40% cut in federal VOCA grants to Indiana expected in October.
The cuts will be particularly detrimental to child advocacy centers, which conduct child abuse investigations. The centers traditionally rely on VOCA grants and private fundraising, but are asking for state funding for the first time this year.
White, from the Indiana Coalition to End Sexual Assault, asked the committee to increase Indiana’s Sexual Assault Victim Assistance Fund from $8 million to $12 million over the biennium to improve access to rape crisis centers.
White called for the creation of a state fund to reimburse hospitals for sexual assault nurse examiner training expenses.
And she is pushing for increased capacity at Indiana State Police labs to alleviate the rape kit backlog.
“We spend millions of dollars in this state for police and prosecutors,” White said. “… What I’m asking you today is to think about how much are we spending to help victims put their lives back together after something so terrible.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: A tech-forward future imagined for New Hampshire at ‘Freedom Summit’
description: More than two decades after the birth of the Free State Project, another group of philosophically united individuals have their eyes trained on New Hampshire, where they envision a home for a new kind of community.  Last week, a gathering of self-described “techno-optimists” drew about 200 attendees to a Manchester event venue to talk about […]
text:
From left: Raechel Lambert, Ryan Lambert, Benjamin Sachs, and Jeremy Hitchcock, prospective developers of a planned community called "Freedom Village," speak during a summit they organized on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)More than two decades after the birth of the Free State Project, another group of philosophically united individuals have their eyes trained on New Hampshire, where they envision a home for a new kind of community. 
Last week, a gathering of self-described “techno-optimists” drew about 200 attendees to a Manchester event venue to talk about the state’s tech industry and stir interest in a “village” planned by four New Hampshire tech workers and prospective founders. 
“Freedom Village” is the name of an exclusive housing and community development imagined for southern New Hampshire “tech people,” according to its designers: entrepreneurs and spouses Raechel and Ryan Lambert; entrepreneur Jeremy Hitchcock, who also chairs the board of a Portsmouth-based nuclear startup; and architect Benjamin Sachs. 
After the two-day event wrapped, some details about the planned community remained murky. But other topics were turned over extensively by the array of speakers, most of whom were tech entrepreneurs and a handful of Republican political figures, including representatives of New Hampshire’s executive branch. 
The central focus throughout was New Hampshire’s high-tech future. Panelists discussed promoting a New Hampshire biotech industry that pushes regulatory envelopes; embracing AI and tech-forward innovation; and growing New Hampshire’s nuclear power sector.
In addition to those sometimes fraught topics, the agenda featured two big New Hampshire names among its array of speakers. Listed as a headline speaker in the promotional materials for the event was New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte, though she was ultimately replaced by an adviser. And on the summit’s second day, attendees heard a presentation on New Hampshire innovation from Dean Kamen, a New Hampshire inventor under fire of late for ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
So what does the techno-optimist vision look like for New Hampshire? Here’s how that question was answered during last week’s Freedom Summit.
Rep. Keith Ammon (left) and Jeremy Hitchcock at the Freedom Summit on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Parallels and new ground
Freedom Village is bound to draw comparisons to the Free State Project, a movement founded in 2001 that brought migrants with Libertarian values to New Hampshire and continues to exert political influence in Concord. 
But Raechel Lambert, in an early August interview with the Bulletin, asserted that Freedom Village is not aligned with the Free State Project.
“Freedom is for everyone,” she said. “I think we have to take back that word.”
Lambert reiterated the idea that Freedom Village was not political on Friday, when she stated that individuals of all persuasions would be welcomed to the planned community.
The politicians involved in the summit were right-leaning, with multiple Republican members of the New Hampshire House of Representatives in the audience. House technology and cryptocurrency advocate Rep. Keith Ammon, a Republican from New Boston, delivered a talk on the theme of sovereignty. And though Ayotte did not appear, an adviser from her office spoke on the first day, while New Hampshire Department of Business and Economic Affairs Commissioner Lucy Lange delivered a recorded message on day two.
Sarah Scott, deputy state director for the conservative, Libertarian-aligned group Americans for Prosperity, also spoke on a panel. 
While Lambert denies that the plan is political in nature, she knows the team’s ideas are not for everyone. (“Lots of people will dunk on this plan,” she wrote on a LinkedIn post before the event.) In fact, they’re not intended to be, she said; the community and gathering were intended for a specific type of person, who Lambert and co-founders variously referred to as “builders” and “tech people.”
That specificity is why the team chose New Hampshire, they said. Hands-off government, a rural atmosphere, and proximity to Boston are among the state’s draws, Lambert wrote in a Substack post in January.
She also wrote about the state’s tax leniency as a major factor.
“There are no billionaire taxes or wealth taxes being debated here,” the Substack post reads, citing a proposed asset tax in San Francisco and an “openly Socialist agenda gaining traction in New York City” as reasons entrepreneurs of the sort she envisions for Freedom Village may land in New Hampshire. 
Skepticism around government and regulations were common threads among speakers over two days of sessions.
Niklas Anzinger (left), CEO of Infinita, speaks during a panel on reducing regulation of biotech at the Freedom Summit in Manchester Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
‘Right to Try’
The first day of the summit, organized around the theme of biotechnology innovation, provided an inside look at New Hampshire’s aggressive “right to try” movement.
New Hampshire’s original Right To Try Act was signed into law a decade ago. Modeled after similar laws in other states, it allowed New Hampshire patients suffering from terminal illnesses to receive treatments that haven’t yet been fully approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration but are through early stages of the process. 
However, in recent years, a group of libertarian-leaning lawmakers have successfully fought to expand the law. In 2025, House Bill 701 updated the Right To Try Act by allowing eligible patients to waive their ability to sue. Proponents argued the fear of medical malpractice lawsuits was scaring pharmaceutical companies from offering experimental treatments.
This year, they went further. Led by Manchester Rep. Brian Cole, Republican lawmakers passed House Bill 1735, which expanded the legal right to try experimental treatments to those with “chronic and debilitating” conditions even if they aren’t dying from the illness. Lawmakers also unsuccessfully attempted to pass House Bill 1734, which would’ve set up experimental treatment centers throughout the state.
At the Freedom Summit, speakers urged lawmakers to go even further yet. A common theme was taking regulatory power away from the federal government and seeking a more industry-driven approach. Speakers challenged mainstream acceptance of the federal pharmaceutical safety system.
“What we’re trying to do is end up changing who is making the decisions around the safeguards,” Jared Rhodes, founder of the free-market think tank Center for Modern Health, said, adding: “It’s OK to ask, ‘Why does this all have to be centralized through the FDA or some sort of other government entity?’”
Ian Huyett, who works for New Hampshire-based conservative advocacy group Cornerstone, decried what he saw as an unfair standard on the biomedical industry where “food additives in the U.S. are largely regulated by after-the-fact remedies like civil liability, whereas drugs and biologics are subject to prospective, pre-market gatekeeping.”
“Food additives are essentially innocent until proven guilty,” Huyett said, in contrast to “biologics and drugs, (which) as we all know, even if there isn’t a big red flag — like ‘this is probably a carcinogen’ — are effectively illegal until proven innocent. Patients can’t get them until they come through a rigorous process, even if there’s nothing alarming in the data. And if you just think about this in first principles, you would expect all of this to be opposite.”
Proponents of “right to try” expansion have often framed their efforts in economic terms. Expansion of the law, they’ve said, will bring economic development to the state by attracting biotech companies interested in the relatively lax regulatory framework.
“Let’s make New Hampshire the best biotech framework in the country and make the Boston companies exit to New Hampshire,” Niklas Anzinger said. Anzinger is the CEO of Infinita, a Libertarian-aligned planned community in Honduras, who has been pushing for this type of legislation in both New Hampshire and Montana.
Speakers evoked countries like China, Japan, and Australia, which they said have adopted more lax regulatory landscapes that they’d like to see adopted in the U.S. and they fear are chipping away at U.S. pharmaceutical dominance.
Organizers had promised a visit from Ayotte Thursday morning. However, at the time of her scheduled visit, they announced that the governor couldn’t make it due to a “last-minute schedule change.”
“I just want to emphasize that the governor is behind you,” Alex Holderith, one of Ayotte’s policy advisers who spoke in lieu of the governor, said. “She’s ready to build. She wants to get out of the way. She wants to support you, and she recognizes just how important it is what you’re doing.”
Inventor Dean Kamen (left) and Jeremy Hitchcock, of StarCube, at the Aug. 21, 2026, Freedom Summit. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Building housing, scoping energy
Discussion on the summit’s second day was framed around the idea of “built futures,” featuring presentations on robot-built modular housing, artificial intelligence, and nuclear energy.
A fireside chat between Hitchcock, of StarCube, and Kamen headlined the day’s agenda — and forced organizers and Kamen himself to address his ties to Epstein. 
Asked about the choice to include Kamen in the lineup despite his connection to the sex offender — Kamen, for example, spent time on the billionaire’s private island — Lambert said she believed he had contributed significantly to New Hampshire’s industrial past, and did not believe in “cancel culture.”
“I didn’t see anything too incriminating. I feel like he already took his lashings,” she said. 
Kamen, who has denied knowledge of Epstein’s activities, took the stage to talk about his work in biotechnology and his STEM nonprofit, FIRST. But he also felt the need to try to clear the air, attributing his connection to the infamous millionaire to his attempts to court supporters for his nonprofits. 
“I’ve kissed every frog I can find,” he said, in what he described as an attempt to get support for his philanthropy. “… One of the frogs I kissed who I thought could be really helpful … it stunned me, it nearly killed me.”
In his talk, Kamen touched on the importance of building more housing in order to retain young talent in New Hampshire and make life affordable. He also shared his vision for a train — inspired by one at Walt Disney World — running through downtown Manchester. 
Other speakers also touched on New Hampshire’s need for housing. Vikas Enti, CEO of Massachusetts-based, AI-forward modular housing company ReFrame Systems, highlighted manufactured homes as a path toward climate resilience and lower housing costs. 
Pardha Ponugoti, a tech entrepreneur from Portsmouth, spoke about integrating artificial intelligence into his life in surprising ways; he advocated for New Hampshire to get ahead of the curve by adopting the technology aggressively. And energy was the focus for Bill Spellane, CEO of StarCube, a company that Spellane says is in the early phase of developing compact nuclear “microreactors.”
Manchester Mayor Jay Ruais speaks during “Freedom Summit” in Manchester on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Ideas for ‘Freedom Village’
The four organizers staged a grand reveal of the Freedom Village plans at the end of the second day. 
The village would take the form of a private housing development where members might “buy in” in order to join, Lambert said. 
“It will pay property taxes to whatever city it belongs to. It’s just like a normal real estate development,” she said in the early August interview.
Yet, she added, plans for the community do have a “specific angle.”
“It’s definitely meant to be, like, a community for entrepreneurs,” she said at the time.
A 100-plus-acre parcel of city-owned land in Manchester is the group’s current focus, they said on Friday, adding that they had already participated in preliminary discussions with Manchester Mayor Jay Ruais. 
When he spoke to kick off Friday’s session, Ruais welcomed the attendees to the Queen City and spoke highly of their mission.
“I believe the city, the state, we are all behind you in this effort to make this work and to make this a centerpiece, and make the centerpiece right here in Manchester,” he said. 
But Ruais’ remarks preceded the developers’ announcement that they were planning to build the development in Manchester, and he did not address the specific city-owned parcel. Ruais’ office did not respond to a question sent by email after the summit about whether Manchester was amenable to selling it to the Freedom Village developers.
There are other unknowns, too. How the village will be funded is still being worked out, Hitchcock said in an email. When an audience member asked about its business structure on Friday, Lambert said the organization would be privately run, but that profit was not the goal.
Some who have reached out about the plan have asked Lambert about Freedom Village’s model for internal governance and conflict resolution, she said. But she’s more focused on long-term outcomes for the people who move to the community, she said. 
“They spend a lot of their time … trying to discuss the governance,” Lambert said. “… And I’m just like, whenever I’m with the tech community, the entrepreneurial community, we’re just kind of all always talking about what we’re going to build.”
Living in community with others in tech carries significant benefits, like networking opportunities and the benefit of being creative around others in your field, Lambert said. But in the U.S., there are only a few cities that can offer that — and that feels limiting, she said. 
“When you work in startups, in tech, you’re constantly dealing with the trade-off of, I can live in San Francisco or New York. Those are basically the only two cities that have meaningful tech communities,” she said. 
Is New Hampshire a likely spot for a third such community to unfold? Lambert owns that it might seem like a stretch for some — but she and the rest of the Freedom Village team are wholehearted believers. 
After the summit wrapped on Friday, attendees milled about the Manchester venue, many heading to an outdoor afterparty nearby. A nature walk was planned for the following morning; then those who traveled from out of state for the event planned to depart.
With the announcements about Freedom Village still fresh, some attendees said they were left with questions — while others were enthusiastic, including Manchester tech worker Chris James.
“I’ll be the first resident,” he said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: We’ve got ‘historic flooding’ and tornadoes. Is this climate change?
description: Storms and tornadoes ravaged our state this month, killing at least seven people. In Hamilton County, the White River surged to a record 24 feet above normal levels, tearing up roads and bridges and destroying homes, sending families fleeing in the dark of the night.   Local meteorologists kept us abreast of the news, warning Hoosiers […]
text:
People work to place sandbags to stop floodwaters from the White River from entering the Indianapolis neighborhood of Rocky Ripple on Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Brett Phelps/Mirror Indy/CatchLight Local/Report for America)
Storms and tornadoes ravaged our state this month, killing at least seven people. In Hamilton County, the White River surged to a record 24 feet above normal levels, tearing up roads and bridges and destroying homes, sending families fleeing in the dark of the night.  
Local meteorologists kept us abreast of the news, warning Hoosiers when they needed to get to high ground or shelter in their basements or bathtubs. The immediacy and accuracy of those reports is job No. 1 for them, and weather emergencies are the top reason that people turn on local TV news.
Given this recent spate of extreme weather, I thought we would also be hearing more from meteorologists about the impacts of climate change. But I was wrong. 
While they cover the weather extensively, meteorologists don’t usually address climate change. It’s a weighty issue to unpack in short news segments. But ignoring the patterns during weather emergencies is a problem for Indy residents as we experience them on a more regular basis.
A news consumer who attended one of my recent Indy Public Editor events asked: To what extent is climate change (and other environmental issues) on the radar of the local press?
I reached out to several local meteorologists and was surprised to discover that they do not want to discuss climate change — with me or on the air. When I asked the leaders at several stations for interviews, they all declined. 
So I sought out journalists who specialize in covering climate change and a representative from the professional association of meteorologists, and I figured out why. 
Both politics and logistics keep climate out of the mouths of local meteorologists
Alan Sealls is the president of the American Meteorological Society. He’s been a meteorologist for close to 40 years.

Meteorologists focus on what the weather is going to do today and tomorrow and maybe next week, he told me. Many of them don’t view the role that climate change plays in our weather as a crucial piece of information when trying to tell people what’s going to happen today. Also, logistically, it’s hard to fit climate change into a two- or three-minute segment, Sealls said. 

Sealls said not every meteorologist avoids the topic. Some “see the link” between weather and climate and want to educate their viewers, so they weave it into their weather reports. “It also depends on who your station owner is and what their somewhat political perspective is, as we’ve seen where TV stations have had their licenses threatened in a sense because of what they broadcast or who was on their airwaves.”

As he’s traveled the country, Sealls said he finds that more meteorologists avoid climate change for logistical reasons, rather than out of the fear of retribution from their boss or the audience. However, the current presidential administration’s habit of characterizing climate change as something that’s not real and shouldn’t be talked about is also a deterrent, Sealls said. 

Elena González agrees with Sealls that meteorologists in the U.S. are mostly avoiding climate change coverage because of time constraints. She is a journalist and engagement manager for Covering Climate Now, a global organization that trains journalists and newsrooms on how best to report on climate change. 

Columbia Journalism Review and The Nation magazine founded Covering Climate Now in association with the Guardian and WNYC, a public radio station in New York City. Over the past two years alone, the organization has trained about 400 journalists in the U.S. and Canada and is expanding into Latin America and other parts of the world.

“If you have four heat waves in a row, and you are not telling that temperatures are intimately linked to climate change – it’s the most clear example – you are not telling your audience the whole story,” González said.

In addition to fearing federal regulatory pressure, some meteorologists worry the audience will tune out if they hear their weather person talking about climate change. 

Both Sealls and González say that the actual number of climate deniers in any audience is relatively small but that they can be noisy. According to Yale Climate Opinion Maps, only 15% of people say that climate change is not happening.

The staff at Covering Climate Now understand many meteorologists avoid climate coverage in their forecast because they don’t want to be rejected by their audience. “But they are not aware that, again, the deniers are a very small proportion,” González said.
What makes for good local climate coverage
Quality climate coverage doesn’t just intersect with weather. Instead, it pops up in multiple beats, including health, sports, social justice and the economy, experts say. 

“It has to be relevant, it has to be understandable, and, ideally, it needs to be local, where people can literally say, ‘Oh, I’ve seen that; I’ve felt that; I’ve experienced that,’” Sealls said.

Covering Climate Now has its own formula for good reporting, a three-pillars approach that focuses on humanizing stories, making them relevant to the local community and pointing toward solutions.  

“We need to try to cover the impacts that are actually affecting our communities and not talking about sad polar bears and shrinking icebergs,” González said. “This is the image that we have, and some editors also have when they are pitched a story about climate change.”
To localize a story, reporters must know how climate change impacts their communities and what their audience is interested in, she said. 
 
“The Midwest has been seeing more tornadoes,” Sealls said. “It’s been seeing more straight-line windstorms recently. So these are all things that people can definitely relate to because it’s not the way it was decades ago.” 

Sealls points to agriculture and economic stories, like this one by local WISH-TV, which notes that rising temperatures are causing financial hardship for area farms as good entry points for reporting on climate change.
Beyond the weather report: where to find good climate coverage in Indy
Mirror Indy’s westside neighborhood reporter, Enrique Saenz, directly addressed the issue in an Aug. 6 story he co-wrote with his colleagues. They talked to several state government officials who tied the recent storms to climate change and climate scientists explained that this could be the new normal.
Saenz regularly cites the Indiana Climate Change Impacts Assessment as well. Researchers tap into that database to see how, for example, temperatures and precipitation have changed since the late 1800s.

“I try to use that information to explain why certain changes that have been observed by scientists, like more frequent heavy rain events, are happening,” he said. Saenz was a founding journalist for the Indiana Environmental Reporter. This story about floods, droughts, and heat domes is an example of that reporting for Mirror Indy, which he wrote with fellow reporters Darian Benson and Elizabeth Gabriel. 

WFYI also zeroes in on what is happening at the local level. 

“We don’t think about it as a do-or-don’t issue,” said WFYI news director Sarah Neal-Estes. “When climate change is the news, we report it. Right now we are reporting an in-depth piece on Tornado Alley expanding and the increase of tornado activity in Indiana.” 

She said the station’s nonpartisan service is to cover significant weather pattern shifts, scientific explanations, leaders’ and residents’ perspectives and economic impacts. The news director doesn’t see the station’s reporting as controversial from any angle.

IndyStar’s Karl Schneider covers the environmental beat and Sophie Hartley has the environment and natural resources beat for the newspaper. Both have reported on the link between climate change and extreme weather events, or attribution science. 

“Referencing climate change in an article depends on how strong that connection is and how pertinent it might be for our readers’ understanding of the topic,” Schneider said. “This could mean a quick sentence or two, or a full section with broader context.”

Hartley said that readers told the paper that some of the stories that resonated the most with them were the ones that affected residents’ backyards. For example, this story about how changing weather patterns are impacting Indiana’s maple syrup makers. 

Other IndyStar climate stories include:

Warming trends and recent flooding 
National Weather Service in Indiana’s reporting on the frequency of flash floods 
The turbulent tornado season
Frustrations of local homeowners considering the cost of adding flood insurance 

“The topic does stir up controversy when government officials craft policy around climate change, but it is our job as journalists to continue to provide a nonpartisan framework for our reporting,” Schneider said.
We need climate change stories to help us stay informed
As a concerned news consumer, unless you read content from a beat reporter like Schneider, you might have to hunt to find coverage that will help you understand how the changing climate is going to change our region. Expect local meteorologists to continue to document forecast records and extreme weather, but not say much about the cause.

Beyond the weather forecast, especially in the days following such events, look to other beat reporters to fill in the details on community preparedness and accountability. 
Are officials insisting on sewer and utility infrastructure improvements that will withstand harsher weather? Do our governments have a plan for the future? Are there things that the government should do in the future? Because science says that these extreme weather events will happen again. 

Local TV stations are missing a key opportunity to include information about climate change in stories when the weather is going wild. That’s when the audience is paying the closest attention and looking for immediate advice, as well as guidance on how to better prepare in the future. Reporting on historical weather records is skimming the surface of a larger story. Additional context educates viewers. 

“If you don’t link the dots, if you don’t put together the whole story; it’s just to say this is another record,” said González. “It means nothing to me.”



				I’d love to hear from you! Please send your questions about Indy’s media ecosystem to indypubliceditor@poynter.org, or reach out to let me know if you’d like me to come speak to your community group. Your input helps strengthen Indianapolis’ local journalism.

name: National
title: Some states raise pay for home caregivers as shortage looms
description: WILMINGTON, Ohio — From her recliner in her tidy townhouse, Donna Logan offers advice to the first baby boomers to hit the big ‘8-0’ this year: Life can be good, especially with someone like Helen Aponte helping with laundry and housekeeping and the drive to the doctor’s office. “I do most things on my own,” […]
text:
Helen Aponte, left, is a home care aide for Donna Logan, 81, of Wilmington, Ohio. Aponte spends Monday mornings helping Logan with daily household chores or a trip to the doctor’s office. Ohio and other states have lifted caregiver pay to address a shortage of workers. (Photo by Anne Saker for Stateline)WILMINGTON, Ohio — From her recliner in her tidy townhouse, Donna Logan offers advice to the first baby boomers to hit the big ‘8-0’ this year: Life can be good, especially with someone like Helen Aponte helping with laundry and housekeeping and the drive to the doctor’s office.
“I do most things on my own,” said Logan, 81, a native of Wilmington, Ohio. “But having Helen come in once a week gives me confidence.”
“I drive her, whatever she needs,” said Aponte, 52. “It makes me happy to help Donna stay in her home.”
Logan and Aponte found each other about a year ago through the Council on Aging in Southwest Ohio in rural Clinton County, about 40 miles northeast of Cincinnati. For three hours on Mondays, Aponte works directly for Logan as a home care aide for $15 an hour, paid by a county property tax for senior services.
Aponte helps Logan with the tasks of daily living, not with medical care. For a senior, that support can mean the difference between aging at home or in an institution charging thousands of dollars a day.
Many seniors who are relatively healthy but need some assistance could see that relationship as an ideal arrangement. But it won’t be possible for many baby boomers, the 65 million Americans who were born between 1946 and 1964.
This year, four million Americans in that generation, including Cher, Sylvester Stallone and President Donald Trump, turned 80. Every day for at least the next decade, another 10,000 will join them. By 2030, Americans over 65 will outnumber those under 18.
For decades, experts have warned that the country was not prepared for this demographic wave.
In 2002, a National Institutes of Health forecast urged states, among other things, to revamp policies to prioritize home caregiving over nursing homes. The study warned  that it was “becoming increasingly difficult for home care agencies and other providers to find and retain qualified caregivers,” and that the problem would only get worse as the U.S population aged.
A big factor then was the poor pay for home care workers. The future has arrived, and little has changed.
Despite the importance of their work, home caregivers are near the bottom of the nation’s pay scale: In 2024, the national median pay for home care aides was $16.78 an hour, or $34,900 per year, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The low pay and the difficulty of the work have created a labor shortage, worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. There are 4.3 million home care aides today, but the federal government forecasts that by 2034, the nation will need more than 5 million of them.
As federal protections fade, disabled Americans fear a return to institutions

Some states that cover nonmedical home care through Medicaid, the joint state-federal healthcare program for people with low incomes, have marginally increased workers’ wages. But those small gains could be wiped out in 2027, when billions of dollars in Medicaid cuts go into effect as part of the broad tax and spending measure that President Donald Trump signed last year.
The spending cuts in that law will put pressure on cash-strapped states to cut home- and community-based services, since the federal Medicaid law only requires them to provide institutional care.
The challenge in Ohio
The structural challenges of a larger older population fall mostly to the states, and Ohio is a bellwether. The population has been aging faster since the 1990s collapse of the state’s industrial base, “so I understood the challenge when I came into office,” said Ursel McElroy.
In 2019, McElroy, a state government veteran on aging policy, became director of the Ohio Department of Aging under Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. In an interview, McElroy defined the challenge, then and now.
“Our health care is a triumph of human ingenuity, but while we’re living longer, we’re spending more years in less than good health,” he said. “That’s the problem we want to solve for. How do we keep pace with the realities of aging?”
One reality is that many seniors, such as Donna Logan, cannot afford to hire an aide on their own, but they are not eligible for Medicaid coverage. Instead, they turn to the nation’s more than 600 area agencies on aging, a network established in the 1965 Older Americans Act.
The Council on Aging of Southwestern Ohio manages senior-services levies in four counties including Clinton, said spokesperson Paula Smith. From that money, the county’s Elderly Services Program can pay home care aides, who can be hired through an employment service or directly.
In 2021, the Biden administration proposed putting $400 billion into Medicaid’s home-based and community programs to support home care workers and improve their pay as they kept older Americans out of nursing homes where COVID-19 was rampant and deadly. The proposal did not pass. The shortage of home care aides worsened.
In the past two years, some states have raised the pay of those workers in their Medicaid programs, often to bring them closer to the state’s minimum wage.
In California, for example, the basic wage for home care workers rose this year to $16.90 an hour, which is the statewide minimum wage. Each of the state’s 58 counties then adds a location adjustment. The Los Angeles County wage went up more than $1 to $19.64 this year.
In New York, the hourly wage for home care aides rose by 55 cents, to $19.65 in New York City, Long Island and Westchester County and to $18.65 in the rest of the state. Other states that have recently adjusted home care aide wages include Illinois, up a dollar to $18.75 and Texas, from $10.60 to $13.
Medicaid cuts could hurt older adults who rely on home care, nursing homes

Ohio, where the minimum wage is $11, also raised its pay in 2025 to an average of $16 an hour because, McElroy said, the Department of Aging and advocates across the state “have come together more so than I’ve seen in years past.”
The nonprofit Councils on Aging across Ohio held roundtable discussions for legislators on the critical shortage of home care aides, and the importance of their work. Raises for the Medicaid-paid workforce of home care aides, advocates said, would help bring up wages for everyone doing that work. A social media campaign pushed for pay raises, and ultimately, the legislature approved them.
Smith, the spokesperson  for the Council on Aging of Southwestern Ohio, said more people are applying to become home care aides. While Smith said no one is quite sure why, the pay raises likely helped.
‘I am doing just fine here’
Donna Logan says baby boomers shouldn’t worry about turning 80. “They’re in a lot better shape, I think, than our parents,” she said one rainy summer morning in her Wilmington townhouse. “I know a lot of them want to stay at home, like me. I tell them, ‘Get Helen.’”
The handicapped tag on the rearview mirror of Aponte’s sedan allows her to ferry Logan to the grocery store or the doctor’s office. She helps Logan with housekeeping. Every week, Aponte shows Logan how to sign on to the computer to sign her time card for $15 an hour. “I’m getting the hang of it,” Logan said with a laugh.
She turned down her son’s offer to live with his family. With Aponte, “I am doing just fine here.”
Logan isn’t the only one. Aponte has 14 other clients, and they love her so much that in May, Aponte received a Council on Aging award as a home aide hero.
“I love doing this so much,” Aponte said. As a teenager, she took care of her grandmother and discovered a calling. She said her work now gives her flexibility to care for a disabled son.
In her years as a home care aide, Aponte has found one thing in common among seniors, no matter the generation.
“They have a lot of stories,” she said, “and they just want someone to listen to them.”
