name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In Bristol, these ‘Old Cranks’ keep CT’s clockmaking history ticking
description: The American Clock and Watch Museum in Bristol harkens back to a time when Connecticut was known as the "Clock Capital of the World."
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

Bruce Thorin ticks when he walks. 
The rhythmic sounds emitted by his trusty gold pocket watch and rotating array of wristwatches provide accompaniment (and the time) as he sets clocks throughout the American Clock and Watch Museum in Bristol.
Thorin, 77, is one of two “Old Cranks” — the other is 73-year-old Michael Dion — who volunteer every Friday to wind 65 clocks. Their tools: white cloth gloves and a cardboard box full of clock keys.
“You’ve got to make sure you’re not cranking like a crazy person,” Thorin said. “Everything is being respectful of the clock itself.” 

Michael Dion shows an example of an Ansonia Crystal Regulator clock at the The American Clock and Watch Museum in Bristol on July 31, 2026. Dion purchased a version of the clock during the Connecticut chapter meeting for the National Association of Watch and Clock Collectors in Newton to add to his collection.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The museum is a time capsule of timepieces. The white temperature-controlled building, a renovated 1801 house, opened in 1954 as the only museum devoted to horology in the country. There were initially 300 clocks on display, but the museum expanded to include another wing as the collection grew. 
It currently holds more than 6,500 timekeeping devices, from shelf clocks to grandfather clocks, railroad watches to character watches from a range of eras. The oldest clock in the collection, a tall-case clock from Philadelphia, dates to 1720. 
Most of these timepieces were acquired from private collections, through auctions and donations. 
The Old Cranks regard the locally made clocks most fondly — like 19th and 20th century Ingraham clocks that were made right in Bristol, or Seth Thomas clocks made in Plymouth.

Michael Dion (left) and Bruce Thorin (right) examine the movement inside a wall clock dated to 1910 in Bristol on July 31, 2026. Both Dion and Thorin volunteer at the museum every Friday.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

When Connecticut kept the time 
The American Clock and Watch Museum celebrates Connecticut’s role in the storied history of clockmaking. 
One of the earliest Connecticut producers of clocks was Thomas Harland, an English immigrant who set up shop in Norwich. At the time, clocks were expensive to make, requiring skilled craftsmen to measure and assemble intricate internal parts from brass.
But many clockmakers were interested in finding a way to speed up the process. 
“These guys used to get together and talk shop time to time,” said Mel Brown, 87, who pioneered the Old Cranks with former curator Chris Bailey and now helps out at the museum with clock repairs. “There was a lot of interest in finding a way to make clocks that average people could afford. People started experimenting.” 

Bruce Thorin winds a clock in The American Clock and Watch Museum in Bristol on July 31, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Then, in 1807, a Connecticut clockmaker named Eli Terry — who had trained in the craft with a protege of Harland’s — developed a new form of wooden clock parts that were interchangeable. 
That innovation made it possible to mass produce clocks at a far lower cost, which made them affordable to a wider swath of Americans. His factory, in Plymouth, took advantage of the plentiful local wood supply and water-powered machinery along rivers in the area.
Soon, his operations were churning out smaller “shelf clocks” that could be sold door-to-door, and timepieces flooded American households. For a time, Connecticut became known as the “Clock Capital of the World.” (The village of Terryville, in Plymouth, was named in Terry’s honor.)
There’s around six Terry-style shelf clocks in the museum, and one of these “clock boxes” was made before 1825, the year his career took off. None of these clocks are wound, though. 
“We don’t really wind any wooden works,” Thorin said. 
Though wooden parts spurred mass production, the gears would warp and swell, making it harder to ship them overseas. Factories shifted to stamping out parts on thin brass sheets.

The American Clock and Watch Museum exhibits a grandfather clock by clockmaker Peter Hill in Bristol on July 31, 2026. While he was enslaved, Hill apprenticed with his master in New Jersey, and when he was freed in 1795, Hill had his own workshop. His clocks are kept in museums, including the Smithsonian collection in Washington D.C. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

With mass production came changes in how factory workers were paid. Piecemeal rates shifted to hourly wages, and workers needed a way to log their time. So they started punching in and out, at the beginning and end of their shifts, on clocks that kept track. 
In a nod to this, the American Clock and Watch Museum placed an 1885 timeclock near the entrance. Visitors can punch a timecard when they arrive. 
With the advent of electricity, it was only a matter of time before mechanical clockmaking went into decline. The Flood of 1955 nearly destroyed one of Connecticut’s major factories in Thomaston, and Brown said the industry never returned what it once was.
The clock had run out. 

Patti Philippon, executive director of the American Clock and Watch Museum, posed in the museum gardens in Bristol on July 31, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The memory is still ticking
While the title of “Clock Capital” doesn’t spring to mind these days in Connecticut, there is a devoted community of timepiece enthusiasts who still celebrate its past. One local chapter of the National Association of Watch and Clock Collectors meets every few months in Newtown, where they share their collections and exchange spare parts and repair tips. 
Patti Phillippon, executive director of the American Clock and Watch Museum, is regularly in attendance. The Old Cranks go too, of course. 
They’re recruiting. 
Anyone who’s interested in clock winding can be an Old Crank, Thorin and Dion will tell you. 
Paul D’Aprile, a late member of the group, recruited Thorin at church. He convinced Dion to join after helping him fix a grandfather clock. Thorin and Dion still remember which clocks in the museum were D’Aprile’s favorites. He took particular care of a 1848 wall clock originally made for Charter Oak Insurance Company; in honor of a son who’d died, the D’Aprile family provided the museum with funds for its maintenance.
Lately, Phillippon has been working to raise the museum’s profile among Connecticut collectors and beyond. Recently, she held focus groups to hear ideas and perspectives as the museum was developing its upcoming exhibition, “The Story of American Watchmaking.”
“We have so many different American watch manufactures, so we really want to make sure everyone is represented,” Philippon said. 
The exhibit is slated to open next February.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: No, Americans haven’t embraced socialism. Suffering people have given up on politics as usual.
description: A clergyman who had spent years in foreign missionary efforts once explained how the work — building housing, digging wells, feeding and clothing people — morphed into a Christian message. Missionaries didn’t show up talking about Jesus and the Bible, he said. They busy themselves trying to meet the immediate needs of the people there. […]
text:
New York Mayor and Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani gained national notice for his supposed ideological differences. (Photo by Ed Reed/Mayoral Photography Office)A clergyman who had spent years in foreign missionary efforts once explained how the work — building housing, digging wells, feeding and clothing people — morphed into a Christian message.
Missionaries didn’t show up talking about Jesus and the Bible, he said. They busy themselves trying to meet the immediate needs of the people there. Otherwise, residents couldn’t hear their Christian witness.
Eventually, the people would finally exhale and ask, “Why would you travel here and do so much for us?”
That gave the missionaries their opportunity to share Christ’s message.
Much of national news media seems to be missing this formula amid talk of an ideological split on the left and an insurgent push by Democratic socialists. Suffering people don’t care about ideology. They care who heard their desperate cries for help.
Since voters swept New York Mayor and Democratic socialist (he’s also a member of the Democratic Party) Zohran Mamdani into office in January, his opponents and some news media chalked his win up to voters swayed by a new ideology.
Balderdash.
The reality? Politicians such as Mamdani and Florida Rep. Angie Nixon, who in recent days upset retired Gen. Alex Vindman in a U.S. Senate race, heard the kitchen table chatter about how soaring food and fuel costs threaten to sink them.
New York voters said the rent is too damn high. They said they live in food deserts. They said they can’t afford childcare. Mamdani could have espoused any faith tradition because voters essentially said: “Whatever Mamdani believes, it’s less important than him listening to us.”
This phenomenon isn’t new.
Religious “brand loyalty” continues to fade. Denominational churches are giving way to nondenominational megachurches. Increasingly, blue voters and red voters have rebranded themselves as independents.
Aside from civics and C-SPAN nerds (like me), I’m not convinced that wide swaths of working Americans care much about political ideologies.
For the record, democratic socialism seeks a democratically run economy dominated by people with decentralized government control and political freedom. Americans have grown weary with our “leave no billionaire behind” economy and increasingly consider news organizations and mainstream politicians as accomplices.
My old boss, Davis “Buzz” Merritt, at the Wichita Eagle, argued that journalism suffered a debilitating addiction to conflict.
Who said what about whom? So, he doesn’t like him? Who is winning the horserace?
Worse, the journalistic elites and the politicians they cover can form an insular loop with shared celebrity status, Merritt said. 
“The increasingly high profile of political reporters, and their constant appearances on television shows as pundits rather than as reporters, the unceasing self-promotion of star anchors by television networks and local outlets, and the fawning celluloid celebration of the Watergate journalists began to meld politicians and political journalists into an amorphous and distant ‘they,’ ” Buzz wrote more than 30 years ago in his book, “Public Journalism and Public Life: Why Telling The News Is Not Enough.”
“Journalists and politicians looked and often acted like a cohesive establishment of elites: imbued with insider status; playing by arcane rules and keeping score with irrelevancies; seemingly indifferent, if not impervious, to outside challenge,” he wrote.
It is understandable then how some journalists and some politicians lose their connection to the struggles of everyday people. Families that can barely afford rent or childcare probably aren’t preoccupied with who controls the means of production.
While the working class and the middle class fret about survival, elites have twisted our democratic republic into something resembling a fascist state. A handful of individuals wallow in more wealth than some nation-states.
They control all three branches of government. They gave themselves tax relief on the backs of society’s most vulnerable. They now seem intent on tightening their grip on power by funding attacks on voting rights. I’m not sure that these figures care about ideology. Their belief system, low-road capitalism, centers power and dominance.
Are we witnessing the emergence of a new political party? Maybe.
What feels more likely is that our economy and politics have grown so hot, so oppressive, so inflamed, that voters no longer care about what’s on the screen. They’re leaping from their seats and following people who’ve won their trust, through the nearest exit.
People understand their basic needs and they are voting accordingly.
Mark McCormick is the former executive director of the Kansas African American Museum, a member of the Kansas African American Affairs Commission and former deputy executive director at the ACLU of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: ‘The time for tolerance has ended’
description: RAYMOND — When Jeff Peterson was hired as principal of Raymond School in 2021, he was coming home to the K-8 school he attended as a child in the small Racine County community where his family has lived for generations. The 30-year education veteran said at a state hearing this year that he’d taken the […]
text:
A once-popular school principal in rural Racine County lost his job after unsupported accusations were circulated through social media. 
(Photo by Heather Asiyanbi)RAYMOND — When Jeff Peterson was hired as principal of Raymond School in 2021, he was coming home to the K-8 school he attended as a child in the small Racine County community where his family has lived for generations.
Jeff Peterson (Courtesy photo)
The 30-year education veteran said at a state hearing this year that he’d taken the job to “finish out my career” in what he called his “dream job.” Peterson’s first year review was full of praise and included a raise. His review also noted teacher complaints to the board had all but stopped.

Journalist Heather Asiyanbi has covered the ongoing conflict at the Raymond School District since 2023. This report is based on interviews with the people involved, documents and recordings obtained through requests under Wisconsin’s open records law, and observation of public meetings, including the Department of Workforce Development hearing conducted over Zoom that investigated Jeff Peterson’s discrimination complaint against the school district.

That changed after the 2022 elections saw the conservative community’s school board taken over by far right-wing figures allied with groups such as Moms for Liberty. Leading the new majority was Gwen Keller, now McCutcheon, who was aligned with Art Binhack, head of the Wisconsin chapter of the right-wing group Convention of States, an organization that pushes states to call a constitutional convention to limit federal power.
Audrey Kostuch had already been on the board since 2021. She was present for Peterson’s hiring and had never publicly said anything negative about him. That changed only after Keller’s election and Dr. Michael Garvey took over as superintendent.
By April 2023, Peterson was put on a professional improvement plan that included a structured timeline but lacked specific metrics by which he would be measured. On September 27, 2023, the board voted 4-1 to issue a preliminary notice of non-renewal, and the next day, Garvey and a few sheriff’s deputies escorted him out of the building. Peterson was told not to speak to anyone.
A final school board hearing on whether to proceed with Peterson’s non-renewal was set for December 2023. In the weeks between, his personnel file began circulating through a Moms for Liberty Facebook page as evidence, campaign organizers claimed, that he’d sexualized and groomed children.
Peterson, who is gay, filed discrimination and retaliation complaints with the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development after he was put on administrative leave. The department found probable cause in November 2024, and a seven-day administrative hearing was held earlier this year. A ruling isn’t expected until 2027. 
Peterson has also filed a federal lawsuit, currently stayed pending the DWD decision, and recently amended it to add former Village President Kari Morgan and Moms for Liberty’s Joann Koenecke as individual respondents.
Neither of the accusations lodged against Peterson was true. Records entered at the DWD hearing show that a campaign by the board’s new majority built its case against Peterson by taking a single staff activity that was investigated and closed and stretching it into something it never was.
Kostuch, McCutcheon, Morgan, Binhack, and Koenecke did not respond to requests for comment or answer questions about what drove them to spread unverified allegations of child abuse. 
The scavenger hunt as it actually happened
In August 2022, Peterson organized a single-day scavenger hunt for staff during inservice week, a team-building exercise meant to familiarize new hires with the community. Among the 20 tasks, staff were sent to take a photo at the local fireworks store, with a local minister, and in front of Peterson’s childhood home. 
Two of the twenty items offered 25 bonus points for a photo “of a student in their swimming pool” and for “reading a book to a student in their bedroom, or under a tree.” Nothing in the instructions told staff to visit a child’s home uninvited or ask them to change clothes.
Staff who took part posted about the day on social media afterward, calling it “memorable” and “fun.” A district secretary filed a complaint that September citing several concerns, including the scavenger hunt, and an outside attorney the district hired that fall substantiated a narrow version of it: Some staff had photographed students at pools or in bedrooms without the district clearly communicating to parents that the activity was voluntary. 
Peterson received a formal written reprimand in November 2022. It was a real, if clumsily handled, personnel matter, and the district treated it as closed.
Raymond School Board President Audrey Kostuch
A year later, Kostuch told a different story. During a September 2023 visit from the Racine County Sheriff’s Office, prompted by a genuinely threatening letter sent to her home, Kostuch barely discussed the letter itself. 
Instead, she described the scavenger hunt as staff being told to “go to a student’s house that has a swimming pool, ask them to put their swimming suits on and take pictures of them in the swimming pool with their suits on,” then to “go to the student’s house and ask them to put their pajamas on and go into their bedroom and sit on the bed and read them a story.” None of that was in the instructions. 
“So, okay, you’ve got the same expression I do,” Kostuch told the deputy. “What the? I don’t like to say it, but some of the things that he’s done, I look at him and think, are you a child groomer?” 
Under cross-examination at the hearing, she acknowledged she’d seen the actual instructions only once.
Making the file public
Sometime after Kostuch talked with the deputy, Peterson’s personnel file was posted on the Moms for Liberty Facebook page, with no explanation of how it got there.
Obtaining a public school official’s personnel file requires an open records request. The affected individual is notified, and they have the opportunity to object. The original request was submitted in August 2023, and the file was released before the district alerted Peterson in early October. 
He responded on Oct. 9 that he would file a court action to prevent the release of his personnel file. Ultimately, he didn’t file because the file had already been released, and there wasn’t anything further he could do.
The Raymond School District building. (Photo by Heather Asiyanbi)
Documents presented at Peterson’s DWD hearing show that Morgan, the then-village president, was searching for a way to oust Peterson but had no jurisdiction over the school district. And, for reasons that remain unclear, she didn’t want her name on the request.
Binhack, a Raymond resident who’d run for the school board twice and lost both times, had spent the prior year building exactly the kind of relationship that made this possible. He campaigned alongside Keller, texting her immediately after the April 2023 election that the board had “the majority, 3-2,” and floating that she could become president. 
“I am hoping for that,” she replied. 
He had standing as an ordinary citizen and no obvious tie to the board members who actually wanted the file. Submitting the open records request under his name meant no public record would connect Raymond’s village president acting outside her authority to a campaign against a school employee.
Metadata on the electronic file later confirmed Morgan wrote the request, and Binhack didn’t dispute the arrangement at the DWD hearing earlier this year. 
“She asked me to file the open records request,” he testified, adding that Morgan supplied a list of specific names to include that he didn’t recognize. “I didn’t know many of the names.”
After receiving Peterson’s personnel file, Morgan drafted a cover letter in which she worked to connect her alleged dots, calling Peterson’s conduct “sexualization of children and things that border on child grooming.” 
Specifically, the letter introduces the district’s “issues” by saying they existed prior to Peterson taking the helm of the school but “have become much worse since he has been principal of the school.” Morgan’s letter urges the public to “evaluate the file of Jeff Peterson and decide” that “tolerance is an admirable mindset, but the time for tolerance has ended.” It condemns Peterson supporters as standing “for a dysfunctional school staff environment and (who) support child grooming.” 
Morgan then put the file and cover letter onto a flash drive and sent it around the community. By October 2023, the letter was posted by Koenecke to the Racine County Moms for Liberty Facebook page. Koenecke since August 2023 had been in direct contact with former school board member McCutcheon. Koenecke also passed it to a local television reporter at FOX 6 within days. 
When Garvey was asked by local reporters to authenticate the accompanying letter, he said it “did not originate from my office.”
What families saw
Some parents of Raymond students spoke up and out about Peterson being targeted and what it was doing to the community and to students.
Nicki O’Brien, a former Raymond parent, watched Peterson get walked out that day in late September 2023. 
“Whatever the hell is happening is not okay,” she told Racine County Eye a few weeks later, “and watching it all unfold was disturbing.”
Megan Rios, whose husband is Mexican and served as PTO president while her children were open-enrolled at Raymond, said the atmosphere reached the students themselves. 
“There was a level of bigotry and hatred brought into the walls of the school, and the kids picked up on it, saying racist things like Mexicans are lazy and worthless,” Rios is quoted in the same  Racine County Eye article. 
She said she watched something change in her daughter that year and pulled her out at the end of the 2022-23 school year, once it became clear Peterson himself wouldn’t survive it. 
“Her light is back,” Rios described her daughter, after enrolling her elsewhere.
Morgan, who pulled her own children from Raymond at the end of the 21-22 school year, said it was because of parents like Rios. 
“Anyone who meets Jeff knows he’s gay, and so what?” she told Racine County Eye in December 2023. “His contract non-renewal is about performance. He’s a great teacher but not a great leader because he doesn’t hold teachers accountable.” 
Yet, just a few weeks prior, Morgan was one of the authors of the file that called Peterson a groomer.
Teacher testimony during the DWD hearing directly disputed the campaign’s characterization of a “toxic staff environment.” A story from Racine County Eye notes a district survey found roughly 70% of respondents rated the teaching staff positively. 
Whatever was driving families like Rios’ out of Raymond, hearing testimony suggests it wasn’t the working relationship between Peterson and his staff and his students. School district data shows that prior to the right-wing takeover of the board in 2022, only about 25 students were open-enrolled out of the district each year. By the 2025-2026 school year, that number had grown to roughly 45, Racine County Eye reported.
What it cost Peterson
Peterson says what the last three years have done to him wasn’t something he could simply ignore or put aside. “It impacted every aspect of my life,” he said. “The things that were said about me are completely untrue, shameful, and hurtful.” 
The accusations followed him as he went through the motions during the day and in his relationships with neighbors and former colleagues. They affected his motivation to just get out of bed. What he says hurt most wasn’t the professional fallout but where it happened. 
“These things were said and done in the same community that I loved, that I lived in, that I grew up in,” he said — the same community that shaped why he became an educator in the first place. 
He describes moving through the world now with his guard up, and he admitted it’s hard not to be a little jaded about work he once found meaningful without a second thought. 
Peterson didn’t land another job for more than a year. Some districts, he believes, never called him back for interviews they might otherwise have offered because they were unwilling to take a chance on someone carrying public accusations tied to children. 
What kept him upright, he says, was people who reached out, “literally on a daily basis for the last three years.” Without them, he said, “I wouldn’t have survived.”
No one has explained why
Binhack’s notes from January 2023 show McCutcheon discussing ending Peterson’s contract that June and a longer-term plan to install a different superintendent candidate, months before the file circulated. 
And, at a December 2022 retreat, Garvey told the room outright that no one in Raymond was “teaching woke” and no critical race theory was taught anywhere in Wisconsin. 
Nothing in Peterson’s curriculum ever changed. What was well known, even as he kept his private life separate from his job, was that he is gay.
The campaign against him was a solution in search of a problem that never existed and could cost the Raymond School District, or its insurer, far more than a quiet non-renewal would have. Legal costs have already run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and a ruling against the district by either the state or in a federal court could add substantially more in legal fees and potential damages. 
With Morgan and Koenecke now named directly in Peterson’s federal complaint, both could be held personally liable alongside the district if a court agrees with what the record already shows: that Raymond school board members had a lawful, quiet way to end Peterson’s employment, and chose instead to manufacture a reason to smear his reputation. 
Kostuch, meanwhile, remains on the board, and is up for re-election in April 2027.

title: With drug prices on the rise, Georgia lawmakers examine role of industry players
description: A business rep was on the phone telling Hugh Chancey’s pharmacy in southwest Georgia to transfer all of an elderly patient’s prescriptions away to another pharmacy.  The patient herself said that’s not what she wanted, Chancey recounted, but the company was relentless. After a three-way phone call where the patient said she wanted to keep […]
text:
Adams Family Pharmacy, a locally owned pharmacy, has locations in Cuthbert and Preston. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderA business rep was on the phone telling Hugh Chancey’s pharmacy in southwest Georgia to transfer all of an elderly patient’s prescriptions away to another pharmacy. 
The patient herself said that’s not what she wanted, Chancey recounted, but the company was relentless. After a three-way phone call where the patient said she wanted to keep using Chancey’s pharmacy, an order came over by fax anyway, saying to transfer the prescriptions.
Chancey relayed that story to high-powered state legislators last month. The group, a House study committee, is taking on the question of medicine regulation in Georgia. The business caller he described was an insurance middleman called a pharmacy benefit manager, or PBM, and is one of the subjects in the committee’s sights.
The insurance middlemen are billion-dollar businesses that say they protect the public good. Their job is to negotiate drug prices between insurance companies and drug makers and pharmacies, to keep prices down. And for that, they take a cut.
But that can get complicated when the middlemen have sister companies that are other pharmacies, competing for customers against all pharmacies. One prominent example of a PBM is CVS Caremark, which shares the same owner as CVS pharmacies and a major insurance company. They serve Georgia’s State Health Benefit Plan.
Chancey did not name the PBM in his anecdote. 
“We’re not asking for special treatment,” Chancey said. “We’re asking for a level playing field.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The insurance middlemen insist they do not game the system; that it’s the other way around. But they are under scrutiny nationwide. Georgia has led the nation in some small steps to prevent potential harms, and the state House of Representatives’ study committee is taking the issue on again during the legislative off season. Its next meeting is planned for Wednesday at the Mercer School of Medicine in Macon. 
The group is called the House Study Committee on Pharmacy Benefits Managers and Consumers’ Access to Prescription Medications. 
The first meeting, held in July, also carried several presentations not about PBMs, but about a controversial federal law mandating discounts for some hospitals on drugs from manufacturers. Like the issue of middlemen, the discount program is hotly contested, high stakes and touted as a life-or-death issue by some rural health businesses.
Rep. Ron Stephens, a Savannah Republican, is leading the study committee. He’s also a pharmacist. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
When it comes to PBMs, independent pharmacists like Chancey believe the middlemen are a blight: driving independent pharmacies in Georgia out of business, costing the state millions of dollars in higher drug payments and depriving rural patients of crucial healthcare options. Independent pharmacies allege that the middlemen make self-serving moves like steering patients away to a competitor – a practice Georgia has already tried to curb – or making them sell a medicine for less than what the pharmacist even spends to fill it.
For their part, the middlemen say they are all that lies between patients and outlandish prices that drug companies like to charge. They say that on the contrary, they save money for the public – and that independent pharmacies cherry-pick their data.
“PBMs have saved the state of Georgia and (organizations paying for health insurance) almost $30 billion over the last 10 years,” said Michael Power, a lobbyist for the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association who spoke at the July hearing. The association represents the middlemen, including CVS Health, Express Scripts and OptumRx.
A spokesman for CVS Health echoed that sentiment, and added that the company’s PBM does not set out to advantage CVS pharmacies. The spokesman, Phillip Blando, said they juggle patients’ interests, including their desire for a nearby pharmacy, with helpful staff and the best price the patient can receive – and it’s up to each pharmacy, independent or chain, to earn that.
“In order to meet our clients’ contractual requirements, we need a broad mix of pharmacies – including independent pharmacies – to serve patients in urban, suburban, and rural areas,” Blando said. 
Georgia stands out for its efforts to rein in pharmacy middlemen 
Losing independent pharmacies is especially a problem in rural Georgia, where five or six counties have no pharmacy at all. In Georgia counties with less than 15,000 people, independent pharmacies outnumber corporate ones by 6-1, according to a 2024 report from the Georgia Center for Rural Prosperity and Innovation. When Bell’s Family Pharmacy closed in Tate in 2024, the town lost its only retail pharmacy. The owner, Katie Bell, said one big factor causing her to close was PBM pricing.  
Bell cited the example of getting reimbursed $1.90 by the state’s insurance middleman for dispensing the popular cholesterol-lowering drug Lipitor – her total reimbursement for buying the drug, paying someone to fill it, buying the bottle, running the label printer and keeping the lights on.
In contrast, the PBM was paying an average of $46.87 to big chains like CVS and Walgreens for the same thing, citing publicly available data from the State Health Benefit Plan.
Rep. Butch Parrish, who is one of the most powerful Republicans in the state House, is a member of the study committee. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
If Bell hadn’t gone out of business, the independent pharmacy’s data would still be secret under a gag clause in the PBM contract, pharmacy advocates said.
But Blando, the CVS spokesman, said that if they averaged together all the drugs on the price list, not just the most common ones, independent pharmacies would have the far better reimbursement figure.
“Focusing on a limited subset of drugs does not provide a complete picture of pharmacy reimbursement,” Blando said this week. “As the industry moves toward more transparent reimbursement models, such as CVS Pharmacy’s Cost Vantage approach, the focus is increasingly on the underlying cost of a drug and the professional services required to dispense it, rather than isolated pricing examples.”
This year’s study committee is small but has unusually influential members. They include the chairman of the powerful House Rules Committee, which decides what bills might get a floor vote, and of the committee that oversees the state budget. 
They drew a standing-room-only audience of lobbyists, including from drug companies, pharmacies and hospitals, some who came from hundreds of miles away.
Trying to wade through the competing data, find out how to best protect patients in the drug market and then make it happen, is a struggle. Georgia has gone at it before, leading the nation in small steps but ones that advocates called meaningful. 
In 2025, Gov. Brian Kemp signed a law, House Bill 196, mandating a basic fee for pharmacists each time they dispense a prescription under the state employees’ health plan. 
But the effort has had uneven progress.
The House this spring voted to create the committee after bigger legislation focused on insurance middlemen died in that chamber.
And in 2024, Kemp vetoed a measure that passed overwhelmingly. That bill would have required PBMs serving the State Health Benefit Plan to reimburse independent pharmacies as much as chain pharmacies for the same drugs. Kemp said in his veto that that could cost the state money that it hadn’t budgeted for. Advocates for the bill believed it would save the state money, though.
 Further, the independent pharmacists say that despite anti-steering legislation, the practice still goes on. 
A push for more transparency? 
The chairman of the study committee, Rep. Ron Stephens, a Savannah Republican, said his legislative goal is transparency.
“You know, whenever our own Department of Community Health (which oversees the State Health Benefit Plan) cannot get information to base decisions on from the very PBM that they’re contracting with, it’s ridiculous.”
 

Committee membership: 
The study committee is chaired by Rep. Ron Stephens, a Savannah Republican, who also chairs the House Economic Development and Tourism Committee and is himself a pharmacist. The other four members are:

Rep. Matt Hatchett, a Dublin Republican, the chairman of the Appropriations Committee, which oversees the state’s budget; 
Butch Parrish, a Swainsboro Republican, chairman of the Rules Committee, which decides which bills might come up for a final House vote; 
Health Committee Chairman Lee Hawkins, a Gainesville Republican; and 
One Democrat, health executive Rep. Debbie Buckner, of Junction City.




But Power, the lobbyist for PBMs, said that new federal rules were taking care of the transparency issue.
The billions of dollars at stake in drug prices are ultimately paid by patients at the check-out window and in their insurance premiums, and by taxpayers.
The legislative panel will also take up the issue of a hotly contested hospital pharmacy discount program. To some attendees’ surprise, that program took up a large portion of the committee’s inaugural meeting.
The program is called 340B, after the federal law that created it. Under the law, drug companies are forced to give some hospitals and clinics that serve the poor the best discounts they offer. Drug makers that say hospitals are gaming the program – like buying a hospital in a poor area just to get the discount that they then use in another location for better-paying patients – and also by using the money for things it was never intended to fund. Hospitals, on the other hand, say it’s a crucial tool to keep indigent care afloat. 
Under the program, designated facilities like hospitals can buy a drug at the company’s most discounted price, but then they get reimbursed by insurance for the full price. Eligible hospitals and clinics wind up with extra money, and they have come to depend on it for just running operations.
This year, a bill that would restrict drug companies’ attempts to rein in use of the discount program never made it out of the House of Representatives. That bill was House Bill 139.
Facing the sea of conflicting claims and complex data, members of the committee said they’re there to learn and that Georgia healthcare is at stake.
“I think there’s a lot of confusion” about the basic issues, said Rep. Butch Parrish, a Swainsboro Republican and member of the study committee who also chairs the House Rules Committee. “A lot of people don’t really understand it, and it depends on who you talk to, sort of what twist you hear. And I think hopefully that’s what we’re going to do in our committee – to really get down into the weeds and get some good information, so we can make intelligent, good decisions going forward.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: In an Ohio congressional race with national scrutiny, Brian Poindexter wants to win on his own terms
description: An Ohio city councilman from a working class suburb near Cleveland’s airport has become something of a darling among national Democrats in recent weeks. Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker and the Democratic nominee for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, launched his campaign out of his garage. Fellow Brook Park councilman Thomas Dufour has served as his […[...]
text:
Ohio 7th Congressional District Democratic candidate Brian Poindexter touring the Feeding Medina County distribution center. (Photo provided.)An Ohio city councilman from a working class suburb near Cleveland’s airport has become something of a darling among national Democrats in recent weeks.
Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker and the Democratic nominee for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, launched his campaign out of his garage. Fellow Brook Park councilman Thomas Dufour has served as his campaign manager, communications director, and treasurer since January. At an Aug. 15 town hall in Medina, he added another job title: cameraman.
“It started with just me and Tom in the garage, and then two became four, four became eight,” Poindexter said in an interview earlier this month, sitting at a picnic table in a small park in Parma.
Cook Political Report initially deemed the race “Likely Republican,” with Poindexter up against incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Max Miller in a district that President Donald Trump won by 11 percentage points in 2024. Ohio’s 7th Congressional District includes Cleveland’s West Side suburbs, as well as Medina, Wayne, and Ashland counties.
When allegations of domestic violence against Miller caused several prominent Republicans to call for his resignation — a movement led by Miller’s ex-father-in-law, U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno — Democrats turned their attention to Poindexter. Miller denies the allegations against him.
Progressives who backed Poindexter in the primary, like U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, have since joined forces with some of the more moderate voices in the party, like former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg and the Blue Dog PAC. Cook Political Report now says the race is a toss-up.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
After Poindexter was interviewed by The New York Times, NBC News, CBS News, ABC News, and Politico in early August, he told the crowd in Medina that going on national television has been “a nightmare.”
Poindexter spoke in Medina about starting an associate’s degree at 27 years old, paying student loans for his daughter, and living with his parents after a divorce in 2020. He has acknowledged the charges he picked up as a young man: a misdemeanor assault charge and two misdemeanor disorderly conduct charges, one that he pleaded no contest for and another that was dismissed. He added that fatherhood changed his perspective.
Between campaigning and serving on Brook Park’s city council, his work as an apprenticeship instructor at Ironworkers Local 17 is still his primary source of income, according to personal financial disclosures.
Poindexter has limited name recognition in his district, but his unusual biography could help, said Cyril Kleem, the Republican mayor of Berea. Brook Park shares a school district with Berea, and Kleem endorsed Poindexter in early August.
“A lot of working class people have felt left out,” Kleem said. ‘Some of those people have gravitated toward the Republican Party, particularly toward Donald Trump, because I think to a certain extent, the Democratic Party has been accused of forgetting about them. I think he represents them.”
Despite having support from almost the entire Democratic Party — including $6 million in committed spending from a super PAC dedicated to flipping the U.S. House of Representatives — Poindexter has repeatedly tried to shed the party label.
“I’m not in this to carry the flag for the Democratic Party,” he said. “I’m in this to flip a seat for working families.”
As Democrats rally behind Poindexter, Republicans splinter on Miller
The U.S. Capitol on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
While Kleem mainly endorsed Poindexter because of their collaboration at the local level, “of course” the allegations against Miller were a factor in his decision, he said.
Kleem said he privately told Poindexter to avoid talking about the scandal frequently, reasoning that protecting Miller’s daughter was more important than winning the race. The Brook Park councilman agreed, Kleem added. When asked about the scandal in interviews, Poindexter usually acknowledges the severity of the situation before pivoting to focus on Miller’s policies.
“If you talk to a strategist, they’re going to go for the throat. I still believe in ethics,” Kleem said. “If my doctor gave me six months to live, I’m not going to be sitting around worried about the elections I won. I’m going to want to spend time with my kids and my wife.”
In a July 8 affidavit for a defamation lawsuit he brought against his ex-wife, Miller wrote that labor unions turned against him because of the allegations. Representatives for three trade unions informed him that they would pull their endorsements, and the international organization for a fourth told him they would endorse Poindexter, he wrote.
Since then, four Republican U.S. senators have called for Miller’s resignation, including both of Ohio’s senators. U.S. Sen. Jon Husted pulled Miller’s endorsement from his campaign website shortly after releasing a statement saying he thought Miller would be “making the right decision” by dropping out of the race and resigning.
Husted’s campaign took $10,000 from Miller’s leadership PAC in 2025. According to campaign finance records as of July 31, he has not returned the donation. Republican candidate for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy’s website still shows Miller’s endorsement.
Voters in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District have had mixed reactions to the allegations.
Victoria Kovach, a registered Republican from Strongsville who works as a server and social worker, said she plans to vote entirely Democratic this year. She usually votes Republican in local elections, she said, but the last time she voted in a federal race was for Hillary Clinton in 2016.
Her elderly father, her friends, and her 20-year-old son’s friends have all heard about the allegations, she said. Her father, who she said voted for Trump, supported Moreno and Husted’s calls for Miller to drop out of the race and resign.
“I know they’re allegations, but those are some pretty serious allegations — enough to ruin your name,” she said. “That’s not what we need to represent our county, which is why I feel like you have Republicans out here who are going to vote Democratic.”
Poindexter is running as a listener. But whom will he listen to?
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Even though they don’t always see eye to eye on policy, Kleem said Poindexter will always hear him out. Poindexter emphasizes a commitment to strong constituent services when speaking to voters, promising to hold quarterly town halls and establish congressional offices throughout the district if elected.
“The [U.S.] House of Representatives is supposed to be made up of people who are representative of the people they serve,” he said. “I do that better than my opponent. I do that better than anybody else who has run for this district in quite a long time.”
He also brings his own ideas, like phasing in universal healthcare by first lowering the minimum age to qualify for Medicare to 55. He supports regulations on data centers, opposes increased military spending for the war in Iran, and doesn’t hide his support for reproductive rights and LGBTQ+ rights.
When asked what legislation he would support on his first day in office, he immediately said the Protecting the Right to Organize Act. Reintroduced in 2025, it would give more power to unions and weaken right-to-work laws. He has also said he would support Moreno’s push to lift the cap on the amount of annual income subject to the payroll tax that funds Social Security.
Some of his more progressive stances may be appealing to Democratic voters in a primary, but Kleem warned that they could alienate Republicans and independents in a general election.
His campaign does not accept corporate PAC money, and personal financial disclosures show that he does not hold stock investments. An outside group with corporate ties is supporting him: Jobs and Democracy PAC, a super PAC in favor of artificial intelligence regulation backed by AI company Anthropic, spent over $512,000 on advertising for Poindexter before the primary.
Poindexter has said he doesn’t know why the Anthropic-backed super PAC is supporting him. Miller has accepted campaign donations from a wide variety of corporate interests, including the Haslam family, Pfizer, John Deere, and more.
“I don’t have to be pro-labor, folks. I am labor,” Poindexter said in a speech at the North Shore AFL-CIO headquarters in July. “My friends, my family — I would not be able to look them in the eye if I went to Washington and forgot where I came from.”
Eileen Velasquez said she listens to the news on the radio in between caring for her grandchildren and shuttling guests from the Best Western in Brook Park to the Cleveland Airport. She doesn’t vote because whether Republican or Democratic, “the rich get richer,” she added.
Her food stamps to feed her family were cut by $175 around three months ago, and she criticized Trump for his attacks on immigrants. But instead of leaning toward one party or another, she simply listens.
“Politicians promise you gold, but they give you copper,” she said.
Neither Kovach nor Velasquez had heard of Poindexter when interviewed, and both said they had little hope that the Democratic Party could offer significant change. A poll conducted by Tavern Research in early August found that 35% of voters in the district were not familiar with Poindexter’s name.
Kleem said that faith cannot be won back in the few months before an election. As he finds his political lane, Poindexter could find himself being pulled in different directions if the people endorsing him have different perspectives, Kleem added.
“At some point, he’s got to find himself,” Kleem said. “The Brian I know is not Bernie Sanders, and he’s not anyone else. He’s Brian Poindexter. He’s a working man … I believe he is the kind that, if he was in a position to take on his own party, I think he would.”

title: Copperwood mine critics raise pollution, tourism concerns as board approves $50M in funding
description: Following several attempts to move ahead with a grant supporting a mining project in the Western Upper Peninsula, members of the Michigan Strategic Fund Board gave the grants a go-ahead, utilizing funds previously approved by state lawmakers. Board members voted Tuesday to approve two grants to support site readiness for the Copperwood Mine in Wakefield […]
text:
Public commenters lined up out the door to speak against a $50 million grant supporting the Copperwood Mine project in the Western Upper Peninsula under consideration by the Michigan Strategic Fund Board on Aug. 25 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Following several attempts to move ahead with a grant supporting a mining project in the Western Upper Peninsula, members of the Michigan Strategic Fund Board gave the grants a go-ahead, utilizing funds previously approved by state lawmakers.
Board members voted Tuesday to approve two grants to support site readiness for the Copperwood Mine in Wakefield and Ironwood Townships, voting 7-2 to approve $44.9 million for Copperwood Resources Inc., and 9-0 for a $5 million grant to the Gogebic County Road Commission. A memorandum on the project says the funds will be used to improve infrastructure in the region, including investments in roads, energy and telecommunications.
While members of the strategic fund board previously approved a $50 million grant for the project in 2024, the funds were never appropriated by the Michigan Legislature, despite several efforts to include the money within the state budget. 
Ahead of Tuesday’s meeting, Michelle Grinnell, the chief communications and attractions officer at the Michigan Economic Development Corporation told reporters that the funds used for the requested grants were appropriated to the strategic fund through a 2022 budget supplemental, which included $50 million for site readiness work. 
Because the Legislature has already transferred the funding, it doesn’t require any additional approval to disburse the funds after the board’s vote, Grinnell explained.
Michelle Grinnell, chief communications and attraction officer for the Michigan Economic Development Corporation discusses a $50 million site readiness grant for benefitting the Copperwood Mine under consideration at the Michigan Strategic Fund Board during its meeting on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Lawmakers and the head of the Michigan Economic Development Corporation have touted the project as an economic boon for the western U.P., with state Rep. Greg Markannen (R-Hancock) noting in public comment that the region had lost several major employers in recent decades, including the White Pine Mine, the Ontonagon Paper Mill and the Waupaca Foundry in Ironwood. 
While Reps. Dave Prestin (R-Cedar River), Karl Bohnak (R-Deerton), Parker Fairbairn (R-Harbor Springs) and Cam Cavitt (R-Cheboygan) and state Sen. Ed McBroom (R-Vulcan) spoke up in support of the project, the individuals who followed them in the in-person comment period were broadly in opposition to the project. 
Map of the area around the Copperwood Mine | DNR
They shared personal stories of trips to the Porcupine Mountains, discussed the legacy of mining pollution in the region and questioned the economic value the mine’s operator, the British Columbia-based Highland Copper, said the mine would bring to the region. 
According to the project memo, the Copperwood Mine is expected to create 380 jobs, operating for approximately 11 years, though Highland Copper CEO Barry O’Shea told the board they anticipate the operating period will be “well in excess” of that amount of time.
Bryan Mitchell of Novi noted that the Michigan Economic Development Corporation is responsible for the Pure Michigan advertising campaign, which aims to draw tourists by promoting the state’s natural features.
State Rep. Greg Markannen (R-Hancock) speaks in favor of a $50 million site readiness grant for the Copperwood Mine during the Michigan Strategic Fund Board’s meeting on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
“By considering $50 million in Michigan taxpayer subsidies for a short-term, 11-year foreign – yes, foreign mining operation – this fund is suffering from financial split personality,” Mitchell said. “Public funds have been used for 20 years to build a world-class tourism brand on one hand, while simultaneously considering funding a foreign corporation to degrade that very asset that makes that brand valuable.”
Emily Smith, the land and conservation policy manager for the Michigan Environmental Council, raised concerns with the mine’s proximity to Lake Superior and Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park, noting that if the dam holding the mine’s tailings were to collapse, the waste would flow into Lake Superior. 
Prior to the vote, O’Shea told the members of the strategic fund board that the grant was incredibly important to the company. 
“I think it sets a path for the broader financing, and without it will certainly be challenging,” O’Shea said.
Following the board’s decision to approve the grant funding, O’Shea said the vote represented an important milestone in the company’s efforts to secure financing for the mine, with the company also receiving a letter of interest from Export-Import Bank of the United States for $250 million in potential debt financing.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Les Wexner stepping down as chair of Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center Board
description: Central Ohio billionaire Les Wexner is stepping down as chair of the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center Board after continued scrutiny over his relationship with the late convicted child sex offender and disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Wexner, 88, will remain on the board as chair emeritus, but he is no longer a voting member, […]
text:
The Ohio State University Medical Center was renamed the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center in 2012. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Central Ohio billionaire Les Wexner is stepping down as chair of the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center Board after continued scrutiny over his relationship with the late convicted child sex offender and disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Wexner, 88, will remain on the board as chair emeritus, but he is no longer a voting member, university spokesperson Ben Johnson said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Les Wexner has stepped back from his role as chair …. Les and Abigail have been great supporters of the university for many years, and we appreciate his ongoing service on the committee,” Johnson said in a statement. 
The Ohio State University Medical Center was renamed the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center in 2012. Wexner was appointed chair in 2013, but has not been at a board meeting since May 2025. 
A spokesperson for Wexner declined to comment. 
Robert Schottenstein will likely replace Wexner’s place as chair, according to a resolution set to be approved at the Sept. 1 meeting. 
“New board chairs always refresh the committee structure and appointments,” Johnson said in a statement. 
Schottenstein is the chief executive officer and president of Columbus-based M/I Homes, Inc. He was a trustee of Ohio State University from 2005-2014 and served as chairman of the board from 2012-2014. 
Schottenstein did not respond to a request for comment by the Ohio Capital Journal. 
Wexner and Epstein
Wexner, the billionaire founder of L Brands who lives in New Albany, was deposed by members of Congress in February about his relationship with Epstein. 
Wexner was listed as an alleged co-conspirator of Epstein’s in a 2019 FBI document. The same document listing Wexner as a co-conspirator says there is “limited evidence of his involvement.”
U.S. House Democrats accused Wexner of facilitating Epstein’s alleged sex trafficking ring. Wexner has denied any wrongdoing. 
Epstein — who died by suicide in a New York jail 2019 after being arrested on federal sex trafficking charges — was Wexner’s personal financial adviser from 1987 to 2007, during which time Epstein reportedly misappropriated millions of dollars. 
Wexner graduated from Ohio State in 1959 and went on to found L Brands in 1963, which created Victoria’s Secret, Bath & Body Works, and Abercrombie & Fitch. Schottenstein previously served as a member of the board of L Brands. 
Wexner previously served on the Ohio State University Board of Trustees, including as the chairman, and was also a founding member of The Ohio State University Foundation. 
Les and his wife Abigail Wexner, and the Limited Brands Foundation, have given, raised or pledged more than $200 million, Johnson said. 
Ohio State University has received 500 requests to remove Wexner’s name from university buildings, which remain under consideration, Johnson said. 
The name requests are not related to Wexner stepping down as chair, Johnson said. 
In addition to the Wexner Medical Center, Wexner’s name is on two other buildings at Ohio State. 
The Wexner Center for the Arts is named after Les’ late father Harry Wexner. 
Wexner’s name is on the Les Wexner Football Complex at the Woody Hayes Athletic Center.

title: Data center debate exposes Ohio’s uneven energy landscape
description: In the battle over data center siting in Ohio, one of the flashpoints is how data centers impact electricity prices. Data centers are indeed energy-intensive and the worry about their impact on local energy prices has moved most developers to work to get their energy generated in behind-the-meter projects that don’t draw from the electrical […]
text:
An aerial view shows a data center situated near single-family homes. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)In the battle over data center siting in Ohio, one of the flashpoints is how data centers impact electricity prices. 
Data centers are indeed energy-intensive and the worry about their impact on local energy prices has moved most developers to work to get their energy generated in behind-the-meter projects that don’t draw from the electrical grid.
So if you are a data center developer, what kind of power are you going to put behind the meter?
Looking at the top sources of power in the United States, you can whittle the options down pretty quickly. 
Coal, once the heavyweight for energy in the United States, has seen its economics turn against itself and the United States has only begun construction on one coal-fired power plant in the past 13 years. 
For all the talk of small modular reactors, nuclear power is still not viable in Ohio due to the massive up-front costs and decades of regulatory hurdles to clear. 
Hydropower and geothermal power demand specific topographic conditions, and biomass has economies of scale that don’t make it competitive with other technologies.
This leaves developers with three choices: solar, wind, and natural gas.
The state has put its thumb on the scale when it comes to choosing between these technologies. A range of state decisions have made siting solar, wind, and natural gas projects very different from one another.
Solar and natural gas projects over 50 megawatts must be approved by the Ohio Power Siting Board. For reference, this would be large enough to power all the homes in Canton with a little bit of energy left over. 
Wind projects, on the other hand, only need to be 5 megawatts to face Ohio Power Siting Board scrutiny. That is only enough to power about half the homes in Athens.
The state has also given considerable latitude to county governments to ban solar and wind projects in unincorporated areas, a barrier gas-powered plants do not have to overcome. 
For projects that are not outright banned, two local representatives get a vote on Siting Board decisions for wind and solar projects, a requirement not faced by natural gas projects.
Solar and wind projects also face a regime of siting rules that do not apply to gas plants. 
Solar facilities face specified setbacks, landscaping, fencing, stormwater, noise, and vegetation requirements. Wind facilities face turbine setbacks and shadow-flicker, ice-throw, blade-failure, communications-interference, noise, and aviation requirements. 
Solar and wind projects also face decommissioning planning requirements that gas-powered plants are not subject to.
Gas-powered plants do have one requirement that solar and wind projects do not: they must submit a range of operational air-quality analyses. This makes sense to a certain extent given solar and wind generation is emissions-free.
In an ideal world, technologies can compete against each other on a level playing field. 
If there are specific costs associated with outcomes like public health, environmental sustainability, or even aesthetics, these can be captured through fees and taxes specifically designed to internalize these costs into the market. 
Creating separate regulatory regimes for different technologies, on the other hand, makes legislators the arbiters of technological superiority rather than the market.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Judge expresses concerns, delays ruling in challenge to redistricting amendment
description: The Anne Arundel County Circuit Court judge overseeing a legal challenge to a proposed constitutional amendment on redistricting said Tuesday there are a "couple things that trouble me about this case," raising hopes of Republicans who brought the lawsuit.
text:
Del. Matt Morgan (R-St. Mary's) (left) and other Republicans expressed optimism at the end of a day-long hearing challenging a proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution setting standards on congressional redistricting. Morgan, chair of the Maryland Freedom Caucus, is a plaintiff in the lawsuit along with Del. Ryan Nawrocki (R-Baltimore County) and Mike Howell (right), president of the conservative Oversight Project. (Photo Bryan P. Sears Maryland Matters) The Anne Arundel County Circuit Court judge overseeing a legal challenge to a proposed constitutional amendment on redistricting said Tuesday there are a “couple things that trouble me about this case.”
The comments by Circuit Judge Robert J. Thompson came at the end of a daylong hearing of a Republican lawsuit challenging the amendment, passed earlier this month in a special legislative session and slated to go to voters in November. Thompson said he originally planned to have a ruling by Tuesday, but instead said he would rule by Wednesday afternoon.
“There are a couple things that trouble me about this case,” Thompson said before adjourning for the day. “In particular, when all of this lawmaking authority, at least statutory lawmaking authority, rests in one branch of the government, and that branch of the government wants to do something that its own laws that it enacted don’t allow or don’t make easy to do, you can just say, ‘Well, you know, we won’t follow those laws.’
“That doesn’t seem right to me because I know that the legislature, that branch of government that has that authority, also has the ability to repeal laws, amend laws, carve out exceptions in laws,” he said.
The comments left Republicans hopeful and Democrats characterizing his ruling as a jump ball at this point.
Thompson was appointed to the bench by Republican former Gov. Larry Hogan in 2018. Prior to the hearing, he disclosed in open court he had “an association” with two of the plaintiffs in the case — Dels. Brian Chisholm (R-Anne Arundel) and Kathy Szeliga (R-Baltimore County), saying he had spoken with both after Hogan appointed him to the bench.
Judge rejects request to move redistricting lawsuit from Dorchester County

“I don’t believe it creates a conflict,” Thompson said as he opened the hearing, and attorneys for both sides declined to raise concerns about the disclosure in open court.
The case filed in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court is one of two legal challenges to House Bill 2100, a proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that could go to voters in November.
A second lawsuit, filed in Dorchester County, has yet to be scheduled for a hearing.
Both cases are expected to head to the Supreme Court of Maryland. Election officials are staring at a deadline of Aug. 31 to certify the roughly 1,200 ballot variations that will be presented to voters across the state Nov. 3.
Maryland State Election Administrator Jared DeMarinis welcomed what he saw as Thompson “understanding the urgency” for a ruling so the appeals process can begin.
“We just want some clarity … so that we can meet all the certification deadlines and make sure that the mail-in ballots go out in a timely fashion,” DeMarinis said. “In the end, voters have to be informed and vote.”
DeMarinis declined to speculate on how Thompson might rule.
“I’ll let the lawyers and the other prognosticators take that one there,” he said. “My job is to create the ballot and make sure that the voters have choices, and that’s what I’m going to do.”
The proposed amendment at the center of the case would nullify a 2022 ruling by Judge Lynne Battaglia that struck down a proposed 2021 congressional map.
Battaglia applied a portion of the state constitution that requires districts be compact, contiguous and mindful of jurisdictional and geographic boundaries — language that had always been applied to legislative districts, not congressional districts.



Quotation







When all of this lawmaking authority ... rests in one branch of the government, and that branch of the government wants to do something that its own laws that it enacted don't allow or don't make easy to do, you can just say, 'Well, you know, we won't follow those laws.' That doesn't seem right to me.


– Anne Arundel County Circuit Court Judge Robert J. Thompson


It was considered a novel ruling. And while not considered a binding legal precedent, the ruling was not appealed. Instead, lawmakers compromised on a revised map that favors Democrats in seven of the state’s eight congressional districts, instead of in all eight as the original plan would have done.
The proposed constitutional amendment would ask voters to approve a change that would make clear that compact and contiguous requirements apply only to state legislative districts.
Republicans see the change as the first step in a process that could result in new maps as early as next year. That map would eliminate the last Maryland Republican member of Congress, Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st), as Democrats seek to join in a flurry of hyperpartisan midcycle redistricting, sparked by President Donald Trump, as states jockey to retain control of Congress in the midterm elections.
The challenge heard by Thompson — mounted by members of the ultraconservative Maryland Freedom Caucus and leaders of the Senate Republican Caucus — primarily focuses on a law passed last year that sets a July 1 deadline for ballot questions to be presented to voters with public comment. The bill passed in special session skirts that deadline.
“All of our constituents’ due process rights were violated,” Del. Ryan Nawrocki (R-Baltimore County), a plaintiff in the case, said outside the courthouse Tuesday afternoon. “All of Marylanders’ due process rights were violated in this process. The legislature can’t make rules for thee and not apply them to me, and that is what this case is fundamentally about. And we are all cautiously optimistic that that is what the judge is going to decide tomorrow.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Maryland Republicans were joined by Oversight Project President Mike Howell, another plaintiff in the case. Jeffrey B. Clark, a former Trump White House official, served as lead attorney Tuesday, arguing the case before Thompson.
“The governor of Maryland and the General Assembly are well within their rights to make mistakes and terrible policy all day long,” Howell told reporters outside the courthouse. “But what they can’t do is just run roughshod over the very rules that they lay out just not too long ago. That’s what this case comes down to: Are there rules, and does the General Assembly have to obey them?”
Clark, who is now vice president of litigation for the Oversight Project, was indicted in connection to Donald Trump’s attempts to overturn the election results in Georgia in 2020. Trump pardoned Clark last year. The case in Georgia was later dropped.
“You have the former acting attorney general of the United States, one of the nation’s leading legal experts, standing up for the rights of Marylanders,” Howell of Clark. “He’s exactly where he needs to be. We have an embarrassment of riches at the Oversight Project with our legal team, and you know, standing behind me are many more lawyers that assisted on this, along with you know my fellow plaintiffs in the Maryland legislature and Senate. And so Jeff Clark makes the case all that much more clear.”
Del. Kris Fair (D-Frederick), a House leader in the effort to pass the amendment, criticized Republicans for bringing Clark in on the lawsuit. He called Clark “infamous” for trying to “overturn a lawful election” in Georgia.
“He’s then coming here to Maryland to try to block the right of Maryland voters just to be able to vote on the issue themselves,” Fair said.
The bill — which included a mandated question for the ballot —passed with the support of Democratic lawmakers who hold supermajorities in both chambers and included a “notwithstanding” amendment supporters said allowed them to bypass those requirements.
U.S. Supreme Court lifts pause on Trump mail-ballot order

Thompson also seemed to express concerns about how the supermajority wields power in the legislature.
“These are the same people who want to set the law aside, who are constantly telling us how we’re a nation of laws. We need to follow the law. We all need to have this fidelity to the law,” Thompson said. “And then when they want something they can’t get in the ordinary way, they want to toss the law out. Doesn’t make a lot of sense to me.”
Republican and Democratic lawmakers in the packed courtroom attempted to read between the lines of Thompson’s closing remarks.
“I’m cautiously optimistic that he saw things the way we saw things as legislators,” said Senate Minority Leader Sen. Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore), a plaintiff in the case.
Fair said he was neither “hopeful or forlorn” as the day ended without a decision from Thompson.
“Obviously, he had some concerns, so I think it’s going to be an interesting ruling tomorrow (Wednesday),” Fair said. “I’m not sure which way it’s going to go.”
When asked if he thought the decision was still a “jump ball,” Fair said “that’s a safe assumption, to think that it could be a toss-up.”
Fair criticized Republicans for attempting to prevent the matter from going to voters.
“Why are the Republicans this scared of the voters of the state of Maryland? Why are they that nervous to bring this issue forward and allow the voters of the state of Maryland to tell us instead of lecturing them?” Fair told reporters.
Del. Matt Morgan (R-St. Mary’s), chair of the Maryland Freedom Caucus and a plaintiff in the case, had a response for Fair.
“They (Democrats) could have avoided this whole situation by following the process that they set up,” Morgan told reporters. “Instead, they come out with this amendment a half-hour before the committee hearing, and it’s supposed to exempt them from all the laws. The General Assembly has to abide by the law. That’s what we’re just asking for.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A speed camera would not have saved him
description: In Fairfield, when we invoke a specific tragedy to justify a specific tool, it's fair to ask whether that tool would have touched that tragedy's cause.
text:
A man was killed on his bicycle Friday night, August 14, in New Haven, at Howard Avenue and Second Street. He was 53. The driver hit him and kept going.
I keep looking at the photo of that intersection. Wide, freshly striped crosswalks. Clear lane markings. A 25 mph sign right on the pole. New Haven has done more of the walkability work than almost any city in Connecticut, and a man still died there, because someone hit him at 11 at night and drove away.

Emily Hau

I’m asking this honestly, not rhetorically: what municipal planning would have prevented this one? Not paint. Not a sign. Probably not a camera that mails a ticket weeks later.
To be clear, I’m not claiming a camera failed here. There was no camera at this corner, and nobody should pretend one would have mattered. A hit-and-run at 11 at night by a driver who kept going is not the crash any of these tools is built to stop. That’s exactly the point.
Every tool prevents the crashes it’s built for. Enforcement against impaired and distracted driving targets impaired and distracted drivers. Road design that slows traffic targets speed. Cameras target one thing: sober drivers speeding past a known camera location. All of these can be worth doing. But here in Fairfield, when we invoke a specific tragedy to justify a specific tool, it’s fair to ask whether that tool would have touched that tragedy’s cause. If it wouldn’t, the tragedy deserves better than to be used as the sales pitch.
That’s not an argument against safety. It’s an argument for honesty about which tool does what. The people we’ve lost deserve remedies aimed at what actually killed them.
Emily Hau is a Fairfield resident and a candidate for State Representative in the 132nd District.  emilyforfairfield.com

description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma Republicans have chosen Robert Franklin as their nominee for the state’s top education office. text:
Republican state superintendent candidate Robert Franklin speaks at a campaign event in Edmond on Aug. 3. He won the GOP nomination for the post in a runoff election Tuesday against fellow Republican James Taylor. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma Republicans have chosen Robert Franklin as their nominee for the state’s top education office.
He defeated James Taylor 54.5% to 45.5% in Tuesday’s GOP runoff for state superintendent, a position that leads the Oklahoma State Department of Education and the state’s top school board. Franklin now advances to the Nov. 3 General Election where he will face Democrat Jennettie Marshall.
Franklin, 66, of Sand Springs, has been a special education teacher, longtime school and CareerTech administrator, and an inductee in the Oklahoma Educators Hall of Fame. He said his decades of experience in educational leadership would be an asset to the state Education Department and the Oklahoma State Board of Education.
He also pledged to collaborate with higher education institutions, tribal nations, state government leaders and local school districts to find solutions to Oklahoma’s yearslong teacher shortage. Putting more counselors and behavioral health specialists in schools to curb discipline issues has been another key piece of his campaign platform.

When reached by phone Tuesday night, Franklin said his victory indicates voters wanted a candidate less like former state Superintendent Ryan Walters, a far-right-wing firebrand, and more like the current, more moderate officeholder, Lindel Fields.
“They said if perhaps we can put a seasoned, tested educational leader in there, much like Lindel Fields has demonstrated, then we can take the toxicity out of things, take the divisiveness out of things and get to the work at hand, and then we can start to see results,” Franklin said. “I think people saw that, and then are saying, ‘I would like to see more of that, please.’” 
Taylor, 67, of Oklahoma City, is a U.S. history and government teacher at Little Axe High School. He leads First Christ’s Church of Norman as the founding pastor.
James Taylor, a Republican candidate for state superintendent, sits in the sanctuary of First Christ’s Church of Norman on July 24. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
He wrote in a social media post Tuesday night that he and his wife, Raphala, “exit this race with zero regrets.”
Taylor declined through a campaign spokesman to comment to Oklahoma Voice.
On the campaign trail, Taylor said he would demand academic excellence in Oklahoma’s struggling public schools and would promote parent empowerment.
Both men were among the last candidates to jump into the state superintendent race before they emerged as the top two vote earners in the June 16 primary election.
Franklin entered the race shortly before the April candidate filing window and ended up in the lead of the crowded Republican primary field. Educators across the state have widely embraced Franklin by endorsing him in droves, donating to his campaign and participating in door-knocking events.
He now advances to the General Election with a crucial GOP nomination. Republicans currently hold all statewide elected offices in Oklahoma, and voters have chosen the GOP candidate for state superintendent in every General Election since 2010.

OKLAHOMA CITY —Oklahoma’s state Constitution will now include voter identification requirements. 
With nearly 55% support in Tuesday’s election, voters approved State Question 846. 
The state question posed by lawmakers asked voters to amend the state Constitution to require voter identification and give the Legislature the ability to enact laws later to specify ID requirements. 
State law already required one of three forms of identification, but supporters said it was important to enshrine the requirement into the Constitution.

Critics of the measure said it would give lawmakers greater authority over Oklahoma election law and could, even unintentionally, allow for the Legislature to pass stricter identification requirements that could disenfranchise Oklahomans. 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, and Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, authored the legislation that placed SQ846 on Tuesday’s ballot. 
Paxton previously said the measure was needed to ensure future lawmakers didn’t remove voter ID requirements without a vote of the people.
