name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Demuth plans to cut $1 billion from Minnesota’s budget, refrains from denouncing tariffs
description: Republican nominee for governor Lisa Demuth said that if elected in November, she would direct her administration to “find $1 billion in savings across all agencies,” in an effort to make life more affordable for Minnesotans, but she refrained from denouncing the Trump administration’s burgeoning trade war with Canada that’s expected to drive up costs. […]
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth and her running mate Ryan Wilson announced their affordability plan at the Minnesota Capitol on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)Republican nominee for governor Lisa Demuth said that if elected in November, she would direct her administration to “find $1 billion in savings across all agencies,” in an effort to make life more affordable for Minnesotans, but she refrained from denouncing the Trump administration’s burgeoning trade war with Canada that’s expected to drive up costs.
Demuth on Tuesday released an affordability agenda, which largely focused on rooting out fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs. Demuth argued fraud is driving up costs for Minnesotans via higher taxes. Republicans this year are hoping Minnesotans’ anger with the fraud that occurred under the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party’s watch will break their 20-year losing streak in statewide races.
“Minnesota has become unaffordable for many families, and fraud is a big part of that,” Demuth said at a Capitol press conference. “How many extra hours did a parent have to work so that the government could tax them, not to cover the costs of a strong economy or strong schools, but actually to feed fraudsters tax dollars?”
The $1 billion in savings Demuth hopes to find amounts to about 1.5% of the state’s current $66 billion, two-year general fund budget.
Demuth will also face voters — for whom cost of living is a primary concern — who have soured on her party’s management of the economy. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran have driven up costs of everything from gasoline to ground beef. Congressional Republicans also allowed special tax credits for health insurance to lapse, causing the number of people insured via the Affordable Care Act marketplace to drop in 49 states.
Demuth declined to criticize Trump directly Tuesday.
Demuth’s affordability plan includes cutting the income tax rate for the state’s lowest earners, eliminating the state tax on Social Security benefits and capping all car tab fees at $99.
It’s unclear exactly how Demuth plans to cut $1 billion across dozens of state agencies, but she cited the hundreds of millions lost to fraud. She also said that the state government has “plenty that we can trim back,” including cutting full-time employees.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the DFL nominee for governor, has her own affordability plans, including spurring construction of 100,000 new homes to push down housing prices and a state tax credit for healthcare premiums if Congress again declines to act.
A pressing issue for Minnesota is also Trump’s tariff war with Canada — Minnesota’s largest trading partner. In 2025, Minnesota exported $5.6 billion in goods to Canada, or 24% of the state’s total exports.
A new study from the Midwest Economic Policy Institute found that Trump’s 2025 tariffs increased costs in Minnesota by about $1,000 per household. But that impact was not felt evenly, with the burden falling most acutely on lower income households.
Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs as high as 50% on hundreds of American products as trade talks collapsed between the two countries. The move came after the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian goods Saturday.
Demuth didn’t criticize Trump’s tariffs when asked about them.
“Tariffs definitely have a purpose, but I think the talks need to continue or restart again,” Demuth said.
Klobuchar has long opposed Trump’s tariffs and sponsored a bill in the U.S. Senate to overturn the tariffs on Canada.
“The new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by Canada’s decision to retaliate, will only make it harder for Minnesota businesses and farmers to compete and will further drive up prices,” Klobuchar said in a statement.
Demuth’s plan would also allow school boards and local governments to opt out of participating in the state’s paid leave program, which grants nearly all Minnesota workers up to 12 weeks of family leave and 12 weeks of medical leave per year, capped at 20 weeks in a single year.
Demuth said granting this opt-out would reduce costs for counties and school districts, which would then keep property taxes affordable.
In a telling moment of GOP acceptance of the popular paid leave program, Demuth said that as governor she would not seek to repeal the program but implement changes to “make it more workable.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Canton and Madison County schools anticipate millions of dollars from Amazon data center fees
description: Kimberly Campbell, second left, with ninth graders in the Principles of Biomedical Science class she teaches at Rosa Scott High School on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026, in Madison. The school district stands to receive millions of dollars from data centers. District leadership want to put that money toward career and technical education and building improvements.
text:
CANTON — Fees from new data centers in Madison County could generate millions of dollars for area public schools starting in January.
Canton and Madison County schools officials say they plan to earmark the money for building improvements and investing in career and technical education. County leaders say the money could be “transformational,” allowing the schools to update their campuses, attract quality educators and offer innovative courses to students.
That transformation is happening amid concerns about traffic and pollution around the data centers, and their water and energy use.
Amazon aims to build 34 data centers in Madison County over the next two years, said Joey Deason, executive director of the Madison County Economic Development Authority. Five are operating and another five are expected to go online this year. The $25 billion project is the biggest capital investment in the state’s history. 
To incentivize Amazon to bring the project to Mississippi, state leaders and county officials worked out a deal for the company to pay discounted fees — a third of what they’d typically owe in property taxes — for the first 10 years of each data centers’ operations over a 30-year term.
Starting in January, Amazon will start paying fees for the first five centers, which are located in Canton. Half of the money — about $14 million — would go toward paying off a loan the county took out to improve infrastructure around the data center project. The other half would be split between community colleges, the city of Ridgeland, Madison County and the county’s public schools. 
And as more data centers crop up around the country and in Mississippi, additional school districts could receive more money from fees data center owners have to pay. 
The Jaguar mascot graphic at the front entrance of Rosa Scott High School, located at 929 Poore’s Pass in Madison, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. Madison County Schools and the Canton district anticipate getting millions of dollars from data centers operating in the county.  Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The county tax collector will give Amazon’s fees to the county board of supervisors, who will then give Canton Public School District its share. The district is projected to receive over $7 million in a lump sum during the first quarter of 2027. The annual payments steadily increase to $17 million in 2029. 
Once the fee agreement ends, Amazon will pay full property taxes for each of their data centers. By 2038, Canton schools could receive upwards of $35 million annually. That’s about half of the district’s budget for the current school year. 
Similarly, Madison County Schools is projected to receive a $7 million annual payment during the first quarter of 2028. The district is getting its share a year later because the Ridgeland data centers began operating a year after Canton’s. The district’s allotment could go up to an annual $33 million payment by 2039. For context, Madison County school district officials approved a $204 million budget this year. 
“These schools have got an opportunity that they’ve never had before to think outside of the box,” Deason said. 
The amount of money the school districts will receive is not yet certain. Amazon Web Services recently challenged the Madison County tax assessor’s valuation of its five data centers in Canton claiming that the county’s assessment is too high, which could result in millions of dollars less for county government and schools. The tax assessor valued each data center at $292 million, but Amazon said each building is only worth $69 million. The Madison County Board of Aldermen upheld the tax assessor’s valuation, but the company could appeal the decision to the courts and could challenge the valuation again in coming years.
Investing in CTE, teachers, buildings
Austin Brown, Madison County Schools’ new superintendent as of July 1, saw the projections for how much money the data centers would bring into his district on his first day. 
“I said, ‘I think I’m gonna retire,’” he recalled. “My day couldn’t get any better, you know? What a blessing.”
Brown said he can’t make promises about how the district will spend the money, but he knows where he’d like to start. 
District leadership is interested in increasing teacher salaries. The state is facing a teacher shortage, and increasing the district’s local supplement could help Madison County Schools stay competitive, Brown said.
Schools in other states have used money from local data centers to boost teacher pay.
Madison County Schools is also renovating several buildings. Brown said he’d like to use the money to continue those efforts. 
“What you’re seeing is basically the first phase of dedicated, intentional upgrades of our facilities,” he said. 
A ninth grade student views organisms through a microscope in Principles of Biomedical Science class at Rosa Scott High School, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026, in Madison. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
A substantial amount of the money could go toward a new career and technical education building. 
“Ultimately, we are going to use it in a way that will provide the right kind of experiences for our students to prepare them for what’s next,” Brown said. “There are no limitations on what we can do.”
Read more of Mississippi Today’s reporting on data centers
Canton’s interim superintendent, Dwight Luckett, has similar plans. Luckett, despite his temporary position, has created a five-year strategic plan that hints at his priorities for the money: Recruiting highly trained teachers, boosting student achievement, focusing on career and technical education and providing students with state-of-the-art facilities. 
He said the district’s central office, for example, is at least 80 years old and needs to be upgraded. Luckett also said district leaders might consider raising teacher pay the next school year and paying off debts they’ve accumulated.
“Those dollars will definitely, first and foremost, be used in the classroom,” he said. Luckett previously served as the district’s superintendent from 2006 until 2014. “There is also a tremendous need for some capital improvements.”
Luckett said he’d also like to see the dollars go toward creating classes focused on science, technology, engineering and math — or STEM.
His interest in career and technical education is in line with a push from the Mississippi Department of Education and state lawmakers to better prepare students for the workforce and bolster the state’s economy. 
Dwight Luckett, superintendent of the Canton Public School District, speaks during an announcement about an Amazon data center in Ridgeland on Thursday, April 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I’d like to see … additional teachers,” Luckett said. “So putting money around those that can come in and really help get us our own program … That’s really good for workforce development.”
Data center tradeoffs
Sen. Bradford Blackmon, a Democrat from Canton, said the infusion of money could be impactful to a district like Canton.
He’s also met with Canton residents who complain about traffic, dust and pollution from the data center site. He knows there are trade-offs. 
“You just have to take the good with the bad because it’s there,” he said. “It’s not going anywhere at the moment or anytime soon.”
Deason said construction at the site stirs up dust. The construction will eventually end, but meanwhile, Amazon and the Madison County Economic Development Authority offered to pay for car washes, humidifiers and house cleaners, Deason said.
“This is a part of growing, a part of getting bigger,” Deason said. “It is what it is.”
Blackmon hopes that despite residents’ concerns, the money could help Canton schools retain teachers, attract talent and offer more to their students. 
“School districts drive communities,” he said. “If the district is good, people would think about making this their home. This type of money is transformational for Canton.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Second Amendment groups weigh in on Bryan Avila’s selection as Byron Donalds’ running mate
description: Byron Donalds’ selection of state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate was received with strong enthusiasm by the Florida Republican establishment, but one group expressed concern. That would be the group Florida Gun Rights, which noted that while serving in the Florida House in 2018, Avila voted for gun-safety legislation following the mass shooting […]
text:
At least one gun-rights group is upset Republican Byron Donalds has chosen state Sen. Bryan Ávila as his running mate in the governor's race. (Photo by Aristide Economopoulos/New Jersey Monitor)Byron Donalds’ selection of state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate was received with strong enthusiasm by the Florida Republican establishment, but one group expressed concern.
That would be the group Florida Gun Rights, which noted that while serving in the Florida House in 2018, Avila voted for gun-safety legislation following the mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland that killed 17 people.
The measure raised the minimum age to buy a rifle or long gun from 18 to 21; banned bump stocks; required a three-day waiting period for gun purchases; and created risk protection orders that allow a judge to temporarily block a person from buying or possessing firearms and ammunition if they pose a significant danger to themselves or others.
Donalds himself has touted his Second Amendment bona fides on the campaign trail and boasts about his vote to oppose the 2018 gunsafety law. The measure was pushed by Florida Gov. Rick Scott and passed just weeks after the school shooting with a mixture of Republican and Democratic votes. The House vote was 67-50.
Of the 76 House Republicans who voted, 57 favored the bill and 19 were opposed. Among the Democrats, 10 voted yes and 31 no. The Democratic House Caucus took a position against the measure because it also allowed for armed educational personnel in schools.
“Very concerning Bryan Avila voted for the largest piece of gun control in Florida history when he was in the state house,” Florida Gun Rights posted on X. “We need to repeal the Parkland gun control not promote its supporters.”
However, another Second Amendment organization says it isn’t bothered by Avila’s vote, because the man at the top of the ticket has vowed to repeal the Parkland measure if elected governor in November.
“Bryan Avila voted for Parkland, but the Governor sets policy, not the Lieutenant Governor,” said Luis Valdes, Florida director of Gun Owners of America, in a text message.
“With Donalds, CFO Blaise Ingoglia, and AG James Uthmeier all opposed to Parkland gun control, three of Florida’s four statewide officers are now aligned against it. GOA expect Donalds to keep his word and repeal Parkland.”
The Phoenix reached out to the Donalds campaign to confirm whether he wants to repeal the Parkland law, but received no immediate response.
Avila did support legislation (HB 543) in 2023 that allow residents to legally carry concealed weapons without having to obtain a permit through the state, a measure supporters called “permitless carry.”
The consensus otherwise from Florida Republicans is that Avila is solid.
“Byron Donalds made a great choice in Bryan Avila,” Ingoglia said in a written statement. “Together, they have the experience, energy, and vision to keep Florida moving in the right direction. I look forward to supporting them and helping deliver a victory for Republicans this November.”
“Congressman @ByronDonalds, you made an incredible choice in @BryanAvilaFL as your running mate,” Florida Senate President Ben Albritton said on X. “He’s a trusted Senator, a great Floridian and an exceptional human being!”
“Senator Avila is a good dude,” declared Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. “I’ve always appreciated his service in the National Guard.”

name: WyoFile
title: Beefing over foreign beef plan, Barrasso breaks with the Trump administration
description:
Wyoming stockgrowers and others also question the president’s plan to waive tariffs on overseas meat in an effort to drive down prices at the supermarket.
The post Beefing over foreign beef plan, Barrasso breaks with the Trump administration appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming cattle ranchers and a sitting senator representing the nation’s most pro-Trump state are pushing back on the president’s plan to import tariff-free foreign beef from unidentified countries in hopes of reducing costs for American grocery shoppers. 
Let out of the chute Friday, the Trump administration’s plan would allow more than 660 million pounds of ground beef to enter the United States over the next 90 days. All that beef could be sold at 25% below market rate. Stockgrowers and conservative rural-state Republicans quickly condemned the market intervention, warning it would harm western ranchers. On Monday, U.S. Sen. John Barrasso joined the fray. 
“Americans want US beef on the table — not foreign imports,” Wyoming’s senior senator posted on social media. “Our ranchers don’t ask for special treatment. They simply want a fair marketplace. It needs to be easier — not harder — for Wyoming ranchers to feed America.” 

U.S. Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyoming, speaks to an audience before the antler auction begins at Elk Fest in Jackson May 20, 2023. (Natalie Behring/WyoFile)

Barrasso’s office did not respond Tuesday to WyoFile’s request for an interview. 
Barrasso’s rebuke marks one of the very few occasions that the senator from Casper has publicly opposed a Trump administration position. The Senate majority whip — the second highest-ranking Republican in the upper chamber — has been in office since 2007 and is typically in lockstep with the president. 
A physician by training, Barrasso told Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in Sept. 2025 that he was “deeply concerned” by the Trump appointee’s vaccine policies. And in November that year, the state’s senior senator also went on record in opposition to Trump’s demands that the U.S. Senate abolish the filibuster — a position he’s held consistently over the years. 
Now this week’s rare beef is the latest well-publicized Trump-Barrasso policy disagreement. 
Some of Barrasso’s cattle-raising constituents are equally concerned about the president’s plans.
“During this time of drought and high-input costs, this does make a setback to the market,” Wyoming Stock Growers Association President Reg Phillips told WyoFile on Tuesday. “It hurts the producers, so that’s not a good feeling.” 
Mark Teichert, standing, manager of the Wyoming Hereford Ranch near Cheyenne and Bill Shain, a veterinarian, preparing to release a Red angus bull after drawing a blood sample on April 13, 2004. (AP Photo/Robert W. Black, File)
The Crook County Cattle Women also have expressed skepticism about the president’s plans. WyoFile’s efforts to interview the group’s board members weren’t immediately successful on Tuesday, but they questioned the president’s efforts on their Facebook page.
“Who is this ‘they’ that sets beef prices? Packers? Feeders? Walmart?” the cattlewomen posted. “How are ‘they’ going to sell foreign beef for 25% less than American beef? I thought country of origin labeling was just impossible.” 
The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association has also criticized the president’s plans. 
“Today’s announcement and other market interventions throw cold water on the prospect of herd expansion and sacrifices long-term stability for short term messaging,” Colin Woodall, the trade group’s CEO, said in a statement Friday.
It remains unclear where the balance of Wyoming’s Congressional delegation stands on Trump’s beef import plans. Neither U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis nor U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman has made any public remarks about Trump’s plans and WyoFile’s inquiries with their offices on Tuesday did not yield a response before publication.
Cattle graze along the Green River near Green River Lakes on Aug. 22, 2026. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Other western Republican senators also have bellowed about the plans.  
“Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand,” Sen. Deb Fischer, a Nebraska Republican, said in a statement.
Montana Republican Sen. Tim Sheehy wrote on social media that the president’s “heart is in the right place,” but importing beef will “harm our ranching families who feed the nation.” And Sen. Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, said that while he appreciates the administration’s focus on grocery prices, “short term policy shifts do not equal long term solutions.” 
When pressed by reporters, Trump did not reveal which country or countries the 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef would be coming from. 
In the wake of a New York Times investigation that found wild horses — including from Wyoming — are being quickly transferred to buyers who are trucking them into Canada to be slaughtered, conspiracy theories and internet jokes have run rampant. 
What exactly is that discounted mystery meat Americans are about to eat?  
—The Associated Press contributed to this story

title: North Dakota approves loans for carbon capture at coal plant
description: The North Dakota Industrial Commission on Tuesday approved $205 million in loans for a project that aims to capture carbon emissions from a coal-fired power plant.  Minnkota Power Cooperative recently partnered with Reliant Carbon Capture & Storage to operate the carbon capture and CO2 delivery system.  The companies will split the loans, $45 million for […]
text:
The North Dakota Industrial Commission hears about Project Tundra on Aug. 25, 2026. 
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Industrial Commission on Tuesday approved $205 million in loans for a project that aims to capture carbon emissions from a coal-fired power plant. 
Minnkota Power Cooperative recently partnered with Reliant Carbon Capture & Storage to operate the carbon capture and CO2 delivery system. 
The companies will split the loans, $45 million for Minnkota and $160 million for Reliant, which will be issued through the state-owned Bank of North Dakota. 
Electric co-op adds partner to renew pursuit of carbon capture at North Dakota coal plant

The money will be used at Minnkota’s Milton R. Young Station near Center in Oliver County, which sits on top of an area geologically suited for permanent underground storage. Minnkota has already secured permits for the underground storage.
Grand Forks-based Minnkota has been working on a carbon capture plan known as Project Tundra since 2015.
Some differences from the earlier version of Project Tundra include Reliant providing its experience and technical expertise on carbon capture and a smaller project cost.
Kelvin Hullet, chief public affairs officer at the Bank of North Dakota, said Reliant has experience working with coal plants. Reliant uses cooling to turn carbon dioxide from a gas into a more liquid form. 
“The science has gotten better, the technology has gotten better,” since early versions of the project, said Gov. Kelly Armstrong, who chairs the three-member Industrial Commission.
Bank of North Dakota Chief Public Affairs Officer Kelvin Hullet answers a question from Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring during a meeting of the North Dakota Industrial Commission on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
Hullet noted the cost estimate for Project Tundra has shrunk from about $3 billion. The project is now estimated to cost about $1.7 billion.
The project also puts more emphasis on the potential for using CO2 in North Dakota’s oil fields, pumping the gas underground to make oil wells more productive.
Federal policy previously offered a smaller tax credit for CO2 used in enhanced oil recovery than for permanent storage. That credit is now the same — $85 per ton of CO2. 
Project Tundra aims to capture about 5 million tons of carbon per year, worth $425 million in tax credits annually.  
The loan application letter from the companies says they are engaged with partnership discussions with oil companies that would use the CO2. 
The application says any pipeline needed to get CO2 to an oil field site would be funded separately. 
State officials have said enhanced oil recovery could extend the life of oil wells and generate more oil and gas tax revenue. 
The Industrial Commission oversees North Dakota’s Clean Sustainable Energy Authority, which last week recommended approving the loans. The authority had previously set aside $250 million in loans for Project Tundra but had not recommended that the Industrial Commission approve grant the loans. 
Minnkota said in a recent news release announcing its partnership with Reliant that it would make a decision on whether to proceed with Project Tundra in 2027.  The 2% loan offer expires after a year. 
The requested payback period is 12 years, but the specific loan terms will be negotiated with the Bank of North Dakota. 
State Sen. Dale Patten, R-Watford City, co-chairs the Clean Sustainable Energy Authority and is a retired banker. 
“I think the risk to the state for loss on these is extremely low,” Patten said, pointing to the size of the assets controlled by Minnkota and Reliant and the potential revenue from the project.
In a presentation last week to the Clean Sustainable Energy Authority, company officials said the project would cut carbon emissions at the power plant by 95%, would create about 350 jobs and would mean no increase in utility bills. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

description: A former Southern Poverty Law Center executive pleaded not guilty Tuesday to conspiracy charges of wire fraud and making false statements as part of the U.S. Department of Justice’s prosecution of the civil rights nonprofit. text:
The headquarters of the Southern Poverty Law Center in Montgomery, Alabama on February 8, 2023. Heidi Beirich, the former director of a covert program that paid confidential informants embedded with white supremacy groups, pleaded not guilty Tuesday to charges brought by the U.S. Department of Justice. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)A former Southern Poverty Law Center executive pleaded not guilty Tuesday to conspiracy charges of wire fraud and making false statements as part of the U.S. Department of Justice’s prosecution of the civil rights nonprofit.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Kelly F. Pate announced that Heidi Beirich, director of the Intelligence Project for SPLC, would plead not guilty during the arraignment Tuesday afternoon, held over videoconference. Beirich did not appear on the teleconference; her attorneys stood in for her.
DOJ charged SPLC in April with 11 counts of fraud over a paid informant system the organization began in the early 1980s to gather information on and disrupt the activities of white supremacist and extremist groups. DOJ alleges that the payments to the informants amounted to fraud on donors to the SPLC, citing the use of shell companies to pay them.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
SPLC says the now-terminated program saved lives and that information gathered was shared with law enforcement, and has accused the Trump administration of prosecuting it for political purposes. The organization said the use of shell companies was essential to protecting the identities of its informants.
Beirich, who supervised the program from 2012 to 2019, was added as a defendant in a case two weeks ago after the federal government filed a superseding indictment that increased the number of charges to 14.
SPLC pleaded not guilty to all 14 counts and has requested the court impose additional rules pertaining to jury selection.
Pate scheduled the trial to begin on the same date as the trial for the SPLC on Oct. 5. However, Michael Proctor, Beirich’s attorney, said due to personal obligations he will not be ready for trial by that date and plans to request a trial start date in late January.
Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Middle District of Alabama Kevin P. Davidson agreed to provide the evidence in the case for the purpose of discovery. The parties anticipate there would be pretrial motions in the case.

title: Longtime corrections officer appointed to WV House following Pritt’s arrest for alleged sex crimes
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Tuesday appointed William “Bill” Vest of Oak Hill, West Virginia, to fill the House of Delegates seat previously held by Del. Elliott Pritt, who was indicted last week on three federal charges, including the alleged sexual exploitation of a child. Vest, a longtime correctional officer for the state, will serve in […]
text:
The West Virginia House of Delegates chamber. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Tuesday appointed William “Bill” Vest of Oak Hill, West Virginia, to fill the House of Delegates seat previously held by Del. Elliott Pritt, who was indicted last week on three federal charges, including the alleged sexual exploitation of a child.
Vest, a longtime correctional officer for the state, will serve in the House for the remainder of Pritt’s term, which ends in January. 
Pritt was first elected as a Democrat to the House in 2022. He switched to the Republican Party in 2023.
He resigned from his House seat last month following his arrest, which stemmed from a federal investigation into alleged sex crimes against a minor. Pritt was initially running for reelection to the seat, which represents Fayette County, but withdrew his name from the ballot earlier this month.
Pritt, a teacher by trade, was arrested on July 22 after the family of a 15-year-old female reported to law enforcement that the child was sexually abused by Pritt. According to a criminal complaint, Pritt, 36, allegedly began communicating with the girl when she was in eighth grade in 2024 through the online game Roblox, then later on Snapchat.
Pritt also allegedly sent sexually explicit photos of himself and requested that the girl send nude photos of herself through Snapchat in 2025 and 2026. Pritt later initiated a physical relationship with the minor and requested that she meet him in his classroom at Oak Hill High School to engage in sexual activity at least five to 10 times, per the criminal complaint.
The grand jury federally indicted him on three charges last week: coercion and enticement of a child, sexual exploitation of a child and tampering with a witness, victim or informant.
Following Pritt’s arrest, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle called for Pritt’s resignation. They urged Morrisey to call a special session to commence impeachment proceedings. Days later — shortly after he appeared in front of a federal magistrate judge and waived his right to preliminary and detention hearings — Pritt sent a one-line resignation letter to House Speaker Roger Hanshaw.
The Fayette County Board of Education previously suspended and terminated Pritt’s employment.
Pritt did not have a challenger in May’s primary election and was set to appear on the November general election ballot. Due to a relatively new law, the state Republican Party is likely unable to fill the vacancy left by Pritt’s withdrawal on the general election ballot. The Democratic challenger in the race is Matthew Anderson, a special education teacher in Fayette County. 
Morrisey said in a news release Tuesday that Vest “brings an extensive background in law enforcement, state corrections administration, and community leadership” to the statehouse and that he “understands the values of hard work and accountability.”
“He will be a strong, reliable voice for his constituents, and I am confident he will serve with distinction in Charleston,” Morrisey continued.
Per the news release, Vest spent more than 30 years working in the West Virginia corrections system before his retirement in 2022. During his tenure, he served as deputy warden and associate warden of security at Mount Olive Correctional Complex and as the acting administrator and superintendent of the Beckley Correctional Center.
He also previously worked as a military police officer and a hospital security officer.
In the spring, Vest ran for a seat on the Fayette County Republican Executive Committee. He initially lost that race, but officially contested the results to the Fayette County Commission. Vest argued that dozens of votes were cast in the closed Republican primary by non-Republican voters, and that the number of votes cast in the specific executive committee race did skew the results. May’s primary election marked the first time in decades that only registered Republicans could vote in Republican primaries across the state.
In July, the Fayette County Commission invalidated the results of the executive committee race after reviewing the evidence brought by Vest. The position and all three candidates running for it, including Vest, will appear again on the November general election ballot for eligible residents to vote on.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Alleged synagogue arsonist will undergo psych exam, federal judge rules
description: A security guard walks outside the Beth Israel Congregation synagogue in Jackson on Monday, Jan. 12, 2026, two days after a fire that investigators determined was intentionally set.
text:
A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Madison County man accused of setting fire to Mississippi’s largest synagogue early this year will undergo a psychiatric examination. 
U.S. Magistrate Judge LaKeysha Greer Isaac granted a request from Stephen Spencer Pittman’s attorney, who wrote in a sparsely worded court filing last week that he believed Pittman is suffering from a mental illness. 
“As such, the defense counsel believes this undefined mental disease makes the defendant unable to understand the nature of the proceedings against him or participate in possible plea negotiations,” Mike Scott, a federal public defender, wrote in the Aug. 20 motion. 
Pittman, who usually goes by his middle name, has remained in jail since his arrest hours after the fire in the predawn hours of Jan. 10. He was swiftly indicted on state and federal charges after investigators said he broke into the Beth Israel Congregation synagogue in northeast Jackson, doused the lobby in gasoline and set it on fire. Security camera footage showed a person splashing a liquid inside the building’s lobby shortly before a fire ignited.
In state court, Pittman is facing an enhanced first-degree arson charge under a Mississippi law punishing “offenses committed for discriminatory reasons.” He has not been charged with a federal hate crime. But in February, federal prosecutors obtained a superseding indictment against Pittman, accusing him of targeting the historic synagogue “because of the religious character of the property.” 
In an affidavit, an FBI agent in the Jackson division wrote that Pittman laughed as he confessed to his father and referred to the congregation as the “synagogue of Satan.”
Pittman comes from an affluent suburb of Mississippi’s capital city and attended a private Catholic school, where he was a multiyear honor roll student and varsity baseball player. But his friends and family noticed a change in his behavior in the months leading up to his alleged arson attack, according to court testimony and interviews conducted by Mississippi Today. 
Weeks before the fire, Pittman allegedly began making antisemitic statements and behaving in such a way that the “family pets were afraid” of him and his mother was considering “locking their bedroom doors at night,” according to testimony from an FBI agent earlier this year. 
The fire reduced the historic synagogue’s library and administrative offices to charred ruins and left smoke damage throughout the building, the same one the Ku Klux Klan bombed in 1967 for its rabbi’s support of civil rights.

name: VTDigger
title: Abuse claimants fight Vermont Catholic Church plan to sell Rice Memorial High to supporters
description:
The state’s largest religious denomination, now in bankruptcy court, wants to save the school in South Burlington from potential liquidation by privately offering it for $4.3 million — 14% of the campus’s $30.5 million appraised value.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Abuse claimants fight Vermont Catholic Church plan to sell Rice Memorial High to supporte[...]
text:
The grade 9-12 Rice Memorial High School in South Burlington. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Creditors in the Vermont Roman Catholic Diocese’s Chapter 11 financial reorganization case are fighting a church plan to sell Rice Memorial High School to supporters to protect the grade 9-12 South Burlington campus from potential liquidation.
In a U.S. Bankruptcy Court filing Monday, lawyers for a creditors’ committee that represents more than 100 clergy abuse claimants questioned the proposed $4.3 million price tag for Rice’s 42-classroom building and 27 acres of athletic fields, parking areas and wetlands. The figure is only 14% of the $30.5 million value reported in a recent church-commissioned appraisal.
“The proposed sale is a functional insider transaction,” the claimants’ counsel wrote in the filing. “The diocese did not list the property. It did not retain a broker. It did not solicit a single competing offer. It contractually promised the buyer that it would not do so. And it now asks the court to bless the result as ‘the highest and best offer,’ a characterization that is true only in the trivial sense that it is the sole offer the diocese permitted itself to receive.”
The creditors’ committee wants the court to limit any sale to a public offering in hopes of raising more money for clergy abuse settlements.
“If the purchaser’s offer is truly the best available, a competitive process will confirm it and the purchaser will prevail,” attorneys wrote. “If it is not, the (diocese), and the over 100 survivors of childhood sexual abuse who are the principal creditors in this case, will have been spared a substantial and irreversible loss.”
Judge Heather Cooper is scheduled to consider the issue at a hearing in Burlington on Sept. 1.
The creditors’ filing comes a month after the state’s largest religious denomination asked the court to approve a private sale of the 400-student campus to a nonprofit entity of supporters identifying themselves only as RMHS Inc.

READ MORE

“Significant concern exists that a fully public sale process would severely and negatively impact student enrollment at RMHS, which the purchaser indicated would force it to reduce and potentially withdraw its offer,” church lawyers wrote in their request. “Additionally, the diocese will not be required to make commission payments to any brokers or agents, increasing the net proceeds available for the bankruptcy estate.”
The diocese filed for Chapter 11 protection in the fall of 2024, arguing that a past series of nearly 70 priest misconduct settlements had reduced its bank-and-building holdings by half — to about $35 million — with more than 100 other abuse claims dating as far back as 1950 yet to be resolved.
As part of the process, the church has received court and creditor permission to publicly sell a few of its properties, including its South Burlington headquarters for $3.13 million and Rutland’s former Loretto Home senior living facility for $1 million. 
Behind the scenes, the diocese has spent the past year discussing a Rice sale with unnamed “dedicated donors,” who initially offered $2 million before increasing the total to $4.3 million after negotiations, according to court records.
“The proposal is intended to preserve Rice’s Catholic identity while providing a strong foundation for future generations,” Christina DeGraff-Murphy, chair of the Rice School Board, said in a statement to VTDigger. “Because this matter remains subject to ongoing legal proceedings, we are limited in our ability to comment further at this time.”
Rice began in 1917 as Cathedral High School in downtown Burlington before moving to a new name and its current South Burlington location in 1959, according to its online history.
Rice is one of three Catholic high schools in Vermont, alongside Mount St. Joseph Academy in Rutland and St. Michael School in Brattleboro. The diocese hasn’t announced any plans for the latter two institutions or its 10 schools for elementary and middle grades.
The potential sale comes as attorneys for the church and clergy abuse claimants are in mediation over who should have access to an estimated $500 million in other local parish properties and possessions that were placed in trusts in 2006. Under federal law, both the court and creditors must approve any Chapter 11 reorganization plan.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa groups ramp up campaigns for and against data centers
description: For 45 years, Hugh Espey worked with Iowa communities in opposition to large scale livestock operations and pipelines. Now as concern toward data centers mounts, Espey said he sees parallels to the previous fights. Espey is retired from Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement, or ICCI, but continues to serve as an adviser for the group, […]
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)For 45 years, Hugh Espey worked with Iowa communities in opposition to large scale livestock operations and pipelines. Now as concern toward data centers mounts, Espey said he sees parallels to the previous fights.
Espey is retired from Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement, or ICCI, but continues to serve as an adviser for the group, which is one of several Iowa organizations that recently launched initiatives raising concerns about data centers. 
The messaging around data center projects, Espey said, is about the “wave of the future,” which he said was the same rhetoric he heard in the 1990s about what he calls “hog factories.” 
“This is never going to stop,” Espey said. “There’s always going to be some corporate powerhouse coming to us, dressed up real nice and smiling, trying to sell us something. And we have to step back and judge those things based on history and where we want to go.” 
Citizen, environmental and economic groups have launched community tool kits, initiatives and outreach to help communities respond to data center proposals, which spark concerns around resource usage, disruption and pollution. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Already, Iowa has more than 100 data centers, either in operation, planned or under construction, with the largest “hub” of data centers in the Des Moines area, according to an economic impact study released by the Technology Association of Iowa. 
The study found that data centers already in operation have an economic impact of $1.6 billion in value added annually, and more than 9,000 jobs. If all of the planned centers became operational, the study estimates the annual value added would top $3.2 billion and account for more than 18,000 jobs. 
Brian Waller, president of the Technology Association of Iowa, said data centers in Iowa do more than run artificial intelligence chatbots. Many of them, he said, help to house the secure information and digital infrastructure necessary for Iowa business, across industries, to operate. 
Waller said community concerns around land use, utility costs and long-term impacts are “legitimate” but he also said data centers are likely going to bring “billions and billions of dollars of investment” in the next decade and communities should have an “honest dialogue of what that looks like.”
“There is a legitimate conversation to be had that in the right community, under the right circumstances, there could be an economic benefit to a data center,” Waller said. “Not to all communities, but there could be, and that is a conversation too that needs to be had that  sometimes gets drowned out.”
Parallels and lessons learned 
ICCI and the Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter held inaugural data center community meetings in August and both noted the seemingly rapid, and sometimes “sneaky,” development of data centers as a friction point with communities.
Espey said the same was true of large-scale animal housing buildouts. When he started working with communities to oppose the projects in the 1990s, there were just a “few hundred” such operations in the state. A recent analysis from the Environmental Working Group estimates Iowa has more than 15,000 animal feeding operations. 
While animal manure is not the sole cause of the high nutrient levels in Iowa’s waterways, it is a contributing factor. Espey said now that Iowa faces what many call a water quality crisis and cancer crisis, it raises the question of if expanding animal feeding operations was the “right path forward.” 
“So that’s why we’re saying, ‘Whoa, whoa!’ Let’s just slow things up; let’s just put a pause,” Espey said. “And what we’ve been saying is that counties and towns should pass moratoriums.” 
Water use was a big concern voiced by those attending ICCI and Sierra Club meetings, likely because large data centers, in order to cool their systems, can use about the same amount of water daily as a small town. 
But many data centers utilize closed-loop cooling systems that recycle water and therefore consume considerably less. Waller said when it comes to water usage, the conversation needs to be more “holistic” and look at other industries, like car washes and food processing, which also use large amounts of water, usually without a system to reuse the water. 
“If we’re going to talk about the water quality, let’s look at every industry and the usage of water,” Waller said. 
Data center growth drives locals to fight for more say

According to ICCI documentation, more than 25 Iowa counties and at least six cities have passed some form of data center moratorium. 
To some degree, Espey said, it seems like communities have learned from past infrastructure projects they have fought and are more prepared to oppose a data center and the “constant” narrative from the industry. 
“I think folks have been through these battles, there’s the hog factory battle, there’s the crude oil pipeline, the Dakota Access battle, there’s the CO2 pipeline, and then this,” Espey said. “ … We have to be just as good about driving our narrative and then organizing thousands and thousands of people.” 
He also said it seems easier for Iowans to be opposed to a data center because “big tech” feels like an outsider to Iowa, especially when compared to the agricultural industry that pushed for large-scale animal ag operations. 
“I think there’s more grassroots pushback because it’s coming from quote unquote outsiders with a lot of money,” Espey said. 
Supporting economic development 
Iowa has data centers from some of the largest names in tech — Google, Microsoft and Meta all have data centers in the Hawkeye state. But Waller said there’s also a lot of small, locally owned, data centers in the state that are critical digital infrastructure for retailers, healthcare providers and schools. 
Waller said when he started at the Technology Association of Iowa 13 years ago, he would walk into businesses in Iowa and they would have rooms with “racks and racks and racks” of servers that held “highly secure, sensitive data for their businesses.”
Now when he walks in, there’s considerably fewer racks because most of that data is being stored in a digital environment — or in a “cloud,”  which he said “is data centers.” Cybersecurity, blockchain technology, artificial intelligence and data mining are all “emerging technologies” he said are run through data centers. 
“Digital infrastructure is what is driving all of our lives right now in the state of Iowa and data centers are just a piece of that,” Waller said.
Several unions, trade councils, economic development alliances and businesses recently joined to form Growing Iowa’s Economy, a coalition to “promote the responsible development of new data centers.” 
In a news release the coalition said it would advocate for policies that would help establish Iowa as “a leading state for technology and innovation.” According to the release, the development of new data centers could bring investments of tens of billions of dollars to the state, millions in local property taxes and create tens of thousands of “high-quality jobs.” The release said a hyperscale data center is expected to require up to 7,000 construction jobs. 
“This level of job creation is absolutely essential to ensure working Iowans in every region of the state have access to the types of economic opportunities that can effectively address the affordability concerns that are so pressing right now,” Andy Roberts, president of the Iowa State Building and Construction Trades Council, said in the release. 
The coalition said its “guiding principles” will require data center operators to pay for energy use and necessary infrastructure upgrades, with continued oversight from the Iowa Utilities Commission. The coalition also said data center operators should “reflect Iowa values” and be a community partner, minimize local impact and respect the quality of life of communities. 
Dan Culhane, president and CEO of the Ames Regional Economic Alliance, said “responsible and regulated” development of data centers will strengthen Iowa’s economy and deliver economic opportunities to residents. 
“In the coming years, tens of billions of dollars will be spent developing data centers in the United States, and when those dollars are invested here in Iowa, it will help support meaningful, long-term economic growth in communities of all sizes across our state,” Culhane said. 
What are Iowans worried about? 
Espey said when factory farms were proposed, opposing Iowans’ first concern was “the stench” associated with a large animal confinement operation. When it comes to data centers, community members are worried about it stressing resources. 
“The major concerns about the data centers are they gobble up our water, they gobble up our energy, they gobble up our tax dollars, they gobble up our farmland,” Espey said. “They just feel like they can come in and do anything they want.” 
Espey said a lot of the data center moratoriums that have cropped up have been “organic” – county boards of supervisors passed them without any sort of outside influence or direction from groups like ICCI. 
Espey said ICCI is recommending counties pass moratoriums on data centers, or ordinances that cap the size of the projects. For example, he said counties could cap the square footage, or the water usage of data centers permitted in the jurisdiction. Or, he suggested counties require data centers run on their own renewable energy.
“And then also say no tax dollars, no tax incentives whatsoever,” Espey said. “ … They’re billion dollar and trillion dollar corporations, why are we giving them tax dollars? Why are we subsidizing them either with sales tax exemptions or property tax exemptions.” 
Size is also a concern raised by Iowans at data center meetings. Jess Mazour, conservation coordinator with Iowa chapter of Sierra Club encouraged participants at the August meeting to “drive by a data center” to fully understand the scale of the projects.



  A video edited and published on behalf of “Save Morgan Valley” a group opposing a proposed gas plant and data centers in Iowa, shows construction of the QTS data center being built in Cedar Rapids. 
Both of Iowa’s gubernatorial candidates have also suggested ending, or limiting state tax incentives for data centers. 
Waller said economic development incentives in Iowa have gone to “a lot of other major employers” in the state, not just data centers. 
“States are competitive through economic development; this is just another industry that’s popping up right now, and it’s really up to the communities,” Waller said. 
Espey said he feels the data center issue is “cutting across political viewpoints.” 
“Data centers will be, we think, a prominent issue at the 2027 legislative session, and one reason why we’re organizing now to kind of build a statewide people power pushback,” Espey said.
The Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club is compiling data center information and examples of county ordinances on its website. ICCI plans to host monthly meetings for members interested in the data center issue and has scheduled several in-person informational meetings around the state to talk about the issue. 
The Hubbell Environmental Law Initiative, or HELI, at the University of Iowa recently launched an “intentionally neutral” data center decision tool to help communities evaluate data center proposals and identify key questions to ask before proposals are approved. 
The Technology Association of Iowa is hosting the Iowa Digital Infrastructure Summit Sept. 29 in Des Moines for a “statewide conversation on the infrastructure powering Iowa’s digital economy.”

title: Active court order still blocking Trump effort to restrict vote-by-mail
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday handed a procedural victory to President Donald Trump on an executive order to curb mail-in voting, but the administration is still fighting a separate ruling that limits a portion of the order and remains in effect — complicating the administration’s temporary win. In light of the ruling in the nation’s highest court, the administration late Monday asked U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts to vacate her decision from earlier in August that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out aspects of Trump’s executive order, while the voting rights groups that brought that challenge argued Tuesday the block should remain in place.Monday’s decision from the Supreme Court also drew the ire of Democrats, who argued that Trump’s executive order ran afoul of the Constitution and threatens democracy. Under the Constitution, states are responsible for administering elections. Many Democrats have said Trump’s order seeks to unlawfully grab that power for the executive branch.The Supreme Court’s ruling halted a June decision from Talwani in a case brought by more than 20 Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C. But that ruling does not apply in a separate case, filed in the same Massachusetts federal court, by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and several other voting rights groups challenging Trump’s executive order. In its emergency motion in the voting rights groups case, the administration wrote that “the Supreme Court’s order leaves no room for any further dispute: this Court lacked jurisdiction to issue the preliminary-injunction in this case, just as it lacked jurisdiction to enter summary judgment in the (states’) case, because there is no justiciable controversy over a proposed rule until it is actually finalized by an agency.”  Final rule publishedFurther complicating the matter, the U.S. Postal Service on Friday issued a final rule that details how the agency would execute Trump’s order. The voting rights groups on Saturday asked Talwani to enforce her August order as a result of the Postal Service issuing the regulation. Regarding that request, Talwani on Tuesday afternoon said the rule violated her order because she specifically said the administration could not take steps to implement the executive order. However, she declined to take action “other than identifying the violation.”The groups redoubled their request earlier Tuesday, writing that the Supreme Court’s decision was based on the lack of a USPS final rule.“That decision addressed a materially different record and did not consider the critical development that occurred last Friday: The USPS Defendants promulgated a Final Rule, transforming the posture of this case and supplying a final agency action that was not before the Supreme Court,” they wrote.Talwani’s order on the administration's request was still pending Tuesday afternoon.Democratic blowbackMeanwhile, Democrats were quick to blast the Supreme Court’s decision, including the top Democrats in the U.S. Senate and House. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said it’s “a disgrace that the highest court in the nation is allowing Trump to put a dagger into the heart of our democracy,” in a Monday statement. The New York Democrat noted that “Trump’s effort to turn the Postal Service into a voter suppression machine is blatantly unconstitutional – yet his MAGA Supreme Court is refusing to stop it from going forward,” while adding that “Senate Democrats will fight every attempt to hijack mail-in voting and rig the rules before voters have their say this November.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries also blasted the decision and vowed to continue fighting, saying “the sycophantic Supreme Court majority’s decision in the vote-by-mail case is sowing chaos in service to Donald Trump’s effort to undermine our free and fair elections.” Jeffries, also of New York, added that “the Trump-aligned justices on the Supreme Court did not and cannot give the President the power to decide how states run elections or who gets to vote by mail.” The respective heads of the Democratic National Committee, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Democratic Governors Association also pushed back against Trump’s executive order.  “This is the latest attempt from Trump to rig the midterms because Republicans know their corrupt, cost-hiking policies are deeply unpopular and hurting people every day,” DNC Chair Ken Martin, DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene, DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, and DGA Chair Andy Beshear said in a statement.“Democrats will not let them get away with it, and we are confident the American people will reject these Republican schemes in November,” they wrote. “We're going to fight every day until Trump's illegal executive order, and all of his other attempts to undermine our free and fair elections, are completely thrown out.” A spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, the party’s U.S. House campaign arm, did not return a message Tuesday.

title: Morrisey: 54K received school clothing allowance so far, including low-income kids who didn’t apply
description: More than 54,000 children have received school clothing allowance funds as of Monday while the Morrisey administration continues to vet applications during the school year. In a new twist in the administration’s handling of the program, some low-income children who didn’t apply for the money have now received the back-to-school financial assistance. West Vir[...]
text:
People look at back to school clothes at a Target store on August 13, 2026 in Downtown Brooklyn in New York City. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)More than 54,000 children have received school clothing allowance funds as of Monday while the Morrisey administration continues to vet applications during the school year. In a new twist in the administration’s handling of the program, some low-income children who didn’t apply for the money have now received the back-to-school financial assistance.
West Virginia’s school clothing allowance program gives low-income students $200 for new  clothes and shoes. The program launched later than expected under Gov. Patrick Morrisey, then ran out of funding after just a week. 
It is now under investigation by Morrisey after he alleged this month that parents could be using the money elsewhere. 
Students returned to school before thousands of applications were processed, frustrating lawmakers who felt the program shouldn’t have faced any disruptions when it was most needed.
A spokesperson Morrisey said 3,696 remaining children will receive their school clothing benefit no later than Aug. 29.
“Based upon those families who are in the final stages of the enrollment process, DoHS projects that it will provide the (school clothing allowance) benefit to an additional 3,696 children this school year for a total of 57,436 kids. This total exceeds the number served last year by nearly 150 children,” Ann Moore, deputy communications director for Morrisey, told West Virginia Watch.
Moore said the administration will spend $11.5 million this year on the school clothing allowance program – $100,000 more than last year. 
The state Department of Human Services also recently automatically deposited the clothing voucher benefit to children ages 4 to 10 who received it last year and met the eligibility requirements this year. 
These children were already receiving help from other federal welfare programs, including Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, but weren’t required to apply this year for school clothing assistance.
“They did not have to reapply,” Moore said. 
The state previously issued automatic school clothing assistance to eligible children during the COVID-era, but returned to required applications last year under Morrisey.
Moore didn’t respond to a question about how the 4 to 10 age range had been selected for the automatic deposit. 
West Virginia pays for the school clothing allowance through federal TANF funding. The money is meant to help low-income families safely remain with their families and avoid the foster care system. States have broad flexibility with how they spend TANF dollars. 
Morrisey has defended decisions around the long-standing clothing assistance program this year, pointing to the state’s looming deficit in TANF funds. The state has less than 13 months — $41 million — in TANF carryover funds at this point, according to Morrisey. TANF spending has increased under his administration.
While Morrisey said he was focused on making sure the federal funding was sustainable in the future, lawmakers pressed for more information about how the governor is spending the money and still have outstanding requests. 
Chris Tatum, mayor of Barboursville, West Virginia, delivers envelopes with school clothing money to Davis Creek Elementary Principal Lee Ann Porter. (Courtesy photo)
While the program and applications were under review, Barboursville Mayor Chris Tatum wanted to make sure children in his area had new clothes before heading back into classrooms.
Tatum launched a fundraiser on his Facebook page this month, quickly raising $20,000. 
“What I learned is how important that $200 actually is,” Tatum said. “That’s two or three outfits for a kid to go to school in. The need is there beyond me.”
Tatum and his daughter filled hundreds envelopes with gift cards and cash, then met families at city hall and made in-person deliveries to schools and homes across Cabell County. The mayor worked with the local schools to make sure they were reaching children in need. 
“This was just about easing the worry and taking one worry off a kid’s plate,” Tatum said. “If that made their day walking into school, that’s all this was about.”

title: Burlington looks to the state for help combating homelessness and drug use downtown
description:
Burlington city councilors approved a resolution Monday asking the governor to direct state resources toward the city. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington looks to the state for help combating homelessness and drug use downtown.
text:
Burlington Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak listens as the City Council discusses a resolution requesting more help from the state to battle homelessness, substance use disorder and the mental health crisis on Monday, August 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON— Burlington city councilors are requesting the governor take new steps to help the Queen City address homelessness and drug use downtown. 
The request from city officials comes in the form of a resolution, which Burlington city councilors approved on a voice vote Monday night with support from Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak. 
In a 10-point list, the resolution recommends ways for Gov. Phil Scott to respond to the city’s persistent struggles with homelessness and drug use. Some of the city’s requests are as broad as requesting more police support while some are as prescriptive as hiring three staff members at an inpatient care facility. 
The resolution takes no action on its own. It solely directs the mayor to bring the city’s requests to the governor. Mulvaney-Stanak said in an interview Tuesday that she is not sure when she will meet with Scott. 
The resolution is the city’s most recent attempt in a long — and at times divisive — battle to address its struggles. The debate has at times put state leaders at odds with the mayor. And recently, it’s divided Democrats and Progressives on the city council. 
The latest resolution, though, seems to keep the peace among the city’s political leadership. Ten of the council’s 12 members from both the Progressive and Democratic parties proposed the resolution and it was drafted by the Progressive mayor’s administration. 
“This is what is most urgently needed and will do the most to meaningfully advance our community health and safety goals,” Mulvaney-Stanak said Monday during her routine update to the council on city affairs. 
The mayor said that Burlington is dealing with a “trifecta of issues”: homelessness, untreated mental illness and substance use disorder. And those issues, she said, extend beyond the boundaries of the city and state. 

READ MORE

“These problems are not within the capacity of any single municipality to solve without  significant state action,” the resolution notes. 
The city’s request to the governor comes after he recently directed Vermont State Police troopers to patrol downtown Burlington without first consulting the mayor. Violent crime is down this year in the Queen City, according to its data, although a spate of violent incidents downtown earlier this month left one dead. 
“The Governor has not reviewed the pending resolution and will consider it if it is sent to him,” Jason Malucci, the governor’s director of policy development and legislative affairs, said in an email Monday, before the council’s vote.
The governor is always willing to have conversations on how to support Vermont communities, Malucci said. “It is also important for communities like Burlington to evaluate policies that they have implemented that have contributed to the current climate,” he said. 
The concerns laid out in the recent resolution are similar to those raised by Mulvaney-Stanak last September when she called on the governor to do more to help Burlington. She blamed Burlington’s struggles — in part — on Scott’s decision to allow mass evictions from  state-sponsored motel rooms last summer. 
Last year, Scott initially responded by saying he wasn’t sure what resources his administration would be willing to provide until the city increased law enforcement and cracked down on drug use. 
Scott later announced a plan to put state resources toward social services, judicial resources and policing in the Queen City for about three months. Shortly after the initiative, state officials largely praised his efforts as a success. 
During Monday’s city council meeting, Mulvaney-Stanak commended parts of the governor’s plan — but emphasized that it “omitted” addressing homelessness. 
The city’s proposed plan, she said, fills gaps that remain in the wake of the governor’s earlier interventions. 
Housing resources were at the top of the list in the resolution. 
The first request outlined in the resolution asks the governor to direct the Vermont Agency of Human Services to aid in the process of securing a location and finding staff for a 100-bed emergency shelter in Chittenden County. 
The Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity, or CVOEO, and the Champlain Housing Trust are in the process of finding a location for the proposed shelter. The organizations hope to open the shelter before this winter and operate it year-round. 
The resolution also asks the governor to direct the human services agency to support daytime spaces for unhoused people, namely CVOEO’s Community Resource Center. It also requests expediting processes and resources for “municipalities with disproportionate unhoused populations” to access state support. 
Along with housing resources, the city is requesting more statewide help with acute mental health care. 

Burlington City Councilor Sarah Carpenter, D-Ward 4, speaks as the council  discusses a resolution requesting more help from the state to battle homelessness, substance use disorder and the mental health crisis on Monday, August 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The resolution asks the Vermont Department of Health “to more strongly partner” with the city, especially to support its syringe service programs. Another request asks for four more inpatient beds and three more positions to support recovery services for inpatient care at an unspecified Vermont Department of Mental Health site in central Vermont. 
The resolution appears to refer to the Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital in Berlin, which recently cut its staff and beds. 
Naming an intention to “address the root causes of recidivism,” the city is asking for more resources to pair social services with court processes, including expanding the capacity of the county’s treatment court docket, which focuses on offering some defendants with rehabilitative alternatives to incarceration. The city also wants the state to prevent juveniles from getting involved with drugs and gun possession. 
The council also asked for coordinated state law enforcement support for city police officers cracking down on drug trafficking, traffic enforcement and retail theft. That request comes as Burlington tries to recruit more local officers and expand its police force. 
City Councilor Laura Sánchez-Parkinson, P-Ward 3, said ahead of the vote that she sees Burlington’s issues downtown as decades in the making, exacerbated by federal divestment from healthcare and housing resources. 
“This is the moment that calls for shared responsibility and coordination across the state. We cannot run from the root causes that continue to take our community in a downward spiral year after year,” she said.

title: University of Dubuque to offer master’s degree in organizational psychology
description: A new master’s program at the University of Dubuque will equip students with the training and education to lead in their future workplace and make it better through study and action. The private university announced in a news release it has received Higher Learning Commission approval for its new master of arts in industrial and […]
text:
The University of Dubuque will offer a new master's program starting this fall. (Photo courtesy of University of Dubuque)A new master’s program at the University of Dubuque will equip students with the training and education to lead in their future workplace and make it better through study and action.
The private university announced in a news release it has received Higher Learning Commission approval for its new master of arts in industrial and organizational psychology — a program created “in direct response to labor market demand in organizational effectiveness, consulting in human resources, and workplace leadership,” the release stated.
“We are grateful for the time and energy of UD’s Graduate Curriculum Committee this past academic year and for their oversight in the submission of the institution’s proposal to HLC,” said University of Dubuque associate professor of psychology Amy Baus in the release. “Receiving approval for this distinct graduate program within our tri-state community better meets a supply gap. Currently, there is no other local graduate program in the discipline of industrial and organizational psychology in Dubuque.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the release, students who graduate from the program can become “industrial and organizational practitioners,” who work to improve quality of business and work life. Baus said in the release this could mean studying employee turnover and job satisfaction indicators, addressing barriers to organizational development and the needs of employees in terms of training and skills development, and assisting management in redesigning positions and programs to provide more opportunities to employees.
Requirements to complete the program include 15 credit hours in core courses and 18 in elective areas alongside practical training, the release stated, and classes are available in online, hybrid and in-person formats. If students take two courses in each seven-week session, the program can be completed in 15 months. The first session will begin this fall.
“The master of arts in industrial and organizational psychology complements our current graduate business offerings by being one of the few programs in the region that examines how the intersection of psychology and business can help our students understand what drives people and organizations,” said Ricardo Cunningham, dean for graduate and adult studies at the University of Dubuque, in the release.

name: WyoFile
title: Judge dismisses citizens’ request for data center permit review
description:
Court says petitioners failed to demonstrate how they were adversely affected by county’s approval of Prometheus Hyperscale’s flagship project near Evanston.
The post Judge dismisses citizens’ request for data center permit review appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
EVANSTON—A formal petition requesting a judicial review of the Uinta County Commission’s issuance of a conditional use permit allowing Prometheus Hyperscale to build a data center near Evanston has been dismissed by Third District Court Judge James Kaste.
 After Uinta County commissioners voted to approve the permit, residents Christy Katzl, Wilhelm Katzl and Marijke Rossi filed a July 16 petition, citing property values, community and environmental safety concerns and a number of other allegations.
The petitioners accused county officials and developers of engaging in private and unadvertised meetings and failing to conduct and provide environmental impact studies, particularly regarding the “closed-loop” system the data center developer has said it will implement. 
Petitioners also accused county commission Chair Mark Anderson and Commissioner Eric South of nepotism in relation to approval of the project.
Uinta County Attorney Loretta Howieson Kallas, who represents the commission, filed a motion to dismiss the petition on July 24. The petitioners had 15 days to respond.
Rossi requested and filed a notice of voluntary dismissal from the petition, which Kaste approved without prejudice on Aug. 4.
On Aug. 17, the remaining petitioners were issued an order of dismissal by the judge in part because the parties did not respond to Kallas’ motion to dismiss within the time allowed by the Wyoming Rules of Appellate Procedure.
Additionally, “the Court finds that the Petitioners have failed to sufficiently allege that they are aggrieved or adversely affected … and, therefore do not have statutory standing,” Kaste’s response states.
“Petitioners make no effort to allege any specific perceptible harm different from any other person in Uinta County … and they have failed to avail themselves of the opportunity to expound upon those allegations in response to the Motion to Dismiss,” the ruling continued. “The Court can only conclude that the Petitioners do not have standing to challenge Uinta County’s decision to issue the Conditional Use Permit.” 
Uinta County Attorney Loretta Howieson Kallas and Prometheus Hyperscale founder Trenton Thornock speak at a June 16, 2026, commission meeting at the Lyman Town Hall. The Uinta County commission subsequently approved a conditional use permit for the Prometheus Hyperscale’s data center with 15 conditions. (Amanda Manchester/Uinta County Herald)
Katzl also filed a formal objection and notice of violation of the Wyoming Open Meetings Act on Aug. 4, outlining identical grievances in addition to accusations that the county failed to respond to her multiple public records requests made on July 14, July 21, July 22 and Aug. 1.
“She [Katzl] asserts that there is an active hiding of public records,” Kallas said, publicly responding directly to each of Katzl’s complaints during an Aug. 4 county commission meeting. 
Kallas said that despite Katzl’s failure to complete the appropriate request forms, the Uinta County Clerk’s office has 30 days to fulfill her records requests should it choose to proceed without the forms.
“Every citizen is asked to fill out a public records request in Uinta County,” Kallas said. “It is a formal provision that we try for equality for all citizens.”
