Who can participate: Students from Delaware public, private, parochial, independent, charter and home schools
Registration deadline: Oct. 30, 2026
Delaware state finals: Feb. 18, 2027, at the Smyrna Opera House
National finals: April 26-28, 2027, in Washington
Register: arts.delaware.gov/poetry-out-loud/pol-registration
Curriculum materials: PoetryOutLoud.org
Contact: Briana Henry, Delaware Poetry Out Loud coordinator, at briana.henry@delaware.gov

name: Delaware
title: Jennings wins temporary order blocking federal access to commercial-driver data
description: The legal fight pits immigration enforcement and highway safety against personal privacy, states’ rights and limits on federal power Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings has joined a multistate legal challenge that temporarily blocked the Trump administration from obtaining personal information on approximately 17 million commercial drivers. The case is[...]
text:
Federal officials say access to the Commercial Driver’s License Information System could help uncover licensing fraud, identify drivers who are not legally eligible to hold commercial licenses. Jennings and attorneys general from 20 other states argue the administration is attempting to take possession of state-owned records without clear legal authority. Image created with AI. 8/25/26
The legal fight pits immigration enforcement and highway safety against personal privacy, states’ rights and limits on federal power
Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings has joined a multistate legal challenge that temporarily blocked the Trump administration from obtaining personal information on approximately 17 million commercial drivers.
The case is more complicated than a straightforward fight between immigration enforcement and privacy.
Federal officials say access to the Commercial Driver’s License Information System could help uncover licensing fraud, identify drivers who are not legally eligible to hold commercial licenses and ensure states enforce national safety standards.
Jennings and attorneys general from 20 other states argue the administration is attempting to take possession of state-owned records without clear legal authority, adequate privacy protections or meaningful limits on how the information could be shared.
A federal judge concluded the states raised substantial legal objections and temporarily stopped the transfer while the case moves forward.
What the court ordered
Senior U.S. District Judge Anthony J. Trenga of the Eastern District of Virginia granted a temporary restraining order preventing the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators from turning the participating states’ records over to the U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration or other federal agencies.
The order also prevents federal officials from terminating more than $10 million in grants and contracts with the association because it has not produced the records.
The ruling is an important early victory for Jennings and the other attorneys general, but it is not a final decision declaring the administration’s actions illegal.
To obtain the temporary order, the states had to demonstrate they were likely to succeed on at least some of their claims, that releasing the information could cause irreparable harm and that temporarily blocking the transfer was in the public interest.
The court will next consider whether to issue a preliminary injunction that could keep the restrictions in place during the litigation.
“What happened here is simple: The Trump administration attempted to expose Delawareans’ sensitive personal data in an effort to extort our state,” Jennings said. “It was outrageous and illegal — I’m glad the court agreed with us that these disclosures should be halted while we are seeking an injunction.”
Her statement reflects the state’s position, although the court has not issued a final ruling on the legality of the federal demand.
What information the government wants
Congress established the Commercial Driver’s License Information System, known as CDLIS, in 1986 to prevent commercial drivers from using licenses issued by different states to conceal traffic violations or disqualifications.
The system allows states to review a CDL applicant’s licensing and driving history. It is operated by the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators, a private nonprofit organization, under an agreement with the federal government.
The records can include a driver’s name, birth date, Social Security number, driver’s license number and licensing state.
FMCSA demanded records for everyone listed in the system during the previous five years. The Department of Homeland Security issued a separate administrative subpoena seeking substantially the same information.
Federal officials reportedly intend to use the records to investigate improper CDL issuance, licensing fraud, commercial-driving schools and licenses issued to people who may not be legally eligible to receive them. The information could also be used for civil immigration enforcement.
The administration’s public-safety argument
The administration argues commercial driving is not merely a state concern.
Commercial trucks routinely cross state lines, and an improperly licensed driver in one state can pose a safety risk throughout the country. The federal government establishes national CDL standards and is responsible for reviewing whether states comply with them.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has accused the participating attorneys general of interfering with efforts to identify unqualified drivers and enforce licensing requirements.
“Every administration since 1988 has had access to this basic database,” Duffy said in a statement responding to the lawsuit.
He said the information is needed to prevent dangerous and improperly licensed drivers from operating commercial vehicles.
The federal government maintains its contract with AAMVA and federal transportation laws entitle FMCSA to obtain the information necessary to oversee state CDL programs.
That argument may resonate with people who believe states have failed to enforce immigration, employment or licensing laws consistently. If licenses were issued to people using fraudulent identities — or to applicants who were not legally eligible — the federal government has a legitimate interest in discovering those failures.
But the court questioned why FMCSA needed possession of the entire database when it has historically been able to query individual driver records.
Enforcement does not eliminate privacy concerns
Support for immigration enforcement does not automatically resolve the privacy and constitutional questions raised by the case.
A person may strongly support identifying unauthorized immigrants and fraudulent CDL holders while remaining skeptical of giving the federal government a database containing Social Security numbers and other information on millions of drivers who are not suspected of wrongdoing.
The states argue they own the records and submitted them to CDLIS for limited licensing and highway-safety purposes — not for the creation of a new federal database available for broader enforcement.
The court cited an FMCSA policy stating CDLIS records are not controlled by the agency. It also found the states were likely to succeed on claims that the wholesale demand conflicted with federal privacy and commercial-vehicle laws.
That raises a broader question about the division of authority between states and the federal government: Can an executive agency substantially expand its access to state records without Congress clearly authorizing the change?
It also raises a fundamental concern about government power. A legitimate enforcement objective does not necessarily give an agency unlimited authority to collect information on everyone in a regulated system.
Funding threat raises another concern
The administration’s alleged threat to terminate AAMVA’s federal funding strengthened the states’ argument.
Federal grants and contracts frequently include conditions. But the Constitution generally requires the federal government to provide clear notice of those conditions rather than adding major new requirements after an organization has accepted the funding.
AAMVA warned losing its federal contracts could disrupt CDLIS and interfere with states’ ability to issue or renew commercial licenses.
The judge found the states were likely to succeed on their claim that federal officials could not impose the new data-transfer requirement by threatening funding that supports the licensing system.
A possible middle ground
The competing positions can be reconciled.
The federal government has a legitimate responsibility to investigate licensing fraud, unsafe drivers, improper state practices and violations of immigration law. States should not be able to use privacy claims to shield illegal conduct or obstruct legitimate federal oversight.
But Washington also should not collect millions of Social Security numbers merely because some records might reveal violations.
A more narrowly tailored approach could allow federal investigators to search for specific individuals, examine records from states with documented compliance problems or compare limited data fields without transferring complete personal records.
Any broader access could be accompanied by rules governing which agencies may use the information, how long it may be retained, whether it may be shared and how drivers can correct inaccurate records.
Congress could also settle the matter by clearly defining federal access to CDLIS and establishing privacy safeguards.
What the decision means for Delaware
For now, the order prevents Delaware’s CDLIS records from being included in the federal transfer. It does not affect the validity of Delaware commercial licenses or prevent federal officials from conducting authorized, individualized investigations.
The case also does not determine whether CDL information may ever be used for immigration enforcement. Instead, it asks whether the administration followed the law in demanding the entire database and threatening AAMVA’s funding.
Jennings has characterized the case as another attempt by the Trump administration to obtain personal information for undisclosed or insufficiently limited purposes. The administration views it as part of a broader effort to strengthen commercial-driver enforcement and identify licenses improperly issued to unauthorized immigrants.
Both concerns deserve scrutiny.
The central question is not whether immigration and CDL laws should be enforced. It is whether the government can enforce them effectively without creating an unrestricted federal repository containing the personal information of millions of people who are not accused of violating the law.
To-go box

What happened: A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from obtaining participating states’ commercial-driver records.
What is involved: Approximately 17 million CDL records containing names, birth dates, license information and Social Security numbers.
Federal argument: The information is needed to detect licensing fraud, enforce safety standards and identify drivers who may not be legally eligible for commercial licenses.
States’ argument: The bulk demand lacks clear legal authority, privacy protections and limits on future use.
What comes next: Jennings and the multistate coalition will seek a preliminary injunction keeping the data transfer blocked while the lawsuit proceeds.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: What really happens in murder investigations? Here’s a fictional take from my experience in SC.
description: Prosecutors and law enforcement agents have enormous powers and how those powers are exercised can have life and death consequences for others and themselves. In “The Color of Death” readers and listeners witnessed up close the relationship between prosecutors and the victims of crime. It is a unique relationship forged through grief, anger, and pain. […]
text:
Trey Gowdy's book, "The Sound of Regret," is a fictional story but reflects his experiences with the criminal justice system in South Carolina. (Book cover photo courtesy of FOX News Books)Prosecutors and law enforcement agents have enormous powers and how those powers are exercised can have life and death consequences for others and themselves.
In “The Color of Death” readers and listeners witnessed up close the relationship between prosecutors and the victims of crime. It is a unique relationship forged through grief, anger, and pain.
There can be no higher calling than to speak up for those too scared, too young, too injured, or too dead to speak up for themselves. Closure is a myth. There is no closure for those victimized by violent crime.
The criminal justice part of processing victimhood does have an end point or a final disposition, but the residue lingers for the remainder of their lives. Being the victim of a violent crime or having someone you love victimized is tantamount to your own life sentence in a different kind of prison.
My mother was a victim advocate at the local district attorney’s office for part of my time at home. Her job was to keep victims and/or their families informed of all court proceedings and to seek their input as to the disposition of the case.
I vividly recall her lamenting that someone charged with a crime can pick “the best criminal defense attorney money can buy but the victim of crime is stuck the prosecutor assigned.”
That word “stuck” did in fact stick with me during my career in prosecution.
If your government is going to assign someone to litigate what could very well be the worst or even final moment of your life, you should have someone who is talented, prepared, and hard-working advocating on your behalf.
Trey Gowdy’s book, “The Sound of Regret,” is a fictional story but reflects his experiences with the criminal justice system in South Carolina. (Book cover photo courtesy of FOX News Books)
The system also requires fairness even amid being an advocate.
As the Supreme Court of the United States so aptly put it in 1935: a prosecutor is entitled to strike hard blows but not foul blows.
And this led to the sequel for “The Color of Death” which goes on sale Tuesday and is titled “The Sound of Regret.”
In this continuation of the characters from the first book, characters Belle, Bones, and Colm are facing new challenges and threats while still trying to solve the ones from yesteryear in the Upstate of South Carolina spanning from Spartanburg to Lake Jocassee.
The “Sound of Regret” is also a stand-alone psychological crime drama with its own twists, turns, and surprises. You do not have to have read “The Color of Death” to enjoy “The Sound of Regret,” but if you did read the first novel you know there were many strings left untied.
Imagine being a young man, and your choice is to spend the next couple of decades in prison or cooperate and spend the next couple of decades being labelled a “rat” or a “snitch” and looking over your shoulder for retaliation.
Those conversations are real and raw, which is why I wanted to highlight how our criminal justice system works in the real world. It’s starkly different from what is typically portrayed in movies and miniseries.
I’ve had those conversations with young men and their parents and seen the consequences, including death, firsthand.
Colm Truesdale is the prosecutor who interacts with these witnesses and informants. The young men have committed drug crimes but not crimes of violence. “The Sound of Regret” tells the real story of how our criminal justice system works — the good and the bad — and how the truth can sometimes set you free and sometimes end your life.
Colm is trying to chase a killer while also being chased himself by a ghost from his past — a ghost he cannot see because he prosecuted so many people and you never know the ones who will resort to revenge or retaliation. Hint: it’s never the ones you suspect.
Belle is in law school and embarking on two innocence projects of her own. She is trying to absolve Colm of the guilt he feels from the passing of his wife and young daughter while also trying to determine whether a serial killer in fact committed the crimes as alleged.
Bones is right at home — in the middle of the action — and bending the rules to reach his own verdicts.
After 16 years as a prosecutor in both state and federal court, these stories draw on the lessons learned and the mistakes made handling thousands of criminal cases.
While fictional, these murder mysteries could very well be real. This book certainly gives readers or listeners an authentic look at the complexities of criminal investigations and prosecutions coupled with the question hanging over many violent crimes, which is “why”?
We are all fascinated by the “why.” Why do people do what they do? What motivates them and are we wasting our time trying to understand or make sense of the unimaginable?
“The Sound of Regret” will take you on an authentic trip through what really happens during murder investigations and, as with “The Color of Death,” I am always interested in when and how the reader or listener figures out what actually happened and who did the deed.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A climate shake-up is jolting one of the most progressive cities in Mass.
description: The question is whether, in the end, it’s more of a mundane municipal reorganization or a sign of retreat in Newton, one of the state’s most climate-forward communities.
text:
THE MAYOR OF an affluent, liberal Boston suburb that has in recent years raced to reach the top of the climate policy mantle is shaking up his city’s approach to the issue.  
The question is whether, in the end, it’s more of a mundane municipal reorganization or a sign of retreat in Newton, one of the state’s most climate-forward communities.  
Marc Laredo, who assumed office as mayor of Newton earlier this year, unveiled a series of personnel and organizational moves in an email to city officials sent on August 13 and obtained by CommonWealth Beacon.  
The most jarring among them: The firing of Ann Berwick, who has worked as the city’s co-director of climate and sustainability for the past 10 years and previously served as the state’s undersecretary for energy and chair of the Department of Public Utilities, and the broader decision to shift the city’s climate division from the mayor’s office to the Department of Public Works. 
The moves, which have not previously been reported, are already generating a swirl of controversy among some in city government. And they’re a window into how the current volatile landscape around climate and energy policy is seeping into local decision making around how a municipal government should best marshal its limited resources to both fight and adapt to a warming world. 
Laredo defends the changes as ones that support his goal to “break down silos” in city government and that will ultimately “enhance” Newton’s climate efforts. 
“I do not want anyone to come away from this thinking that we are lessening in our commitment to sustainability. In fact, I think it’s quite the contrary,” he said in an interview. “We are increasing our commitment to sustainability throughout the city because we are going to deliver even more than we have been, and I expect that Newton will continue to be a leader in these efforts.” 
City Councilor Susan Albright doesn’t think the changes reflect an increased commitment to the issues and said the moves suggest the administration may be undercutting Newton’s more ambitious climate policies. 
“Let’s put it this way: It reads like a lack of understanding of the complexities of the issue,” she told CommonWealth Beacon. 
Albright, who serves on the council’s public facilities committee, said the restructuring deserves public scrutiny. She said she plans to bring up the changes and staffing needs for the city’s climate work in an upcoming council meeting and will ask Laredo or someone from his staff to appear to answer questions about the reorganization. 
At least some of the intrigue stems from the surprise nature of Laredo’s decision to let go of Berwick, who is widely respected among advocates and the utilities alike and has been a major player in the state’s climate policy.  
Laredo wrote in the email that Berwick is going to be “transitioning from her position,” seemingly insinuating an agreed upon departure or retirement — a characterization that she disputes. 
“There was no mutual decision. It was not my choice to leave,” Berwick said in a short statement, in which she also wished the team “great success.” 
Laredo praised Berwick as someone who will leave an “immense” legacy and said she “did a great job,” but that the restructuring is simply a “rethink” of how to best deliver services to residents. 
Laredo wrote in the August 13 email that a key challenge to the city’s progress on climate is that “we have not had a single organizational structure that brings these areas together into a coordinated sustainability program.” Citing climate resilience, stormwater management, and waste reduction efforts as key areas aligning with DPW’s work, he said climate policy will now be overseen by a new deputy commissioner of sustainability and administration.  
Laredo wrote that his “vision” is to establish a unified sustainability and materials management division within DPW. One arm of that division would be the climate and energy branch that Berwick currently co-leads.  
Caroline Weiss, currently the city’s climate action coordinator, will become the director of climate and energy, while Sam Nighman, Berwick’s co-director, will move into a new role as director of organizational performance, according to Laredo’s email. 
The mayor’s announcement follows the elimination of the city’s sustainability director in its public schools system earlier this year amid a budget crunch, leaving much of that work to the team now led by Weiss. Laredo, who has tried to carve out somewhat of a moderate lane, has also reshaped leadership in the city’s planning department, nominating a new director after the former director and deputy director left earlier this year. 
It’s a fraught time for climate politics and those looking to pursue a green transition as the Trump administration has rapidly pulled support at the federal level for clean technologies like offshore wind, solar, and electric vehicles. Meanwhile, Gov. Maura Healey is trying to pull off a balancing act amid soaring utility bills as she attempts to lower energy costs for Bay Staters by touting an “all of the above” agenda that embraces clean energy technologies but makes clear that natural gas is still a vital a part of the state’s energy mix.  
Newton had positioned itself at the vanguard of climate action, taking aggressive steps to rein in greenhouse gas emissions across its energy, building, and transportation sectors.  
The wealthy city of 90,000 people, with the state’s seventh-highest per capita income, is aiming to reach carbon neutrality by 2050. 
To do so, Newton officials signed a landmark agreement earlier this year with Eversource and National Grid, the state’s two largest utilities, to coordinate an ambitious transition off natural gas for heating homes.  
Berwick, buoyed by her past work dealing with the utilities, was instrumental in reaching that accord, and she and her team were just getting into its implementation phase. Albright said her departure could, as someone with “experience and gravitas in the field that National Grid and Eversource could feel very good about working with,” throw a wrench in the work executing on that agreement, especially since DPW isn’t a particularly natural fit for hammering out a broad transition off gas. 
Newton is also one of just a handful of communities to adopt stringent green building code standards, and is one of 10 in Massachusetts to pledge to go “fossil fuel free” by banning gas and oil hookups in new construction and major renovations to existing buildings.  
Plus, on top of aggressive deployments of solar energy and electric vehicle charging stations, the city’s local electricity program has in the past offered residents power that’s produced with a higher rate of renewable energy sources. 
Laredo insists that the changes do not mark any kind of retreat from that record and said that even amid all the concrete climate gains the city has made, he wants to see more results and thinks the new restructuring will yield them — a position that’s puzzling to some inside city government. 
“Planning is very good and advocacy is very important,” he said. “But if you don’t then implement, if you don’t have deliverables, if you don’t actually get things done, the planning, in some ways, becomes meaningless. You’ve got to act, and this way we’re going to do both.” 
“I don’t think anything was lacking in the current team at all,” Laredo said when asked about Newton’s status as a state leader in addressing climate issues with the city’s existing personnel and structure, adding that the new organization is “simply a way of improving” the city’s ability to both engage in planning and implementation “seamlessly.” 
As for tangible targets for the new structure, he said, “It’s a little too early for me to set specific goals,” but he added that stormwater management is a significant area of concern, there are “greater efforts” to come on trash, recycling, and composting, and he wants to keep pushing to electrify and ween off fossil fuels. 
Others involved in the city’s climate efforts aren’t sure Laredo’s changes will be particularly harmful. 
“I’m willing to trust the mayor,” said Jon Slote, vice chair of the Newton Energy Commission. 
But Albright said she still hasn’t been given a convincing answer from Laredo or his team regarding why the reorganization is necessary or why DPW is a better home for sustainability-focused work than where it currently lives in the mayor’s office.  
What might seem like a fairly innocuous city government rejiggering could trigger blowback in a community of vocal climate activism, if residents with strong views on the issue smell a trace of backtracking.  
“It was a big shock to me,” Albright said. “I called the mayor’s office and I said I really want to talk about this, and they assured me that this was the right thing to do, and that since it’s been announced, lots of people have called to congratulate us. I frankly don’t know who those people would have been because everyone I talked to was also shocked.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Attorney general race: Why would we enlist a Trump ally in our fight against Trump?
description: The most pressing issue for the next Minnesota attorney general will be the ongoing fight to force the Trump administration to govern by the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution.  When Trump’s minions were withholding evidence from state and local law enforcement in the federal killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, Attorney General […]
text:
Federal immigration officers on the scene where an officer shot a man Wednesday, Jan. 14, 2026, in north Minneapolis. (Photo by Max Nesterak/MInnesota Reformer)The most pressing issue for the next Minnesota attorney general will be the ongoing fight to force the Trump administration to govern by the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution. 
When Trump’s minions were withholding evidence from state and local law enforcement in the federal killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, Attorney General Keith Ellison and Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty sued the feds. Last month, they announced that the feds had turned over key evidence, like Good’s car. 
After prosecutors charged ICE agent Christian Castro, alleging he shot an innocent man in the leg and then lied about it, Trump’s ally Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has been holding up Castro’s extradition. Ellison again sued. 
On another front, when Trump assumed monarchical powers and levied tariffs, which has raised the price of nearly everything for American consumers, Ellison was among the attorney generals who successfully sued to stop him (though Trump is at it again on that front). 
Minnesotans have been in the fight of our lives against the Trump administration, which has to rank among the most lawless in American history. It’s gotten so bad that — as ProPublica reported recently — federal judges across the country have called Trump’s Justice Department at various times “unlawful,” “unethical,” “unseemly” or otherwise dishonest. 
Which is why it wouldn’t make any sense to elect a Trump ally to the job of attorney general, who is Minnesota’s chief legal officer. (That’d make as much as sense as the federal government hiring someone from the American Chemical Council to regulate chemical safety; oh, wait, they did that.) 
And, to be sure: Republican nominee for attorney general Ron Schutz is very much a Trump ally. 
The Republican Attorneys General Association is dropping a seven-figure ad buy against Ellison. Check out this photo of Don Jr. Trump with association leaders. 
RAGA, as it’s known, is connected to the mastermind of the Trump Supreme Court, Leonard Leo. 
Leo, who is co-chairman of the board of the Federalist Society, is closely connected to RAGA and various big money GOP groups, which shrewdly see state attorneys general as a key policy, political and legal lever.
Schutz, a successful trial lawyer and fixture of the Minnesota conservative legal establishment, has been a member of the Federalist Society for more than 30 years. 
The group has successfully implanted their right-wing judicial philosophy on the federal bench, including the current supermajority on the U.S. Supreme Court. 
We’re talking overturning Roe v. Wade, giving President Donald Trump immunity from criminal prosecution and gutting the Voting Rights Act.
Beyond the company he keeps, what Schutz has said he’ll do as attorney general is not comforting — insofar as he’s said anything.
How did Schutz react to ICE’s lawless assault on the constitutional rights of Minnesotans? He attacked Ellison for “wasting taxpayer money suing the Trump admin to block ICE from doing their job — enforcing immigration laws in Minnesota.”
Were they “enforcing immigration law” when they killed Good and Pretti? Or dragged an American citizen out of his home without a warrant? Or racially profiled countless Minnesotans? Or stopped clergy and lawyers from visiting people in detention? 
I asked Schutz’s campaign what he would do as attorney general to get Castro back here to face justice. And which, if any, of the more than 70 lawsuits filed by Ellison against the Trump administration that Schutz would drop or continue. 
Schutz didn’t respond. 
I also asked about another high-profile Ellison case, in which he alleges Big Oil defrauded Minnesotans by lying about what they knew about climate change. As multiple investigations have found, the oil companies knew humans burning fossil fuels were causing climate change but then seeded the information atmosphere with phony doubt while the problem only worsened. 
Again, no response from the Schutz campaign, but he did tweet that the lawsuit was part of a “radical green agenda.” 
There’s nothing radical about expecting the world’s largest and most powerful corporations to be truthful with the public. 
I’ve written critically of Democratic-Farmer-Labor elected officials’ lackadaisical initial response to the raiding of our state and federal treasury by fraudsters. Including Ellison’s foolish decision in the fall of 2021 to meet with people who sought his help getting the executive branch to go easier on what we politely call program integrity, just weeks before the raids that finally put an end to the Feeding Our Future debacle. 
Ellison came across during the leaked audio of the meeting as utterly oblivious to what was happening, while inappropriately criticizing the Walz administration, i.e., his client.
I don’t doubt that he didn’t come into office hoping to focus on Medicaid fraud, and I’m sure he doesn’t love touting the work, especially when so much has been found in one community. Regardless, his office informs me they’ve charged 377 people with Medicaid fraud and secured 358 convictions since his tenure began in 2019. That’s a conviction about every eight days since he took office in 2019. 
Every year the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General puts out a statistical report on states’ Medicaid fraud control units, and Minnesota has ranked in the top 10 in fraud convictions, despite our relatively low population compared to places like other top-ranking states like Florida and California. 
Ellison also hired a 20-year veteran of the FBI as a lead investigator. 
Point being: Ellison seems to have gotten the message.
As for Schutz, here’s what he said during a TV interview when asked what he would do in the case of an “unlawful decision” on the part of the Trump administration. 
“What I can tell you is my goal is to protect the citizens of Minnesota.” 
OK, sounds good. 
But then this: “I, I doubt if President Trump is going to be, you know, taking some action that would be blatantly illegal. I know Dems think he has done that. I can tell you from having spent a lot of time in the courtroom, there can be differences of opinion on this.”
Enough said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Appeals court sends UK professor’s case back to lower court
description: A federal appeals court is sending a University of Kentucky law professor’s case to restore his teaching duties back to a lower court.
text:
Ramsi Woodcock has been reassigned from teaching and banned from entering the University of Kentucky College of Law, where he is an assistant professor.A federal appeals court is sending a University of Kentucky law professor’s case to restore his teaching duties back to a lower court. 
A panel of judges on the U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that the U.S. Eastern District Court of Kentucky should reconsider Ramsi Woodcock’s case where he is seeking to regain his teaching duties after UK removed him from them following his criticism of Israel and support of Palestine, including circulating an online petition calling for military action against Israel. 
Last summer, UK President Eli Capilouto shared a public message that did not name Woodcock directly, but indicated the university was aware of the petition and called his views “if accurately attributed … repugnant.”
The appeals court said that UK placed him on administrative leave and started an investigation, but Woodcock argued “that the district court erred because the University’s investigation is not an ongoing state proceeding for purposes of abstention.” 
“The appeals court made clear today that if the University of Kentucky uses an investigation, suspension, and ban to retaliate against a professor for speech that the University dislikes, the professor has a right to challenge the retaliation in federal court on First Amendment grounds,” Woodcock said in a statement. “Like every American scholar, I have a constitutionally protected right to not like Israel and I look forward to vindicating that right in federal court.”
UK spokesperson Jay Blanton said the university is “disappointed in the Sixth Circuit’s ruling.”
“We are considering next steps,” he added. “We look forward to litigating the preliminary injunction.”
Woodcock has a similar case pending in state court and another case challenging the appointment of College of Law Dean Judge Gregory VanTatenhove.

title: Virginia students make gains in reading, math as schools push toward pre-pandemic levels
description: Virginia students continued to make progress in reading and math last school year, posting gains that moved them closer to pre-pandemic performance levels, the Virginia Department of Education announced Tuesday. Across the commonwealth, students’ proficiency in math and reading increased by 0.4% from the prior school year. Over the past five years, proficien[...]
text:
Students in a classroom. (Photo courtesy of Getty Images)Virginia students continued to make progress in reading and math last school year, posting gains that moved them closer to pre-pandemic performance levels, the Virginia Department of Education announced Tuesday.
Across the commonwealth, students’ proficiency in math and reading increased by 0.4% from the prior school year. Over the past five years, proficiency rates rose 5% in reading and 19% in math. 
“Behind the numbers are the dedicated efforts of thousands of students, educators, and families working hard every day to strengthen foundational literacy and numeracy skills,” Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith said in a statement.  “We also know that a lot of hard work is ahead of us, and I am convinced that together, we will continue to address learning gaps.”
Virginia uses the Standards of Learning assessments to measure student learning and achievement in mathematics, reading, science, writing, history, and social science. The results also help determine school accreditation, which affects funding, support, and intervention efforts.
A push to reform SOL assessments was led by former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s Board of Education and administration from 2022 to 2026. In January, Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s team took over and is now celebrating the gains while also seeking ways to ensure more students reach proficiency in all content areas.
Statewide, 72% of students in grades 3 to 8 passed their reading SOLs, and 69% passed their math SOLs. 
Beyond those results, the state’s history and social sciences pass rates increased by 3.2% between the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 school years. A nominal decrease of 0.2% was found in science.
Roughly 53 school divisions, or 40%, achieved increases in both math and reading pass rates last year compared with the 2024-2025 school year.
The results are based on previous proficiency benchmarks, or cut scores, for state assessments. This school year, Virginia rolled out new proficiency benchmarks that students must meet, and these benchmarks will continue to increase over the next four years. 
 A look back

The assessment results come as the Spanberger administration makes its mark on Virginia’s education system, following the Youngkin administration’s broader effort to raise academic expectations beginning in 2022. 
Youngkin pushed for greater rigor in academic standards and assessments with the help of his appointed Board of Education and the state legislature. 
In 2023, the executive branch and lawmakers appropriated $418 million for the ALL In VA plan to address learning loss and other problems that worsened during the pandemic, with a priority on tutoring, literacy and school attendance. 
The agency said Tuesday that the sustained improvement over several years reflects students’ resilience and educators’ ongoing efforts to close learning gaps and strengthen foundational skills statewide.
“We know there is still work ahead to ensure every child develops the knowledge and skills needed to be successful anywhere, but this growth demonstrates that our schools are moving in the right direction,” Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway said in a statement.  
“We will continue using this information to inform targeted and meaningful support for our students’ long-term academic success.”
 What’s next

The department said it will release the results of the School Performance and Support Framework for the 2025-2026 school year in October. Schools are rated on multiple measures of school quality and student achievement, including mastery, growth in reading and mathematics, readiness, and high school graduation rates.
The education board is scheduled to hold a briefing on the results at its work session Wednesday, where members will discuss them. A breakdown of student performance, including grade-level and course-specific pass rates for schools, school divisions and the commonwealth, is available on the agency’s website. 
The department’s  School Quality Profile reports will be updated in the coming week.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Nothing changes yet with SCOTUS elections order. But it could open door to ‘chaos’
description: Nearly one-third of the US votes by mail. US Supreme Court preliminary approval of Trump's order restricting mail voting creates uncertainty.
text:
The Supreme Court’s decision giving preliminary approval for President Donald Trump’s order restricting mail voting may not lead to a single election procedure changing during the November midterms, but it has already thrown into uncertainty the method that nearly one-third of the country uses to vote.
Rather than saying that Trump’s order is legal, the high court said Monday it was too early for Democratic-run states to challenge it in June, when they convinced a federal judge in Boston to freeze the order for November’s election. That effectively restarts the legal fight over the order in an incredibly compressed timeline, with initial ballots scheduled to be sent to North Carolina’s overseas and military voters in just over a week, on Sept. 4.
A second injunction barring the U.S. Postal Service from making changes to comply with Trump’s directive remains in effect. Still, the administration late Monday filed a motion asking that the second hold be removed, and has posted new regulations from the Postal Service that would go into effect Tuesday if the legal pathway is fully cleared.
That new rule requires specific formatting for envelopes containing mail ballots — which may force some jurisdictions to completely revise theirs — and makes states use an electronic system to identify to the Postal Service who is voting by mail. If states don’t comply with the rule, their mail ballots won’t get sent.
The prospect of such a potential sweeping overhaul in mere days boggled critics’ minds. In her dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warned that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.”
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, agreed, saying the majority “seemed to create complete chaos leading up to the midterm elections” and it’d be “impossible” for states to comply with the new rules at this late date.
Some ballots for the November election are set to go out within days
Jesse Salinas, the registrar of Yolo County in California and president of that state’s association of election officers, noted that ballots in his state start going out in 11 days and his county already printed its envelopes.
“You look at the timeline, and it’s a bit chaotic,” Salinas said, noting he doesn’t know precisely which envelope designs comply with the new rules.
He dismissed the idea of a last-minute revision in procedures. “The capacity to do that, I just don’t see it,” Salinas said.
Tammy Patrick, chief program officer at the Elections Center, an association of 2,500 election officers, warned that it’s impossible for any state to comply with the rule and that no one she talked to has tried.
“There isn’t a single state that does their elections in a way that this postal rule lays out,” Patrick said in an interview. “There has been this assumption that this is not going to happen because it could not happen the way it’s laid out, because no one does it this way.”
Cisco Aguilar, the Democratic Secretary of State in Nevada, where every registered voter gets a mail ballot, noted the post office had already misdelivered three dozen mail ballots from his state’s June primary.
“They’re going to come in within seven days and build a massive database that has 100% accuracy?” Aguilar said in disbelief. “It is impossible to implement this system in that time frame.”
Trump votes by mail, but has sought to curb it for others
Trump has long sought to make voting by mail largely impossible, though he himself has repeatedly cast his ballots by mail.
Trump falsely blamed his 2020 loss on mail voting and spun up baroque conspiracy theories that he’s tried to prove while back in office. Judges blocked him from creating new voting restrictions by executive order last year, and he only issued his latest order after his bill to revamp voting procedures stalled in the Senate amidst Democratic opposition.
The Election Assistance Commission found that 29% of voters in 2024 cast their ballots through the mail. Democrats are more likely to use mail voting than Republicans, a reflection of how the process has become polarized since Trump began attacking it in 2020. Still, the president has to date been unable to make the sweeping changes he’s sought because the Constitution grants control of voting rules to states, and in federal elections, to Congress — not the president.
Legal experts stressed that’s why they view it as unlikely Trump’s order will actually be implemented. Not only did the majority in the Supreme Court’s unsigned order note that it hasn’t determined whether the measure is constitutional, but every victory the administration has won so far has only been because it’s argued that it’s premature to talk about its constitutionality. Opponents are already weighing new lawsuits since the final rule was published Friday night.
More litigation is expected
Becker, a former Department of Justice lawyer who co-wrote a book debunking Trump’s 2020 election lies, added that he expects the next round of litigation to keep the order from being implemented in November. Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said after the ruling: “This doesn’t necessarily mean anything in terms of November.”
Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor, said the Supreme Court still ensured a fraught court battle in the coming days.
“It puts courts in a terrible place, because whatever happens is super close to the election,” Muller said. “If it permits it, it creates super disruption for the states. If it suspends it, it visibly angers the administration.”
Hasen said it’s inconceivable that the regulation will impact voters in November.
“Both legal and practical reasons make this practically impossible to enforce,” he said of Trump’s mail voting order.
Elections are run by local officials in thousands of scattered offices, many of which don’t even have a full-time employee. Patrick said that those who work in the field have been left reeling.
“Election officials just feel like punching bags at this moment because they plan one way of conducting their elections, and have contingency plans if a fire breaks out, or one location loses power,” Patrick said. “But how do you plan for something that affects one-third, one half, or all of your voters?”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Military sexual trauma survivors can’t sue the government. A new bill could change that.
description: This article first appeared on The War Horse, an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter. When Mayra Diaz opened the door of her Army barracks room in 2022, she didn’t realize it was the beginning of the end of her military career. She had never met the soldier standing in […]
text:
Teal shoes are displayed outside Naval Medical Center Portsmouth in April 2018 as part of Sexual Assault Awareness and Prevention Month. (MASS COMMUNICATION SPECIALIST 2ND CLASS KRIS R. LINDSTROM/U.S. NAVY)
This article first appeared on The War Horse, an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter.
When Mayra Diaz opened the door of her Army barracks room in 2022, she didn’t realize it was the beginning of the end of her military career.
She had never met the soldier standing in front of her, Sgt. Greville Clarke. She didn’t know he had sexually assaulted three other women on base over the past 15 months, including one he threatened at knifepoint.
Diaz remembers Clarke lifting his uniform top to show he was armed with a handgun. She can’t recall much else after he forced his way into the room, where she lived alone, and assaulted her. It wasn’t until a full day later that a friend found her on the floor with fresh bruises on her neck. Clarke went on to attack a fifth woman before he was finally caught.
In April 2025, Clarke was convicted in a court martial at Fort Hood, Texas, on 29 specifications—including rape, attempted premeditated murder, and kidnapping—for attacking five women. Not long after he was given a life sentence, in September, he died of an apparent suicide in his cell at the Army’s prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, according to Stars & Stripes.
Meanwhile, Diaz soured on her dream to serve until retirement, leaving the Army just two years after she joined.
“I wanted to make it far in the military,” she said. “But I couldn’t stand being in the same uniform.”
This year, Diaz filed a claim against the Army, accusing Fort Hood leadership of failing to provide a safe environment on base. Historically, lawsuits from service members against the military have faced a near-insurmountable barrier: a legal principle known as the Feres doctrine, which bars troops from suing the government for harms incurred during military service.
A new bill in Congress could change that. The Military Sexual Trauma Accountability Act, which has bipartisan support, would allow service members to sue the military for sexual misconduct and related issues, such as failing to investigate reports of misconduct or for negligence in creating an unsafe environment where sexual assault or harassment is allowed to fester.
In 2024, the military received more than 8,000 reports of sexual assault, the majority allegedly committed by service members. That’s a decline of about 4% from the previous year. But researchers with Brown University’s Costs of War project estimate that the total number of sexual assault cases is two to four times higher than the reported cases.
“Accountability doesn’t end with the perpetrator being found guilty and going to jail,” said Josh Connolly, senior vice president of Protect Our Defenders, a nonprofit group that works to end sexual misconduct in the military.
“If the military was on the hook for millions, if not billions, of dollars,” he said, “I think that would create an incentive for the military to take this more seriously.”
 ‘Be careful. It’s Fort Hood’

When Diaz joined the Army in 2021, she was excited to see the world beyond her hometown of Fresno, California.
“I wanted to go to Germany. I wanted to go to Korea,” she said. “I wanted to do all that the military had to offer.”
Her first duty station, however, was closer to home. At basic training, Diaz learned that she would be stationed in Texas at one of the Army’s largest bases.
“Be careful,” a drill sergeant warned, ominously. “It’s Fort Hood.”
Roughly two years earlier, the dismembered remains of Spc. Vanessa Guillén had been found near a river not far from the base next to Killeen. A fellow soldier had murdered Guillén inside an armory at Fort Hood, not long after she confided to her mother that she was being sexually harassed. Guillén’s death spurred a public outcry for greater accountability and protection of women in the ranks, which led to changes in how the military prosecuted sexual misconduct cases.
But when Diaz reported to the base in 2022, she noticed that fellow soldiers still didn’t take rape and sexual harassment seriously. The culture of the Army apparently hadn’t changed much. After her own assault, for instance, a fellow soldier asked why she had opened her door.
“We’re talking about an institution that has had a tendency to blame victims,” Connolly said.

Army Spc. Vanessa Guillén. (U.S. Army)
Diaz found some measure of justice within the military system when Clarke was arrested and convicted. But she still thinks the military could have done more to keep her safe. Army criminal investigators did not investigate Clarke’s first attack, and military police on base closed the case after DNA evidence proved inconclusive. But even after Clarke attacked two other women, none of Diaz’s leaders warned anyone in the barracks about the assaults, according to her legal claim.
“If we were warned properly, [then] maybe this wouldn’t have happened to me,” Diaz said. “They failed to take accountability for where they went wrong.”
Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, citizens can sue the government for negligence or wrongdoing. But Feres limits service members from bringing claims against the military for harms that are “incident to service.”
The principle, according to experts, is rooted in the idea that service members must accept some risk to join the armed forces, and that a lawsuit could undermine the military command structure. But advocates bristle at the persistent denial of claims from military sexual assault survivors due to Feres.
“What they’re saying is that being raped is somehow incident to your military service,” said Christine Dunn, Diaz’s lawyer. “Which is appalling.”
 Unequal justice

Although Feres has served for more than 70 years as a barrier to claims against the military, it hasn’t stopped some service members from trying. For decades, courts have cited Feres to dismiss most cases brought by service members against the government. But in recent years, Feres critics have sensed a shift.
In 2021, for example, the Supreme Court declined to hear a case from a West Point cadet who sued the Army for failing to keep her safe from being raped by a fellow cadet. The decision allowed the lower court’s decision to stand, which dismissed the cadet’s claim due to Feres. But Justice Clarence Thomas dissented.
“Under our precedent, if two Pentagon employees—one civilian and one a servicemember—are hit by a bus in the Pentagon parking lot and sue, it may be that only the civilian would have a chance to litigate his claim on the merits,” Thomas wrote, arguing that the Supreme Court should revisit the doctrine.
Then, two years later, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with a lower court’s decision on a sexual assault case against Air Force Gen. John Hyten that Feres did not apply because the assault could not be considered as “incident to [military] service.”
“It is not conceivable that his military duties would require him to sexually assault Plaintiff, or that such an assault would advance any conceivable military objective,” the lower court wrote.
The case settled out of court and the government paid the plaintiff, Col. Kathryn Spletstoser, nearly $1 million. It was the first known payment from the military in a sexual assault case against a service member.
That ruling could provide an opening to challenge the doctrine in court, said Dunn, Diaz’s lawyer. She also represents survivors in another high-profile case involving Dr. Blaine McGraw, a former gynecologist at Fort Hood and Tripler Army Medical Center in Hawaii, who is facing charges for allegedly abusing nearly 100 patients, many of whom he secretly recorded.
“When you have so many victims complaining about the exact same thing, it’s hard to argue there wasn’t some negligence,” Dunn said.
Dunn points out that Feres creates a parallel—and unequal—justice system. Both Army spouses and service members were victims of McGraw’s alleged abuse. But only the civilian spouses are able to sue the military.
“Feres has so long protected the institution and not the service member,” said Rita Graham, policy director at Service Women’s Action Network, which advocates for women in the military.

The 20th Fighter Wing courtroom at Shaw Air Force Base includes a jury box, witness stand, and gallery, and is used for courts-martial and other military legal proceedings. (Airman 1st Class Daniel Blackwell/U.S. Air Force)
 The path ahead

Military justice reform advocates argue that relying on courts to limit the Feres doctrine is a slow and inefficient way for survivors to get justice. They see a better path through legislation.
In 2019, Congress passed the SFC Richard Stayskal Military Medical Accountability Act, which carved out an exception to Feres for service members harmed due to negligence or wrongdoing in the military medical system.
The Military Sexual Trauma Accountability Act builds on that idea, allowing sexual misconduct survivors in the military to sue the government.
“Servicemembers give up a lot to defend this country, but they should not have to give up their right to hold the government accountable when its negligence contributes to sexual assault or harassment,” said Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a cosponsor of the bill with Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire.
Military justice reformists hailed the passage of the Military Medical Accountability Act, but implementation of the law has been anything but smooth. The law allowed service members to submit malpractice claims to the military, which are reviewed by military lawyers. But fewer than 10% of claims filed since 2020 have been approved, according to recent reporting from the military news site Task & Purpose. Even the bill’s namesake, Richard Stayskal, was denied his claim against the military for overlooking symptoms of Stage 4 lung cancer.
To avoid a similar fate, the new bill would allow sexual assault survivors to directly sue the government in civilian court, instead of filing a claim with the military.
“Just cleanly giving people the ability to go to court for an assault would be the best policy,” said Connolly, who advised lawmakers on the bill.
Survivors hope that, if passed, the bill would force the Pentagon to root out sexual misconduct in the ranks or face serious financial and reputational consequences.
“If the perpetrators are never held accountable, if the people that convince you not to really press charges aren’t held accountable, if you take it to court [martial] and they’re still not held accountable, well, then the military should be held accountable,” said Cairey Williams, a former soldier who said she had been sexually assaulted at all three bases where she was stationed after joining the Army in 2003.
“Until somebody is held accountable, it’s just going to keep going,” she said.
Ultimately, survivors and advocates say it isn’t about the money. Instead, they hope the threat of financial penalties will force the military to do more to prevent sexual assault and harassment for future generations of Americans who decide to serve.
“Regardless of them giving me money, not giving me money, I still have to live with what happened to me for the rest of my life,” Diaz said. “And as much as I could try, money can’t buy off the trauma that I go through now.”
This War Horse article was edited by Paul Szoldra, fact-checked by Jess Rohan, and copy-edited by Mitchell Hansen-Dewar.

 Catching Our Eye

• Privatizing education. Jessie Balmert reports in the Columbus Dispatch, “Ohio could close, convert struggling schools under proposed changes.”
Chronically struggling public schools could be converted into charter schools, have their leadership replaced or be forced to close, according to proposed changes Ohio wants federal education officials to approve.
The proposal lists 16 ways to improve the state’s lowest-performing schools, which include high schools where at least a third of students do not graduate. But Ohio school leaders worry that the changes go too far and weren’t properly vetted.
• Living with disabilities. Cleveland.com’s Karan Singh reports, “An alternative to guardianship? Ohio bill promises more independence for adults with disabilities. Critics see risks.”
For Ohio adults with developmental disabilities who need help navigating major decisions, the legal options can present a stark choice: retain full control or, if a court finds them legally incompetent, have a guardian appointed with authority to make certain decisions for them.
A bill moving through the Ohio legislature seeks to establish a middle ground.
• Flock. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s David Ferrara and Quinlan Bentley report, “More than 1,000 Flock cameras watch Cincinnati area. Resistance is growing.”
Police are using a private network of Flock license plate cameras to track people. While law enforcement credits the technology with solving crimes, its use has sparked a backlash from privacy advocates and some residents.
The growing network of more than 1,100 cameras in Greater Cincinnati creates a vast surveillance web with inconsistent usage policies.
• Youth homes. The Dayton Daily News’ Avery Kreemer reports, “Local lawmakers picked for new committee to address delinquent youth group homes.”
A new Ohio legislative study committee will soon begin evaluating the impacts of courts ordering delinquent youth to stay in residential group homes, a practice that has drawn concern and scrutiny in the area due to Montgomery County’s outsized number of group homes.
The committee, set to convene Monday, Aug. 24, will feature state Rep. Andrea White, R-Kettering, as co-chair, Rep. Phil Plummer, R-Butler Twp. and a handful of other select lawmakers; alongside representatives from various state departments, county children services agencies, juvenile courts, group homes, law enforcement agencies and more.
• SNAP cuts. The Toledo Blade’s Chantal Eulenstein reports, “SNAP funding cuts leave Lucas County with $2.5 million gap.”
Lucas County Job & Family Services will see a significant funding cut this fall as it administers programs that provide food, cash, and other assistance to low-income residents.
The agency oversees local administration of programs including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP, and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF.
The reductions stem from the federal tax and spending law signed by President Trump, which is expected to cut SNAP spending by $187 billion through 2034.
