name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Weeks after school’s closure, private student records remain in empty building
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Confidential student records are sitting in a vacated building nearly eight weeks after a charter school permanently closed its doors, officials from the state and the school said, though both sides disagree on who is at fault.  Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, known as PTPLA, ceased operations on July 1 after the […]
text:
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, pictured May 19, is now closed, but school and state officials say paper copies of student records remain inside its former building in southwest Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Confidential student records are sitting in a vacated building nearly eight weeks after a charter school permanently closed its doors, officials from the state and the school said, though both sides disagree on who is at fault. 
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, known as PTPLA, ceased operations on July 1 after the Statewide Charter School Board canceled its charter contract over financial, operational and academic quality concerns. 
The charter high school’s 100 students have either graduated or transferred elsewhere, but paper copies of their academic transcripts, vaccination records and enrollment documents still remain at PTPLA’s former building in southwest Oklahoma City, raising concerns over privacy protections and potentially racking up thousands of dollars in rental fees, according to email correspondence Oklahoma Voice obtained from the state.
Representatives of the shuttered school told Oklahoma Voice that state employees haven’t worked with the building’s landlord to pick up the records.
A spokesperson for the Statewide Charter School Board, Shelly Hickman, said board staff has contacted the landlord, who indicated the student records are under lock and key and “it is the PTPLA team, and not he, who has that key.”
The Statewide Charter School Board meets for a termination hearing for Proud To Partner Leadership Academy on April 29 at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The state received electronic copies of the student records and has been providing them daily to school families upon request, Hickman said. A lack of paper copies hasn’t stopped any students from attending school elsewhere, she said, because enrollment commonly involves an electronic exchange of records.
Recovering the physical copies from the empty school building, though, has turned into a monthslong dispute.
The state board’s staff tried to retrieve the files multiple times in June when the school still occupied the building, but PTPLA leadership declined to provide them because the records were incomplete, Hickman said. 
Emails that Oklahoma Voice obtained show state officials have asked PTPLA representatives repeatedly in July and August to either hand over the physical documents or agree to a time that state employees could pick up the records.
School representatives on a “transition team” overseeing the closure had a deadline of Aug. 12 to transfer all financial, student and personnel records, the emails show. Days after the deadline, state employees still were sending emails seeking a response.
“We could be at the building today if the PTPLA transition team arranged for us to enter and finally produced these hard copy records for us, which has been their legal responsibility all along,” Hickman said.
The state needs to contact the building’s landlord to gain entry because the school no longer has access to the facility, said Marva Williamson, a PTPLA board member and the school’s only remaining representative on the transition team. 
School board member Charlesetta Jossell also was part of the team but resigned on Aug. 18, email records show.
The school board president of PTPLA, Sharri Coleman, returned the building’s keys to the landlord on July 31, according to a written memorandum, which Oklahoma Voice obtained. 
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy school board President Sharri Coleman, center, speaks during a board meeting May 19 at the charter high school in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The memorandum states that student records and some desks still remained inside at the time of the key transfer. Any further access to the building must be coordinated with the landlord, the document states.
Coleman said she isn’t part of the transition team. Her responsibility was to ensure the building was secure and the keys were returned, not to transfer records, she said.
But, she said she became concerned with the lack of progress toward final closure, so she decided to notify the news media, multiple state lawmakers and state Superintendent Lindel Fields on Friday of the documents remaining in the former school facility.
“The reason why I went to state officials is so that someone on the outside can say, ‘Hey, get the records. The records have been left there for you. They weren’t abandoned. There was documentation saying that they’re in the building,’” Coleman told Oklahoma Voice on Monday. “That’s just a part of the transition process, and I just felt like the transition process had stalled.”
Her email to state leaders only stoked frustrations among the statewide board and its staff.
State employees have made “numerous attempts” to obtain the documents from PTPLA, Statewide Charter School Board Chair Brian Shellem wrote in an email to Coleman on Sunday evening.
Abandoning the documents could violate student privacy laws, he wrote. His email argues that the school at any point could have hired a courier service to deliver the records to the statewide board’s offices.
Meanwhile, the leftover items have accrued two months of rental fees, totaling $39,469, according to an email Thursday from the building landlord, Cameron Kaspereit.
Kaspereit, who did not return requests for comment from Oklahoma Voice, wrote in emails to state officials last week that another $118,800 is owed for a “building expense due from the early termination,” along with “fees for damages previously submitted.”
The last of PTPLA’s funds will go toward its outstanding bills, according to a July 21 email from the state board’s legal compliance officer, Emily Witwer.
“Following closure, the landlord’s only recourse would be to sue the defunct entity, as the Statewide Charter School Board does not inherit the debts of PTPLA,” she wrote.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Health officials warn of ‘unprecedented’ blood shortage
description: New Jersey is one of many states now facing a lack of blood products. The New York Blood Center declared an “unprecedented” second blood emergency in July.
text:
New Jersey is one of many states now facing a lack of blood products. The New York Blood Center declared an “unprecedented” second blood emergency in July. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)New Jersey is facing a blood shortage – part of a national dip in supplies – and the state’s health commissioner plans to roll up his sleeve and donate Tuesday in hopes that others will follow his lead.  
Health Commissioner Dr. Raynard Washington is scheduled to visit the New Jersey Blood Services’ Freehold donor center Tuesday afternoon as part of an event to boost blood product donations statewide. Washington said giving blood takes less than an hour and can save lives. 
“Donated blood is an essential part of healthcare New Jerseyans rely on, used for everything from routine surgeries and cancer treatments to trauma care. But blood and platelets can’t be manufactured — they come from generous donors who step up to help,” Washington said.
New Jersey is one of many states now facing a lack of blood products, state health officials said, noting warnings from the American Red Cross.  
The New York Blood Center, which operates New Jersey Blood Services, declared an “unprecedented” second blood emergency in early July after an initial shortage was announced around Memorial Day. Donors can find a location to give blood here.  
University Hospital’s Dr. Scott Pasichow, who teaches emergency medicine at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, said he has yet to see the shortage impair emergency department operations or emergency response connected to the Newark hospital. 
“But if the blood banks are concerned, then it is only a matter of time. Donations now will keep us ready when blood is needed to save lives,” Pasichow told the New Jersey Monitor.  
Summer traditionally involves an increased need for blood products, since trauma cases rise as more people are traveling, boating, and active outdoors. This regularly coincides with a decline in donations, but the dip has been more pronounced this year, experts said.  
“August is traditionally one of the most challenging times of year for the blood supply, and this summer has been especially difficult as extreme weather has disrupted blood donations across our region,” Jeannie Mascolino, vice president of operations for the New York and New Jersey blood programs, said in a statement earlier this month.  
When the New York Blood Center announced the second blood emergency in early July — unprecedented in its 60-year history — blood supply in the region had fallen to approximately two days of products, far below the level needed to sustain the more than 200 hospitals, emergency response units, and labs that the center works with, according to the group. 
Bhishma Patel, the chief technologist at University Hospital’s blood center, said hospital officials proactively manage blood supply to ensure there’s enough for patients, increasing demand in advance of scheduled complex procedures. The hospital also benefits from a diversified supply chain, with 60% of its products from the New York Blood Center and 40% from the Red Cross, she said.   
“This dual-supplier strategy further strengthens our ability to maintain a reliable blood inventory and support patient care during periods of regional or national blood shortages,” Patel told the New Jersey Monitor.

name: WyoFile
title: Old rift reopens as Trump administration amends Grand Teton pathway decision
description:
Conservation groups decry the federal government’s do-over as both a dubious procedural maneuver and threat to wildlife. But longtime trail advocates are pleased. 
The post Old rift reopens as Trump administration amends Grand Teton pathway decision appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Even though the 7.1-mile Moose-Wilson Road represents a sliver of the 310,000-acre Grand Teton National Park, its fate has fueled years of debate.
And when the National Park Service recently amended a 10-year-old park management plan to allow for the construction of a multiuse path along the busy road, it reopened a rift over the agency’s obligation to balance multiple concerns, including wildlife protection, archeological preservation, recreation and safe visitor access. That same pathway was excluded from a 2016 decision. 
The narrow roadway, which is closed to RVs and mostly signed for 25 miles per hour, is prized for its wildlife-watching potential. That quality makes additional infrastructure controversial. 
For the conservation groups who argued back in 2015 that a separate paved pathway would damage rich wildlife habitat at a ridiculous cost to taxpayers, the federal government’s reversal stung.
“I was really disappointed and, and quite frankly, shocked,” said Joan Anzelmo with Friends of the Moose-Wilson Corridor. “It appeared the agency was being forced to add a rejected alternative with no further scientific analysis, no supplemental EIS.”
But on the other side of that coin are transportation advocates like Tim Young, who has worked for decades to build out a safe network of multi-use pathways for cyclists, pedestrians and others in the region. High-profile cycling fatalities such as the 1999 death of 13-year-old Gabriella Axelrad, who was struck by a van while riding the Moose-Wilson Road, underscore the need for a pathway separate from the heavily trafficked road, he said. He considers the pathway construction an appropriate agency action. 
The 7.1-mile Moose-Wilson Road in Grand Teton National Park is a popular scenic route for cyclists and vehicles. The narrow road is not open to RVs. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
“I thought it was outstanding to reconsider this,” the former director of Wyoming Pathways said.  
The pivot was the result of an executive order signed by President Donald Trump, according to the park service. The agency announced in March it was reopening the 2016 decision, and in June it released a draft “programmatic agreement,” identifying additional scoping work related to multi-use pathway construction. 
According to that document, recreational opportunities, newly stipulated by Trump’s executive order, were not considered during the previous scoping process. On Aug. 14, the park service approved the amendment, authorizing the pathway’s construction and partial realignment of the road. 
“We remain committed to providing appropriate recreational opportunities while maintaining the natural and cultural resources that sustain a healthy, functioning ecosystem,” Grand Teton National Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins said in a press release. “We are balancing visitor access with long-term stewardship.”
Pavement priorities
The road is the main artery running through what’s known as the Moose-Wilson Corridor — a swath of roughly 10,300 acres with exceptional wildlife habitat that also provides access to destinations like the Death Canyon trailhead, Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve and Murie Ranch historic district.
A mix of aspens, chokecherries, willows and conifers alongside pristine riparian zones draw species including moose, wolves, grizzly and black bears — which can create “wildlife jams” as slowing or stopping vehicles clog the road. Along with growing visitation, some local residents rely on the road as a shortcut between Teton Village and the Jackson Hole Airport or Wyoming Route 390 and destinations in the park and beyond.
In 2016, the park service estimated that roughly 400,000 visitors traveled the corridor annually.

Though a sign warns users that cycling on the Moose-Wilson Road is not for beginners, cyclists of every level pedal the heavily trafficked road. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)

With its location between Teton Village and park destinations, Young said, it’s a major jumping-off point for visitors heading into the park. But it also draws cyclists — including young riders who may not have the skills or vigilance to navigate the road-sharing required, he said. 
The narrative that the pathway’s approval represents Trump administration overreach fails to address a much longer and more complex story, he said while standing astride his gravel bike on a smoky August morning. The deaths of Axelrad and, two years later, cyclist Jeff Pool helped lead to a 2007 Grand Teton Transportation Plan environmental impact study. The final decision is no longer on the agency’s website, but Young said a majority of public comment supported a significant pathway system. 
The high-profile fatalities, he said, “kind of broke the dam in terms of public demands for trying to do something to improve safety … in making the case that bicycling is an appropriate means of access to see, visit, explore, enjoy the national park.” 
Young was instrumental in that effort, which led to the construction of pathway sections from Moose to Jenny Lake and Jackson to Moose. Users loved the new transportation options, Young said, but that Moose-Wilson gap remained.
The National Park Service initiated the Moose-Wilson Corridor Comprehensive Management Plan process in 2013. Following a year-long scoping, the agency released four alternatives for managing the corridor — and received more than 4,000 comments. 
In its 2016 record of decision, the park service selected alternative C, which generally restricted development within the corridor to the existing footprint. Notably left out of that preferred alternative was a proposal to build a multi-use pathway, separated from the road, for bicycles and pedestrians. 
“The emphasis of the selected action is to balance preservation and public use and enjoyment by exemplifying conservation legacies within the corridor,” the agency’s record of decision read. 
Cyclist Tim Young near the Granite Entrance Station of Grand Teton National Park in August 2026. The entrance station marks one end of the 7.1-mile Moose-Wilson Road, a narrow and heavily trafficked stretch that Young and other trail advocates say would be improved with a separate multiuse pathway. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
On his bike in early August, Young pedaled the Moose-Wilson Road, pointing out blind corners and a pathway route along an existing two-track that could take users to the Rockefeller Center. Though a sign near the entrance station warned the road ahead was for experienced cyclists, a family without helmets pedaled on cruiser bikes, and a girl of around 9 rode alongside a woman.  
With minuscule shoulders and vehicles traveling at various speeds around corners, Young said, the road is not bike-friendly. But he doesn’t like the way this issue has been reduced to “recreation versus conservation,” he said. 
“When you look at the full corridor, rather than drill down to a singular action among dozens of management steps, the National Park Service made the right decision for the Moose-Wilson Corridor,” Young told WyoFile. “I look forward to the day people can safely bike and walk between Teton Village to Moose on a safe pathway, and leave their car behind.”
Wildlife worries
When the agency announced it was revisiting the 2016 decision, it cited a 2025 executive order that “calls for improving visitor services, enhancing access, and reviewing policies that may unnecessarily restrict recreation in national parks.”
The announcement got the hackles up of people who participated in the Moose-Wilson Corridor plan the first time around. 
“Ten years ago, significant concerns from park leadership and the local community, including NPCA, led to a final plan for this important corridor to be protected,” Allison Michalski, Grand Teton Senior Program Manager for National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement. “We are disappointed to see many years of science, policy,  and public engagement overturned to satisfy special interests [that] will leave parks like Grand Teton National Park and others open to damaging changes.”
Those opposed to pathway construction say it poses harm to wetlands the road crosses, to sensitive species including grizzly bears and to archeological resources found in the corridor. 
When Anzelmo became involved in the earlier EIS, she said, the corridor “was a favorite place to be able to observe wildlife, so I was very aware of the specialness of that corridor, but also the fragility of the corridor.” What ensued was a robust, careful and scientific process, she said. 
“In September of 2016, when the National Park Service completed that process and signed the record of decision selecting the alternative,” she said, “we were really pleased.”
The Moose-Wilson Road is a common place to view wildlife, as its name suggests. (C. Adams/NPS)
She was deeply disappointed to see it revived. The costs of an 8-mile separated pathway — to wildlife, habitat and taxpayers — do not justify the benefits, she said. She would rather see the park service experiment with management strategies such as timed one-way vehicle traffic. 
“Instead of spending [tens of millions of dollars] and taking out thousands of trees and damaging grizzly bear habitat and elk calving grounds, perhaps other things could be done to achieve the same goal,” she said. 
A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service analysis for the amended record of decision determined the effects associated with the proposed action “are likely to adversely affect but are not likely to jeopardize” the continued existence of the grizzly bear.
Not over yet
Friends of Moose-Wilson Corridor is working alongside other organizations to find a better solution, Anzelmo said. 

Joan Anzelmo on Feb. 9, 2020, at her home near Jackson. (Ryan Dorgan)

“We are going to do anything we can to raise awareness and try and stop this,” she said. “We don’t want to see bulldozers coming down the Moose-Wilson Corridor.”
She hopes officials press pause and consider “smarter visitation strategies that could be used to work within the existing footprint.”
But Young, who also formerly worked for the National Parks Conservation Association, said a close study of the National Park Service’s mission is merited in this context. 
“The National Park Service preserves unimpaired the natural and cultural resources and values of the National Park System for the enjoyment, education, and inspiration of this and future generations,” the mission reads.
“It’s a complicated mission,” Young said. It’s not solely about protecting resources; it’s also for human access. “So the balance of what you provide, that’s the challenge for park managers.”

name: WyoFile
title: Why the Bear Lodge mine plan needs a closer look
description:
Sundance deserves clear, factual data showing how rare earth mining will affect local water and air, writes guest columnist Justin Johnson.
The post Why the Bear Lodge mine plan needs a closer look appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A massive decision about the public land right next to our homes in Sundance is being rushed through its review process. The U.S. Forest Service just opened a public comment window for the proposed Bear Lodge rare earth mine at Bull Hill. Because the government put this project on a fast track, our normal right to object to final plans has been cut short. That makes this current comment window, closing Aug. 28, our only real chance to stand up and speak out to protect our water, our air and our rights as citizens. This sets a precedent which should concern our entire state.

Opinion

We simply cannot afford to guess when it comes to our water. The Forest Service must demand thorough scientific studies before a single shovel hits the ground. The Sundance community deserves clear data and baseline testing to prove this mine won’t ruin our local aquifers, dry up our residential wells or destroy our natural springs. If we don’t demand these water studies right now, our families risk paying the price for generations. Digging a deep open pit will require pumping out massive amounts of groundwater. That heavy pumping risks draining local water tables and neighboring ranch wells. Any chemical or waste leaks at the mine site could directly contaminate the regional aquifers that our town and ranches rely on every single day.
Clean air is just as critical. Because this is a rare earth mine, digging and crushing the rock will expose radioactive materials. This work turns buried elements into airborne dust and releases radon gas. Since the mine is positioned on a high ridge, our strong mountain winds can carry that fine dust straight down into our valleys and schools. We need strict, independent wind modeling to prove our air will stay safe for our kids.
Beyond these significant concerns about our air and water, the Bear Lodge Project attempts to rewrite the rules of the Black Hills National Forest. The mine is seeking a specific “forest plan amendment” to exempt this mine from standard environmental rules. Our public forests belong to everyone. Protected forest regulations should never be rewritten or waived for a mining operation without telling us what that project will actually do to our land, our views and our wildlife.
The U.S. Forest Service is accepting public comment until Aug. 28. Anyone can voice their concerns, either through the U.S. Forest Service’s online portal or by mail at the address below. Please don’t let this deadline pass by silently.
Send physical written comments to:Wendy Schuyler, Project ManagerBlack Hills National Forest, Bearlodge Ranger District101 S. 21st Street, P.O. Box 680Sundance, WY 82729

name: WyoFile
title: Frothy emotional appeal seldom suffices
description:
Voters showed the Wyoming Freedom Caucus last Tuesday that politicking has to lead to effective, sensible governance, writes guest columnist Gunnar Malm.
The post Frothy emotional appeal seldom suffices appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
There is a line in a very important book in my life that I return to often: “Frothy emotional appeal seldom suffices.” 

Opinion

It wasn’t written about politics. It was written about something far more personal. But watching the rise of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus over the last several years — and then watching voters deliver a very different message in last week’s primary — I couldn’t help but think about those words. 
There are lessons here, and they aren’t only for the Freedom Caucus. They’re lessons for all of us who have the privilege of serving the public. 
The first is that anger is powerful, but it is not the same thing as leadership.
Anger can win an election. Frustration can build a movement. A clever social media post can generate thousands of reactions. Politics makes it remarkably easy to convince people that every complicated problem has a simple solution being prevented by someone with bad intentions. 
That kind of politics can be intoxicating. But governing is different. 
Eventually, you have to produce something. 
You have to pass a budget, maintain roads, keep law enforcement staffed and work with people you don’t particularly like. You have to understand that while the person sitting across the table may disagree with you, that doesn’t mean they’re corrupt, stupid or evil. 
Most importantly, you have to make decisions where there isn’t a perfect answer. That is where frothy emotional appeal runs into reality. 
The Freedom Caucus’ rise was not an accident, and dismissing it as one would be a mistake. Its members tapped into something real. Many Wyoming voters felt ignored. They were frustrated with government spending, skeptical of institutions and tired of politicians who seemed more interested in managing government than challenging it. 
Those voters deserved to be heard. And in 2024, they were. 
The Freedom Caucus took control of the Wyoming House of Representatives and received an opportunity few political movements ever receive: the chance to turn rhetoric into effective governance. 
Then came the harder part. 
This week’s election suggests that a meaningful number of Wyoming Republicans decided that what followed the caucus’s takeover wasn’t what they had signed up for. 
That brings me to the second lesson: A mandate is borrowed, not owned. 
Winning an election doesn’t mean voters have endorsed everything you will ever do afterward. It means they have entrusted you with an opportunity. 
Politicians of every stripe eventually make the mistake of confusing the two. A big victory becomes proof that “the people are with us.” Criticism becomes evidence that opponents simply haven’t accepted the election. Compromise becomes betrayal. Before long, elected officials begin speaking for voters more often than they listen to them. 
But voters are remarkably good at reminding us who works for whom. 
Last Tuesday was one of those reminders. 
The third lesson may be the most important: Being willing to fight is valuable; knowing when not to fight is leadership. 
There are things worth fighting for. I’ve learned during my years in public service that some decisions require you to plant your feet and accept the consequences. Leadership cannot simply mean finding the loudest group in the room and doing whatever keeps them happy. But if everything is a battle, eventually nothing is. 
Government requires relationships and trust. It requires sometimes accepting half a loaf so you can come back tomorrow and keep working. It requires understanding that today’s opponent on one issue may be tomorrow’s indispensable partner on another. 
Compromise isn’t always surrender. Sometimes it is how representative government among people with different interests actually functions. 
And there is another lesson for those who opposed the Freedom Caucus: Don’t become what you criticized.
Political pendulums swing. It would be easy for traditional Republicans to look at Tuesday’s results, declare the Freedom Caucus experiment dead and return to business as usual. That would be every bit as foolish as believing the 2024 election represented a permanent revolution. 
The concerns that fueled the Freedom Caucus’ rise didn’t disappear Tuesday night. People still expect fiscal discipline. They still want government held accountable. They still distrust institutions that appear insulated from ordinary citizens. They still expect Republicans in one of the most conservative states in America to govern conservatively. 
Those messages should not be discarded simply because some of the messengers were defeated. 
The challenge now is to separate legitimate concerns from political theater — and turn them into durable policy. 
Which brings me back to that line: “Frothy emotional appeal seldom suffices.” 
Emotion can start something. It can fill a room, fuel a campaign, dominate Facebook and turn frustration into an electoral wave. 
But sustained, meaningful change requires something more. 
It requires depth. It requires weight. It requires humility. 
It requires doing the homework when nobody is watching, building coalitions with people who don’t agree with you on everything, admitting when you’re wrong and occasionally making a decision that earns fewer likes but leaves your community better than you found it. 
Perhaps most importantly, it requires remembering that no election result — good or bad — is the final word. 
I’ve won elections. I’ve made mistakes. I’ve taken criticism. I’ve changed my mind. And after years in public service, I am increasingly convinced that leadership has much less to do with winning every argument than I once thought. 
It is about accomplishing something that lasts. 
Wyoming’s Freedom Caucus taught our state some lessons during its remarkable rise. Its setbacks this week should teach us some lessons too. 
Not about which faction won or lost, but about the difference between a movement and governing. Between attention and accomplishment. Between outrage and leadership. Because froth rises quickly. 
But only things with depth and weight endure.

name: Daily Montanan
title: The five horsemen of the apocalypse
description: The Trump Administration has released five horsemen to run roughshod over America the Beautiful, playing out their version of Manifest Destiny 2.0 at the expense of all that is good and whole. In seemingly separate, but connected actions, the very agencies entrusted with protecting our national heritage seek to drive threatened and endangered wildlife off […[...]
text:
A grizzly bear killed by hunter gunfire in the Aspen Creek drainage west of Cody in 2014. Grizzly bears have died at a high rate so far in 2024. Some 16 deaths are being investigated, which means the bears were likely killed in self-defense. (Courtesy of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)The Trump Administration has released five horsemen to run roughshod over America the Beautiful, playing out their version of Manifest Destiny 2.0 at the expense of all that is good and whole.
In seemingly separate, but connected actions, the very agencies entrusted with protecting our national heritage seek to drive threatened and endangered wildlife off the landscape like the native Americans before them. Under a cloak of “efficiency” and “local control,” they are wreaking havoc leading to plunder and lawlessness, clearing the way for bulldozers and industrial anarchy.
First, the Department of Interior redefined “harm” under the Endangered Species Act so that habitat destruction is no longer considered harmful to threatened and endangered species. That’s like saying we could take away food, shelter, heat, water and clothing from people and it would have no effect on their well-being. No harm, no foul.
Second, the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service proposed to remove Endangered Species Act protection for grizzly bears less than two years after concluding that a host of cumulative threats puts the species at increased risk of extinction throughout their range in the lower 48.
Third, the Fish & Wildlife Service proposed an expanded “4(d) rule” that Interior Secretary Doug Burgum says turns grizzly bear management over to the states that want trophy hunting and to kill them whenever near livestock, even on public lands. Like failed state management of wolves, the proposed rule creates expanded exemptions for killing grizzly bears and would give out kill permits like Halloween candy.
Fourth, the Department of Agriculture proposed canceling the Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Tens of millions of acres of the wildest National Forests would be opened to new roads, logging, motorized use and other development. This despite that 99% of the comments from the American people oppose this industrial land grab. Say goodbye to connecting isolated grizzly bear populations and say hello to dramatic reductions in elk, Montana’s five-week general hunting season, bull trout, salmon, old growth forests and clean water supplies for humans.
Fifth, the Department of Agriculture has proposed to shred National Travel Management Planning on National Forests, opening the way to off-trail cross-country travel by ATVs, snowmobiles and 4-x-4s. Management of motorized access to seasonally protect sensitive wildlife and fish habitat would go out the window, replaced with a system of motorized mayhem.
Taken in sum, these five horsemen would unleash an environmental apocalypse.
Other actions have already eroded the National Environmental Policy Act, limited public comment and other mechanisms meant to maintain checks and balances. They are dismantling a system of land and wildlife management years in the making that has sustained ecosystems, restored elk populations and brought wildlife back from the brink of extinction. These connected actions also undermine the public’s right to have a say over management of its own lands.
Many organizations are fighting the good fight but they need your help. Please get informed and involved. These connections actions must be stopped before the soul of America is permanently wounded.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Nashville state lawmakers enter fray over fight for fairground speedway
description: Five years after a proposal surfaced to renovate the Nashville fairground racetrack with $84 million in taxpayer funding, area state lawmakers are split over the concept of racing at the speedway. Former Nashville Mayor John Cooper announced a proposed deal with Speedway Motorsports in 2021 that would cost city taxpayers $50 million in bonds to […]
text:
An anti-racing group started a campaign this summer to gather the 40,000 signatures required to put an amendment before Nashville voters in 2027 that would remove the fairgrounds racing requirement from the city charter. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Five years after a proposal surfaced to renovate the Nashville fairground racetrack with $84 million in taxpayer funding, area state lawmakers are split over the concept of racing at the speedway.
Former Nashville Mayor John Cooper announced a proposed deal with Speedway Motorsports in 2021 that would cost city taxpayers $50 million in bonds to renovate the city’s fairground speedway. Then, Gov. Bill Lee and the Nashville Visitors and Convention Bureau agreed to chip in another $17 million each.
But nearly five years later, the cost to renovate the Nashville Fairgrounds Speedway has likely increased to more than $100 million, and cost has barely factored into the debate over whether city voters should repeal the requirement for racing at the fairgrounds.
The Nashville Fairgrounds Speedway has not hosted a NASCAR event since 2000. But in 2011, 70% of Nashville voters approved an amendment to the city’s charter that requires racing at the fairgrounds, essentially preventing the city from tearing down the facility without another vote.
An anti-racing group, called Restore Our Fairgrounds, started a campaign this summer to gather the 40,000 signatures required to put an amendment before Nashville voters in 2027 that would remove the fairgrounds racing requirement from the city charter. As part of its push, the group has been selling voters on the idea that the track could be torn down and replaced by affordable housing.
In response, another pro-racing group, called Decline to Sign, has emerged, arguing the anti-racing group is gathering signatures under false pretenses.
NASCAR close to returning to Nashville after Cooper reaches deal with Bristol Motor Speedway

State Rep. Bob Freeman, a Nashville Democrat who came out publicly in favor of keeping the track, said he didn’t have an opinion on whether public money should go toward a renovation but was against the group gathering signatures under the guise of “affordable housing.” He called their petition drive “intellectually dishonest.”
“Should they be racing there?” Freeman said. “I don’t know that I care. I’ve been to the track. I enjoy it. But the people of Nashville have spoken. We voted on it. Had the referendum. Now it’s up to the city to figure out what to do with it.”
Freeman joins state Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, in opposing the latest effort from the anti-racing group. Behn, in a post to her Substack blog, compared the track to the Ryman Auditorium — the iconic downtown music venue that was threatened with demolition in 1974 —adding that it has such a high historical value that it should be preserved.
On the other side favoring a charter amendment vote are state Reps. John Ray Clemmons and Caleb Hemmer, both Nashville Democrats and former Nashville fair board commissioners.
Hemmer said he feels Nashville has been “constrained” by the charter since it was revised, especially as the fairgrounds and surrounding neighborhood changed in the last generation, getting new homes and businesses. He contends the Metro government and fair board need “more flexibility” to manage the property.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“I think the site and the neighborhood and the city have evolved to where that is not the best use of the property and we should evaluate other options outside of racing,” Hemmer said.
Ingram (Nashville SC) vs. Speedway Motorsports
Behind the scenes, the political fight over the speedway is between Nashville billionaire John Ingram and Speedway Motorsports.
Ingram, owner of Nashville Soccer Club and chairman of family business Ingram Industries, has opposed racing because it conflicts with play at Geodis Park, the team’s stadium, built next to the racetrack in 2022.
Speedway Motorsports, which owns Bristol Motor Speedway, the Nashville Superspeedway in Lebanon, and nearly a dozen other tracks, has wanted to hold a NASCAR race within the city limits for years.
The political fight is also between two Nashville lobbying firms. Cooley Strategies, run by former Gov. Phil Bredesen advisor Dave Cooley, represents the anti-racing side. Calvert Street Group, founded by Darden Copeland, represents the pro-racing side.
Copeland is currently running for U.S. Congress as the Democratic nominee for House District 7.
Any deal to build a new racetrack in Nashville could also allow Speedway Motorsports to sell the Nashville Superspeedway in Wilson County, which the company purchased in 2021 for $131.5 million. 
Tennessee Republican lawmakers in leadership haven’t publicly weighed in on a deal in years. Lee has previously supported the renovation plan in 2022 but will leave office in January. Speedway Motorsports hosted a Major League Baseball game at its Bristol speedway in 2025 with several lawmakers in attendance.
If the anti-racing group’s signatures are certified by the mid-September city charter amendment deadline, the vote will go before Nashville voters during the mayoral election in 2027.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Lowndes County residents demand transparency in hyperscale data center development
description: HAYNEVILLE — At least 150 Lowndes County residents gathered at the local courthouse Monday evening to demand transparency from the county commission about the development of one of Alabama’s largest planned data centers. One resident, John Urquhart, said in an interview before the regularly scheduled County Commission meeting that the development, known as P[...]
text:
Residents of Lowndes County holding up signs that read "No Data Center" at a County Commission meeting on Aug. 24, 2026, in Hayneville, Alabama, in the Lowndes County Courthouse. The residents demanded more transparency from the commission on Monday in the wake of a $1.5 billion proposed data center a few miles from the courthouse. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)HAYNEVILLE — At least 150 Lowndes County residents gathered at the local courthouse Monday evening to demand transparency from the county commission about the development of one of Alabama’s largest planned data centers.
One resident, John Urquhart, said in an interview before the regularly scheduled County Commission meeting that the development, known as Project Red Clay, is “depressing.” He lives on 230 acres adjacent to the planned location of the data center. 
“It’s depressing to think we put our life savings into buying all this, and getting it together, and they move in, and they destroy it,” he said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Urquhart attended the meeting with many of his peers through a resident-organized group called Protect Lowndes County to protest the planned 800-acre data center. 
About 350 people signed the group’s petition demanding more transparency from the commission. Urquhart was chosen to read the petition to the commissioners during the meeting.
The facility has requested 1,500 megawatts of energy capacity from Alabama Power – enough to power roughly one million homes. The entire state of Alabama has about 2 million households and about 2.4 million housing units.
John Urquhart, a Lowndes County resident, speaking to the Lowndes County Commission on Aug. 24, 2026, in the Lowndes County Courthouse in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
“I’m not against new technologies. I mean it’s made all of our lives better,” Urquhart said. “There are just so many negatives to it. We’ve asked for answers since April. Our commissioners have given us absolutely nothing.”
Data centers have emerged as a top issue for Alabamians ahead of the midterm elections, and they have become a partisan issue. Democrats at the top of Alabama’s ticket are calling for a one-year moratorium on the facilities due to local and expert concern. Republicans have tended to tout the facilities for economic development possibilities. 
The petition asked the commissioners to comply with an open records request submitted on July 27 seeking documentation on the project. It also demanded a list of the entities involved in the project, disclosure of infrastructure impacts and the creation of an accessible online dashboard to share up-to-date information on the project for the public. 
Members of the commission said Monday they did not have any information to share with the public. 
In a statement Monday evening, the developers of Project Red Clay said it created a separate LLC, Sandstone Cliffs DevCo, to operate the beginning phases of the project. Cloverleaf owns the LLC and is responsible for it, the statement said. 
The statement also said the company would not reveal the operator of the large-scale data center because an agreement has not been finalized. The project is estimated to cost at least $1.5 billion in the development stage, according to the statement.
Ryan Anderson, a staff attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC), also spoke at the meeting. 
“I understand the county staff are busy and that records requests take time to process, but I do want to remind the commission of the legal obligations that apply here, because a project of this scale deserves to be conducted in full view of the public,” she said.
Ryan Anderson of SELC speaking to the Lowndes County Commission on Aug. 24, 2026, in the Lowndes County Courthouse in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
In the middle of her prepared remarks about the public records request, Commissioner Charlie King, Jr., repeatedly struck his gavel, signalling Anderson was out of time. 
As Anderson returned to her seat, Commissioner Dickson Farrior, the vice chair, motioned for King to allow her to finish her prepared remarks. The commission approved the motion, and Anderson returned with applause and cheers from the audience.
“Transparency isn’t a courtesy the commission extends to the public. It’s the law, and it’s the foundation of the public’s trust and how this decision gets made,” she said.
Anderson said in a phone interview on Monday afternoon prior to the meeting that the documents the records request would allow them to see would give an unbiased view of the resources Project Red Clay will need.
“Understanding the scope of the impacts can really only be done if you can look at these factual documents, from an unbiased source. Right now, all that we have is a website run by the developer,” Anderson said. “Of course, they’re going to make it seem like all daisies and roses, but residents really deserve to have an unbiased source of information.”
Part of the issue, Anderson said, is that Cloverleaf was able to buy the land and start developing the data center in Lowndes County because the county lacks planning or zoning authority. That is the case for most counties in the state.
The Association of County Commissions of Alabama unanimously passed a resolution at its annual meeting last week supporting a comprehensive approach to land use authorization. 
“Granting planning and zoning authority for a single industry raises practical and constitutional concerns,” said ACCA Executive Director Sonny Brasfield in a statement. “Rather than pursuing an industry-specific approach, counties believe a broader conversation is needed about how county governments can effectively support strategic and productive growth in Alabama’s unincorporated areas.”
Lowndes County Commissioner Robert Harris put forward a resolution at the end of the meeting Monday to support
Negatha Holt speaking at the Lowndes County Commission meeting on Aug. 24, 2026, in the Lowndes County Courthouse in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
legislation that would allow the county to have planning and zoning authority. The resolution passed unanimously. 
“The people who are showing up here tonight and at the other meeting, if they get behind it as if they’re behind that on stopping this particular company from coming, then I think it may be in favor of happening,” Harris said in an interview after the meeting. “If there’s no support behind it, then you’re gonna get the same thing.” 
Negatha Holt, another resident who spoke during the meeting, addressed residents more than the commission, and encouraged those living in Lowndes County to resist apathy. 
“Since May of 2024, communities across this country have blocked or delayed over many $98 billion dollars in data center projects,” she said. “The power of the people is greater than the people in power.”

title: Push back on book bans by reading Tennessee authors
description: Our legislature has an obsession with getting books out of the hands of young people, via a 2022 measure called the “Age Appropriate Materials Act” that was updated in 2024.  A different approach would be more beneficial. What books involving Tennessee or Tennesseans should people be reading? My list is, by definition, subjective and incomplete […]
text:
How to push back on book bans? Read an expansive selection of works by Tennessee authors, including Alex Haley’s “Roots.” (Photo: Angela Dennis for Tennessee Lookout)Our legislature has an obsession with getting books out of the hands of young people, via a 2022 measure called the “Age Appropriate Materials Act” that was updated in 2024. 
A different approach would be more beneficial. What books involving Tennessee or Tennesseans should people be reading? My list is, by definition, subjective and incomplete — and I welcome others to add to it. 
Let’s start with some authors with strong Tennessee connections. Alex Haley’s “Roots” is a must, as are any of Cormac McCarthy’s novels. McCarthy moved to Knoxville when he was four, attended the University of Tennessee – Knoxville, and his first four novels were based on Appalachian or East Tennessee themes. Poet Nikki Giovanni spent formative years in Knoxville, as one can read in her essay “400 Mulvaney Street” and her poem “Knoxville, Tennessee.”
James Agree’s autobiographical novel “A Death in the Family” was based on his Knoxville childhood; it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1958. Tad Mosel adapted the novel into the play “All the Way Home” which won the  Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1961. Mosel, one of my instructors at Syracuse University, confided to me that many of the Knoxville city scenes were based on his hometown of Steubenville, Ohio.
Historian Jack Neely has published some thoughtful works of Knoxville area history. Jack McElroy, former Knoxville New Sentinel editor, recently published “Citizen Carl [Magee]: The Editor Who Cracked Teapot Dome, Shot a Judge, and Invented the Parking Meter.”
Biographer and historian Jon Meacham, a Nashville resident, won the 2009 Pulitzer Prize for his book on President Andrew Jackson. (Photo: J. Holly McCall/Tennessee Lookout)
Nashville is the setting for “Nothing to See Here”, by Kevin Wilson, a dark humor piece that includes a group of children who spontaneously combust when agitated. The iconic Tennessee singer and personality Dolly Parton and prolific mystery writer James Patterson collaborated on “Run, Rose, Run,” a thriller built around Nashville’s country music scene. Parton also deserves special praise for her Imagination Library, getting free books into the hands of more than three million kids every month.
For those who like historical romance novels, there’s “Christmas at Carnton” by Tamera Alexander. This piece is set in 1864 and wraps around brutal action and plantation life following the Battle of Franklin.
William Faulkner’s final novel, “The Reivers,” is a coming-of-age story of a boy and his friends who steal a relative’s car to go to Memphis in 1905. Vince Vawter’s award-winning “Paperboy” looks at 1950s Memphis society through the lens of an 11-year-old who takes over a friend’s paper route.
“Shiloh,” a sprawling 1952 work by Shelby Foote, who became known to many through his contributions to documentarian Ken Burns’ 1990 epic “The Civil War,” takes the reader along the banks of the Tennessee River to craft a fictional recreation of the Battle of Shiloh in1862, using narrators both blue and gray.
The non-fiction list should include the major environmental and political works by former Vice President Al Gore, notably the bestsellers “Earth in the Balance,” “An Inconvenient Truth, “ “The Assault on Reason” and “The Future: Six Drivers of Global Change.”
Jon Meacham, a biographer and historian based in Nashville, writes about American politics and civil rights, including “His Truth is Marching On: John Lewis and the Power of Hope.”  Meacham’s “American Lion: Andrew Jackson in the White House” won the 2009 Pulitzer Prize for Biography.
Legendary editor John Seigenthaler of the Tennessean led a fascinating life and was a superb journalist. A collection of his best interviews, “A Word on Words,” is worth a read.  
Both adult and children’s books are available on the native American Sequoyah. He was born in the late 1770s at Tuskegee, which now lies under Tellico Lake in Tennessee and effectively crafted and promoted a written language for Cherokee speakers.
These suggestions barely scratch the surface of Tennessee authors and subjects that make for good reading, and a good book is a summer vacation we all can enjoy spontaneously in any season.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Coloradans to vote on ballot measure to increase funding for conservation, wildfire mitigation
description: Colorado voters will decide this November whether to boost funding for conservation and wildfire mitigation projects by exempting tax revenue from sporting goods sales from constitutional limits set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. Proposed Initiative 308, backed by The Nature Conservancy and a handful of other environmental groups, qualified for the ballot[...]
text:
Slash piles from a "hand thinning" wildfire mitigation project along Stillwater Ditch in southern Routt County, in a section of the Routt National Forest, are pictured on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado voters will decide this November whether to boost funding for conservation and wildfire mitigation projects by exempting tax revenue from sporting goods sales from constitutional limits set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights.
Proposed Initiative 308, backed by The Nature Conservancy and a handful of other environmental groups, qualified for the ballot after submission of a sufficient number of petition signatures to state elections officials, the Colorado secretary of state’s office said Friday. Backers submitted more than 205,000 signatures, well above the 124,238 signature requirement for statutory measures.
The initiative, which will be assigned a new proposition number when it appears on the ballot, would raise up to $175 million in new revenue by exempting sporting goods sales tax collections from TABOR limits. It would not raise taxes, but could reduce the size of TABOR refunds in years when state revenue exceeds the annual growth cap.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nearly all of the new funding would be split evenly between Great Outdoors Colorado, a state entity that invests in conservation and outdoor recreation projects, and a constellation of state programs that fund wildfire mitigation efforts. Two additional small slices of the funding would be directed to Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s Outdoor Equity Grant Program and economic development projects under the state’s Outdoor Recreation Industry Office.
“We want to protect many of the most critical and beautiful places in this state — for recreation, for protection of our water resources that (are) filtered through those lands, and for wildlife,” Aaron Citron, Colorado policy director at the Nature Conservancy and one of Initiative 308’s sponsors, said last week during a presentation on Initiative 308 at the summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress.
Vast scale of wildfire threats to Colorado watersheds far exceeds funding

More than 13 million acres of mountain watersheds across western and central Colorado are now covered by a Wildfire Ready Action Plan, or WRAP, developed as part of a watershed protection program administered by the Colorado Water Conservation Board, the state’s lead water agency.
The Colorado State Forest Service estimated in 2020 that 10% of Colorado’s roughly 24 million acres of forest “need urgent attention to address forest health, wildﬁre risk and threats to water supplies.” Depending on factors like equipment and terrain, the cost of wildfire mitigation treatments typically runs to thousands of dollars per acre — making even the state’s highest-priority to-do list a multibillion-dollar proposition.
“There is far more work than there is funding, so this initiative, should it come before voters and be approved, would be a key source of dollars to reduce wildfire risk,” Madelene McDonald, manager of watershed planning for Denver water, which voted earlier this month to endorse the measure, said in a statement. “Every project we can complete helps ensure a clean water supply and reduces property damage — saving enormous amounts of money and resources down the line.”
An issue committee registered in support of the measure has reported over $3 million in contributions, about half of which came from The Nature Conservancy. Other major donors include Western Resource Advocates, the Trust for Public Land, and Tom and Olivia Walton, of the ultra-wealthy Walton family.
Some grassroots environmental groups remain skeptical of wildfire mitigation efforts that they fear could open up Colorado forests to large-scale logging. But Citron told Newsline last week that the measure’s proponents don’t expect any “funded opposition.”
“What we’re talking about is thinning, pile burning, prescribed fire, fuels mitigation — around communities, around reservoirs,” he said. “It’s projects that are identified by HOAs, local governments, fire districts.”
As a statutory measure, the initiative can’t tie the hands of future legislatures that may seek to divert the funding elsewhere, Citron said at the Water Congress. But sponsors hope its passage would send a clear message to lawmakers that wildfire mitigation should rank high on the state’s priority list, even in tight budget years.
“We’re bullish about the fact that this is so critical, it has to be in line for funding when it’s available,” said Citron. “The wildfire mitigation grant programs have received pretty consistent funding from our general fund, (but) it’s been small … We need to substantially increase that.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: When it comes to early voting, North Carolinians won’t be fooled
description: When North Carolina’s State Board of Elections met August 20 to decide early voting options for 20 counties where local boards couldn’t agree, it surprised no one that Auditor Dave Boliek’s GOP majority largely chose plans crafted by Republicans. What was surprising, was the immediacy of the campaign to rehabilitate Boliek’s reputation by couching 2026 […]
text:
State Board of Elections members meet to discuss early voting sites at their August 20, 2026 meeting. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)When North Carolina’s State Board of Elections met August 20 to decide early voting options for 20 counties where local boards couldn’t agree, it surprised no one that Auditor Dave Boliek’s GOP majority largely chose plans crafted by Republicans.
What was surprising, was the immediacy of the campaign to rehabilitate Boliek’s reputation by couching 2026 early voting plans as a victory for all voters after local whistleblowers revealed Boliek’s office, including former “elections liaison,” Dallas Woodhouse, pressured county elections chairs to pass plans favoring Republicans.
Attempting to distance himself from the elephant in the room, State Board Chair Francis DeLuca kicked off the marathon meeting admitting, “I hope we never hear the name Dallas Woodhouse in here again.”
But if Boliek and DeLuca think they can fool voters into believing this summer’s efforts haven’t hurt voters, Woodhouse provided a taste of how they’d try.
First, Woodhouse suggested that the Auditor’s board may tout overall increases in sites or hours compared to 2022. 
But registered voters in North Carolina have grown by 6% since 2022. Adding handfuls of sites or a few percentage points in hours this year doesn’t keep up.
Even in the 80 unanimous counties decided locally, analysis from political scientist Chris Cooper shows that while the total number of sites increased by five (+1.8%) since the last midterm, sites available per 10,000 voters actually dropped (-3.2%), signaling a shift away from where voters actually live.
Simply put, many of the sites and hours approved under Boliek’s watch meet his demands, not voters’.
The Auditor might argue that while he meddled in county options, it prevented bigger early voting cuts.
Preventing “bigger cuts” doesn’t mean chosen sites work for all voters.
Public records show the Auditor’s effort to add or protect sites that may help certain Republican candidates. Woodhouse’s texts focused on what sites and hours “GOP voters need” in counties like Columbus and Anson. These partisan add-ons may pad the State Board’s stats, but they distract from devastating site closures, including the site serving the poorest part of Columbus, multiple sites in Lenoir where 40% of voters are Black, and the most popular site for Black (and all) voters in Granville.
The Auditor could repeat tired excuses that unprecedented cuts to Sunday voting address poll worker fatigue, religious preferences, or costs.
But when the Auditor’s appointees cut Sunday access in 23 North Carolina counties that had it in 2022, they failed to mention their true motives.
Fortunately, Lee County Board of Elections member Jay DeLancy did it for them.
DeLancy’s testimony to the State Board revealed that Woodhouse told him to slash Sunday voting because the US Supreme Court’s 2026 Callais decision, gutting the Voting Rights Act, greenlit Republican cuts to options used by Black voters.
“I had not thought about getting rid of Sunday until [Woodhouse] planted that seed,” DeLancy told the Board.
Woodhouse started planting seeds a decade ago when, as state GOP chair, he sent a memo to GOP elections chairs in every county demanding they eliminate Sunday voting. His ultimately unsuccessful loyalty test followed a federal ruling that struck down legislative efforts to cut Sundays because doing so targeted African-American voters “with surgical precision.”
Thanks to the Auditor, the surgeons are back. And their amputations of Sunday voting will be felt throughout the state.
The Auditor’s State Board might try to justify their decisions by saying campus voting largely survived. 
But campuses with some of the largest and most diverse populations likely disagree.
Public records show State Board Member Angela Hawkins worked with Woodhouse to make sure Wake County moved its NC State site off of the main campus. Woodhouse approved moving Pasquotank’s site to its under-renovation elections office rather than keep it on a historically-Black college or university (HBCU). In Guilford, none of the 168 public comments to the State Board supported the plan it ultimately approved, leaving no site at NC A&T, the nation’s largest HBCU.
Finally, the Auditor may try to say with a straight face that 2026 early voting planning was a transparent process, full of compromise. 
But his partisan manipulations were only revealed after threats of litigation over unfulfilled public records requests —he has since admitted Woodhouse deleted many of those conversations.
If you “read the documents and check the record,” as Woodhouse suggests, the only thing in public view is the Auditor’s staff pressuring counties to adopt plans that led to some of the most toxic local debates over early voting in recent history and forcing only the voters to compromise.
These controversial changes so conflicted with community interests that even GOP elections board members in counties like Cabarrus, Jackson, Moore, and Randolph pushed back.
Like them, North Carolinians won’t be fooled.
Sailor Jones is state director of Common Cause North Carolina.

title: Former Michigan House speaker slated for Sept. 21 trial amid accusations of misusing political funds
description: Former Michigan’s House Speaker Lee Chatfield’s final pretrial concluded without any major developments, as attorneys for the state and the ex-lawmaker met Monday in chambers with Judge Morgan Cole of the 30th Circuit Court of Ingham County. While the attorneys opted against on-the-record proceedings, Assistant Attorney General Kahla Crino told Michigan Adva[...]
text:
Former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield (right) and his wife Stephanie Chatfield (left) leave court after their preliminary exam as the couple face multiple charges related to embezzlement on Feb. 28, 2025 | (By Anna Liz Nichols/Michigan Advance) Former Michigan’s House Speaker Lee Chatfield’s final pretrial concluded without any major developments, as attorneys for the state and the ex-lawmaker met Monday in chambers with Judge Morgan Cole of the 30th Circuit Court of Ingham County.
While the attorneys opted against on-the-record proceedings, Assistant Attorney General Kahla Crino told Michigan Advance they still plan to proceed to trial on Sept. 21. 
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel first announced charges against Chatfield in 2024, however the investigation into the ex-speaker began with the Michigan State Police in December 2021, when Chatfield’s sister-in-law filed a report saying Chatfield had sexually assaulted her for more than a decade beginning when she was 14 or 15 years old.
Nessel’s office took over the case in 2022 and expanded the investigation to include allegations of financial misconduct. However, her office later closed the sexual assault investigation without issuing charges, telling reporters they did not have sufficient evidence to bring the matter to trial.
Chatfield faces 13 felony charges, including conducting a criminal enterprise and several embezzlement charges, with the attorney general accusing Chatfield of misusing funds from his political action committees as well as the Peninsula Fund, a 501(c)(4) social welfare organization.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Through their investigation, Nessel said they found evidence Chatfield had received improper mileage reimbursements from state monies for trips he did not take and that he had used money from the Peninsula Fund for personal use, including renting an apartment, subletting it and pocketing the money from the sublease.
Chatfield has pleaded not guilty.
His wife, Stephanie, was recently sentenced to six months probation and 25 hours of community service and was fined $2,000 after she pleaded guilty to embezzling from the Peninsula Fund.
During a previous hearing on July 22, Gongwer News Service reported that the court accepted testimony from two former Chatfield aides, Anné and Rob Minard, as evidence. The Minards were sentenced to 36 months of probation as part of a plea agreement with the Michigan Department of Attorney General, agreeing to offer truthful testimony in future proceedings.
The admitted evidence included apartment-related reimbursements, which Crino said showed the intent to embezzle from the Peninsula Fund, and proof  of improper travel. According to Gongwer, Chatfield’s attorney, Mary Chartier-Mittendorf, argued the Minards had “every incentive to lie.”

title: Hearings planned in southwest North Dakota power line project
description: The Public Service Commission will hold two public hearings in September on a proposed power line project covering more than 240 miles across six counties in southwest North Dakota.  The North Plains Connector plans to go through Golden Valley, Slope, Hettinger, Oliver, Morton and Grant counties in North Dakota.  The full line would run about […]
text:
Towers support electrical transmission lines in western North Dakota. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)  The Public Service Commission will hold two public hearings in September on a proposed power line project covering more than 240 miles across six counties in southwest North Dakota. 
The North Plains Connector plans to go through Golden Valley, Slope, Hettinger, Oliver, Morton and Grant counties in North Dakota. 
The full line would run about 422 miles from near Colstrip, Montana, to two separate end points in North Dakota – one near Center and one near St. Anthony. 
The project is estimated to cost $6 billion with the North Dakota portion at $3.2 billion. 
Grid United and Minnesota-based Allete are the joint developers of the project. Other utilities that would use the power line include Montana-Dakota Utilities and Minnkota Power Cooperative. 
The power line requires approval from the Public Service Commission.
The public hearings are:

8:30 a.m. Sept. 2 at Mandan City Hall, focused on Oliver, Morton and Grant counties.
9:30 a.m. Mountain Time Sept. 3 at the Enchanted Castle in Regent, focused on Golden Valley, Slope and Hettinger counties.

Members of the public must testify in person for comments to be included in the PSC record.
The North Plains Connector power line would cross into North Dakota from Montana and branch into two separate endpoints. (Map courtesy of Public Service Commission)
A technical hearing going over details of the project will also be held at 8:30 a.m. Sept. 1. in the state Capitol. No public comment is expected to be taken at this hearing.
Hearings are livestreamed on the PSC website, www.psc.nd.gov.
Major construction on the project is expected to begin in 2028, and the line is expected to be operational in 2032, according to the project’s website. About 800 workers will be needed at the peak of construction.  
The project includes 168 miles of high-voltage direct current line and about 74 miles of 345 kilovolt transmission lines. Electricity could flow in either direction on the lines.

title: With lifecycle campus plan, is Idaho getting ready to buy a nuclear waste pig in a poke?
description: Editor’s note: This is the first in a series of three op-eds written by columnist Jim Jones that will discuss Idaho’s application to become the host of one of three Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses in the U.S. The second column will run Tuesday, and the third will run Wednesday. Back in the early 1990s, Idaho’s […]
text:
Located in Eastern Idaho, Idaho National Laboratory is one of 17 U.S. Department of Energy labs. It is known for its work on nuclear energy, cybersecurity, AI, homeland security and defense. (Photo courtesy of Idaho National Laboratory)Editor’s note: This is the first in a series of three op-eds written by columnist Jim Jones that will discuss Idaho’s application to become the host of one of three Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses in the U.S. The second column will run Tuesday, and the third will run Wednesday.
Back in the early 1990s, Idaho’s former Attorney General and Lt. Gov., Dave Leroy, was a very lonely nuclear waste salesman. 
During his three years (1990-93) as United States Nuclear Waste Negotiator, he wandered the country and beyond, trying to find some state, tribal or territorial government willing to become the nation’s nuclear waste repository. He was treated as a pariah. 
The New York Times reported Leroy as saying that all the people with whom he needs to negotiate will not be caught dead talking to him. My, how times have changed.
New nuclear campus deal would require Idaho to accept, store spent nuclear fuel, radioactive waste 

Now, five states, including Idaho, are begging to be one of three repositories of high-level nuclear waste in exchange for undefined and unfunded future benefits. 
According to the U.S. Department of Energy, the country has more than 90,000 metric tons of spent nuclear fuel from commercial nuclear power plants and about 90 million gallons of radioactive waste from the nation’s nuclear weapons program. That makes it easy to calculate Idaho’s one-third share of the nuclear waste pie. 
There is no indication of the benefits to be bestowed on the three states and absolutely no money available in the federal till to pay for them. It’s all a matter of faith. 
Perhaps it is better stated that Idaho and the other states are being asked to buy a nuclear waste pig in a poke – just commit up front to take the waste and the feds will tell you the payoff sometime down the road.
The proposal to make Idaho a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus” was apparently initiated with Gov. Brad Little’s issuance of Executive Order 2025-06, which established the Idaho Advanced Nuclear Energy Task Force last September. The task force includes about 20 Idaho luminaries – the lieutenant governor, attorney general, director of the Idaho National Laboratory and a variety of others. 
They worked together to formulate a proposal to the DOE. Idaho was picked as one of the five finalist states. They all signed a memorandum of understanding with the Department of Energy to negotiate a Host Agreement “for the acceptance of out-of-state used nuclear fuel, spent nuclear fuel, and high-level radioactive waste.” The word “temporary” appears nowhere in the MOU.
If Idaho is selected as one of three repositories, we will start receiving nuclear waste from around the country and will undoubtedly start searching for another location dumb enough to act as a permanent dumping ground. Let’s be honest, it will even be a tougher job than that which confronted Dave Leroy those many years ago. 
Gov. Little fantasizes that Utah might be willing to take the nuclear waste from Idaho, but that is a pipe dream. Why would Utah take the waste if it does not get the commensurate benefits that are being dangled to attract the three repository states?
The fact is that no other state or tribal government will take any finalist’s third of the waste. All three will become the de facto final repositories for existing waste, as well as the 2,000 metric tons per year that the Department of Energy expects to be generated in the future.
That being the case, Idahoans should ask some searching questions and get some firm commitments from the federal government before blundering into a Host Agreement that will be legally binding upon the state. Where and how will the waste be stored? What will be its effect on the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer? What safeguards will be imposed by the federal government? Exactly what projects will Idaho receive at the INL in exchange for being a permanent repository, and how will funding be guaranteed? 
All branches of the federal government must provide binding funding and safeguard guarantees because it would be too easy for disputes to arise between agencies, as well as current and future Congresses and presidents. Our current senators, Jim Risch and Mike Crapo, as well as Congressman Mike Simpson, are cheerleaders for the task force nuclear waste plan. 
The plan originated with Donald Trump. If Idaho is to become a final dumping ground for the nation’s nuclear waste, there must be some sort of hefty trust fund established and funded to back up the promises and guarantees.
These are just a few of the questions that must be answered before Idaho buys into this nuclear waste pig in a poke. 
Don’t get me wrong. I have been a steadfast supporter of the INL since my Valley High School class took a field trip to the INL in the late 1950s. Both the state and nation should support its pioneering work into the future. However, all Idahoans have an unqualified right to express their opinion and communicate their concerns to the proponents of this loosey-goosey proposal.
